T: What security checks do you apply to uploaded files?
K: secure file upload, file upload security, validate uploaded files, malware scan upload, upload vulnerabilities
X: File uploads are a very common attack route, so I put several checks in place.

X: And every upload gets logged for audit. That's pretty much my checklist.
@p17-89
S: secx
D: A
T: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric JWT signing?
K: hs256 vs rs256, symmetric vs asymmetric signing, jwt signing algorithm, rs256 jwks, which jwt algorithm
X: JWTs can be signed two ways, and for microservices the choice really matters.
X: Symmetric signing, like HS256, uses one shared secret for both signing and verifying. It's simple and fast. The problem is every service that verifies tokens needs that same secret, and anyone with the secret can also create valid tokens. So if any one service leaks it, an attacker can forge tokens for the whole system. It's only okay when the issuer and the verifier are the same application.
X: Asymmetric signing, like RS256 with RSA or ES256 with elliptic curves, uses a private key to sign and a public key to verify. Only the identity provider holds the private key. APIs just need the public key, which isn't secret, so even a compromised API can't create tokens. The public keys are published at the JWKS endpoint with a key id, and that makes rotation easy. The provider adds a new key, starts signing with it, and APIs pick it up automatically.
X: So for distributed systems, asymmetric is the right choice, no question.
X: One classic attack to know is algorithm confusion. The attacker changes the header's algorithm to "none", or to HS256 and uses the public key as the secret. So validation must only accept the expected algorithms. ASP.NET Core's JWT handler handles this properly when you configure it with the authority. That's how we have it set up.

S: secx
D: A
T: What is a threat model, and how do you do one for a new feature?
K: threat modeling, stride, threat model feature, security design review, attack surface
X: A threat model is just a structured way of thinking about what could go wrong with a feature's security before you build it. So security is designed in, not patched on later.
X: I keep it lightweight, honestly mostly a one-hour session with the team. We start by drawing a simple data-flow diagram, users, services, data stores, external systems, and the trust boundaries between them, like the internet to our API, or our service to a vendor.
X: Then we go through each element using STRIDE as a checklist. Spoofing, can someone pretend to be another user or service? Tampering, can data be changed in transit or at rest? Repudiation, can someone deny doing something because there's no audit trail? Information disclosure, can data leak through APIs, logs or errors? Denial of service, can someone overload it? Elevation of privilege, can a user do more than they should?
X: For each real threat, we agree a mitigation, like resource-level authorization, signing a webhook, rate limiting, and track it as a work item with an owner. Anything we decide to accept gets written down.
X: And we revisit the model when the design changes.
X: [When we threat-modelled the drug accountability return screens, it showed the return quantity API needed a site ownership check, which we added before release.] So it does catch real things.
@p17-91
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you secure webhooks you send and receive?
K: webhook security, verify webhook signature, hmac webhook, secure webhook endpoint, webhook replay attack
X: Webhooks are just HTTP calls between systems, so both sides need to be able to trust each other.
X: When we're receiving, the big risk is someone calling our endpoint pretending to be the provider. So I verify a signature. The provider signs the request body with a shared secret using HMAC-SHA256 and sends it in a header. I recompute the HMAC over the raw body and compare using a constant-time comparison. I also check a timestamp header and reject old requests, say older than five minutes, so nobody can replay them. And I store the event id to ignore duplicates, because providers do retry. The endpoint replies quickly with a 2xx and queues the work, so the provider doesn't time out and send it again.
X: When we're sending, it's the same thing in reverse. Sign each payload, include a timestamp and unique id, HTTPS only, retry with backoff on failure, and let customers rotate their secrets. And since customers give us the URLs, I protect against SSRF, block internal addresses like localhost, private IP ranges and metadata endpoints.
X: Payloads carry minimal data, often just an id, and the receiver fetches details through the authenticated API.
X: [Our vendor status callbacks in the newer data transfer API verify an HMAC signature and timestamp before queuing the message.] That's how we did it.
@p17-92
S: secx
D: A
T: What is SSRF, and how do you prevent it?
K: ssrf, server side request forgery, prevent ssrf, metadata endpoint attack, url fetch vulnerability
X: SSRF, server-side request forgery, is when an attacker gets our server to send a request to a URL they choose. It's a risk anytime the server fetches a user-provided URL, like importing an image from a link, previewing a URL, or calling a webhook URL a customer gave us.
X: The danger is our server sits inside the network. So the attacker can reach stuff they normally can't, internal admin APIs, databases with HTTP interfaces, or the cloud metadata endpoint, like 169.254.169.254 on AWS, which can hand out temporary credentials. Honestly, some well-known cloud breaches happened exactly like this.
X: To prevent it, first I avoid fetching user-supplied URLs if I can. If I really need to, I validate against an allow-list of domains, resolve the host name, and block private, loopback, link-local and metadata IP ranges. I check again after redirects, or just disable redirects, because an allowed URL can redirect to an internal one. DNS rebinding is another trick, so I connect to the exact IP I validated.
X: At the infrastructure level on AWS, I require IMDSv2, which uses session tokens and blocks simple SSRF access to metadata. And outbound traffic gets restricted with security groups or an egress proxy.
X: Least-privilege roles then limit the damage if something still gets through. So it's layers, like always.

T: A critical CVE is reported in a transitive NuGet or npm dependency. What do you do?
K: vulnerable dependency, nuget vulnerability, npm audit, dependency scanning, cve in package, dependabot
X: First I assess it. Are we actually using the vulnerable package, and is the vulnerable code path even reachable? How severe is it, is there a known exploit? Which apps and environments use it? And transitive dependencies matter, because mostly the vulnerable package is pulled in by some other package.
X: The tools help here. dotnet list package with the vulnerable flag, NuGet audit warnings during restore, npm audit, and scanners like Dependabot, Snyk or GitHub's dependency graph, which open pull requests with the fixed version.

X: After that, if the risk was high, I check logs for any signs of exploitation, and document everything.
X: To avoid surprises next time, the pipeline runs dependency scanning on every build and fails on high or critical findings, and we keep dependencies reasonably current so upgrades stay small.
X: In a validated environment even a security patch goes through change control, but we fast-track the critical ones. That's how we handle it.
@p17-94
S: secx
D: A
T: What is the Data Protection API in ASP.NET Core?
K: data protection api, asp.net core data protection, key ring, data protection keys, protect unprotect, cookie encryption keys
X: The Data Protection API is ASP.NET Core's built-in system for encrypting and signing data that the app needs to read back later. The framework itself uses it for authentication cookies, anti-forgery tokens and TempData, and you can use it for things like protecting a token in a URL.
X: You get an IDataProtector from IDataProtectionProvider with a purpose string, and then call Protect and Unprotect. The purpose string keeps uses isolated, so something protected for "password reset" can't be unprotected as something else. And ToTimeLimitedDataProtector adds expiry.
X: Now the important production part is the key ring. Keys get generated and rotated automatically, every 90 days by default. By default they're stored locally, which is fine on one machine. But with several instances behind a load balancer, or containers that restart, each instance ends up with different keys. So a cookie issued by one instance can't be read by another, and users randomly get logged out or see anti-forgery errors.
X: So in production, I persist the keys to a shared location, Redis, a database, blob storage or S3, set the same application name on all instances, and protect the keys at rest with Azure Key Vault, a certificate, or AWS KMS.
X: Honestly, this is a classic one when you move an app from a single server to a load-balanced or containerised setup.
@p17-95
S: secx
D: A
T: What is a Content Security Policy, and how do you roll it out without breaking the site?
K: content security policy, csp, csp rollout, csp report only, nonce csp, csp angular react
X: So a Content Security Policy is a response header that tells the browser which sources are allowed for scripts, styles, images, fonts, frames and API calls. If an attacker injects a script, the browser refuses to run it because it doesn't match the policy. It's one of the strongest XSS defences.
X: A strict policy would be something like default-src self, script-src self, object-src none, frame-ancestors none, and connect-src for our API and identity provider. Inline scripts get blocked unless they have a nonce, a random value per response, or a hash.
X: The thing is, rolling it out on an existing site can break stuff. Inline scripts, inline event handlers, third-party analytics, fonts from CDNs, older libraries that use eval.
X: So I start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only. It doesn't block anything, it just reports violations to an endpoint. I collect reports for a couple of weeks, fix or allow the legitimate sources, move inline code out where possible, and only then switch to enforcing. And I keep reporting on, to catch new issues later.
X: Modern React and Angular builds with Vite or the Angular CLI work nicely with a strict CSP, because scripts are external files anyway. Angular also supports nonces for its inline styles. So for newer apps it's honestly not that painful.

@p17-97
S: secx
D: A
T: What is the difference between a WAF and a firewall?
K: waf vs firewall, web application firewall, aws waf, network firewall, what is waf
X: So a normal network firewall works at the network and transport layers. It allows or blocks traffic based on IP addresses, ports and protocols. Like "allow HTTPS on 443 from anywhere, block everything else", or "only the app servers can reach the database on 1433". In the cloud, security groups, network ACLs and Azure network security groups do that job.
X: A WAF, web application firewall, works at layer 7, the application layer. It actually understands HTTP and looks inside the requests, URLs, headers, query strings, bodies. So it can block common attack patterns, SQL injection strings, cross-site scripting payloads, known bad bots, traffic from certain countries, or too many requests from one IP. Examples are AWS WAF on CloudFront, an ALB or API Gateway, Azure's WAF on Front Door or Application Gateway, and Cloudflare.
X: They work together. The firewall limits who can talk to what, and the WAF filters bad content inside the traffic that's allowed.
X: But I'd say a WAF is a safety net, not a replacement for secure code. People bypass it with clever encoding, and it gives false positives too. So I start new rules in count mode, review what would've been blocked, and then turn on blocking. And the application still has to validate input and use parameterised queries. The WAF doesn't let you skip that.
@p17-98
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you rotate secrets and certificates without downtime?
K: secret rotation, rotate database password, certificate rotation, zero downtime rotation, key rotation
X: The trick is having two valid credentials during an overlap period, so nothing breaks while you switch.
X: For database passwords or API keys, it's dual credentials. You create the new secret while the old one still works, and update the secret store. Applications pick up the new value, either by reloading config periodically, or by fetching a fresh secret when authentication fails and retrying. Once every instance is on the new one, you revoke the old one. AWS Secrets Manager actually automates this with rotation Lambdas using alternating users, so one is always valid.
X: For signing keys, like JWT keys, the identity provider publishes both old and new public keys in its JWKS. It starts signing with the new key, and once old tokens have expired, the old key is removed.
X: For TLS certificates, I automate renewal well before expiry, with AWS Certificate Manager, Key Vault auto-renewal, or Let's Encrypt with cert-manager, and for anything manual, an alert at 30 days before expiry. Honestly, expired certificates cause a surprising number of outages.
X: Even better is not having secrets at all where possible. IAM roles and managed identities rotate credentials automatically.
X: And on the app side, don't cache secrets forever, and don't need a restart to pick up a new one. Otherwise rotation means downtime anyway.

@p17-101
S: secx
D: A
T: What is the difference between TLS termination at the load balancer and end-to-end TLS?
K: tls termination, ssl offloading, end to end encryption, https load balancer, tls passthrough, re encryption
X: With TLS termination, or SSL offloading, the load balancer or gateway handles the HTTPS connection with the client, decrypts it, and forwards to the backend, often as plain HTTP inside the private network. It's simple and efficient. Certificates live in one place, like AWS Certificate Manager on an ALB, backends don't burn CPU on encryption, and the load balancer can look at the HTTP content to route it and apply a WAF.
X: The risk is the hop between the load balancer and the backend is unencrypted. In a well-isolated private network, a lot of teams are fine with that. But for sensitive data, compliance requirements, or a zero-trust approach, it's not enough.
X: End-to-end TLS means it's encrypted all the way. Two ways to do it. Re-encryption, the load balancer terminates TLS, inspects the request, and then opens a fresh TLS connection to the backend. Or TLS passthrough, the load balancer just forwards the encrypted bytes using a layer 4 balancer, and the backend terminates TLS. But then the load balancer can't route by path.
X: In ASP.NET Core behind a terminating proxy, I set up the forwarded headers middleware, so the app knows the original request was HTTPS and gets the right client IP and scheme. People forget that and then redirects go wrong.
X: For healthcare data, I'd prefer re-encryption to the backend.
@p17-102
S: csx
D: A
T: What is the difference between == and Equals() in C#?
K: double equals vs equals, == vs equals, reference equality vs value equality, operator equality c#, referenceequals
X: For reference types, the double equals operator by default compares references, meaning do both variables point to the same object in memory. Equals is a virtual method, and by default it also compares references, but a class can override it to compare values.
X: The difference shows when a type overrides them. String is the classic example. Both are overridden to compare the characters, so two different string objects with the same text are equal either way.
X: But here's the catch. Double equals is resolved at compile time, based on the variable's declared type, while Equals is resolved at runtime, based on the actual object. So if two strings are sitting in variables of type object, double equals compares references and can return false, but Equals still compares the text and returns true. Interviewers love that one, honestly.
X: For value types like int or a struct, Equals compares values. A struct's default Equals uses reflection, which is slow, so for performance-sensitive structs I implement IEquatable of T.
X: Records generate value-based Equals and the operator for you.
X: And if I override Equals, I must also override GetHashCode, and usually the equality and inequality operators too, so they behave the same. If I really want a reference check, I use ReferenceEquals. That's the full picture.
@p17-103
S: csx
D: A
T: What is the contract between Equals and GetHashCode?
K: gethashcode, equals and gethashcode, override gethashcode, hash code contract, dictionary key custom class, hashcode.combine
X: The rule is, if two objects are equal by Equals, they have to return the same hash code. The other way isn't required, different objects can share a hash code, that's just a collision.
X: Why it matters, hash-based collections like Dictionary and HashSet first use the hash code to find the bucket, and only then call Equals inside that bucket. So say I override Equals to compare by value but leave the default GetHashCode, which is based on the reference. Two "equal" objects will mostly land in different buckets. Then a dictionary lookup with an equal key just doesn't find the entry, and a HashSet happily stores duplicates. Honestly those bugs are really confusing to debug.
X: So whenever I override Equals, I override GetHashCode using the same fields. In modern .NET, HashCode.Combine of the fields does it neatly.
X: One more rule, the hash code shouldn't change while the object is being used as a key. If I change a field that's part of the hash after adding it to a dictionary, it's basically lost in the wrong bucket. That's why keys should be immutable.
X: Records and value tuples generate correct Equals and GetHashCode automatically. So for value-like keys, like a composite key of study id and site id, I just use a record struct. Saves a lot of trouble.
@p17-104
S: csx
D: A
T: Why are strings immutable in C#, and when do you use StringBuilder?
K: string immutability, stringbuilder, string concatenation in loop, string vs stringbuilder, immutable string c#
X: In C#, once a string is created, it can't be changed. Anything that looks like it's modifying a string, concatenation, Replace, ToUpper, actually creates a new string and leaves the original alone.
X: There are good reasons for that. It's thread-safe, nobody can change a string another thread is reading. It's safe as a dictionary key, since its hash never changes. It allows interning, where identical literals share one instance. And it's secure, because something you validated, like a file path, can't be changed afterwards.
X: The cost shows up with repeated concatenation in a loop. If you build a string from 10,000 pieces with plus-equals, it copies the growing string every time, which is roughly quadratic, and creates tons of garbage for the GC.
X: StringBuilder fixes that. It keeps a growable internal buffer, appends into it, and only creates the final string when you call ToString.
X: My rule of thumb, for a few concatenations, or one expression, plain concatenation or interpolation is fine and more readable, the compiler optimises it anyway. In loops, or when building large text like a CSV export or an email body, I use StringBuilder, or string.Join for collections.
X: For really hot paths, there's also Span-based formatting and string.Create. But honestly I rarely need to go that far.

S: csx
D: A
T: What are required members and init-only setters in C#?
K: required keyword, init only setter, init accessor, required members c# 11, object initializer immutability
X: Both are about creating objects safely with the object initialiser syntax.
X: An init-only setter, where you write init instead of set, lets a property be assigned during object initialisation, but not after. So I can create a new Shipment with Id 5 and Status Pending, and after that the object is effectively read-only. You get immutability without writing a long constructor. Records use init properties by default.
X: The required modifier, from C# 11, goes a step further. The compiler forces the caller to set that property in the initialiser. If someone creates a Shipment without setting a required property, it's a compile error, not a null reference at runtime later. It plays nicely with nullable reference types too, because a required non-nullable string won't give you that "might be null" warning.
X: If a constructor already sets all the required members, I mark it with SetsRequiredMembers, so callers using that constructor aren't forced to set them again.
X: I use these a lot for DTOs, options classes and commands. Required plus init gives you objects that are always complete and can't be changed by accident.
X: One thing to watch, System.Text.Json respects required since .NET 7, so a missing JSON property causes a deserialisation error. For incoming requests, honestly that's usually exactly what I want.
@p17-106
S: csx
D: A
T: What are primary constructors in C# 12?
K: primary constructor, c# 12 primary constructors, class primary constructor, primary constructor dependency injection
X: Primary constructors let you declare constructor parameters right on the class or struct declaration. Like a ShipmentService class that takes an IShipmentRepository and a logger directly in its declaration. Those parameters are in scope throughout the class body, so I can use them in methods without declaring private fields and writing a constructor just to assign them.
X: Records already had this, but C# 12 brought it to normal classes and structs. It removes a lot of boilerplate, especially for dependency injection in services and controllers.
X: There are some differences from records worth knowing. In a class, primary constructor parameters don't become public properties, they're just captured parameters. They're not readonly either, so the class could accidentally reassign one. If I care about that, I assign it to a readonly field explicitly. And if the class has other constructors, they have to call the primary one using this.
X: One subtle trap, if I capture a parameter and also use it to initialise a property, the class ends up with two copies of the state. The compiler does warn about it though.
X: I find them great for small services and handlers with a few injected dependencies. For classes with complex validation in the constructor, I still go with a regular constructor, because it's just clearer to read.
@p17-107
S: csx
D: A
T: What does yield return do, and how do iterators work in C#?
K: yield return, iterator c#, yield break, lazy sequence, custom ienumerable, state machine iterator
X: yield return lets you write a method that produces a sequence one item at a time, lazily, without building the whole collection in memory.
X: When a method returns IEnumerable of T and uses yield return, the compiler turns it into a state machine class behind the scenes. Nothing runs when you call the method. Code runs only when someone enumerates the result, like with foreach. Every time the consumer asks for the next item, the method runs until the next yield return, hands that value back, and pauses, remembering where it was. yield break ends the sequence early.
X: That's useful for reading large files line by line, paging through an API, or generating sequences on demand. Only one item is in memory at a time, and if the consumer stops early, say with Take of 10, the rest never gets produced.
X: But there are gotchas. Since execution is deferred, argument validation inside an iterator doesn't run until enumeration starts. So I put validation in a non-iterator wrapper method, or use a local function. Enumerating twice runs the whole method twice. And a using block inside an iterator stays open until enumeration finishes or the enumerator gets disposed.
X: For async sources, like paging through an API, I use async iterators, IAsyncEnumerable with yield return and await foreach. Same idea, just async.
@p17-108
S: csx
D: A
T: What is multiple enumeration of IEnumerable, and why is it a problem?
K: multiple enumeration, possible multiple enumeration warning, enumerate twice, ienumerable evaluated twice, tolist materialize
X: See, an IEnumerable is often not actually a collection. It's more like a recipe that gets executed every time you enumerate it. That's deferred execution. So if I enumerate the same IEnumerable twice, the work happens twice.
X: Let me take an example. A method gets an IEnumerable that's really a LINQ query over the database, or an iterator reading a file. The code calls Count, and then later does a foreach. That's two database queries or two file reads. If the source is expensive, it's slow. If the source changes in between, the two passes see different data and you get inconsistent results. And some sources can't be enumerated twice at all, like a stream reader or a network response.
X: That's why ReSharper and Rider show that "possible multiple enumeration" warning.
X: The fix depends. If I need to go over it several times, I materialise it once with ToList or ToArray and use that. If I only need one pass, I write the logic in one loop. And in method signatures, if the method needs the count or multiple passes, I take IReadOnlyCollection or IReadOnlyList instead of IEnumerable. That tells the caller clearly, give me a materialised collection.
X: [I once found a report that ran the same query three times because of this, and a single ToList fixed it.] Small thing, but it made a real difference.
@p17-109
S: csx
D: A
T: How does Dictionary work internally, and what is its lookup complexity?
K: dictionary internals, hash table c#, dictionary lookup o(1), dictionary vs list lookup, hash collision, dictionary capacity
X: A Dictionary is basically a hash table. When you add a key, it calls GetHashCode on the key, maps that hash to a bucket index, and stores the entry there. If two entries land in the same bucket, that's a collision, and they get chained together.
X: On lookup, it computes the hash, goes straight to the bucket, and then compares keys inside that bucket using Equals. With a decent hash function, buckets have very few entries, so lookup, insert and remove are O(1) on average. Compare that to searching a List, which is O(n), since it might check every element.
X: When the dictionary grows past its capacity, it resizes. It allocates a bigger array, roughly double, and re-inserts every entry, which is an O(n) operation. So if I roughly know the size, I pass the capacity to the constructor and avoid all that resizing.
X: Performance really depends on the key's hash. A bad GetHashCode, say one that returns the same value for everything, turns the dictionary into a slow linked list, O(n) per lookup.
X: A couple more points. Dictionary isn't thread-safe for writes, so for concurrent use I'd go with ConcurrentDictionary. Insertion order isn't guaranteed. And for string keys, I often pass StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase so lookups are case-insensitive. That one saves a lot of small bugs.
@p17-110
S: csx
D: A
T: When would you use a HashSet instead of a List?
K: hashset vs list, hashset c#, contains performance, unique values collection, set operations c#
X: I go for a HashSet when I need fast "is this in there?" checks, or uniqueness, and I don't care about order or duplicates.
X: A List keeps order and allows duplicates, and Contains has to scan the whole list, so it's O(n). A HashSet stores unique items using hashing, so Contains, Add and Remove are O(1) on average. Add returns false if the item's already there, which is handy for de-duplication.
X: The difference gets huge in loops. Say for each of 10,000 incoming records, I check whether its id is in a list of 10,000 existing ids. With a List, that's around 100 million comparisons. With a HashSet, about 10,000 hash lookups. Big difference.
X: HashSet also has nice set operations, UnionWith, IntersectWith, ExceptWith, IsSubsetOf. Perfect for things like "which kit ids in the file aren't in the database".
X: The trade-offs, it uses more memory than a List, there's no index access, and order isn't guaranteed. And it depends on good Equals and GetHashCode for the element type.
X: In LINQ, Distinct, Except and Intersect already use a set internally. But if I'm doing repeated lookups, I build the HashSet myself once.
X: In our CSV import, actually, I load the existing kit numbers into a HashSet once, so validating each row is just a quick lookup. That made the validation step much faster.
@p17-111
S: csx
D: A
T: What are the common pitfalls of ConcurrentDictionary?
K: concurrentdictionary, getoradd pitfall, concurrentdictionary thread safe, lazy getoradd, addorupdate
X: ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe for individual operations, yes. But there are a few traps people fall into.
X: The biggest one is the value factory in GetOrAdd and AddOrUpdate isn't guaranteed to run only once. If two threads ask for the same missing key at the same time, both might run the factory, and only one result gets stored. If the factory is expensive, like a database call, or has side effects, like creating a connection, that's a real problem. The usual fix is storing Lazy of T values. The dictionary only stores the Lazy wrapper, and the expensive work runs once when Value is accessed, with the thread-safe Lazy mode.
X: Then, compound operations aren't atomic. Checking ContainsKey and then adding, or reading a value and then updating it, can race with other threads. So I use the atomic methods instead, GetOrAdd, AddOrUpdate, TryUpdate with a comparison value, TryRemove.
X: Another one, the values themselves aren't protected. If the value is a mutable List, two threads can still change it at the same time.
X: Then some operations, like Count, Keys or ToArray, take all the internal locks, so calling them a lot under load hurts.
X: And honestly, a ConcurrentDictionary used as a cache just grows forever unless something evicts entries. For caching I'd rather use IMemoryCache or HybridCache, which have expiry and size limits.
@p17-112
S: csx
D: A
T: lock vs SemaphoreSlim vs Monitor: when do you use each?
K: lock vs semaphoreslim, monitor c#, async lock, semaphoreslim waitasync, mutex vs semaphore, thread synchronization
X: All three limit concurrent access to something, but they fit different situations.
X: lock is the simplest one. Only one thread at a time runs that block of code, using some object as the lock. Under the hood it's Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit in a try-finally. It's fast, and right for small synchronous critical sections, like updating a shared counter or list. But you can't await inside a lock. The compiler stops you, because the continuation might run on a different thread, and that breaks the lock's ownership. In .NET 9 there's also a dedicated System.Threading.Lock type which is a bit faster.
X: Monitor is what lock uses underneath, with extra things like TryEnter with a timeout, and Wait and Pulse for signalling. Honestly I rarely use it directly.
X: SemaphoreSlim lets a set number of threads in at once, not just one, and it supports async with WaitAsync. So that's my choice when I need mutual exclusion around async code, like "only one refresh of this cache at a time", with a count of one. Or for throttling, like "at most five concurrent calls to the vendor API". Just always release it in a finally block.
X: Mutex and Semaphore, the non-Slim ones, work across processes, but they're heavier. I only use those when coordinating separate processes on one machine. So mostly it's lock or SemaphoreSlim for me.
@p17-113
S: csx
D: A
T: What is the Interlocked class used for?
K: interlocked, interlocked increment, atomic operations c#, compareexchange, lock free counter
X: Interlocked gives you atomic operations on shared variables, without taking a lock.
X: See, a simple counter plus-plus looks like one step, but it's actually three. Read the value, add one, write it back. If two threads do it at the same time, both can read the same value and one increment just gets lost. With Interlocked.Increment, the whole read-modify-write happens as one atomic CPU instruction, so nothing is lost, and it's much cheaper than a lock.
X: The main methods are Increment, Decrement and Add for counters. Exchange, which sets a value and gives you the old one back atomically. And CompareExchange, which sets a value only if it currently equals what you expect. CompareExchange is the building block for lock-free algorithms. Like to update a shared reference safely, I read the current value, compute a new one, and call CompareExchange. If another thread changed it in between, the call fails and I retry.
X: Where I typically use it, counting requests or processed messages, generating sequence numbers inside one process, making sure something runs only once by flipping a flag from 0 to 1, or swapping in a new configuration object.
X: But it only works for single variables. If several values have to change together consistently, I still need a lock. That's the limit.
@p17-114
S: csx
D: A
T: Why is async void dangerous?
K: async void, async void exception, async void event handler, fire and forget async, avoid async void
X: An async void method can't be awaited, and that causes two big problems.
X: One is exceptions. In an async Task method, an exception gets captured in the returned Task, and the caller sees it when it awaits. In async void, there's no Task to hold it, so the exception is raised directly on the synchronisation context or the thread pool. In ASP.NET Core or a console app, that unhandled exception can crash the whole process. And no try-catch around the call can catch it, because the caller has already moved on.
X: The other one, the caller has no idea when it finished. Can't await it, can't wait for it in tests, can't sequence work after it. So you get race conditions. Like a DbContext getting disposed at the end of the request while the async void method is still using it, and you get ObjectDisposedException at random. Those are painful to debug, honestly.
X: The only legit use is event handlers, like a button click in WinForms or WPF, because the event signature forces void. Even then, I wrap the body in try-catch.
X: Everywhere else, Task or ValueTask. And if I really want fire-and-forget, I don't hide it in async void. I put the work on a background queue processed by a hosted service, with proper error handling, logging, and a fresh DI scope. That's the safe way.
@p17-115
S: csx
D: A
T: Task.WhenAll vs Task.WhenAny: how do they work and how are exceptions handled?
K: task whenall, task whenany, whenall exceptions, run tasks in parallel, aggregateexception, parallel async calls
X: Task.WhenAll takes several tasks and gives you a task that completes when all of them finish. That's how I run independent async operations concurrently, like calling three services at once, so total time is roughly the slowest call, not the sum. With tasks of T, you get back an array of results.
X: Now exceptions, this is where people get surprised. If any task fails, the WhenAll task faults. But when you await it, only the first exception gets thrown. All the exceptions are still there in the WhenAll task's Exception property, as an AggregateException, and each task has its own status and exception. So if I need every failure, I keep a reference to the WhenAll task and inspect it, or check each task.
X: Also, WhenAll doesn't cancel the other tasks when one fails. They just keep running. If I want that behaviour, I pass a shared CancellationTokenSource and cancel it on the first failure.
X: Task.WhenAny completes as soon as any one task finishes, and returns that task. Useful for timeouts, racing a task against Task.Delay, or handling results as they come in. It doesn't throw if the winner failed, so I await the returned task to see its result or exception. And since .NET 6, WaitAsync with a timeout is a cleaner way to add a timeout. I use that more now.

S: csx
D: A
T: How do you limit concurrency when running many async operations?
K: throttle async calls, parallel foreachasync, limit concurrent tasks, semaphoreslim throttling, max degree of parallelism async
X: Say I have 5,000 items and each one needs an API call. If I start them all at once with Task.WhenAll, I'd open thousands of connections, overload the downstream service, hit rate limits, maybe even run out of sockets. So I limit how many run at the same time.
X: The cleanest way in modern .NET is Parallel.ForEachAsync, available since .NET 6. You pass the items, ParallelOptions with MaxDegreeOfParallelism, say 10, a CancellationToken, and an async lambda per item. It runs at most 10 at once and starts the next one as soon as one finishes.
X: Before that, the common pattern was SemaphoreSlim with a count of 10. Each task awaits WaitAsync before the call and releases in a finally, then Task.WhenAll over all of them. It works fine, but all the tasks get created up front.
X: For producer-consumer pipelines, I use System.Threading.Channels with a fixed number of consumer tasks reading from a bounded channel, or TPL Dataflow blocks with bounded capacity.
X: What the right limit is depends on the downstream, its rate limits, the connection pool size, database capacity. I keep it configurable and measure.
X: Put that together with retries and backoff, and batch jobs stay fast without hammering the services they call. That's usually my approach.

T: What is IAsyncDisposable and await using?
K: iasyncdisposable, await using, disposeasync, async dispose, async cleanup c#
X: IAsyncDisposable is the async version of IDisposable. It has one method, DisposeAsync, returning a ValueTask. It exists because some cleanup naturally involves I/O, like flushing a buffered stream to disk, closing a network connection gracefully, or committing and closing a database connection. With the synchronous Dispose, that I/O would block a thread, which hurts scalability and can even cause deadlocks.
X: To use it, you write await using, either as a block or as a declaration, like await using var connection equals a new SqlConnection. The object gets disposed asynchronously at the end of the scope, even if an exception is thrown.
X: Lots of framework types implement it already. Streams, SqlConnection, DbContext, Utf8JsonWriter, and DI scopes. ASP.NET Core's DI disposes scoped services asynchronously at the end of the request if they implement it.
X: When I write my own class that holds async resources, I implement IAsyncDisposable, and usually IDisposable too, so callers who can't use async still work. The recommended pattern has a protected virtual DisposeAsyncCore method, so derived classes can add their own cleanup.
X: One gotcha I've actually hit, if a service only implements IAsyncDisposable and someone disposes the DI scope synchronously, .NET throws. So in background workers, I use CreateAsyncScope. That avoids it.
@p17-118
S: csx
D: A
T: What is a finalizer, and how is it different from Dispose?
K: finalizer, destructor c#, dispose pattern, gc.suppressfinalize, safehandle, unmanaged resources
X: A finalizer, the one written with the tilde like a destructor, is a method the garbage collector calls before reclaiming an object's memory. Dispose is a method my code calls explicitly, usually through using, to release resources at a known time.
X: The main difference is timing and reliability. Dispose runs immediately, deterministically. A finalizer runs at some unknown later time, on the finalizer thread, after the GC notices the object is unreachable. And it might not run at all if the process exits abruptly.
X: Finalizers are also expensive. Objects with finalizers survive at least one extra GC, because they go to the finalization queue first. That promotes them to an older generation and increases memory pressure.
X: So the classic dispose pattern was, Dispose releases resources and calls GC.SuppressFinalize so the finalizer doesn't run, and the finalizer is only a safety net for unmanaged resources in case someone forgot to dispose.
X: Honestly, in modern .NET, I almost never write a finalizer. Unmanaged handles should be wrapped in a SafeHandle, which has its own reliable finalization, and my class just implements IDisposable and disposes the SafeHandle. For classes that only hold managed disposables, like a DbContext or HttpClient, I implement Dispose without any finalizer at all. That's enough.
@p17-119
S: csx
D: A
T: What is the Large Object Heap, and how do ArrayPool and pooling help?
K: large object heap, loh, arraypool, memory pooling, loh fragmentation, recyclablememorystream
X: The Large Object Heap is a separate part of the managed heap for objects of 85,000 bytes or more, big arrays, large strings, big byte buffers. It's handled differently because copying large objects is expensive. LOH objects only get collected with generation 2, the most expensive collection, and by default they aren't compacted. So the heap gets fragmented, with free gaps too small for new large objects.
X: So if a service keeps allocating big buffers, like reading every uploaded file into a new byte array, or building large JSON strings, you get frequent gen 2 collections, longer pauses, and memory that keeps growing.
X: Pooling fixes that by reusing large buffers instead of allocating new ones. ArrayPool of T, usually the shared byte pool, lets you rent an array of at least the size you need and return it when done, in a finally block. Same buffers get reused again and again, so garbage drops a lot. Two things to remember, the rented array can be bigger than what you asked for, and you must not use it after returning it.
X: Related tools, RecyclableMemoryStream from Microsoft for pooled memory streams, ObjectPool for expensive objects, and streaming APIs, so you never need the whole payload in memory in the first place.
X: But first I confirm it's actually the problem, with dotnet-counters, watching gen 2 collections and the LOH size. No point pooling blindly.
@p17-120
S: csx
D: A
T: What are readonly struct and ref struct?
K: readonly struct, ref struct, span ref struct, stackonly struct, defensive copy, struct performance
X: Both are special kinds of structs, mainly for correctness and performance.
X: A readonly struct says all its fields are readonly, so the struct is immutable. Apart from making the intent clear, it helps performance. See, when you call a method on a struct through a readonly reference, like an in parameter or a readonly field, the compiler normally makes a defensive copy, because it can't be sure the method won't modify the struct. With a readonly struct it knows nothing can change, so it skips those copies. I use them for small value types, like a Money or Coordinates type.
X: A ref struct is a struct that has to live only on the stack. It can't be boxed, can't be a field in a class or a normal struct, traditionally couldn't be a generic type argument, can't be captured in lambdas, and historically couldn't be used across await in async methods. Span of T is the famous example. These rules are what make it safe for Span to point at stack memory or slices of arrays, because it can never outlive the memory it points to.
X: C# 13 relaxed some of that. Ref structs can now implement interfaces, be used as generic arguments with the allows ref struct constraint, and be used in async methods and iterators, as long as they don't cross an await or a yield. So it's a bit more flexible now.
@p17-121
S: csx
D: A
T: What are covariance and contravariance in C#?
K: covariance contravariance, in and out generic, variance c#, ienumerable covariance, func contravariance
X: So variance is basically about whether a generic type can be used with a more specific or a more general type argument than what's declared.
X: Covariance, marked with the out keyword, lets you use a more derived type where a base type is expected, for types that only produce values. IEnumerable of T is covariant, so an IEnumerable of string can be assigned to an IEnumerable of object. That's safe because you can only read from it, and every string is an object.
X: Contravariance, marked with in, goes the other way, for types that only consume values. Action of T and IComparer of T are contravariant, so an Action of object can be used where an Action of string is needed. Makes sense, right? A method that accepts any object can definitely accept a string.
X: Func is both, contravariant in its inputs and covariant in its return type.
X: List of T is invariant, so a List of string can't be assigned to a List of object. If that were allowed, you could add an integer through the object list into what's really a list of strings.
X: Arrays are covariant for historical reasons, and honestly that isn't type-safe. Putting the wrong type into a covariant array compiles fine but throws ArrayTypeMismatchException at runtime.
X: And variance only applies to interfaces and delegates, and only with reference types. That's the whole idea in short.
@p17-122
S: csx
D: A
T: What are source generators, and why use them instead of reflection?
K: source generators, roslyn source generator, reflection vs source generator, compile time code generation, aot friendly
X: Source generators are compiler plug-ins that run during the build. They look at your code, like classes marked with a certain attribute, and generate extra C# code that gets compiled along with it.
X: The main reason to use them over reflection is that the work moves from runtime to compile time. Reflection discovers types and members while the app is running. That costs startup time and CPU, allocates memory, and it's a problem for Native AOT and trimming, because the trimmer can't see what's used through reflection and might remove it. Generated code is just normal code, fast, visible, debuggable, and trimming-safe.
X: .NET itself uses them a lot. System.Text.Json source generation creates serialisation code for your types, which speeds up startup and supports AOT. GeneratedRegex compiles regular expressions at build time. LoggerMessage generates high-performance logging methods. And the configuration binder and minimal API request delegates have generators for AOT too.
X: Popular libraries use them as well, like Mapperly for object mapping, which generates mapping code instead of the reflection-based approach AutoMapper uses.
X: Writing your own generator is more advanced. If I did, I'd use the incremental generator API for performance, and honestly only for real repetitive boilerplate across a codebase.
X: In our newer services, I mainly use LoggerMessage and GeneratedRegex. Easy wins.
@p17-123
S: csx
D: A
T: What are expression trees, and where are they used?
K: expression trees, expression of func, linq expression, iqueryable expression tree, build dynamic query
X: An expression tree represents code as data. When you assign a lambda to an Expression of Func type, the compiler doesn't compile it to executable code. Instead it builds an object tree that describes it, a parameter, a member access, a comparison, a constant, and so on. Other code can then walk that tree and translate it into something else.
X: That's exactly how LINQ providers work. When I write a Where clause on an EF Core IQueryable, the lambda becomes an expression tree, and EF Core walks it and translates it into SQL. With a plain IEnumerable, the same lambda is a compiled delegate and runs in memory. That's actually why some C# methods can't be used inside EF queries, the provider just doesn't know how to translate them.
X: Other places I've seen it used. Building dynamic queries at runtime, like combining filters a user picks on a search screen, using Expression.AndAlso or something like LinqKit's PredicateBuilder. Strongly typed property selectors, like FluentValidation's RuleFor, or Moq's Setup, which read the property name from the expression. And generating fast code at runtime by compiling an expression into a delegate, which used to be a common trick to avoid slow reflection.
X: Compiling expressions is fairly expensive though, so you should cache the compiled delegates. I learned that one from a profiler.
@p17-124
S: csx
D: A
T: Static class vs singleton pattern: which and when?
K: static class vs singleton, singleton pattern c#, thread safe singleton, static vs singleton di, lazy singleton
X: A static class can't be instantiated, all its members are static. It's fine for stateless helpers, extension methods, simple calculations, constants.
X: A singleton is a normal class with exactly one instance. The classic way is a private constructor and a static Instance property, made thread-safe with Lazy of T or a static readonly field.
X: The singleton has real advantages over a static class. It can implement interfaces and be passed around as a dependency, so you can mock it in tests. It can hold state that's initialised lazily. And it can inherit from a base class.
X: But honestly, in modern .NET, I almost never write the classic singleton pattern. I just register a normal class in the DI container with AddSingleton. The container makes sure there's one instance, my class stays a plain, testable class with constructor injection, and consumers depend on an interface instead of some static Instance property.
X: Static classes and classic singletons share one problem, they're global state. Hidden dependencies that make testing and reasoning harder.
X: So my rule is, static for pure, stateless functions. DI singletons for shared services, like a cache, a configuration provider or an HttpClient wrapper. And any singleton has to be thread-safe, because lots of requests hit it at once. People forget that part.

S: csx
D: A
T: What is the difference between decimal, double and float, and which do you use for money?
K: decimal vs double, money in c#, floating point precision, double rounding error, float vs double vs decimal
X: Okay, so float and double are binary floating-point. float is 32-bit with around 7 significant digits, double is 64-bit with about 15 to 17. They're very fast, since CPUs support them in hardware, and the range is huge. But they store numbers in base 2, so lots of decimal fractions, like 0.1, can't be stored exactly. That's why 0.1 plus 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 in double, and small errors build up over repeated calculations.
X: decimal is a 128-bit decimal floating-point type, with 28 to 29 significant digits, and it stores numbers in base 10. So 0.1 is exact. It's slower and the range is smaller, but it's precise for decimal values.
X: So for money, prices, quantities with fixed decimal places, anything where exact decimal results and rounding matter, I use decimal. For scientific stuff, measurements, graphics or statistics, where tiny errors are okay and speed matters, double.
X: A few related things I keep in mind. Never compare doubles with double-equals, use a tolerance. Use Math.Round with an explicit MidpointRounding mode, because the default is banker's rounding, which surprises people. And in SQL Server, use decimal with fixed precision and scale for money columns, not float, and make sure EF Core maps the precision explicitly. Otherwise you get silent truncation.

T: DateTime vs DateTimeOffset vs DateOnly: which should you use?
K: datetime vs datetimeoffset, dateonly timeonly, datetime kind, utc in c#, date handling c#
X: DateTime stores a date and time, with a Kind property that says UTC, local or unspecified. The problem is Kind gets lost very easily, like when reading from a database or JSON, and you end up with an unspecified value where nobody knows which time zone it was. DateTime.Now on a server is especially risky, because it depends on the server's time zone.
X: DateTimeOffset stores a date and time plus an offset from UTC, like plus 5:30. So it represents an exact instant without any confusion. That's what I use for timestamps, when something happened, created and modified dates, API values. SQL Server has a matching datetimeoffset type.
X: DateOnly and TimeOnly, which came in .NET 6, represent just a calendar date or just a time of day. They're right for a date of birth, a visit date, a store opening time, where a time or time zone doesn't make sense. If you store a birth date as midnight DateTime, it can shift by a day when time zones get converted. I've seen that happen.
X: One thing to note, an offset isn't a time zone. Plus 5:30 tells you nothing about daylight saving rules. For future local times, like "every day at 9 AM in New York", I store the IANA time zone id and convert with TimeZoneInfo.
X: And I use TimeProvider instead of calling the clock directly, so tests can control time.

D: A
T: What is the difference between ReadOnlyCollection, ImmutableList and FrozenDictionary?
K: immutable collections, readonly collection vs immutable, frozendictionary, frozenset, ireadonlylist, collections c# 8
X: Honestly, they all stop changes, but in different ways.
X: A read-only collection, like ReadOnlyCollection or IReadOnlyList, is a read-only view over some other collection. My code can't modify it through that view, but whoever owns the underlying List can still change it, and I'll see those changes. So it's more about API design, exposing a collection without letting callers modify it.
X: Immutable collections, from System.Collections.Immutable, like ImmutableList and ImmutableDictionary, can never change. Methods like Add give you back a new collection that shares most of its structure with the old one, so it's efficient. They're great for thread-safety, because readers never need locks, and for snapshot semantics, like a configuration state that gets swapped atomically. Lookups are slower than a normal List or Dictionary though, since they're tree-based.
X: Frozen collections, FrozenDictionary and FrozenSet, came in .NET 8. Also immutable, but optimised for read speed instead of updates. Creating one is relatively expensive, because it analyses the data to build the fastest lookup it can, but after that lookups are faster than a normal Dictionary.
X: So how I use them, IReadOnlyList for exposing data from methods, immutable collections for shared state that changes now and then, and frozen collections for data built once at startup and read all the time, like lookup tables or permission maps.

S: csx
D: A
T: What are default interface methods, and when are they useful?
K: default interface methods, default implementation interface, interface with method body, c# 8 interface
X: Since C# 8, an interface can give a default implementation for a member. Classes implementing that interface get the behaviour automatically, unless they provide their own.
X: The main reason it was added is evolving an interface without breaking existing implementations. Earlier, adding a new method to a published interface broke every class that implemented it, which is a real headache for libraries with lots of consumers. Now the library can add the method with a default body, and old implementations keep compiling.
X: It also allows a kind of trait-like reuse, where small bits of shared behaviour are written in terms of other interface members. Like an ILogger-style interface could have a default LogError method that just calls the core Log method with an error level.
X: A few rules worth knowing. The default member is only accessible through the interface type, not through the class variable, unless the class implements it itself. Interfaces still can't have instance fields, so no state. And you can get diamond-inheritance ambiguities if two interfaces provide the same default, which the class then has to resolve.
X: Honestly I use them sparingly, mostly for API evolution in shared libraries. For sharing actual behaviour and state, an abstract base class or composition is usually clearer to read.
@p17-129
S: csx
D: A
T: What are static abstract interface members and generic math?
K: static abstract members, generic math, inumber, static virtual interface, c# 11 generic math
X: Okay, so since C# 11, interfaces can declare static abstract members. So each implementing type has to provide a static method, property or operator. Before this, generics couldn't call static members or operators on a type parameter, so you couldn't write one generic Sum method that works for int, double and decimal.
X: Generic math is built on top of that. .NET 7 added interfaces like INumber of T, IAdditionOperators and IParsable, and all the numeric types implement them. So I can write a generic Sum where T is an INumber of T, and inside it use T.Zero and the plus operator. It works for every numeric type with full performance, because the JIT generates specialised code for value types.
X: Other uses beyond maths. A static abstract factory method, like a static Create, so a generic method can create instances without reflection. Or a static abstract Parse, which is exactly what IParsable gives you, so a generic method can parse strings into any parsable type.
X: In everyday business code, honestly, I don't use it much. But it's useful in libraries, like a generic statistics helper, or a strongly typed id that can be parsed from route values.
X: It's also a nice example of how C# keeps adding features that remove the need for reflection or duplicate code.
@p17-130
S: csx
D: A
T: What are Native AOT and trimming in .NET?
K: native aot, ahead of time compilation, trimming, publish aot, startup time .net, aot limitations
X: Native AOT, ahead-of-time compilation, compiles a .NET app straight to native machine code at publish time, instead of shipping IL that the JIT compiles at runtime. What you get is a self-contained executable that doesn't even need the .NET runtime installed.
X: What you gain is very fast startup, often a few tens of milliseconds, lower memory, smaller deployments. That's really valuable for serverless like AWS Lambda where cold starts matter, for containers that scale quickly, and for command-line tools.
X: Trimming is part of it. The publish process analyses the app and removes unused code from the framework and libraries, to cut size.
X: The limitations come from the fact that everything has to be known at compile time. No runtime code generation, so no Reflection.Emit, and no dynamic assembly loading. Reflection over types the trimmer can't see may break, so libraries need to be AOT-compatible. Serialisation needs source-generated System.Text.Json contexts. And not everything supports it yet, like EF Core's AOT support is still limited, and some popular libraries depend on reflection.
X: ASP.NET Core supports AOT for minimal APIs with the slim builder, and the compiler warns you about anything incompatible.
X: So I'd use it for Lambdas and small, focused services, and stay on normal JIT for big apps with heavy reflection-based libraries. That's a practical split.
@p17-131
S: csx
D: A
T: What is tiered compilation and ReadyToRun in .NET?
K: tiered compilation, readytorun, jit compilation, dynamic pgo, startup performance .net, r2r
X: Both are about how .NET turns IL into machine code, basically balancing startup speed against peak performance.
X: The JIT compiles a method the first time it's called. With tiered compilation, it first compiles quickly with few optimisations, that's tier 0, so the app starts fast. Methods that get called a lot are recompiled in the background with full optimisations, tier 1. And long-running loops can switch to optimised code mid-execution, which is on-stack replacement.
X: Then there's dynamic PGO, profile-guided optimisation, on by default since .NET 8. While tier 0 code runs, the runtime collects data on how the code is actually used, like which types get passed to an interface call, and the tier 1 compile uses that to optimise. Like devirtualising and inlining the common case. Honestly, a lot of apps got a noticeable speed-up for free from this.
X: ReadyToRun is a publish option that pre-compiles IL to native code ahead of time, but keeps the IL too. The app starts faster because there's less JIT work at startup, and the JIT can still re-optimise hot methods later. The files are bigger though.
X: So for a service where startup matters, containers that scale often or Lambdas, I'd turn on ReadyToRun, or look at Native AOT. For long-running services, the defaults with tiered compilation and dynamic PGO work really well. I wouldn't touch them.
@p17-132
S: csx
D: A
T: What is thread pool starvation, and how do you detect it?
K: thread pool starvation, threadpool starvation, sync over async, blocking calls async, slow requests low cpu
X: So thread pool starvation is when all the thread pool threads are busy, mostly just blocked and waiting, so new work, like incoming requests or async continuations, has to wait for a free thread. And the thread pool adds new threads slowly, roughly one or two a second once you're above the minimum. So under load, response times explode while CPU stays low. That low CPU is the giveaway.
X: The most common cause, honestly, is sync over async. Calling .Result, .Wait or GetAwaiter().GetResult on async code. The thread blocks waiting for an operation whose continuation also needs a thread pool thread, so under load all the threads end up waiting on each other. Other causes are long synchronous I/O, like a sync database or file call, Thread.Sleep, or long locks in hot paths.
X: What you see is requests getting very slow or timing out, the thread count climbing and climbing, and CPU not high at all. Health checks can time out too, so you get restarts on top.
X: To detect it, I use dotnet-counters and watch thread pool queue length and thread count. A growing queue is the signal. A memory dump, or dotnet-stack, shows lots of threads blocked in the same place, like waiting on a Task.
X: The real fix is making the call chain async all the way, removing blocking calls, and using async APIs for I/O. Raising the minimum threads only buys you time.
@p17-133
S: csx
D: A
T: How do you call async code from synchronous code safely?
K: sync over async, call async from sync, getawaiter getresult, task result deadlock, async in constructor
X: Best answer, honestly, avoid it. Make the calling code async too, all the way up. In ASP.NET Core, controllers, middleware, hosted services, even Main can be async, so there's almost always a way.
X: But when I really can't, like a legacy interface I'm not allowed to change, or a constructor, then there are options and risks.
X: Blocking with .Result, .Wait or GetAwaiter().GetResult works, but it blocks a thread. In apps with a synchronisation context, like classic ASP.NET on .NET Framework, WinForms or WPF, it can deadlock. The async method tries to resume on the context that's blocked waiting for it, so both just wait forever. ASP.NET Core has no synchronisation context, so it won't deadlock there, but blocking still wastes threads and can cause thread pool starvation under load. If I must block, I prefer GetAwaiter().GetResult over .Result, because it throws the original exception instead of an AggregateException. And in libraries, ConfigureAwait false reduces the deadlock risk.
X: For constructors, I just avoid async work entirely. I use an async factory method like CreateAsync, or lazy async initialisation, or do the work in a hosted service at startup.
X: For event handlers in desktop apps, async void with a try-catch is acceptable.
X: Our legacy .NET Framework code actually had a few of these deadlocks, so for us it's a real concern during the migration.
@p17-134
S: csx
D: A
T: What is a race condition? Give an example.
K: race condition, race condition example, check then act, thread safety bug, concurrency bug
X: A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of two or more operations running at the same time. So it works most of the time and fails once in a while, which makes it really hard to reproduce.
X: Classic example is check-then-act. Two requests try to reserve the last kit at a site. Both read the stock and see one available. Both pass the check. Both reserve it. Now we've allocated two kits when only one existed. Each request was correct on its own, the problem is just the interleaving.
X: Another one is a shared counter incremented by many threads without synchronisation, where updates get lost. Or a lazy cache that gets initialised twice.
X: They happen in memory and in databases. And with multiple server instances, an in-memory lock doesn't help at all, which people sometimes forget.
X: The fix depends on where the shared state lives. In memory, locks, Interlocked, or concurrent collections. In the database, make the check and the update one atomic operation, like an UPDATE with a WHERE condition on the available quantity and then check rows affected. Or optimistic concurrency with a row version, or a unique constraint so the second insert just fails. Across instances, a distributed lock, or a single queue consumer per key.
X: In our IRT, kit allocation uses database transactions and concurrency checks for exactly this reason. You really can't afford a double allocation there.
@p17-135
S: csx
D: A
T: What is Lazy<T>, and how does it work?
K: lazy of t, lazy initialization, lazy thread safety mode, lazy loading object c#, deferred initialization
X: So Lazy of T basically delays creating an object until it's first needed, and then caches it. You give it a factory function, and the first time you read its Value property, it runs the factory and stores the result. After that, reads just return the same instance.
X: It's useful when something is expensive to create, like loading a big lookup table or building a complex client, and it might not even be needed in every code path. So you don't pay the cost at startup, or at all if it's never used.
X: It's thread-safe by default too. In the default mode, ExecutionAndPublication, if many threads read Value at the same time, only one runs the factory, the rest wait and get the same result. So it's an easy way to do a thread-safe singleton or a one-time initialisation. And it's the standard trick to make ConcurrentDictionary's GetOrAdd run the factory only once.
X: One gotcha though. If the factory throws, Lazy caches the exception by default, and every later access rethrows it. That's bad for transient failures, like a network blip at startup, because now it's stuck failing forever. In that case I use PublicationOnly mode, or a custom approach that retries.
X: For async initialisation, Lazy of Task of T works, but libraries like AsyncLazy handle retry and cancellation better. So I'd lean on those.
@p17-136
S: csx
D: A
T: throw vs throw ex: what is the difference?
K: throw vs throw ex, rethrow exception, preserve stack trace, exceptiondispatchinfo, wrap exception
X: Both rethrow an exception from a catch block, but they treat the stack trace very differently.
X: Plain throw, on its own, rethrows the current exception and keeps the original stack trace. So I can still see where the error actually happened, deep down in the call chain.
X: throw ex resets the stack trace to the current spot, the catch block. Everything about where the exception really came from is gone, and that makes production debugging so much harder. Code analysis tools flag it as a warning for that reason.
X: So inside a catch block, if I want to log something and let the exception carry on, I use plain throw.
X: If I want to add context, I wrap it. Throw a new ShipmentProcessingException with a useful message and pass the original as the inner exception. Then both the new context and the original stack trace are kept.
X: If I need to rethrow later, outside the catch block, like capturing it on one thread and rethrowing on another, ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture and Throw preserve the original stack trace. That's actually what await does internally.
X: And honestly, often the best choice is not catching at all. I only catch when I can handle it, add useful context, or translate it, and let the global exception handling deal with everything else.
@p17-137
S: csx
D: A
T: What are exception filters in C#?
K: exception filters, catch when, when keyword catch, filter exceptions c#, catch specific condition
X: Exception filters let you add a condition to a catch block using the when keyword, like catching HttpRequestException only when the status code is NotFound. The catch block runs only if the condition is true. Otherwise the exception just keeps going, as if that catch block wasn't even there.
X: Why is that better than catching and then rethrowing inside an if? A few reasons.
X: The stack isn't unwound when the filter is evaluated. So if the filter returns false, the exception continues with its original state intact, and debugging and crash dumps are more useful.
X: The code is cleaner, especially with several catch blocks for the same exception type but different conditions. Like handling a SqlException differently for a deadlock, error number 1205, versus a unique constraint violation, 2627 or 2601.
X: There's also a neat trick, logging inside a filter. You write a filter that calls a LogAndReturnFalse method. It logs the exception right where it happened, with the full stack, and returns false, so the exception isn't actually caught and continues upwards. I've used that one.
X: Transient error checks for retries benefit too, like catching only specific HTTP status codes.
X: Just keep filters quick, and they must not throw, because an exception inside a filter gets swallowed and treated as false. Then you're scratching your head wondering why your catch never ran.

S: csx
D: A
T: Exceptions vs the Result pattern: which do you prefer for business errors?
K: result pattern, exceptions vs result, error handling without exceptions, oneof, either type, railway oriented
X: For me, exceptions are for exceptional, unexpected stuff, like the database being down, a bug, or a broken invariant. They're expensive to throw, they're invisible in method signatures, and if you use them for normal business outcomes, like "validation failed" or "stock not available", your control flow turns into hidden jumps.
X: The Result pattern makes the expected outcome explicit. The method returns a Result that's either success with a value, or failure with an error, like a code and a message. The caller has to handle both, and the signature itself tells you this can fail. It's faster too, since nothing is thrown.
X: In practice, I use both. Expected business failures, a validation error, a not-found entity, a rule like "site not active", or a conflict, return a Result. The API layer maps that to the right HTTP response, 400, 404, 409 or 422 with ProblemDetails. Unexpected technical failures throw exceptions, which go to the global exception handler, get logged, and become a 500.
X: Libraries like FluentResults, ErrorOr or OneOf help, or honestly a small custom Result type is enough.
X: The downside is the code gets a bit more verbose, and the team has to apply it consistently.
X: In our newer IRT APIs, MediatR handlers return results for business rules, and FluentValidation errors become 400 responses automatically. That's worked well.
@p17-139
S: csx
D: A
T: System.Text.Json vs Newtonsoft.Json: what are the differences?
K: system.text.json vs newtonsoft, json.net vs system text json, json serialization c#, migrate newtonsoft, jsonserializeroptions
X: Okay, so System.Text.Json is the built-in serialiser in modern .NET, and the default in ASP.NET Core. Newtonsoft.Json, Json.NET, is the older, hugely popular third-party library.
X: System.Text.Json is faster and allocates less, because it works on UTF-8 bytes and spans, and it supports source generation for even better performance and Native AOT. It's secure by default and strict. Case-sensitive property matching by default outside ASP.NET Core, no comments or trailing commas unless you turn them on, and no loose conversions like a number sitting in a string.
X: Newtonsoft is more feature-rich and flexible. Very lenient parsing, JObject and LINQ to JSON for dynamic JSON, rich converters, reference loop handling, tons of settings. And a lot of older code and libraries depend on it.
X: To be fair, System.Text.Json has caught up a lot. Polymorphic serialisation with JsonDerivedType, JsonNode for dynamic documents, required properties, ReferenceHandler for cycles, naming policies including snake case.
X: When you migrate, what bites you is case sensitivity, how enums, dates and nulls are handled, private setters, and custom converters, which you have to rewrite.
X: My approach, System.Text.Json for new code with web defaults, and Newtonsoft only where some legacy behaviour or library needs it. In our legacy .NET Framework code, Newtonsoft is still there.
@p17-140
S: csx
D: A
T: Ordinal vs culture-sensitive string comparison: why does it matter?
K: string comparison ordinal, stringcomparison, culture sensitive comparison, turkish i problem, case insensitive compare c#
X: See, string comparisons can be ordinal, which compares the raw character codes, or culture-sensitive, which follows the language rules of a culture, like how accented letters sort.
X: The problem is some methods are culture-sensitive by default, like string.Compare, StartsWith with a string, ToUpper and ToLower. So the result can change depending on the server's culture settings. The famous one is the Turkish I problem. In Turkish culture, uppercase of small i isn't capital I, so a check like "file" ToUpper equals "FILE" fails on a Turkish machine. And these bugs only show up for certain users or servers, which makes them nasty.
X: Culture-sensitive comparison is slower too.
X: So my rule is, for identifiers, codes, keys, file paths, URLs, HTTP headers, config keys, anything machine-readable, use ordinal, StringComparison.Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase. For dictionary keys that should be case-insensitive, pass StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase. Culture-sensitive comparison only for text shown to and sorted for users, with the user's culture set explicitly.
X: I always pass the StringComparison argument explicitly, and the code analysers, CA1307 and CA1309, help enforce that.
X: For normalising case, ToUpperInvariant, not ToUpper.
X: In a global product with sites in so many countries, like ours, this really matters.

T: Explain the Strategy pattern with a real example.
K: strategy pattern, strategy design pattern c#, replace switch with strategy, pluggable algorithm, strategy with dependency injection
X: So the Strategy pattern puts a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, and the calling code picks one at runtime without knowing the details. It basically replaces those big if-else or switch blocks that choose behaviour based on a type or a setting.
X: Let me take an example. Calculating resupply quantities for sites, where different studies use different methods. One uses a simple min and max level, another uses a predictive method based on upcoming visits. Instead of one method with an ever-growing switch, I define an interface, IResupplyStrategy, with something like CalculateQuantity. Then I write a MinMaxResupplyStrategy and a PredictiveResupplyStrategy, each with its own logic and its own unit tests. The calling service gets the right strategy based on the study's configuration and just calls CalculateQuantity.
X: With DI, I register all the strategies, inject an IEnumerable of them, and pick by a key property. Or in .NET 8, use keyed services and resolve by strategy name.
X: What you get is each algorithm isolated and testable, adding a new one doesn't touch existing code, that's open-closed, and the choice can come from configuration.
X: The pluggable SFTP providers I built are also a Strategy, one interface, three provider implementations, picked by configuration.
X: But honestly, for just two simple cases, I won't bother. An if statement is fine.

T: Explain the Decorator pattern and how you use it with dependency injection.

X: The Decorator pattern wraps an object with another object that implements the same interface, and adds behaviour before or after calling the wrapped one. The caller has no idea it's talking to a decorator. And you can stack them.
X: It's perfect for cross-cutting stuff I don't want inside the business class, caching, logging, retries, timing metrics, authorization checks.

T: Explain the Factory pattern, and when you need a factory with DI.

X: A factory is just an object or method whose job is creating other objects, so the calling code doesn't need to know which concrete class to create or how to build it.

S: csx
D: A
T: Explain the Observer pattern and how C# events relate to it.
K: observer pattern, observer design pattern c#, events c#, publish subscribe in process, iobservable
X: Okay, so the Observer pattern lets one object, the subject, notify a bunch of other objects, the observers, when something changes, without knowing who they are. Observers subscribe and unsubscribe, and the subject just raises a notification. It keeps them loosely coupled.
X: In C#, events are basically the built-in implementation. A class declares an event, like ShipmentStatusChanged, other objects subscribe with plus-equals and a handler, and when the class raises the event, every subscriber gets called. IObservable and IObserver are the more formal interfaces, and Rx.NET builds a powerful reactive library on them. RxJS in Angular follows the same idea actually.
X: The big gotcha with events is memory leaks. The subject holds references to the subscribers' handlers, so a long-lived subject, like a singleton, keeps short-lived subscribers alive if they never unsubscribe. So I always unsubscribe, usually in Dispose.
X: Exceptions are another issue. If one handler throws, the handlers after it don't get called.
X: Honestly, in modern web back ends I rarely use C# events for business logic. Inside a service, I use domain events with MediatR notifications, which play well with DI and scoped services. And across services, the same idea becomes publish-subscribe messaging through RabbitMQ or Kafka. So the pattern is everywhere, just in different forms.

T: Explain the Adapter pattern with an example.
K: adapter pattern, adapter design pattern, wrapper class, wrap third party library, interface adapter c#
X: The Adapter pattern takes a class with an incompatible interface and makes it usable where a different interface is expected, by wrapping it in an adapter that translates the calls. Like a travel plug adapter, basically.
X: I mostly use it to isolate third-party libraries and external systems. Let me take a real one. X: Same idea applies to the anti-corruption layer for legacy systems, which is really an adapter at the service boundary.
X: And just to compare, Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour, and Facade simplifies a complex subsystem behind one easier interface. Adapter is purely about translating one interface into another.
