S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you seed reference data with EF Core?
K: ef core seed data, hasdata, seeding reference data, useseeding, migration data seeding, lookup tables seed
X: Honestly it depends on what kind of data it is, I've done it a few different ways.
X: HasData, in the model configuration, defines seed rows for an entity with explicit primary key values. EF Core puts inserts, updates and deletes for that data into migrations, by comparing with the previous model. It works well for small, stable reference data, statuses, country codes, types, stuff that should be identical in every environment. But keys have to be hard-coded, it can't depend on data already in the database, and changing large seed sets creates noisy migrations.
X: EF Core 9 added UseSeeding and UseAsyncSeeding, configured on the DbContext options, which run custom seeding code when EnsureCreated or Migrate runs. That's more flexible. It can check whether the data's already there and use any logic you like.
X: Custom migration code with migrationBuilder.Sql, or a post-deployment script in a database project, is another option. Especially when the data change has to happen at a precise point in the schema's evolution.
X: For test data and local development, I keep it separate from reference data, in a seeding tool or test fixtures. Never in production migrations.
X: In regulated systems, reference data changes are part of the validated release, reviewed just like code. And configuration that differs per study or customer isn't seed data at all. That belongs in configuration tooling, like our Admin console.
@p17-255
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is row-level security in SQL Server?
K: row level security, rls sql server, security policy predicate, tenant isolation database, session_context
X: Okay, row-level security basically lets the database itself filter which rows a user can see or change, based on who's running the query, without changing the queries at all.
X: You create an inline table-valued function, the predicate, that returns a row when access is allowed. Like when the row's TenantId equals the tenant id stored in the session context. Then a security policy applies that function as a filter predicate on the table. So SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE silently see only allowed rows. Optionally you add a block predicate too, which stops anyone inserting or updating rows into another tenant.
X: For apps that connect with one shared database login, the user or tenant identity gets set per connection with sp_set_session_context. For example through an EF Core connection interceptor right after the connection opens. And the predicate reads it with SESSION_CONTEXT.
X: For multi-tenant databases it's a strong extra layer of defence. Even if a developer forgets a WHERE clause, or a reporting tool queries the table directly, other tenants' data isn't exposed.
X: A few cautions though. The predicate runs on every query, so it has to be simple and backed by indexes, or performance suffers. Session context must be reset properly on pooled connections, that one's easy to miss. Admin and maintenance processes need a safe way to bypass it. And it doesn't replace authorization in the application, which still decides what each user is allowed to do.
@p17-256
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is zone.js, and what does zoneless Angular mean?
K: zone.js, zoneless angular, ngzone, provideZonelessChangeDetection, run outside angular, change detection trigger
X: So zone.js is a library that patches the browser's async APIs, setTimeout, promises, DOM events, XHR, so Angular knows whenever some async work finishes. After any of those, Angular runs change detection to update the view. That's why in classic Angular, changing a component property inside a click handler or an HTTP callback just works, without calling anything.
X: But there are downsides. It's a fairly heavy library. It triggers change detection very often, even when nothing relevant changed. Async stack traces get harder to read. And native async await can't be patched, so Angular had to downgrade it during builds.
X: The NgZone service lets you control it a bit. Like runOutsideAngular for frequent events, mousemove or a polling timer, so they don't trigger change detection on every tick.
X: Zoneless Angular removes zone.js completely. Change detection is triggered explicitly by things Angular knows about, signals changing, the async pipe, event handlers bound in templates, and markForCheck. It was experimental in Angular 18, stable in 20, and it's the default for new apps since Angular 21. In older versions you configure it with provideZonelessChangeDetection.
X: You get smaller bundles, better performance and cleaner debugging. To migrate though, components need to work properly with OnPush and signals, because code that changes state outside those triggers just won't update the view anymore. That's where most of the migration effort goes.
@p17-257
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is the new control flow syntax in Angular, like @if and @for?
K: angular control flow, @if @for @switch, built in control flow, ngif vs @if, track in @for
X: Since Angular 17, templates have built-in control flow blocks that replace the structural directives, ngIf, ngFor and ngSwitch.
X: At-if with an expression shows a block, with else-if and else branches, and you can alias the result, like at-if user async as user. At-switch with case and default replaces ngSwitch. At-for loops over a collection, and it requires a track expression, like track item.id. That tells Angular how to identify each item so it can reuse DOM elements instead of recreating them when the list changes. There's also an empty block that shows when the collection is empty, and implicit variables like index, first, last and count.
X: Why it's better, it's built into the compiler, so no importing CommonModule or the directives. It's more readable, especially else branches, which used to need ng-template references. Type narrowing works better inside if blocks. And it's faster. The mandatory track also fixes a really common performance mistake, because lots of teams forgot trackBy with ngFor and got full re-rendering of lists.
X: The Angular CLI has a migration schematic for control-flow that converts existing templates automatically, so moving over isn't painful.
X: In our newer Angular 17 study builder, we use the new syntax, while the older Angular 8 and 12 sub-apps still use the directives. So I go back and forth between both, honestly.
@p17-258
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are @defer blocks in Angular?
K: defer blocks, @defer angular, deferrable views, lazy load component template, on viewport, on idle
X: Okay so defer blocks came in Angular 17. A defer block lazily loads part of a template and its dependencies. Components, directives and pipes used only inside the defer block get split into a separate JavaScript chunk, which is downloaded and rendered only when some trigger condition happens.
X: The triggers are on idle, which is the default, when the browser's idle. On viewport, when the placeholder scrolls into view. On interaction, when the user clicks or types in the placeholder. On hover. On timer, after a delay. On immediate. And when, with a condition. There's also prefetch, so you can download the code earlier, like on idle, but render it later, on interaction.
X: Related blocks control what shows in the meantime. Placeholder before loading starts, with an optional minimum display time so it doesn't flicker. Loading while the chunk downloads. And error if loading fails.
X: It's useful for heavy parts of a page that aren't needed straight away. Charts below the fold, a rich text editor, a comments section, a big dialog. The initial bundle gets smaller and the first render is faster, which helps metrics like Largest Contentful Paint.
X: Before defer, lazy loading in Angular was mostly at the route level, or manual dynamic imports with ViewContainerRef. Now it's declarative and fine-grained. And with server-side rendering, Angular 19 added incremental hydration, where deferred blocks hydrate only when they're triggered.
@p17-259
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are signal inputs, model inputs and the output function in Angular?
K: signal inputs, input function angular, model signal, output function, input required, two way binding signals
X: Actually since Angular 17.1, components can declare inputs with the input function instead of the Input decorator. Like name equals input of string, or input.required of string. The input is a read-only signal, so in the template you read it as name with brackets, and in code you can use it in computed signals, like fullName as a computed of first plus last. Angular updates the signal whenever the parent passes a new value. So this replaces ngOnChanges and setters for reacting to input changes. And with required inputs, the compiler errors if the parent doesn't provide them. Transforms like booleanAttribute still work.
X: The model function creates a writable input for two-way binding. A child declares value equals model of number, and can set it with value.set. The parent binds with the banana-in-a-box syntax, square brackets and parentheses, to a property or a signal, and changes flow both ways. Way simpler than the old pattern of an Input plus an Output with the Change suffix.
X: The output function replaces the Output decorator with EventEmitter. Like saved equals output of Shipment, and you call saved.emit. It's lighter, and outputFromObservable can turn an RxJS stream into an output.
X: There are also signal-based queries, viewChild, viewChildren, contentChild and contentChildren, which return signals instead of being set later.
X: Put together, they make components fully signal-based, which plays really well with OnPush and zoneless change detection.
@p17-260
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are computed and effect in Angular signals, and what are the pitfalls of effect?
K: computed signal, effect angular, signal effect pitfalls, untracked, derived state signals, allowsignalwrites
X: Okay, so a computed signal derives its value from other signals, like total as a computed of the items reduced to a sum. It's lazy and memoised. It only recalculates when one of the signals it read has changed, and only when someone actually reads it. It's read-only and should be a pure function. That's the right tool for derived state, filtered lists, totals, flags.
X: An effect runs a side-effect function whenever the signals it reads change. It tracks dependencies automatically, runs at least once, and gets cleaned up when its component is destroyed. Effects are meant for syncing with stuff outside Angular's signal world. Writing to local storage, logging, calling a third-party chart library, manual DOM work.
X: Now the pitfalls, and I've seen people fall into these. Using effects to derive state, like an effect that sets another signal whenever some signal changes. That's what computed is for. The effect version causes extra change detection cycles, timing issues, and maybe even loops. Angular originally blocked signal writes inside effects by default for exactly this reason. Then unintended dependencies. Every signal you read inside the effect becomes a dependency, so reading something incidental re-runs it. untracked lets you read a signal without tracking it. And async work inside effects can race, so use the cleanup function, onCleanup, to cancel the previous work.
X: For data loading driven by signals, the newer resource and httpResource APIs are usually a better fit than effects.
@p17-261
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are linkedSignal and the resource API in Angular?
K: linkedsignal, resource api angular, httpresource, rxresource, async data signals, loading state signals
X: These are newer signal APIs, from around Angular 19 and 20. They fill the gaps between computed and writable signals, and between signals and async data.
X: linkedSignal creates a writable signal whose value is derived from other signals, but the user can also set it. When the source changes, it resets to a new computed value. Classic example is a selected option. The list of options comes from an input, and the selected item should default to the first option, but the user can change it. When the options list changes, the selection resets. Before this, people did it with an effect writing to a signal, which was honestly messy.
X: resource connects signals to async data. You give it a params function that reads signals, like the selected site id, and a loader function that fetches data. Whenever the params change, it calls the loader again and cancels the previous request with an AbortSignal. It exposes signals for value, status, isLoading and error, so the template can show a spinner or an error easily. rxResource does the same with an Observable loader, and httpResource wraps HttpClient directly, so interceptors still apply.
X: They kill a lot of boilerplate for the common "reload data when a filter changes" pattern. And they avoid race conditions where a slower response arrives after a faster one and overwrites it.
X: They're still evolving though, so I check their stability status for whichever Angular version we're on.
@p17-262
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do toSignal and toObservable work, and when do you use them?
K: tosignal, toobservable, rxjs signals interop, rxjs-interop, convert observable to signal
X: So basically they're the bridge between RxJS and signals, from the rxjs-interop package.
X: toSignal subscribes to an Observable and gives you back a signal with its latest value. I use it when a service exposes an Observable, like an HTTP call, route parameters or a store selector, but I want the value in a template or in computed signals. It subscribes immediately and unsubscribes automatically when the component or service is destroyed, so no manual subscription management. Since an Observable might not emit synchronously, the signal's initial value is undefined, unless you give an initialValue, or use requireSync for observables that emit right away, like a BehaviorSubject. Errors from the Observable are thrown when the signal is read, so I handle them in the stream first.
X: toObservable goes the other way. It turns a signal into an Observable that emits when the signal changes. Useful when you need RxJS operators on signal values, like debounceTime and switchMap on a search term signal, to call an API and cancel outdated requests. And then often I convert the result back with toSignal.
X: Both have to be called in an injection context, like a constructor or a field initialiser, or be given an Injector. People forget that and get an error.
X: My general approach is signals for synchronous state and templates, RxJS for complex async event streams, and these two functions right at the boundary between them.
@p17-263
S: ngx
D: A
T: inject() function vs constructor injection in Angular: what is the difference?
K: inject function angular, constructor injection angular, injection context, functional injection, inject vs constructor
X: Right, so Angular has two ways to get dependencies. Constructor injection declares them as constructor parameters, like private http of type HttpClient in the constructor. The inject function, available since Angular 14, gets them from inside the class body or a function, like private http equals inject HttpClient.
X: Both use the same injector hierarchy, so you get the same dependency either way. The differences are practical.
X: inject works in functions, not just classes. That's what enabled functional route guards, resolvers and HTTP interceptors, which are much shorter than the class-based ones. It also allows reusable helper functions that inject things, like an injectStudyId function that reads the route.
X: Inheritance gets easier. With constructor injection, a subclass has to repeat all the base class's dependencies and pass them to super. With inject, the base class just gets its own.
X: It also works better with modern TypeScript and the useDefineForClassFields setting, where constructor parameter properties had ordering issues with field initialisers.
X: The constraint is that inject only works in an injection context. During construction, in field initialisers, in factory functions, or inside runInInjectionContext. If you call it later, like in ngOnInit or a click handler, it throws.
X: The Angular team recommends inject now, and there's a migration schematic to convert constructor injection. For unit tests, both work the same with TestBed, so that's not a concern.
@p17-264
S: ngx
D: A
T: How does Angular's hierarchical dependency injection work?
K: hierarchical injectors angular, providedin root, component providers, environment injector, element injector, service instance per component
X: So Angular has a tree of injectors, and where you provide a service decides how many instances exist and who shares them.
X: At the top you've got the environment injector hierarchy. providedIn root in the Injectable decorator registers a singleton for the whole app, and it's tree-shakable, so if nothing injects it, it's removed from the bundle. Services provided in the application's providers, or in a lazy-loaded route's providers, live in environment injectors. A lazy route with its own providers gets its own child injector, so a service provided there is a separate instance just for that feature.
X: Then there's the element injector hierarchy, which follows the component tree. If a component lists a service in its providers array, each instance of that component gets its own instance of the service, shared with its children and destroyed with the component. That's handy for state that belongs to one part of the screen, like a form wizard's state service, or one editor instance per tab. viewProviders limits visibility to the component's own view, not projected content.
X: When a component injects something, Angular searches up the element injectors first, then the environment injectors, until it finds a provider. Modifiers change the search, Optional, Self, SkipSelf and Host, and those are options on the inject function.
X: A really common bug I've seen is accidentally providing a "global" service in a component's providers. You get separate instances, and shared state looks completely broken.
@p17-265
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is an InjectionToken, and what are useClass, useValue, useFactory and useExisting?
K: injectiontoken, usefactory usevalue useclass useexisting, angular providers types, inject config angular, provide token
X: Okay, so an InjectionToken is a key for dependency injection when there's no class you can use as the key. Like a config object, a primitive value, an interface, which doesn't exist at runtime in TypeScript, or a function. You create it with new InjectionToken of AppConfig with a description, and optionally a factory that gives a default value.
X: Providers then tell Angular what to hand out for a token or class.
X: useValue gives a fixed value, like an API base URL or a config object loaded at startup.
X: useClass gives an instance of a class, which lets you swap the implementation. Provide LoggerService, useClass ConsoleLoggerService. That's useful for environment-specific implementations or test doubles.
X: useFactory calls a function to create the value, and it can use inject inside, or a deps array in older code. It's for values that depend on other services or runtime conditions, like picking a storage implementation based on configuration.
X: useExisting creates an alias, so asking for one token returns the same instance as another. Like a component providing itself under an abstract token, so child components can inject it through an interface.
X: And the multi flag lets several providers contribute to the same token, so you get an array. Angular uses that for HTTP interceptors, form validators and app initialisers.
X: In our Angular apps, actually, the API base URL and feature settings come through an InjectionToken filled from a runtime configuration file.
@p17-266
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are functional route guards and resolvers in Angular?
K: functional guards, canactivatefn, canmatch, resolver angular, resolvefn, route guard function
X: Actually since Angular 15, guards and resolvers can be plain functions instead of classes implementing interfaces like CanActivate. A guard has a type like CanActivateFn, gets the route and router state, and uses inject to get services. It returns true to allow, false to block, or a UrlTree to redirect, like to the login page, and it can return an Observable or Promise of those. Class-based guards are deprecated now.
X: The guard types are canActivate, whether a route can be entered. canActivateChild for child routes. canDeactivate, whether the user can leave, usually to warn about unsaved changes. And canMatch, whether a route definition should even be considered. canMatch is great for loading different components for the same path based on a role or feature flag, and it stops the lazy-loaded code from even downloading when the user isn't allowed.
X: Resolvers, ResolveFn, fetch data before the route activates, and the component gets it through the route data, or as an input when withComponentInputBinding is on.
X: Honestly, I use resolvers sparingly. Navigation waits until the data arrives, so on slow requests the user sees nothing happening, and errors are harder to show nicely. Often it's better to navigate immediately and let the component show a loading state.
X: And guards are for user experience, not security. The API still has to enforce authorization, because anyone can call it directly.
@p17-267
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you handle token refresh on 401 in an Angular interceptor?
K: token refresh interceptor, 401 retry angular, refresh token interceptor, queue requests during refresh, httpinterceptorfn auth
X: In my project, the auth interceptor adds the access token to outgoing requests and deals with expired tokens without the user noticing.
X: How it flows, the interceptor attaches the bearer token to requests going to our API, and only to our API's URLs, never to third-party domains. If a response comes back 401, it tries to refresh the token, and if that works, retries the original request with the new token. If the refresh fails, it logs the user out and sends them to the login page.
X: The tricky part is concurrency. A screen often fires several requests at once, and they might all get 401 together. Without care, each one triggers its own refresh, and with refresh token rotation, the second refresh uses an already-used refresh token and fails, and the user gets logged out for no reason. So the interceptor keeps a single in-flight refresh, a flag plus a BehaviorSubject, or a shared Observable with shareReplay. The first 401 starts the refresh, and the other requests wait for it with filter and take one, then retry with the new token.
X: A few more details. Don't intercept the refresh call itself, or you get loops. Retry each request only once. And refresh proactively before expiry when you can, which avoids most 401s anyway. Libraries like angular-auth-oidc-client or keycloak-angular handle a lot of this.
X: In our apps, the Keycloak adapter refreshes tokens before expiry, and the interceptor just attaches the current token.

T: How do you write custom sync and async validators in Angular reactive forms?
K: custom validator angular, async validator, validatorfn, asyncvalidatorfn, cross field validation angular, form group validator
X: Okay, a synchronous validator is just a function that gets an AbstractControl and returns null if it's valid, or an errors object, like noFutureDate true, if not. X: So yeah, server-side validation is still the source of truth though, and I map server validation errors back onto the form controls.

T: What is ControlValueAccessor, and when do you implement it?
K: controlvalueaccessor, custom form control angular, ng_value_accessor, formcontrolname custom component, writevalue registeronchange
X: Basically ControlValueAccessor is the interface that connects an Angular form control to a UI element. There are built-in accessors for inputs, selects and checkboxes. T: How do you create a custom structural directive?

X: A structural directive changes the DOM structure by adding or removing elements, like the built-in ngIf used to. I write one when there's reusable display logic, like showing content only if the user has a certain permission.

@p17-273
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you write a custom pipe, and when should it be impure?
K: custom pipe angular, pipe transform, pure vs impure pipe example, standalone pipe, format pipe
X: Okay, a pipe transforms a value for display in a template, like formatting a date or a status label. To make one, you write a class with the Pipe decorator, give it a name, and implement PipeTransform with a transform method that takes the value and optional arguments and returns the display value. In modern Angular, pipes are standalone by default, and components import them directly.
X: Like a kitStatus pipe that turns a status code into a friendly label, or a siteTime pipe that formats a UTC timestamp in the site's time zone. You'd use it as kit.status piped into kitStatus, or created piped into siteTime with the time zone as an argument.
X: Pipes are pure by default. A pure pipe only re-runs when its input value changes by reference, or its arguments change. That makes them very efficient, much better than calling a method in the template, which runs on every change detection cycle. So pure pipes should be pure functions, no side effects, same output for the same input.
X: An impure pipe, pure set to false, runs on every change detection cycle. You need it when the output depends on something other than the input reference, like a mutable array that changes internally, or some external state. The async pipe is the famous impure one. Impure pipes have to be really cheap, or they slow the whole page down.
X: Honestly, a better alternative to an impure pipe is often immutable data, or a computed signal.
@p17-274
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is the async pipe, and why is it recommended?
K: async pipe, async pipe benefits, subscribe in template, observable in template, async pipe change detection
X: Honestly the async pipe is one of my favourites. It subscribes to an Observable or Promise right in the template and gives you the latest emitted value. Like shipments dollar piped into async.
X: Why it's recommended, a few reasons. Subscription management is automatic. It subscribes when the component renders and unsubscribes when the component is destroyed, so no memory leaks from forgotten subscriptions. It works nicely with OnPush, because it marks the component for check whenever a new value comes in, so the view updates even though no input changed. And it pushes you toward a declarative style. The component exposes streams, the template consumes them, no manual subscribe calls copying values into fields.
X: A few things to watch though. Each async pipe on the same Observable creates a separate subscription. So for an HTTP Observable used in three places, you'd make three HTTP calls. I've seen that in network tabs more than once. The fix is subscribing once with an if block, using the as syntax to alias the value, or sharing the stream with shareReplay. And errors in the stream need catchError in the component, otherwise the subscription just ends.
X: With signals, toSignal plays a similar role. It converts the Observable to a signal once, and the template reads it without a pipe. In newer code I often go that way, but the async pipe is still a perfectly good pattern, especially in existing RxJS-heavy apps like our older Angular sub-apps.

D: A
T: What are ng-template, ng-container and ngTemplateOutlet?
K: ng-template, ng-container, ngtemplateoutlet, template reference angular, reusable template, no extra dom element
X: So ng-template defines a block of template that isn't rendered on its own. It's a template that something else can render later, maybe several times, with different data. Structural directives use it behind the scenes, and in older code, else branches pointed to an ng-template.
X: ng-container is a grouping element that doesn't produce any DOM element at all. It's useful when you need to apply logic to several elements without adding a wrapper div that would break the layout or CSS, like inside a table row or a flex container. People used it a lot to combine ngIf and ngFor, since you can have only one structural directive per element.

And this is the key to customisable components. Let me take a reusable data table component. It can accept an ng-template for how to display a cell, through a content child query or an input. The table renders that template for each row with ngTemplateOutlet, passing the row as context. So the consumer controls the cell markup, and the table controls the layout, sorting and paging.
X: The same idea lets you define a piece of markup once in a template, like a status badge layout, and render it in a few places without creating a separate component. That's how I'd explain the three of them.
@p17-276
S: ngx
D: A
T: How does view encapsulation and component styling work in Angular?
K: view encapsulation, emulated encapsulation, shadow dom angular, :host selector, ng-deep, component styles
X: So Angular scopes component styles, so one component's CSS doesn't leak out and mess up other components. The ViewEncapsulation setting controls how.
X: Emulated is the default. Angular adds unique attributes to the component's elements and rewrites its CSS selectors to include those attributes, so styles only apply inside that component's template. ShadowDom uses the browser's real Shadow DOM, which gives true isolation, but then global styles, like a design system's base styles, don't reach inside. None makes the component's styles global, which people occasionally use for theme files, but it risks conflicts.
X: There are special selectors too. Colon host styles the component's own host element, like making it display block, and host with a class lets the component react to a class on itself. Host-context applies styles based on an ancestor, like a dark theme class higher up the tree.
X: To style inside a child component, especially third-party ones like Angular Material, people use ng-deep, which turns off encapsulation for that rule. It's deprecated, but honestly still everywhere, because there's no full replacement. Better options are the child component's inputs, CSS custom properties, which pass through encapsulation, or the library's theming APIs.
X: In a big app, I keep component styles small, use a shared design system for consistency, and rely on CSS variables for theming. We keep the Angular sub-apps visually consistent with the React shell through shared design tokens.
@p17-277
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is server-side rendering and hydration in Angular?
K: angular ssr, hydration angular, angular universal, prerendering, incremental hydration, ssr benefits
X: Okay, so server-side rendering means the Angular app runs on the server, in Node.js, and returns fully rendered HTML for the requested page. The browser can show content immediately, before the JavaScript has even downloaded. That improves first paint and Largest Contentful Paint, helps SEO, and gives good link previews on social media, because crawlers see real content.
X: It used to be called Angular Universal. Since Angular 17, SSR is built into the CLI, ng new with the ssr option, or ng add the angular ssr package. Prerendering, or static site generation, renders pages at build time for content that doesn't change per request.
X: Hydration is what happens next in the browser. Instead of throwing away the server HTML and re-rendering everything, which used to cause flicker, Angular reuses the existing DOM and attaches event listeners and state to it. Full hydration has been stable since Angular 16. Event replay captures clicks that happen before hydration finishes and replays them. And incremental hydration, Angular 19 onwards, hydrates defer blocks only when they're triggered, which cuts JavaScript work further.
X: The tricky bits, code must not touch browser-only objects like window or localStorage during server rendering, so you guard with isPlatformBrowser or afterNextRender. And HTTP data fetched on the server gets transferred to the client, so it isn't fetched twice.
X: Honestly, for internal, login-only business apps like ours, SSR adds very little, so we don't use it. It really matters for public, content-heavy sites.

T: How do you load runtime configuration in an Angular app instead of build-time environments?
K: runtime config angular, app initializer, provideappinitializer, environment.ts vs runtime config, config.json angular, build once deploy many
X: See, Angular's environment files get compiled into the bundle at build time. That means a separate build for every environment, which goes against build once, deploy many, where the same tested artifact moves from test to UAT to production. In a validated environment that really matters, because a rebuilt artifact isn't the artifact that was tested.
X: So I load configuration at runtime instead. The app ships with a config.json file, or the server serves one at a known URL, with environment-specific values like the API base URL, the identity provider URL, the client id and feature flags. Another way is fetching the config in main.ts before calling bootstrapApplication and passing it into the providers.
X: Only non-secret values go in this file though, since the browser can read everything.

T: How do you upgrade an Angular application across many versions, like 8 to 17?
K: angular upgrade, upgrade angular 8 to 17, ng update, angular migration versions, update angular major version
X: Honestly, Angular officially supports upgrading only one major version at a time. So going from 8 to 17 is nine steps, not one jump, and I'd plan it as a proper project.
X: The first thing is preparation. Make sure there's a decent test suite and an end-to-end smoke test, because every step needs verifying. Check the third-party libraries, because honestly they're usually the real blocker. Each library needs a version compatible with each Angular version, and some are abandoned, so you have to replace them. Also check the Node.js and TypeScript versions each Angular version needs.

Standalone components in 14 and 15. And the esbuild builder plus the new control flow in 17. Those later features are optional migrations, which I'd do after the upgrade itself.

@p17-281
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do NgRx store, actions, reducers, selectors and effects fit together?
K: ngrx, ngrx store, ngrx effects, ngrx selectors, redux in angular, ngrx actions reducers
X: So NgRx is basically a Redux-style state management library for Angular, built on RxJS.
X: The store holds the application state as one immutable object tree. Components never change it directly. Instead they dispatch actions, which are plain objects describing events, like "Shipments Page Opened" or "Shipment Cancelled", created with createAction or grouped with createActionGroup.
X: Reducers are pure functions. They take the current state and an action and return a new state, built with createReducer and on handlers. No side effects in there, so state changes are predictable and easy to test.
X: Selectors read and derive data from the store, created with createSelector. They're memoised, so derived values, like pending shipments for the selected site, only get recalculated when their inputs change. Components use store.select, or selectSignal to get a signal.
X: Effects handle side effects, like API calls. An effect listens for specific actions, calls a service, and dispatches a success or failure action with the result, usually with switchMap or exhaustMap and catchError. Then the reducers update state from those actions.
X: Redux DevTools shows every action and state change, with time-travel debugging, which honestly helps a lot when debugging.
X: The downside is boilerplate and indirection. For simple apps or local component state, it's overkill, and services with signals are enough. It pays off in big apps with lots of shared state and complex async flows, with several developers who need consistent patterns.
@p17-282
S: ngx
D: A
T: How is the new SignalStore different from the classic NgRx store with reducers and effects?
K: ngrx signalstore, signal store, signalstate, withstate withmethods, ngrx signals, lightweight state angular
X: Okay, NgRx SignalStore is a newer, lighter state management approach from the NgRx team, built on Angular signals instead of RxJS and the Redux pattern.
X: You create a store with signalStore and compose it from features. withState defines the initial state, which becomes signals for each property. withComputed adds derived signals. withMethods adds methods that update state with patchState, or do async work, using rxMethod for RxJS-based flows or plain async functions. And withHooks runs logic on init and destroy. There are reusable features too, like withEntities for collections with ids, and community features for devtools and request status.
X: The store is an injectable service, so you can provide it at root for global state, or at component level for local, feature-specific state. I like that flexibility.
X: Compared with the classic NgRx store, there are no separate actions, reducers and effects files, so way less boilerplate. Components just call methods directly. It's signal-based, so it works naturally with OnPush, zoneless change detection and signal inputs. And it's more modular, stores per feature rather than one big global tree. What you lose is some of the strict event-driven traceability that actions give you, though NgRx has added an events plugin for people who want that back.
X: For new Angular apps, I'd start with SignalStore or simple signal-based services, and only use the classic store where the Redux pattern clearly adds value.
@p17-283
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you handle errors in RxJS streams?
K: rxjs error handling, catcherror, retry rxjs, error kills observable, retry with delay, finalize rxjs
X: In RxJS, when an Observable errors, the stream terminates. No more values come through. So in a long-lived stream, like a search box or a polling feed, one single error stops it working until the page is reloaded. That's honestly the most common RxJS bug I see.
X: catchError intercepts the error and returns a replacement Observable. A fallback value, like an empty array, with of. Or EMPTY to complete quietly. Or rethrow a friendlier error with throwError. The key trick for long-lived streams is putting catchError inside the inner Observable, inside switchMap, not at the end of the outer stream. Then only that one request fails, and the outer stream keeps listening for the next search term.
X: retry resubscribes to the source after an error, a number of times. Since RxJS 7, retry takes a config with count and a delay function, which allows exponential backoff, like retry with count 3 and a delay based on a timer and the retry count. I only retry for transient errors, network failures or 503, not 400 or 404.
X: finalize runs when the stream completes, errors or gets unsubscribed, which is useful for turning off a loading spinner.
X: In Angular, HTTP errors can also be handled centrally in an interceptor, for logging, notifications or redirects on 401, while components handle the errors specific to their screens. That split works well for us.
@p17-284
S: ngx
D: A
T: combineLatest vs forkJoin vs withLatestFrom vs zip: what is the difference?
K: combinelatest vs forkjoin, withlatestfrom, zip rxjs, combine observables, parallel http calls rxjs
X: So these all combine multiple Observables, but they emit at different times, and honestly that's the whole difference.
X: forkJoin waits until all the sources complete, then emits once with the last value from each. It's like Promise.all. The right choice for running several HTTP calls in parallel and using all the results together, like loading a site, its inventory and its users before showing a page. If any source errors, the whole thing errors. And if any source never completes, forkJoin never emits, so it's not for long-lived streams.
X: combineLatest emits whenever any source emits, once each source has emitted at least once, giving the latest value from each. It's for combining ongoing streams, like filters. When the status filter, the date range or the search term changes, recalculate with the latest of all three. A common surprise is nothing emits until every source has emitted once, so startWith helps there.
X: withLatestFrom is driven by one primary stream. When the primary emits, it combines that value with the latest of the others, but the others emitting doesn't trigger anything. Perfect for "when the user clicks save, take the current form value and the selected site".
X: zip pairs values by index, first with first, second with second, and so on. I rarely need it, mostly when values correspond one to one.
X: And with signals, computed covers a lot of combineLatest's use cases more simply.
@p17-285
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you build a search typeahead with RxJS?
K: typeahead rxjs, debouncetime distinctuntilchanged, search as you type, autocomplete angular, switchmap search, cancel previous request
X: Let me walk through it. A typeahead calls an API as the user types, so it has to avoid flooding the server and deal with responses arriving out of order.
X: I start with a stream of the input's values, from a reactive form control's valueChanges, or a signal converted with toObservable. Then a pipeline of operators.
X: debounceTime of about 300 milliseconds waits till the user pauses typing, so we're not calling the API on every keystroke.
X: map to trim the text, and filter out terms that are too short, like under two characters, maybe returning an empty result for those.
X: distinctUntilChanged skips the call if the term is the same as last time, like when the user types a letter and deletes it.
X: switchMap calls the search API, and this is the key one. When a new term arrives, it unsubscribes from the previous request, and Angular's HttpClient cancels it. So a slow response for an old term can never overwrite the results for a newer term. That's the race condition people hit with mergeMap or plain promises.
X: Inside switchMap, catchError returns an empty result on failure, so one failed request doesn't kill the stream. And I can track loading state with a signal or startWith.
X: The template shows the results with the async pipe, or a signal from toSignal.
X: On the server side, the search endpoint should be fast, limited and indexed, because even with debouncing it gets hit a lot. So that's the full picture.
@p17-286
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are hot and cold observables, and what does shareReplay do?
K: hot vs cold observable, shareReplay, share rxjs, multicast, duplicate http calls angular, cache http observable
X: Okay, a cold Observable starts producing values separately for each subscriber. Angular's HttpClient calls are cold, so each subscription sends a new HTTP request. If a template has two async pipes on the same HTTP Observable, or two components subscribe to the same service method's result, the request goes out twice.
X: A hot Observable produces values regardless of subscribers, and all subscribers share the same source. Like DOM events, a WebSocket stream, or a Subject. Late subscribers miss earlier values, unless the stream replays them.
X: share and shareReplay turn a cold Observable into a shared hot one. share multicasts to all current subscribers through one subscription to the source. shareReplay also replays the last N values to new subscribers. So shareReplay with bufferSize 1 is the common way to cache an HTTP result. The first subscriber triggers the request, and everyone after gets the cached value with no new call.
X: There are pitfalls though. With the old shareReplay of 1 signature, the source subscription stays alive even when all subscribers leave, which can leak for long-lived sources. Using the config with refCount true unsubscribes when nobody's left. A cached error or stale value stays cached, so you need a way to refresh, like a Subject that triggers reloading. And caching in a root service means the data sticks around for the whole session.
X: For simple shared state, honestly, a signal or BehaviorSubject in a service is often clearer.

S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you display very large lists efficiently in Angular?
K: virtual scroll angular, cdk virtual scroll, large list performance angular, render thousands of rows, infinite scroll angular
X: See, rendering thousands of rows with a simple loop creates thousands of DOM elements and component instances. Initial render gets slow, scrolling gets janky, and change detection gets expensive.
X: The main thing I'd reach for is virtual scrolling. The Angular CDK's virtual scroll viewport, with the cdkVirtualFor directive, only renders the rows visible in the viewport plus a small buffer, and recycles them as the user scrolls. The list can have 50,000 items, but only about 30 are in the DOM. It works best with a fixed row height, set with itemSize. Variable heights are harder. Data grids like AG Grid have virtualisation built in, even for columns.
X: Then server-side paging or infinite scrolling. Often the user doesn't need all items at once, so loading pages on demand, with filters and search on the server, beats sending everything to the browser.
X: After that, reduce the work per row. OnPush on row components, a proper track expression in the for block so rows get reused when data refreshes, pure pipes instead of method calls in templates, and no heavy components inside each row. Like rendering a dropdown only when a row is being edited.
X: You can also use defer for parts of each row that aren't needed immediately.
X: And I'd measure with Angular DevTools' profiler and the browser's performance panel, to see whether time goes to change detection or DOM rendering.
X: [Our material forecasting dashboard was the kind of screen where server-side paging and OnPush made the difference.]

S: ngx
D: A
T: How does internationalization work in Angular?
K: angular i18n, localize angular, translation angular, ngx-translate, transloco, multiple languages angular
X: So Angular has a built-in i18n system. You mark text in templates with the i18n attribute, and in code with the dollar-localize tagged template. The CLI extracts all marked text into a translation file, XLIFF or JSON, which translators fill in for each language. Then the build produces a separate compiled version of the app per locale, with the translations baked in. Locale data also drives the built-in date, number, currency and percent pipes, and plural and select expressions handle the grammar rules.
X: The good thing about the built-in approach is performance. Translations are compiled in, so no runtime lookup cost. The bad part is a separate build and deployment per language, usually served under a path like slash fr, and switching language means loading a different version of the app, a full page reload.
X: Runtime libraries, like Transloco or the older ngx-translate, load translation files at runtime and translate with a pipe or directive. One build serves all languages, and users can switch instantly. You pay a small runtime overhead and lose some compile-time checking. Honestly, a lot of business apps choose this for the flexibility.
X: Either way, I keep dates and numbers in neutral formats in the data, format them in the UI with the user's locale, think about right-to-left layouts if needed, and avoid concatenating translated fragments. Word order differs between languages, so glued-together sentences come out wrong.
@p17-289
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you read route parameters, and what is component input binding?
K: activatedroute, route params angular, query params angular, withcomponentinputbinding, parammap, route data
X: Okay, so Angular's router gives a component the current route's info through ActivatedRoute. Route parameters, like the id in shipments slash colon id. Query parameters, like status equals pending. The fragment, resolved data, and static data defined on the route.
X: You can read them two ways. The snapshot, like route.snapshot.paramMap.get id, gives the value at the moment the component was created. Fine if the component always gets recreated when the parameter changes. But Angular reuses the component when you navigate from shipments 1 to shipments 2 within the same route, so the snapshot goes stale. I've seen that bug in code reviews. The Observables, paramMap and queryParamMap, emit every time the parameters change, so I combine them with switchMap to load the right data, which also cancels the previous request.

Route parameters, query parameters and resolver data get bound directly to component inputs with the same name. So the component just declares an id input, or a signal input, and reacts to changes. No ActivatedRoute dependency, easier to test and reuse, and it works nicely with computed signals and resource for loading data.
X: To update query parameters, like when the user changes a filter, I navigate with queryParams and queryParamsHandling set to merge. That keeps the URL shareable and the back button works.
@p17-290
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are preloading strategies in the Angular router?
K: preloading strategy, preloadallmodules, custom preloading strategy, lazy loading preloading, quicklink angular
X: Right, so with lazy-loaded routes, each feature's code downloads only when the user navigates to it. That keeps the initial bundle small, but the first navigation to a feature waits for its chunk, which feels slow on bad networks.
X: Preloading downloads lazy-loaded route chunks in the background after the app has loaded and become interactive. So later navigation is instant, and the initial load stays fast.
X: Angular has built-in strategies. NoPreloading, the default, only loads on demand. PreloadAllModules preloads every lazy route once the app is stable. That's simple and fine for small to medium apps, but in big apps it downloads a lot of code that many users never touch, which wastes bandwidth.
X: A custom preloading strategy gives you more control. You implement PreloadingStrategy and decide per route. Like preloading only routes marked with data preload true, the ones most users visit. Or only routes the current user's role can access. Or skipping preloading on slow connections using the Network Information API. Libraries like ngx-quicklink preload routes whose links are currently visible on screen, which is a smart middle ground.
X: You configure it with withPreloading in provideRouter for standalone apps.
X: Defer blocks and canMatch guards complement this. canMatch stops users from even downloading features they're not allowed to use, which I like.
@p17-291
S: ngx
D: A
T: What causes ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError, and how do you fix it?
K: expressionchangedafterithasbeencheckederror, ng0100, change detection error, value changed after checked, angular dev mode error
X: Actually this error shows up in development mode when a value bound in a template changes after Angular has already checked it in the same change detection cycle. In dev mode, Angular runs an extra verification pass to make sure the view is stable. If a binding's value is different on the second pass, it throws, because the view would be showing inconsistent data.
X: What usually causes it? A child component, or a lifecycle hook like ngAfterViewInit, changes a property on the parent that the parent's template already rendered. Like a child emitting an event in ngOnInit that sets the parent's title. Or a getter or method in the template that returns a new value every time, like new Date or a new object or array, so the second check sees something different. Or a service shared between parent and child that gets updated during rendering.
X: The fix is to correct the data flow, not hide the error. Move the logic earlier, into ngOnInit or the constructor, so the value's set before the view is checked. Don't update parent state from a child's lifecycle hooks. Let the parent compute it, or restructure into a shared service or signal that's set before rendering. And make template expressions stable, with computed signals or pure pipes instead of methods that create new objects.
X: Workarounds like setTimeout or calling detectChanges again do make the error go away. But honestly they hide a design problem and cause an extra render, so they're my last resort.

T: How do you profile and debug change detection performance in Angular?
K: angular devtools profiler, change detection profiling, slow angular app debug, too many change detection cycles, ng.profiler
X: Honestly, when an Angular screen feels sluggish, the first thing I want to know is whether the time goes to change detection, rendering, or our own code.
X: Angular DevTools, the browser extension, is my first tool. The component explorer shows the component tree with inputs, outputs and state. The profiler records change detection cycles while I click around. It shows how many cycles ran, what triggered them, and how long each component took. What I usually find is a mousemove or scroll listener, or a setInterval, triggering change detection constantly. Or one expensive component, often with a method call in the template doing heavy work. Or the whole tree getting checked because nothing uses OnPush. Recent versions also show signal graphs and injector trees.
X: The browser's Performance panel gives the full picture. Scripting versus rendering versus layout, long tasks, memory.
X: The fixes come from what you find. OnPush on components, so they're only checked when inputs change or events happen inside them. Signals, for more targeted updates. Running noisy events outside the Angular zone with runOutsideAngular, or going zoneless. Pure pipes or computed signals instead of template methods. Proper tracking in for loops. And defer or virtual scrolling for heavy parts.
X: And I always measure before and after. Guesses about performance are wrong surprisingly often, I've been wrong myself plenty of times.
@p17-293
S: ngx
D: A
T: What are bundle budgets in Angular, and how do you reduce bundle size?
K: angular bundle size, budgets angular.json, source map explorer, reduce bundle size angular, tree shaking angular, esbuild angular
X: So budgets are just size limits you configure in angular.json. Like a warning if the initial bundle goes above 500 KB and an error above 1 MB, plus limits for individual component styles. If a build crosses the error budget, it fails. It's a simple guard against bundle size slowly creeping up as dependencies and features get added, which hurts load times bit by bit.
X: To figure out what's making the bundle big, I build with source maps and analyse with source-map-explorer, or esbuild's metafile with a visualiser. That shows a treemap of which libraries and files take up the space.
X: Then the usual fixes. Lazy load feature routes, so each feature's code isn't in the initial bundle. Use defer for heavy components inside a page, like charts or editors. Replace heavy libraries or import only what you need. moment.js with all its locales is the classic culprit, replaced by date-fns or the built-in Intl APIs. lodash should be imported per function, or replaced by native methods. Make sure libraries are tree-shakable, ES modules, and don't import whole icon sets. Remove unused dependencies. Use providedIn root services, which are tree-shakable. And check for duplicate packages, two versions of the same library.
X: Since Angular 17, the default esbuild-based builder is faster and produces efficient output anyway.
X: For us, smaller bundles matter for users on slow hospital or clinic networks, which is a real thing for site users.

T: What are Angular Elements, and how do they help with micro-frontends?
K: angular elements, web components angular, createcustomelement, custom elements, micro frontend angular
X: Okay, Angular Elements packages Angular components as standard web components, also called custom elements. With createCustomElement, you turn a component into a custom element class, and register it with the browser's customElements.define under a tag name, like shipment-summary. Then any HTML page can use that tag, whatever the framework. Plain HTML, a server-rendered MVC page, React, or another Angular app. Inputs become attributes and properties, and outputs become DOM custom events.
X: So they're useful in a few situations. Gradual migration, embedding new Angular components into a legacy app without converting the whole page. X: The challenges are real though. Each element bundle includes Angular's runtime unless you share it carefully, so several separately built elements can mean duplicate framework code and bigger downloads. Global styles and Shadow DOM interactions need thought. Communication between elements should go through attributes, events, or a small shared event bus, not shared internal state. And versioning has to be managed across teams.
X: For micro-frontends, Module Federation, or Native Federation in the Angular world, is another option that shares dependencies at runtime more efficiently.
X: In our case, actually, the React shell uses npm feature packages instead of runtime micro-frontends.
