S: ngx
D: A
T: What is the difference between markForCheck and detectChanges?
K: markforcheck vs detectchanges, changedetectorref, onpush manual update, detach change detection, view not updating onpush
X: So both are methods on ChangeDetectorRef, and you use them when Angular doesn't automatically notice a change, usually with OnPush components.
X: markForCheck marks the current component and all its ancestors up to the root as dirty, so they get checked in the next change detection cycle. It doesn't run change detection right away. It's the right tool when an OnPush component's state changed because of something Angular didn't see, like a value pushed from a service subscription, or a callback from a third-party library. The async pipe calls markForCheck internally, that's why it works with OnPush.
X: detectChanges runs change detection immediately and synchronously, but only for this component and its children. Useful when you need the view updated right now, like before measuring the DOM. Or for a component you've detached from the change detection tree with detach, and then update manually for performance, like something that redraws only on a timer. Calling it at the wrong moment, like during another change detection cycle, can cause errors.
X: There's also checkNoChanges, used in dev mode for verification.
X: In modern Angular with signals, you need these much less. When a signal read in a template changes, Angular marks the component for check automatically. Honestly, when I find myself calling them a lot, it usually means the state should be in signals, or Observables with the async pipe.
@p17-296
S: ngx
D: A
T: Smart vs presentational components: how do you structure an Angular feature?
K: smart vs dumb components, container presentational, angular component design, feature structure angular, reusable components angular
X: I split components into two kinds, and it makes features much easier to test, reuse and change.
X: Smart components, or containers, know about the application. They inject services or stores, load data, handle routing parameters, call APIs, and decide what happens on user actions. Usually they map to a page or a major section, like ShipmentListPage. Their templates mostly compose presentational components and pass data down.
X: Presentational components, the dumb ones, only know their inputs and outputs. They get data through inputs, render it, and emit events through outputs when the user does something. Like a ShipmentTable emitting a cancelClicked event with the shipment id. No services, no HTTP, no store. So they're easy to reuse in different places, easy to test with simple inputs, and perfect for OnPush, since they only change when inputs change.
X: A feature folder usually has the routes, the page-level smart components, the presentational components, the feature's data service or store, and its models. Shared generic UI components, buttons, dialogs, form fields, live in a shared library or the design system.
X: I don't follow it dogmatically though. A small component with one simple service call doesn't need splitting. But for anything substantial, keeping data logic separate from display pays off, especially when the same table or form shows up in several places. In my project, that's saved us a lot of duplicate code.
@p17-297
S: ngx
D: A
T: What is a route reuse strategy in Angular?
K: route reuse strategy, routereusestrategy, keep component state on navigation, cache route component, tabs keep state angular
X: See, by default when the user navigates away from a route, Angular destroys its component, and when they come back, it creates a new one. Any state in there, the scroll position, filters, an expanded row, data already loaded, is gone, and the data gets fetched again.
X: A RouteReuseStrategy lets you customise this. It's a class with methods the router calls during navigation. shouldDetach decides whether to keep a route's component when leaving. store saves the detached component tree. shouldAttach and retrieve decide whether to restore a stored component when coming back. And shouldReuseRoute decides whether to reuse the current component when navigating between two URLs that match the same route config.
X: A common use is a list-detail flow. The user filters a long list, opens a detail page, and comes back expecting the list exactly as they left it. By detaching and storing the list route, it reappears instantly with its state. Another is a tabbed interface where each tab is a route.
X: There are pitfalls. Stored components stay in memory with their subscriptions active, so you have to limit what's stored and clear it, like on logout. And lifecycle hooks like ngOnInit don't run again on reattach, so components may need to refresh data explicitly.
X: Honestly, a simpler solution is often keeping filter state in the URL's query parameters, or in a service or store, so a brand new component can just restore it.
@p17-298
S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you write a custom attribute directive with HostListener and HostBinding?
K: custom attribute directive, hostlistener, hostbinding, host property directive, autofocus directive, directive example angular
X: Basically an attribute directive changes how an existing element looks or behaves, without adding or removing elements. You create a class with the Directive decorator and a selector in square brackets, like appAutofocus or appHighlightOverdue, and apply it as an attribute.
X: Inside, you can inject ElementRef to get the host element, and Renderer2 to change it in a platform-safe way, which also works with server-side rendering.
X: HostListener subscribes to events on the host element, or globally on the window or document. Like a directive that listens for paste events on an input and strips spaces from pasted kit numbers. Or one that closes a dropdown on a document click outside it.
X: HostBinding binds a property of the host element to a directive property. Like adding a CSS class, class.overdue, when an input date is in the past, or setting attr.aria-label.
X: In modern Angular though, the recommended way is the host property in the Directive decorator. You map class.overdue to isOverdue, and click to onClick with the event, instead of using the decorators. That keeps all host bindings in one place and works well with signal inputs.
X: Directive composition, with hostDirectives, lets a component include existing directives on its own host, so behaviours like focus handling or tooltips can be reused.
X: Directives are a great way to package small behaviours once, autofocus, input masks, permission checks, click-outside detection, and use them everywhere. I've got a few of those I reuse all the time, that's how I like to package them.
@p17-299
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you avoid race conditions when fetching data in useEffect?
K: useeffect race condition, abortcontroller react, useeffect cleanup fetch, stale response react, ignore flag useeffect
X: So this is a classic bug. A component fetches data in useEffect based on a prop, like the selected site id. The user switches from site A to site B quickly. Both requests are in flight, and if A's response comes back after B's, the component shows site A's data while site B is selected.
X: The fix is the effect's cleanup function. React runs the cleanup before running the effect again, and when the component unmounts. And you can use it two ways.
X: One is an ignore flag. Inside the effect, declare let ignore equals false, and in the cleanup, set ignore to true. When the response arrives, only update state if ignore is still false. The stale response just gets thrown away.
X: The other is AbortController, which I prefer. Create a controller in the effect, pass controller.signal to fetch, or to axios through its signal option, and call abort in the cleanup. Now the outdated request actually gets cancelled, which saves bandwidth, and the aborted promise rejects with an AbortError, which I ignore instead of showing as an error.
X: The cleanup also stops you setting state after unmount.
X: Honestly though, in real apps I avoid hand-written fetching in effects. Libraries like TanStack Query or RTK Query handle caching, deduplication, race conditions, retries and loading states for you, keyed by the query parameters. Effects are better kept for syncing with external systems.
@p17-300
S: rx
D: A
T: Why do effects run twice in development with React StrictMode?
K: strictmode double render, useeffect runs twice, react 18 strict mode effects, double api call development, strict mode react
X: Okay, so in React 18 and later, when a component is wrapped in StrictMode, React deliberately mounts it, unmounts it, and mounts it again in development. So every effect runs, its cleanup runs, and then it runs again. Render functions get called twice too. This only happens in development. Production builds run effects once.
X: The point is to surface bugs early. React is moving towards features, like keeping state when components are hidden and shown again, where components might be mounted and unmounted multiple times. If an effect doesn't clean up properly, like a subscription that isn't removed, a timer that isn't cleared, or an event listener added twice, the double run exposes it as duplicate behaviour. And double rendering exposes impure render functions with side effects.
X: So the right response isn't to disable StrictMode. Honestly, I've seen people do that. The right thing is making effects resilient. Every effect that sets something up should return a cleanup that tears it down, and the effect should work correctly when run twice. For data fetching, the abort or ignore pattern handles it, and the second request is the one that counts. For stuff that truly has to happen once per app, like initialising analytics, I do it outside components, at module level, or guard it with a ref.
X: The duplicate API call in development looks scary in the network tab, but it's expected, and libraries like TanStack Query deduplicate it anyway.
@p17-301
S: rx
D: A
T: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect: what is the difference?
K: uselayouteffect vs useeffect, layout effect, measure dom react, flicker react, useinsertioneffect
X: See, both run after React has updated the DOM, just at different moments.
X: useEffect runs after the browser has painted the screen. It doesn't block painting, so the user sees the update quickly. That's the right default for most side effects, data fetching, subscriptions, logging, timers, syncing with external systems.
X: useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after the DOM updates but before the browser paints. The browser waits for it to finish. It's for when you need to read the layout and change something before the user sees it, otherwise there'd be a visible flicker. Typical example is positioning a tooltip or popover. You measure the target element's position and size with getBoundingClientRect, then set the tooltip's position. With useEffect, the tooltip would first show up in the wrong place and then jump.
X: Since it blocks painting, heavy work in useLayoutEffect makes the UI feel slow. So I keep it small and only use it when there's an actual flicker problem.
X: During server-side rendering, layout effects don't run, and React used to warn about it, so components using it need some care in SSR apps.
X: There's also useInsertionEffect, which runs even earlier, before layout effects, and it's really only meant for CSS-in-JS libraries to inject styles.
X: Honestly, in practice I use useEffect almost always, and useLayoutEffect maybe a few times a year.
@p17-302
S: rx
D: A
T: When does React.memo not help?
K: react memo not working, react.memo pitfalls, memo with object props, unnecessary memo, when to use react memo
X: Okay, React.memo makes a component skip re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to the previous props. It's useful for expensive components that re-render often with the same props, like rows in a big list or a heavy chart.
X: But a lot of the time it doesn't actually help, and here's why.
X: New object, array or function props on every render. If the parent passes style as an object literal, items as data.filter of something, or onClick as an arrow function, those are new references every time. So the shallow comparison always fails, and memo does nothing except add comparison cost. The fix is useMemo for derived objects and arrays, useCallback for functions, or moving constants outside the component.
X: Children as props is another one. JSX children are new elements on every render, so a memoised component that receives children re-renders anyway.
X: Then context. If the component uses a context that changes, it re-renders regardless of memo. And its own state or hooks changing triggers re-renders too. memo only affects re-renders caused by the parent.
X: And sometimes it's just not needed. If the component is cheap, re-rendering costs less than the memo bookkeeping. React's rendering is fast, and re-rendering isn't the same as touching the DOM.
X: So I measure first with the React DevTools Profiler, and memoise where it shows a real cost. The React Compiler, which is stable now, does a lot of this memoisation automatically anyway.
@p17-303
S: rx
D: A
T: What is automatic batching in React 18?
K: automatic batching, react 18 batching, setstate batching, multiple setstate one render, flushsync
X: So batching means React groups several state updates into a single re-render, instead of re-rendering after each one. If a click handler calls setLoading, setData and setError, React renders once with all three changes. That's faster, and you don't get intermediate, inconsistent states on screen.
X: Before React 18, batching only happened inside React event handlers. Updates inside promises, setTimeout, native event listeners or other async callbacks weren't batched. So after an API call, setting three state values caused three separate renders.
X: React 18 brought automatic batching. With the new createRoot API, all updates are batched, wherever they come from, async callbacks, timeouts, promises. Apps get fewer renders without changing any code. One thing to note, apps still using the old ReactDOM.render, like React 17 apps upgraded without switching to createRoot, keep the old behaviour.
X: In rare cases you need an update applied immediately. Like reading the updated DOM right after setting state, say scrolling to a newly added item. flushSync forces React to apply the updates inside it synchronously. It hurts performance, so I use it sparingly.
X: And related to this, because of batching, state isn't updated right after calling the setter. The new value shows up on the next render. So for updates based on the previous value, I use the functional form, setCount with c goes to c plus one. People get bitten by that one a lot.
@p17-304
S: rx
D: A
T: What are useTransition and useDeferredValue?
K: usetransition, usedeferredvalue, concurrent rendering react, starttransition, non urgent updates, keep ui responsive
X: Actually these are concurrent features from React 18 that keep the UI responsive when some update triggers expensive rendering.
X: The idea is to separate urgent updates, like typing in an input, which has to feel instant, from non-urgent ones, like filtering a big list based on that input, which can lag a little. React can interrupt rendering a non-urgent update if something urgent comes in, and work on it in the background.
X: useTransition gives you a startTransition function and an isPending flag. You wrap the expensive state update in startTransition. The input's own state updates immediately, while the filtered list update becomes a transition. If the user keeps typing, React throws away the outdated render. isPending lets you show a subtle loading indicator. In React 19, transitions can also wrap async functions, called Actions, which track pending state across the whole async operation.
X: useDeferredValue gives you a deferred version of a value. It lags behind the real value during heavy rendering. You pass the deferred value to the expensive child, ideally memoised, so the input stays responsive while the child catches up. It's handy when you don't control where the state is set, like when the value comes from props.
X: Honestly, the thing people misunderstand is that neither makes the work faster. They just prioritise it. If filtering 50,000 items is slow, virtualisation or server-side filtering is still the real fix.
@p17-305
S: rx
D: A
T: How does Suspense work, and how is it used for data fetching?
K: react suspense, suspense data fetching, suspense fallback, suspense boundaries, use hook react 19, suspense query
X: So basically Suspense lets a component "wait" for something before rendering, and shows a fallback, like a spinner or skeleton, from the nearest Suspense boundary above it, until the content's ready.
X: It started with React.lazy for code splitting. A lazily loaded component suspends while its JavaScript chunk downloads, and the Suspense boundary shows the fallback.
X: For data, a component suspends when it reads data that isn't ready yet. Under the hood, the data source throws a promise. React catches it, shows the fallback, and retries rendering when the promise resolves. You don't do this manually in app code. Suspense-enabled data libraries do it. TanStack Query's useSuspenseQuery, RTK Query with suspense patterns, Relay, and frameworks like Next.js. React 19's use hook can read a promise passed in, usually created by a framework or a parent, and suspend until it resolves.
X: What you get is components that can assume data is there, without loading checks everywhere. Loading states get coordinated declaratively by where you place boundaries, so one skeleton can cover a whole section, or you have separate ones per widget. And with server rendering, content can stream in as it becomes ready.
X: Errors aren't handled by Suspense though. They go to the nearest error boundary, so I always pair the two.
X: One pitfall, creating promises during render without caching causes infinite suspending. That's exactly why libraries manage it for you.
@p17-306
S: rx
D: A
T: What is new in React 19: Actions, useActionState, useOptimistic and use?
K: react 19 features, useactionstate, useoptimistic, use hook, react actions, ref as prop react 19
X: Okay, so React 19 came out in December 2024, and it was mainly about making async data mutations and forms simpler.
X: Actions are functions that run inside a transition, including async functions. React tracks the pending state, errors and optimistic updates for them automatically. A form element can take a function as its action prop, so submitting calls the function with the FormData, and React handles the pending state and resets the form after success.
X: useActionState wraps an action and gives you back the current state, like the result or an error message from the last submission, a wrapped action to pass to the form, and an isPending flag. It cuts a lot of boilerplate around loading and error state for submissions.
X: useFormStatus lets a child component, like a submit button, read whether its parent form is pending, without prop drilling.
X: useOptimistic shows an optimistic value immediately while an async action runs, like showing a new comment instantly, and automatically reverts to the real state when the action finishes or fails.
X: And use reads a resource during render. A promise, suspending until it resolves, or a context. Unlike other hooks, you can call it conditionally.
X: Some other changes too. ref is now a normal prop for function components, so no more forwardRef. Context can be used directly as a provider. Document metadata, like title tags, can be rendered in components. And better error reporting.
X: Our shell is on React 17 though, so using these would come after an upgrade.
@p17-307
S: rx
D: A
T: What are React Server Components?
K: react server components, rsc, server components vs client components, use client directive, next.js app router
X: See, React Server Components are components that run only on the server. They render to a special serialised format that gets streamed to the browser, and their own code never goes to the client. They can be async functions that hit databases, the file system or internal APIs directly, and secrets stay on the server.
X: Client components are the familiar kind, marked with the "use client" directive at the top of the file. They're sent to the browser, hydrated, and can use state, effects, event handlers and browser APIs.
X: The two get combined in one tree. Server components fetch data and render the static parts, and pass data as props into client components for the interactive bits. Server Functions, marked "use server", let client components call server-side functions, like for form submissions, without you writing an API endpoint.
X: The upside is smaller JavaScript bundles, since server-only code and heavy rendering libraries stay on the server. Faster initial loads, because data fetching happens close to the data. No client-server request waterfalls. And simpler data access.
X: The cost, they need a framework with a server, most commonly the Next.js App Router. There's a new mental model about which code runs where. And props passed to client components have to be serialisable.
X: For a single-page app like our React shell, built with Vite and served as static files with .NET APIs, Server Components don't really apply. Honestly, they make most sense for content-heavy, public-facing apps.
@p17-308
S: rx
D: A
T: What is the React Compiler, and does it replace useMemo and useCallback?
K: react compiler, auto memoization react, react forget, babel plugin react compiler, do we still need usememo
X: So the React Compiler is a build-time tool, a Babel plugin, that memoises components and hooks automatically. It analyses the code, works out which values depend on which props and state, and inserts memoisation so components, calculations and callbacks only get recomputed when their inputs actually change. It hit its stable 1.0 release in October 2025, after being used in production at Meta.
X: So the result is like wrapping things in React.memo, useMemo and useCallback everywhere it matters, but done correctly and automatically, without cluttering the code or missing dependencies.
X: In projects using the compiler, most manual useMemo and useCallback calls become unnecessary, and new code can be written more simply. They still work and can stay, like where a memoised value is used as an effect dependency and the exact identity has to be guaranteed, or where you want precise control.
X: The catch is the compiler relies on the code following the Rules of React. Components and hooks must be pure during render, props and state must not be mutated, and hooks must be called unconditionally. Code that breaks these rules just gets skipped, so the compiler's ESLint plugin is useful for finding violations. In an existing codebase, you usually adopt it gradually, directory by directory, with testing.
X: It works with React 19 natively, and with React 17 and 18 through a runtime package. So actually even our React 17 shell could adopt it later.
@p17-309
S: rx
D: A
T: Vite vs Create React App or webpack: why use Vite?
K: vite vs webpack, vite vs create react app, why vite, vite dev server, esbuild rollup vite, cra deprecated
X: Create React App used to be the standard way to start a React project. But it's been deprecated since early 2025, and honestly it was slow for big projects, because it bundled everything with webpack, even in development.
X: Vite works differently in development. It serves source files as native ES modules straight to the browser, and only transforms the files the browser asks for, using esbuild, which is written in Go and extremely fast. So the dev server starts almost instantly, no matter how big the project is, and hot module replacement updates the browser in milliseconds after a change. Dependencies are pre-bundled once.
X: For production, Vite builds optimised bundles with Rollup, or Rolldown in newer versions, with code splitting, tree shaking, hashed file names and CSS handling. Config is much simpler than webpack's, and there's a big plugin ecosystem. TypeScript, JSX, CSS modules and environment variables work out of the box, and there's library mode for building packages.
X: webpack is still powerful and very flexible, and plenty of existing projects and tools use it, like Module Federation's original implementation. But it's more complex to configure, and slower.
X: Vitest, a test runner built on Vite, shares the same config and is really fast.
X: Our React shell and feature packages use Vite, and developer experience got a lot better compared with the older webpack setups we had. Startup time alone was a big win for the team.
@p17-310
S: rx
D: A
T: How do environment variables work in Vite, and what are the pitfalls?
K: vite env variables, import.meta.env, vite_ prefix, env files vite, runtime config react, mode vite
X: Okay so Vite loads environment variables from .env files. .env for all modes, .env.development and .env.production for specific modes, and .local variants that don't get committed to Git. Only variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed to client code, as import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL. There are built-ins too, like import.meta.env.MODE, DEV and PROD. For TypeScript, I declare the variables in a vite-env.d.ts file so they're typed.
X: Now the thing to really understand is these values get replaced at build time. They're baked into the JavaScript bundle as plain strings. And that leads to two pitfalls.
X: One is secrets. Anything with the VITE_ prefix is visible to anyone who opens browser dev tools. So only public values belong there, API URLs, public client ids. Never API keys or secrets.
X: The other is build once, deploy many. If the API URL is baked in, you need a different build per environment, which means production isn't running the exact artifact that was tested in UAT. In regulated environments, that's a real concern. The workaround is runtime configuration. The app fetches a config.json at startup, or the server injects a small script that sets window variables, and the deployment pipeline writes the right values per environment.
X: Our React shell uses Vite environment variables for things like the API and Keycloak URLs.
@p17-311
S: rx
D: A
T: What are portals in React, and when do you use them?
K: react portals, createportal, modal portal, render outside root, tooltip overflow hidden
X: Basically a portal renders a component's children into a different DOM node, outside the parent component's DOM hierarchy. You use createPortal with the JSX and a target element, often document.body or a dedicated modal-root element.
X: The main use is overlays. Modals, dialogs, tooltips, dropdown menus, toasts. If a modal is rendered inside some deeply nested component, CSS can break it. A parent with overflow hidden can clip it, a parent with a transform or a lower z-index stacking context can push it behind other content, and positioning gets messy. Rendering it directly under body avoids all that.
X: The nice part is a portal still behaves like a normal child in React's tree. It gets props and context from its React parent, like the theme or the current user. And events bubble up through the React tree, not the DOM tree. So a click inside the modal still reaches onClick handlers on React ancestors, which honestly surprises people and sometimes needs stopPropagation.
X: Accessibility needs care with portals. Focus should move into the modal when it opens, stay trapped inside while it's open, and go back to the triggering element when it closes. The rest of the page should be hidden from screen readers, and Escape should close it.
X: In practice, component libraries like MUI handle this for you. MUI's Dialog, Popover and Menu use portals and manage focus internally, so I rarely write a raw portal myself.
@p17-312
S: rx
D: A
T: What replaced forwardRef in React 19, and when do you use useImperativeHandle?
K: forwardref, ref as prop react 19, useimperativehandle, expose methods from child component, focus input from parent
X: So a ref gives you direct access to a DOM element or a component instance, for things like focusing an input, scrolling, measuring, or plugging in non-React libraries.
X: Before React 19, a function component couldn't receive a ref as a normal prop. If a parent wanted to focus an input inside my custom TextField component, I had to wrap it in forwardRef, which passed the ref as a second argument, and attach it to the inner input. Reusable component libraries had forwardRef literally everywhere.
X: In React 19, ref is just a regular prop for function components. The component takes ref from its props and passes it to the inner element. forwardRef isn't needed anymore, and it'll be deprecated in a future version.
X: useImperativeHandle customises what the parent gets through the ref. Instead of exposing the whole DOM node, the component exposes a small controlled API, like an object with focus, clear or scrollToRow methods. A data grid component, say, might expose scrollToRow and resetFilters, and keep its internal DOM private.
X: But honestly, it's an escape hatch. React's normal flow is props down and events up, and most things that look like "call a method on the child", like opening or closing a dialog, are better as props, like an open prop. I use imperative handles only for genuinely imperative actions, focus, scrolling, playing media, triggering animations.
@p17-313
S: rx
D: A
T: Higher-order components vs render props vs custom hooks: which pattern do you use?
K: higher order component, hoc vs hooks, render props, reuse logic react, withauth hoc, custom hooks vs hoc
X: Okay, so all three are ways to reuse logic across components, and they kind of reflect React's history.
X: A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a new one with extra props or behaviour. Like withAuth wrapping a Dashboard, which checks authentication, or Redux's old connect. They work, but there are problems. Wrapper hell, with lots of nested wrappers in DevTools. It's unclear where a prop came from. Prop name collisions between HOCs. And awkward TypeScript types.
X: Render props pass a function as a prop, or as children, and the component calls it with its data, like a MouseTracker with a render prop that gets the mouse position. More explicit than HOCs, but you end up with deeply nested JSX, people call them callback pyramids.
X: Custom hooks, since React 16.8, replaced most uses of both. A hook like useAuth, useDebounce or useShipments wraps up stateful logic, and any component calls it directly and gets the values. No extra component in the tree, it's clear where values come from, they compose easily, and TypeScript types are simple.
X: So these days I use custom hooks by default. HOCs still have a place for wrapping components with cross-cutting behaviour at the route level, like requiring a permission to render a page. And render props, or children as a function, are still useful for flexible UI components where the consumer controls rendering, like a virtualised list's row renderer.
@p17-314
S: rx
D: A
T: What is the compound components pattern?
K: compound components, compound component pattern react, tabs component pattern, context compound component, flexible component api
X: Actually compound components are a set of components that work together to form one UI element. They share state implicitly, but let the consumer arrange them freely. The classic HTML example is select and option. In React, think of Tabs with Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab and Tabs.Panel, or an Accordion with Item, Header and Content.
X: The parent component holds the shared state, like which tab is active, and provides it through a React context. The child components read the context to know if they're active and to change the state, like a Tab calling setActive on click. So the consumer writes clean, declarative JSX, puts the pieces wherever they want, even adds custom elements between them, without passing state or callbacks around by hand.
X: What you get is a flexible API without dozens of config props, like those tabsConfig arrays with render functions. The structure is clear right there in the JSX. And the component's internal state stays hidden.
X: A few details I take care of. The children should throw a helpful error if used outside their parent, by checking for a missing context. The parent can support both uncontrolled use, with internal state, and controlled use, with value and onChange props. And accessibility lives inside, ARIA roles and keyboard navigation for tabs.
X: MUI and headless libraries like Radix use this pattern a lot, and honestly it's how I build reusable UI pieces in a design system.
@p17-315
S: rx
D: A
T: What is prop drilling, and how do you avoid it?
K: prop drilling, avoid prop drilling, pass props many levels, context vs composition, component composition react
X: So prop drilling is basically passing data through several layers of components that don't use it themselves, just so some deeply nested child can get it. Like the current user going from App to Layout to Sidebar to Menu to MenuItem. The middle components get noisy, tightly coupled, and harder to refactor.
X: There's no single fix, I pick based on the situation.
X: Composition first. Often the intermediate components can accept children or element props, so the parent renders the deep component directly and passes it down as a ready-made element. Then the data only goes where it's used. Honestly, this is underused and really effective.
X: Context, for data that lots of components at different levels need and that changes rarely. Current user, theme, locale, permissions, the selected study. It's built in and simple, but every consumer re-renders when the value changes, so I keep contexts small and focused and memoise the value.
X: A state management library, like Redux Toolkit or Zustand, for app state that's shared widely and updated often, because components subscribe to just the slice they need through selectors.
X: A server-state library, like TanStack Query or RTK Query, for API data. Any component calls the same query hook and gets cached data, so you don't pass fetched data down at all.
X: And passing props one or two levels is fine. It's explicit. I don't treat every prop as drilling.
@p17-316
S: rx
D: A
T: What are the performance pitfalls of React Context, and how do you avoid them?
K: context performance, context re render, split context, usememo context value, context selector, context vs redux performance
X: Okay, when a context's value changes, every component that consumes that context re-renders, even if it only uses a tiny part of the value. And React.memo doesn't stop it.
X: The common pitfalls I see. Passing an object literal as the value, like value equals user and setUser in braces. That's a new object on every render of the provider, so all consumers re-render whenever the provider re-renders, even if nothing changed. Fix is memoising the value with useMemo.
X: Putting too much in one context, like user, theme, notifications and filters all together. A change to notifications re-renders every component that only uses the theme. Fix is splitting into separate focused contexts, one per concern.
X: Mixing frequently changing state with stable functions. A common trick is splitting state and dispatch into two contexts. Components that only trigger updates consume the dispatch context, which never changes, so they don't re-render when the state changes.
X: And using context for high-frequency updates, like form input values or real-time data. Context just isn't designed for that.
X: If part of the app needs fine-grained subscriptions, a store library like Redux Toolkit or Zustand is better, because components subscribe through selectors and only re-render when their selected value changes. There's also use-context-selector as a library.
X: So for me, context is for low-frequency, app-wide values, and a store or server-state library handles the rest.
@p17-317
S: rx
D: A
T: Zustand vs Redux Toolkit: when would you choose each?
K: zustand vs redux, zustand, state management comparison react, lightweight state management, redux alternatives
X: Honestly both are popular state libraries for React, but with pretty different philosophies.
X: Redux Toolkit is the official, modern way to use Redux. Single store, slices with reducers and actions from createSlice, Immer for simple immutable updates, createAsyncThunk for async logic, and RTK Query for API caching. It gives you a strict, predictable structure, excellent DevTools with time travel and action history, middleware, and patterns that scale well across big teams. It costs you more concepts and some ceremony, though way less than old Redux.
X: Zustand is minimal. You create a store with a function that defines state and actions together, and components use a hook with a selector, like useStore picking selectedSite, and re-render only when that selection changes. No providers, very little boilerplate, small bundle, and it works outside React too. It can use the Redux DevTools and middleware like persist and immer. The flip side is less enforced structure, so big teams need their own conventions.
X: How I choose, for large apps with many developers, complex shared state, and a need for strict patterns and traceable state changes, Redux Toolkit. For small to medium apps, or local feature state, Zustand. Either way, server data belongs in a server-state library like RTK Query or TanStack Query, which removes most of the state that used to go into Redux.
X: Our React shell uses Redux Toolkit, so that's where most of my experience is.
@p17-318
S: rx
D: A
T: What is normalized state, and how does createEntityAdapter help?
K: normalized state redux, createentityadapter, entity adapter, ids and entities, normalize nested data redux
X: So normalised state means storing each type of data like tables in a database. Each entity type in its own collection, keyed by id, with references by id instead of nested copies. So instead of an array of shipments where each shipment has a full site object and an array of kit objects, I store shipments, sites and kits separately, as objects mapping id to entity, plus an array of ids for ordering.
X: Why bother? Each item exists in exactly one place, so updating a site updates it everywhere it's referenced, no inconsistent copies. Lookups by id are O(1) instead of searching arrays. And updates are simpler and cheaper, which cuts unnecessary re-renders, because components can select single items.
X: Redux Toolkit's createEntityAdapter makes this easy. It creates the standard shape, ids and entities, and gives you reducer helpers like addOne, addMany, setAll, updateOne, upsertMany and removeOne, which you use inside a slice's reducers. It also generates memoised selectors, selectAll, selectById, selectIds and selectTotal. You can set a sortComparer to keep ids sorted, and a custom selectId if the id field isn't called id.
X: When API responses are nested, I flatten them when storing, either by hand or with a library like normalizr.
X: With RTK Query though, a lot of server data is cached per query instead. So honestly I normalise mainly for client-side state with lots of cross-references or frequent individual updates.
@p17-319
S: rx
D: A
T: Why do Redux selectors need memoization, and how does createSelector work?
K: reselect, createselector, memoized selectors, selector re render, derived data redux
X: See, a selector is a function that reads data from the Redux store, like state.shipments.items. With useSelector, a component re-renders whenever the selector's result changes, compared by reference.
X: The problem comes with derived data. A selector like "pending shipments", which filters the array, returns a new array every single time it runs, even if the shipments haven't changed. useSelector runs selectors after every dispatched action, sees a new reference, and re-renders the component on every action in the whole app. And the filtering re-runs every time, which is wasteful for big lists.
X: createSelector, from Reselect and re-exported by Redux Toolkit, creates memoised selectors. You give it input selectors, like selectShipments and selectStatusFilter, and a result function that combines them. It only recomputes when an input's result changes by reference. Otherwise it returns the cached previous result, same reference, so the component doesn't re-render.
X: There are some subtleties. The cache size used to be one by default, so a selector used with different arguments in several components, like selectShipmentsBySite with a site id, kept recalculating. Newer Reselect versions use weakMapMemoize by default, which handles multiple arguments better, or you create a selector instance per component with useMemo. And input selectors themselves must be simple and not create new objects.
X: Redux Toolkit's dev checks actually warn when a selector returns a new reference for the same inputs, which catches a lot of these.
@p17-320
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you build forms with React Hook Form and Zod?
K: react hook form, zod validation, zodresolver, form validation react typescript, schema validation forms
X: Okay, React Hook Form is a form library that manages form state with uncontrolled inputs and refs by default, so typing in one field doesn't re-render the whole form. That makes it fast even for big forms, with very little code.
X: You call useForm, which gives you register to connect native inputs, handleSubmit to validate and submit, and formState with errors, isSubmitting and isDirty. For controlled components, like MUI inputs or date pickers, you use the Controller component or useController. useFieldArray handles dynamic lists of fields, like adding multiple kit lines to a return.
X: Zod is a TypeScript-first schema library. I define the form's schema once. Like quantity is a number, at least 1, at most the dispensed quantity. Reason is a string with a minimum length, required when the status is Damaged, using refine or superRefine for cross-field rules. Then z.infer gives me the TypeScript type from the schema, so the type and the validation rules can never drift apart. Honestly, I really like that part.
X: zodResolver connects them. useForm with the resolver set to zodResolver of the schema. Validation runs on submit, or on blur or change if you configure it, and errors show up in formState.errors with messages from the schema.
X: When the server sends back validation errors, I map them onto fields with setError.
X: The same Zod schema can even be shared with a Node backend. With a .NET backend though, the server has its own FluentValidation rules.
@p17-321
S: rx
D: A
T: Why validate API responses at runtime with Zod when you already have TypeScript types?
K: runtime validation api response, zod parse api, typescript types not runtime, validate json react, safeparse
X: See, TypeScript types only exist at compile time. When I write data equals await response.json as Shipment, TypeScript just trusts me. If the API returns something different, like a renamed field, a null where I expected a string, a date as a number, or an error object instead of data, nothing catches it at runtime. Then the app fails somewhere far from the cause, like "cannot read property of undefined" deep in a component, and that's painful to debug.
X: Runtime validation closes that gap. You define a Zod schema for the response and parse the JSON with it. If the data matches, you get a correctly typed object. If not, you get a clear error saying exactly which field is wrong, right at the API boundary. safeParse returns a success flag instead of throwing, so you can log the problem and show a friendly error.
X: Zod can also transform data while parsing, like converting ISO date strings into Date objects, or applying defaults.
X: It's most valuable for data from external or less trusted sources. Third-party APIs, local storage, URL parameters, messages from other windows. For our own APIs, where types are generated from the backend's OpenAPI spec, the contract is already strong. So I use runtime validation selectively, for critical screens and during API changes.
X: It costs a little bundle size and CPU, which is usually nothing to worry about.
@p17-322
S: rx
D: A
T: Which TypeScript utility types do you use most?
K: typescript utility types, partial pick omit record, readonly typescript, returntype parameters, required typescript
X: Utility types transform existing types, so you don't repeat definitions. Honestly, a handful of them I use almost daily.
X: Partial of T makes all properties optional, perfect for update payloads or patch functions, like updateShipment taking a Partial of Shipment. Required of T does the opposite.
X: Pick of T with some keys creates a type with only those properties, like Pick of Shipment with id and status, for a summary component. Omit of T removes properties, like Omit of Shipment and id for a create form, where the server generates the id.
X: Record of K and V describes an object with keys of type K and values of type V, like Record of ShipmentStatus to string for status labels. With a union of string literals as K, TypeScript makes sure every status has a label. So adding a new status shows errors wherever a mapping is missing, which is really handy.
X: Readonly of T makes properties read-only, useful for state and props that mustn't be mutated.
X: ReturnType and Parameters pull types out of functions, like getting the type of what a hook returns without exporting it separately. Awaited unwraps promise types.
X: NonNullable removes null and undefined, and Extract and Exclude filter union types.
X: The point is these keep types derived from one source. When the base type changes, everything derived from it updates automatically, and I don't chase copies around.
@p17-323
S: rx
D: A
T: What are discriminated unions, and how do you use them for UI state?
K: discriminated unions typescript, tagged union, loading success error state, exhaustive switch never, union types state
X: So a discriminated union is a union of object types that share a common literal property, the discriminant, which TypeScript uses to narrow the type.
X: The classic UI use is request state. Instead of separate isLoading, error and data fields, which allow impossible combinations, like loading true with data and an error at the same time, I define one type. Either status idle, or status loading, or status success with data as a Shipment array, or status error with an error message. Each state carries exactly the data it needs, nothing more.
X: When I check that status equals success, TypeScript narrows the type, so state.data is available and typed. In the error branch, state.error is available. In other branches, touching data is a compile error. Impossible states just become unrepresentable.
X: For exhaustiveness, in a switch over the status, the default case assigns the value to a variable of type never. If someone adds a new status, like cancelled, without handling it, the compiler errors in every switch that misses it.
X: The same pattern fits loads of domain concepts. Redux actions with a type property, form steps, permission results, or events like KitDispensed versus KitReturned, each with different fields.
X: For me, it's one of the most valuable TypeScript features for front-end correctness, because it moves bugs from runtime to compile time.
@p17-324
S: rx
D: A
T: What do the satisfies operator and as const do in TypeScript?
K: satisfies typescript, as const, const assertion, literal types typescript, satisfies vs type annotation
X: Okay, so as const is a const assertion. It tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest, most specific type and make everything read-only. Without it, an object with status pending gets inferred as status string. With as const, it's the literal pending, and arrays become read-only tuples. A common use is defining a list of values once, like statuses as pending, shipped, delivered, as const, and then deriving a union type from it with typeof statuses indexed by number. So the runtime array and the type stay in sync.
X: satisfies came in TypeScript 4.9. It checks that a value matches a type without changing the value's inferred type. With a normal type annotation, like config typed as a Record of string to Route, TypeScript checks the value but then forgets the specific keys. config.shipments isn't known, and any string key is allowed. With satisfies Record of string to Route instead, TypeScript validates every entry against Route, catching typos and missing properties, but still remembers the exact keys and literal values. So autocomplete and narrowing keep working.
X: And they combine nicely. as const satisfies some type gives you an immutable, precisely typed object that's also validated against a contract. Like a route table, a permission map, or a config object.
X: I use satisfies a lot for configuration objects, and as const for lists of literal values and lookup tables. Honestly they've cleaned up a lot of our typing.
@p17-325
S: rx
D: A
T: What are keyof, typeof, mapped types and conditional types in TypeScript?
K: keyof typeof, mapped types, conditional types, infer keyword, advanced typescript types, indexed access types
X: These are the building blocks of TypeScript's type-level programming, and actually the built-in utility types are made from them.
X: keyof T gives a union of T's property names. For Shipment, keyof Shipment is id or status or site. It's useful for type-safe functions, like a sortBy function whose key parameter has to be a real property of the item type.
X: typeof in a type position gets the type of a value, like typeof defaultConfig, so you derive types from constants instead of writing them twice. Put together, keyof typeof some object gives you the keys of an object value.
X: Indexed access types, like Shipment indexed by status, give the type of one property.
X: Mapped types build a new type by transforming each property of another. For each K in keyof T, map to some new type. That's how Partial and Readonly are built. You can also remap keys, like turning status into an onStatusChange handler.
X: Conditional types pick a type based on a condition, like if T extends string then A, otherwise B. With infer, they can pull out parts of types, like the element type of an array, or the resolved type of a promise. That's how Awaited and ReturnType work.
X: In everyday app code, I mostly use keyof, typeof and indexed access. Mapped and conditional types matter more when you're writing shared libraries, generic hooks, or typed API clients, where one generic definition gives precise types for lots of cases.
@p17-326
S: rx
D: A
T: What are type guards and assertion functions in TypeScript?
K: type guards, user defined type guard, is keyword typescript, assertion functions, asserts keyword, narrowing typescript
X: Okay, so type narrowing is how TypeScript refines a broad type to a more specific one inside a code block. The built-in checks narrow automatically. typeof x equals string, instanceof, the in operator, equality checks, and checking a discriminant property.
X: A user-defined type guard is a function whose return type is a type predicate, like value is Shipment. Inside, you write the runtime check, say it's an object with a numeric id and a string status. When the function returns true, TypeScript narrows the variable to Shipment in that branch. It's useful for unknown data. JSON from local storage, errors in catch blocks, which are unknown, or filtering arrays. items.filter with isShipment gives a Shipment array, and newer TypeScript versions can even infer simple predicates automatically.
X: An assertion function has a return type like asserts value is Shipment, or asserts condition. Instead of returning a boolean, it throws if the check fails, and after the call, TypeScript treats the value as narrowed for the rest of the scope. Handy for invariants, like an assertDefined on the current user at the start of a function.
X: The important caution, TypeScript trusts these functions completely. If your runtime check is wrong or incomplete, the types lie, and bugs show up later. So for complex shapes, honestly, I'd rather use a schema library like Zod, which generates both the check and the type from one definition.
@p17-327
S: rx
D: A
T: TypeScript enums vs union of string literals: which do you prefer?
K: enums vs union types typescript, string literal union, const enum, typescript enum pitfalls, enum alternative
X: Honestly, TypeScript enums, like an enum ShipmentStatus with Pending and Shipped, look familiar to C# developers, but they've got some quirks.
X: Numeric enums let you assign any number, and they have reverse mappings, so they're less type-safe than they look. Regular enums generate runtime JavaScript objects, so extra code. const enums get inlined, but they cause problems with isolated module compilation, which tools like Vite, esbuild and Babel use. And enums are a TypeScript-only construct. Node's native TypeScript type stripping, and the erasableSyntaxOnly option, don't support them, because they're not just types.
X: A union of string literals, like type ShipmentStatus equals Pending or Shipped or Delivered, has no runtime cost. It works directly with JSON from APIs, which are plain strings anyway. You get autocomplete and exhaustiveness checks. And it's just JavaScript once the types are erased.
X: When I also need the values at runtime, for a dropdown or validation, I define a const array or object with as const and derive the union type from it, so one definition does both jobs.
X: So for new code, I prefer string literal unions, or as const objects. Enums are fine where a codebase already uses them consistently, and string enums are way safer than numeric ones.
X: For API contracts generated from a .NET backend, I configure the generator to produce string unions, which matches our enums being serialised as strings.
@p17-328
S: rx
D: A
T: Which tsconfig options matter most for a React project?
K: tsconfig options, strict mode typescript, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, tsconfig react vite, moduleResolution bundler, typescript configuration
X: So the tsconfig controls how strict TypeScript is and how it understands the project. Honestly, a few options matter way more than the rest.
X: strict set to true, which turns on a group of checks, especially strictNullChecks, so null and undefined have to be handled explicitly, and noImplicitAny. It catches a huge class of bugs. For an existing JavaScript-heavy codebase, I'd turn it on gradually, but new projects start strict.
X: noUncheckedIndexedAccess, which makes array and record lookups include undefined in their type, because the item might not exist. It's stricter, but it catches real bugs with lookups by id or index.
X: exactOptionalPropertyTypes, which separates a missing property from one explicitly set to undefined. Useful for patch-style objects.
X: noUnusedLocals, noUnusedParameters and noFallthroughCasesInSwitch, for clean code, though linting covers some of this.
X: For a Vite React project, jsx set to react-jsx, the modern transform without importing React. module ESNext with moduleResolution bundler, which matches how Vite resolves imports. isolatedModules true, since Vite transpiles each file separately. noEmit true, because Vite does the building and TypeScript only type-checks. And types for vite/client, so import.meta.env is typed.
X: paths for import aliases, like at-sign pointing to src, which has to match the Vite config.
X: And I run tsc with noEmit in the pipeline, because Vite's dev server doesn't type-check at all. People forget that.
@p17-329
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you customise MUI with themes, and sx vs styled?
K: mui theme, material ui theming, sx prop vs styled, mui createtheme, design system mui, mui component overrides
X: See, MUI, Material UI, is customised mainly through the theme. You create a theme with createTheme and define the palette, primary and secondary colours, error and warning colours. Typography, like font family and sizes. Spacing. Breakpoints. Shape, like border radius. And component defaults and style overrides, like making all buttons non-uppercase, or giving every TextField a small size by default. The ThemeProvider at the root makes it available everywhere.
X: That's really the foundation of a consistent design system. Components use theme values, so changing a brand colour happens in one place. A company design system built on MUI usually ships as a theme package plus extra components.
X: For one-off styling, there are two main tools. The sx prop applies styles directly on a component, with access to theme values through shorthand, like p 2 for padding on the spacing scale, or color primary.main, and responsive values by breakpoint. Great for small layout tweaks. styled creates a reusable styled component, like a StatusBadge, with styles defined once, which is better for anything reused or complex.
X: Performance-wise, sx is fine for most cases. But in very large lists, a styled component or theme override avoids recalculating styles per item.
X: I avoid hard-coded colours and pixel values in components, everything stays tied to the theme.

@p17-330
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you handle large data grids in React with MUI or AG Grid?
K: mui datagrid, ag grid react, large table react, server side pagination grid, virtualized table, grid performance react
X: Actually large grids are really common in business apps, lists of kits, shipments, subjects. And performance and usability both matter.
X: The first decision is client-side or server-side data. For a few thousand rows, loading everything and letting the grid sort, filter and page in the browser is simple and fast. For tens of thousands or more, or data that changes often, I go server-side. The grid sends sort, filter and page parameters to the API, and the API returns one page with a total count. MUI's DataGrid supports this with paginationMode, sortingMode and filterMode set to server, and AG Grid has the server-side and infinite row models.
X: Virtualisation is essential. Both MUI DataGrid and AG Grid render only the visible rows and columns, so the DOM stays small even with thousands of rows loaded.
X: For React performance, keep the columns definition stable with useMemo, or outside the component. A new columns array on every render makes the grid recalculate, and I've seen that make a grid crawl. Memoise custom cell renderers. And avoid heavy components inside cells.
X: Usability-wise, column visibility and ordering saved per user, export to CSV or Excel, keyboard navigation, and accessible markup.
X: And licensing is part of it. MUI DataGrid's free version covers the basics, while advanced features like row grouping, tree data and Excel export are in the paid tiers, similar to AG Grid's enterprise edition. So the licence choice is part of the decision.
@p17-331
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you make a React application accessible?
K: accessibility react, a11y react, aria attributes, keyboard navigation, screen reader react, wcag
X: Okay, accessibility means people using keyboards, screen readers, magnification or other assistive tech can actually use the app. It's often a legal or contractual requirement too, usually targeting WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 level AA.
X: The basics come first. Use semantic HTML, button, nav, main, table, label, instead of clickable divs, because they come with keyboard support and meaning for screen readers. Every input has an associated label. Images have meaningful alt text, or empty alt if they're decorative. Headings follow a logical order.
X: Then keyboard support. Everything must work with the keyboard, with a visible focus indicator, a logical tab order, and no keyboard traps, except on purpose inside open modals.
X: Focus management in SPAs is the one people miss. When a modal opens, move focus into it and return it afterwards. After client-side navigation, move focus to the new page's heading, so screen reader users know the page changed.
X: ARIA, used carefully, for custom widgets. Roles, states like aria-expanded or aria-selected, and aria-live regions to announce dynamic updates like "Shipment saved" or validation errors. But the first rule of ARIA is prefer native elements where you can.
X: Enough colour contrast, and never colour alone to convey meaning, like statuses shown only as red or green.
X: Component libraries like MUI handle a lot of this. On top, I add eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, axe checks in tests, and manual keyboard and screen reader testing. That's how I'd approach it.
@p17-332
S: rx
D: A
T: How do nested routes and data loading work in React Router?
K: react router nested routes, outlet react router, react router loaders, createbrowserrouter, react router v6 v7, route layout
X: So React Router basically lets you define routes as a tree, where parent routes render shared layout and child routes render inside the parent through the Outlet component. Like a parent route for sites slash siteId renders the site header and tabs, and child routes render the inventory, shipments or users tab inside it. Index routes define what shows at the parent path itself, and layout routes without a path group routes that share a layout, like all the authenticated pages.
X: Hooks give you the routing info. useParams for path parameters. useSearchParams for query strings, which is a good place to keep filter state, so it's shareable and works with the back button. useNavigate for programmatic navigation, and useLocation.
X: Since version 6.4, with createBrowserRouter, routes can have loaders and actions. A loader fetches data before the route renders, and the component reads it with useLoaderData, so data loading starts in parallel with the code download, no waterfalls. Actions handle form submissions and mutations, and loaders revalidate automatically after. errorElement shows an error UI for failures in that branch, and lazy loads route code on demand. In version 7, these ideas merged with the Remix framework.
X: Honestly, many teams, ours included, still use simpler component-based routing, with data fetching through RTK Query or TanStack Query inside components, and that works fine too.
X: And route-level code splitting with lazy imports keeps the initial bundle small.
@p17-333
S: rx
D: A
T: Module Federation vs npm packages for micro-frontends: what are the trade-offs?
K: module federation, micro frontends react, npm packages micro frontend, runtime vs build time integration, shell app feature modules
X: Okay, so both let separate teams build features independently and combine them into one app, but they integrate at different times.
X: With npm packages, each feature module is built and published as a versioned package to a registry, and the shell installs specific versions and builds everything together. So it's build-time integration. It's simple, you get full type checking across packages, one optimised bundle with shared dependencies deduplicated, and a clear, tested combination of versions in each shell release. That last part is really important for validated releases. The downside is that releasing a feature change means publishing a new package version and then rebuilding and redeploying the shell.
X: With Module Federation, from webpack 5 and now available for Vite and Rspack, each feature is deployed separately as a remote, and the shell loads it at runtime from a URL. Teams can deploy their part without redeploying the shell, and shared libraries like React get loaded once and shared at runtime. But you can get runtime failures if shared dependency versions are incompatible, setup is more complex, type sharing needs extra tooling, and the exact combination in production changes whenever any team deploys. That makes testing and validation a lot harder.
X: In my project, our React shell uses the npm package approach. Feature modules like drug accountability and material block are separate repos published to the Azure DevOps feed, which fits our regulated release process, where every production combination has to be validated.
@p17-334
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you set up a monorepo for front-end packages?
K: monorepo frontend, npm workspaces, nx turborepo, pnpm workspaces, monorepo vs polyrepo, shared packages monorepo
X: Basically a monorepo keeps several related projects, like a shell app, feature packages and a shared component library, in one repository, with tooling that understands how they relate.
X: The basic building block is workspaces, from npm, pnpm or Yarn. The root package.json lists the workspace folders, dependencies get installed once at the root, and local packages are linked to each other automatically. So the shell can use the latest local version of a feature package without publishing it. pnpm is popular because it's fast and strict about dependencies.
X: On top of that, build orchestrators like Turborepo or Nx add a lot. Running build, test and lint across packages in the right dependency order. Caching, so unchanged packages aren't rebuilt or retested, locally and in CI with remote caching. And affected detection, so the pipeline only builds and tests the packages a commit changed, plus their dependants. Nx also adds generators, dependency graphs and boundary rules that stop forbidden imports.
X: What you gain is atomic changes across packages in one pull request, consistent tooling and versions, easier refactoring, and simpler code sharing.
X: What it costs is a growing repo, CI that needs smart caching to stay fast, and access control that's per repo, so if teams need strict separation, separate repos are easier.
X: Actually our feature modules are separate repositories published as npm packages, so that's the polyrepo approach. A monorepo would be a reasonable alternative for tighter integration.
@p17-335
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you publish a React component library without bundling two copies of React?
K: publish react library, peerdependencies react, invalid hook call two reacts, vite library mode, npm package react components
X: See, when you build a reusable React package, like a feature module or a component library, the most important rule is that React itself must not be bundled into the package, or installed as its own dependency.
X: If the package lists react as a normal dependency, or bundles it, the consuming app can end up with two copies of React. Then hooks fail with the "Invalid hook call" error, because the package's components use a different React instance than the app's renderer. And context providers from the app aren't visible inside the package. Honestly, that error confuses everyone the first time.
X: So in package.json, react and react-dom go in peerDependencies, with a compatible version range, like React 17 or 18, and in devDependencies for local development and tests. Same for other libraries that must be singletons, MUI, Emotion, React Router, Redux, because their contexts have to be shared.
X: In the build, with Vite's library mode or tsup, I mark these as external, so they come from the host app at runtime instead of being bundled. The output is ES modules with TypeScript declaration files, and the package.json exports field points to them. sideEffects false allows tree shaking.
X: For local testing with the shell, npm link can cause duplicate React copies too, so I prefer a workspace setup, or tools like yalc.
X: Versioning follows semver with a changelog, because the shell pins versions. That's how our feature packages work with the React shell through the Azure DevOps feed.

T: How do you implement feature flags in a React application?
K: feature flags react, feature toggle frontend, launchdarkly, gradual rollout ui, flag based rendering
X: Okay, so feature flags let you turn features on or off without deploying new code. So incomplete work can be merged and deployed safely, features can roll out gradually to some users or customers, and if something's causing trouble, you switch it off quickly.
X: In a React app, flags are usually evaluated per user or tenant. @p17-338
S: rx
D: A
T: What are Core Web Vitals, and how do you improve them in a React app?
K: core web vitals, lcp inp cls, largest contentful paint, interaction to next paint, cumulative layout shift, page speed react
X: Actually Core Web Vitals are Google's main user-experience metrics, measured from real users.
X: Largest Contentful Paint measures loading, when the largest visible element, like a main image or text block, gets rendered. Good is under 2.5 seconds. Interaction to Next Paint, which replaced First Input Delay in 2024, measures responsiveness, how quickly the page visibly responds to clicks, taps and key presses through the whole visit. Good is under 200 milliseconds. Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability, how much content jumps around unexpectedly. Good is under 0.1.
X: For a React single-page app, improving LCP means a smaller initial bundle through code splitting and lazy routes, compressing and caching assets, serving from a CDN, preloading critical fonts and images, and showing meaningful content quickly. Not a blank page waiting on several API calls one after another.
X: Improving INP means keeping the main thread free. Avoid long JavaScript tasks, memoise expensive renders, virtualise big lists, use transitions for non-urgent updates, debounce expensive handlers, and move heavy computation to web workers.
X: Improving CLS means reserving space for images, ads and content that loads later, with width and height or skeleton placeholders of the right size, and not inserting banners above existing content. That one's annoying for users.
X: I measure with Lighthouse and tools like GTmetrix in the lab, and with the web-vitals library sending real-user data to monitoring. Lab numbers alone can fool you, honestly.
@p17-339
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you write a useDebounce hook, and when do you debounce?
K: usedebounce hook, debounce react, debounce search input react, throttle vs debounce, custom hook debounce
X: So debouncing delays an action until some time has passed with no new events. You use it for search inputs, so the API gets called after the user stops typing, for auto-saving forms, and for resize handlers. Throttling is different, it runs the action at most once per time interval, which suits scroll or mousemove handlers.
X: A simple useDebounce hook debounces a value. It takes the value and a delay, keeps a debounced copy in state, and in a useEffect sets a timeout to update that copy after the delay. The effect's cleanup clears the timeout, so if the value changes again before the delay's up, the previous timer is cancelled and a new one starts. The hook returns the debounced value.
X: In a search component, the input updates its own state immediately, so typing stays snappy, and the debounced value, maybe 300 milliseconds behind, is what drives the API query. With TanStack Query or RTK Query, putting the debounced value in the query key means only settled terms trigger requests, and stale responses are handled by the library.
X: Sometimes you need a debounced callback instead of a debounced value, like for auto-save. Then I keep the latest callback in a ref, so the debounced function doesn't capture stale state, and create the debounced function once, cancelling it on unmount. Honestly, libraries like use-debounce give you well-tested versions of both, so I usually just use that.

S: rx
D: A
T: How do you implement infinite scrolling with IntersectionObserver?
K: infinite scroll react, intersectionobserver, load more on scroll, useinfinitequery, sentinel element scroll
X: Okay, infinite scrolling loads the next page of data automatically when the user scrolls near the bottom of a list.
X: The modern way to detect that is IntersectionObserver. It tells you when an element enters the viewport, without listening to scroll events, which fire constantly and hurt performance. You place an empty sentinel element after the last item. An observer watches it, with a rootMargin of say 200 pixels, so loading starts a bit before the user actually hits the end. When the sentinel becomes visible, and there's a next page, and no request is already running, you fetch the next page.
X: In React, I attach the observer to the sentinel with a ref, in a useEffect or a ref callback, and disconnect it in the cleanup. Libraries like react-intersection-observer wrap this in a useInView hook.
X: For the data, TanStack Query's useInfiniteQuery fits perfectly. It fetches pages with a cursor, gives you fetchNextPage, hasNextPage and isFetchingNextPage, and keeps the pages cached. The API should use cursor-based pagination, so items don't shift or repeat as new data comes in.
X: Once there are hundreds of loaded items, I add virtualisation so the DOM stays small.
X: And I think about usability. Infinite scroll makes it hard to reach a footer or get back to a specific position. For business data, lists users work through and come back to, classic pagination or a Load more button is often better. That's what I'd usually push for.
@p17-341
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you implement optimistic updates in React?
K: optimistic updates react, optimistic ui, rollback on error, react query optimistic, useoptimistic
X: See, an optimistic update shows the result of an action immediately, before the server confirms it, and rolls back if the request fails. It makes the app feel instant, which is great for frequent, low-risk actions. Marking a notification as read, toggling a favourite, reordering items.
X: With TanStack Query, I use the mutation's lifecycle callbacks. In onMutate, cancel any in-flight queries for that data so they don't overwrite the optimistic change, save a snapshot of the current cached data, and update the cache with the expected new state. In onError, restore the snapshot and show an error message. In onSettled, invalidate the query, so the data gets re-fetched from the server and is definitely correct. RTK Query has the same pattern with onQueryStarted, updateQueryData and an undo patch.
X: React 19's useOptimistic hook gives a simpler version for component state during an action.
X: A few cautions though. I don't use optimistic updates for important or irreversible operations. Dispensing a kit, randomising a subject, financial transactions. There the user has to see the real, confirmed result, and the server might reject it based on rules the client doesn't even know about. In our domain, that's a hard rule for me. Concurrent changes and server-generated values, like ids and timestamps, need handling. And failures have to be very visible, because the user may have moved on thinking it worked.

T: How would you upgrade a React 17 application to React 18 or 19?
K: upgrade react 17 to 18, react 19 upgrade, createroot migration, react upgrade breaking changes, react version upgrade plan
X: I'd upgrade in steps, 17 to 18 first, then 18 to 19, because 18.3 adds deprecation warnings that prepare you for 19.
X: For React 18, update react and react-dom, and replace ReactDOM.render with createRoot. That turns on concurrent features and automatic batching. Code that depended on synchronous, unbatched updates in async callbacks might behave differently, so I'd test flows with timeouts and promises. In StrictMode, effects run twice in development, which exposes missing cleanups that need fixing. Types changed too. React.FC doesn't include children implicitly anymore, so components that take children have to declare them.
