X: For React 19, run the official codemods, which handle a lot. Removed APIs include propTypes and defaultProps on function components, string refs, legacy context and ReactDOM.render. ref becomes a normal prop, so forwardRef can go over time. Error handling changed slightly.
X: Testing is critical. Unit tests, the end-to-end suite, and manual checks of key screens. In a regulated product, the upgrade is a validated change with regression testing.
X: Our shell is on React 17, so for us this is a real roadmap item.
@p17-343
S: rx
D: A
T: What is useSyncExternalStore, and when do you need it?
K: usesyncexternalstore, external store react, subscribe to store react, tearing concurrent rendering, browser api hook
X: So useSyncExternalStore is a React 18 hook for subscribing to data that lives outside React. Like a state library's store, browser APIs, or any custom event source, in a way that's safe with concurrent rendering.
X: You give it a subscribe function, which registers a callback and returns an unsubscribe function, a getSnapshot function that returns the current value, and optionally getServerSnapshot for server rendering. React re-renders the component when the snapshot changes.
X: Why does it exist? Tearing. With concurrent rendering, React can pause rendering in the middle and continue later. If an external store changes during that pause, different components in the same render could read different versions of the data, and you'd show an inconsistent UI. useSyncExternalStore guarantees a consistent snapshot for the whole render.
X: Library authors are the main users. Redux's useSelector, Zustand and others use it internally. In app code, I use it for browser state. Like a useOnlineStatus hook that subscribes to the online and offline events and reads navigator.onLine. Or a hook that reads from localStorage and listens for storage events from other tabs. Or media queries.
X: One important rule, getSnapshot has to return the same value, by reference, if nothing changed. Returning a new object every time causes an infinite re-render loop. I learned that one the hard way, so now I return primitives or cached objects.
@p17-344
S: rx
D: A
T: How do you update nested state immutably, and how does Immer help?
K: immutable state update react, nested state update, spread operator nested, immer, produce immer, mutating state react bug
X: Okay, React and Redux detect changes by comparing references. If you mutate an object or array in place, like pushing to an array in state, or setting user.address.city directly, the reference doesn't change. So React may not re-render, memoised components and selectors miss the change, and you get bugs that are hard to trace.
X: So updates have to create new objects for every level that changes. For nested state, that means spreading at each level. A new state object, with a new user object, with a new address object, with the new city. For arrays, use map to replace an item, filter to remove, and spread or concat to add, instead of push, splice or assigning by index. Newer array methods like toSorted and with return copies too.
X: Honestly, deep nesting gets verbose and error-prone, and that's a hint you should flatten or normalise the state.
X: Immer fixes the verbosity. Its produce function gives you a draft copy you can "mutate" with normal assignment and push, and Immer records the changes and produces a new immutable object, structurally sharing the unchanged parts. Redux Toolkit uses Immer inside createSlice reducers, which is why reducers there can be written in mutating style. use-immer gives a useImmer hook for component state.
X: The one rule to remember with Immer in Redux Toolkit is either mutate the draft or return a new value. Not both.
@p17-345
S: nodex
D: A
T: process.nextTick vs setImmediate vs setTimeout: in what order do they run?
K: nexttick vs setimmediate, microtask vs macrotask, event loop phases node, settimeout 0, promise then order
X: So they all schedule code to run later, but they go into different queues.
X: Microtasks run as soon as the current operation finishes, before the event loop moves on. In Node, process.nextTick callbacks run first, then promise callbacks, like then handlers and the continuation after await. Both queues get drained completely before anything else happens.
X: Macrotasks run in the event loop's phases. setTimeout and setInterval callbacks run in the timers phase, once their delay has passed. setTimeout of zero actually means at least about one millisecond. setImmediate callbacks run in the check phase, right after the poll phase, where I/O callbacks are processed.
X: So within the same synchronous block, nextTick runs first, then promises, then the timers and immediates. Between setTimeout zero and setImmediate, the order from the main module isn't guaranteed, because it depends on how fast the loop starts. But inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before setTimeout zero, since the check phase comes right after poll. That's a classic interview trick, actually.
X: In browsers there's no nextTick or setImmediate. Promise microtasks run before the next macrotask, like a timer or a rendering step.
X: The practical lesson is, recursively scheduling nextTick or promise callbacks can starve the event loop, because I/O never gets a turn. When I need to yield so I/O can run, I use setImmediate.
@p17-346
S: nodex
D: A
T: Worker threads vs child processes vs cluster in Node.js: when do you use each?
K: worker threads, child process node, cluster module, cpu intensive node, multi core node, pm2 cluster
X: See, Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread, so CPU-heavy work blocks everything else, and one process uses only one CPU core for JavaScript. These three deal with that in different ways.
X: Worker threads run JavaScript in separate threads inside the same process, each with its own event loop and memory. They talk through message passing, and can share memory with SharedArrayBuffer. They're for CPU-intensive tasks, parsing a large file, image processing, encryption, complex calculations, so the main thread stays responsive. A pool of workers, with a library like Piscina, saves the cost of starting threads over and over.
X: Child processes start separate OS processes with spawn, exec or fork. They're for running external programs, like a command-line tool or a Python script, or isolating risky work, since a crash doesn't take down the parent. More overhead than threads though.
X: The cluster module starts several copies of the whole Node server, usually one per CPU core, sharing the same port, with the primary process distributing connections. It's for using all cores to handle more HTTP requests. PM2 does this for you.
X: In containers though, I usually prefer one Node process per container and scaling the number of containers with the orchestrator, like ECS or Kubernetes. That's simpler, and you get better health checks and restarts. Then workers are only for specific CPU-heavy tasks. That's how I'd set it up.
@p17-347
S: nodex
D: A
T: What are streams in Node.js, and how does backpressure work with pipeline?
K: node streams, readable writable transform, backpressure node, stream pipeline, process large file node
X: Basically streams process data piece by piece, in chunks, instead of loading it all into memory. You've got four types. Readable, like reading a file or an HTTP request. Writable, like writing a file or an HTTP response. Duplex, both, like a TCP socket. And Transform, a duplex that modifies data passing through, like gzip compression or CSV parsing.
X: With streams, you can process a 5 GB file with a few megabytes of memory, and start sending output before the input is fully read.
X: Backpressure is what keeps memory under control when the writer is slower than the reader. A writable stream's write method returns false when its internal buffer is full. A well-behaved producer then pauses until the drain event says it can carry on. If code ignores that and keeps writing, data piles up in memory and the process can crash.
X: The pipe method handles backpressure automatically, but it was bad with errors. An error in one stream didn't destroy the others, so you got leaks. So the recommended way is stream.pipeline, or the promise version from stream/promises. It connects the streams, handles backpressure, forwards errors, and cleans up every stream when any of them fails or finishes.
X: Readable streams are also async iterable, so for await over a stream is a clean way to process chunks one by one, with backpressure handled naturally.
X: [I used a pipeline of a file read stream, a CSV parser and a batching transform to load large extract files without memory spikes.]
@p17-348
S: nodex
D: A
T: What is a Buffer in Node.js?
K: buffer node, binary data node, buffer vs string, buffer encoding, buffer.from, uint8array
X: So a Buffer represents raw binary data in Node.js, a fixed-size sequence of bytes. JavaScript strings are text, made of UTF-16 characters, so they're not suitable for binary stuff like files, images, network packets, encrypted or compressed data. Buffers fill that gap. These days Buffer is a subclass of Uint8Array, so it works with the standard typed array APIs too.
X: You create buffers with Buffer.from, from a string with an encoding, an array, or another buffer, and Buffer.alloc for a zero-filled buffer of a given size. Going back uses toString with an encoding, like utf8, base64 or hex. That's how I'd encode binary data as Base64 for JSON, or compute a hex digest.
X: A few things matter here. Encoding matters a lot. Reading UTF-8 bytes as Latin-1 garbles text, and cutting a buffer in the middle of a multi-byte character breaks it, which is why streams use a StringDecoder when turning chunks into text. Buffer.allocUnsafe is faster because it doesn't zero the memory, but it might contain old data, which can leak sensitive information if you don't fully overwrite it. So I only use it when I fill it immediately. Comparing buffers with secrets, like HMAC signatures, should use crypto.timingSafeEqual, not a normal equality check. And large buffers count against the process's memory, so for big data, streams beat reading whole files into buffers.
@p17-349
S: nodex
D: A
T: CommonJS vs ES modules in Node.js: what are the differences?
K: commonjs vs esm, require vs import, es modules node, type module package.json, cjs esm interop, dual package
X: Okay, so CommonJS is Node's original module system. require to import, module.exports to export. It loads modules synchronously at runtime, and you can call require anywhere, even conditionally.
X: ES modules are the JavaScript standard, import and export statements, used in browsers and modern tooling. Imports are static and analysed before the code runs, which enables tree shaking in bundlers and top-level await. Loading is asynchronous.
X: In Node, a file is treated as an ES module if it has the .mjs extension, or if the nearest package.json has type set to module and the file is .js. Otherwise .js is CommonJS, and .cjs is always CommonJS.
X: The differences that actually bite you. In ESM, file imports need the extension, like importing from utils.js with the .js. dirname and filename globals don't exist, so you use import.meta.dirname or import.meta.url. JSON imports need an import attribute. ESM can import CommonJS packages, though named exports aren't always detected. CommonJS historically couldn't require ES modules at all, only use dynamic import, but since Node 22, requiring synchronous ES modules works, which honestly removed a lot of pain.
X: For TypeScript projects, the module and moduleResolution settings, like NodeNext, have to match whichever system you pick.
X: New projects should go with ES modules. Libraries often publish both formats, using the exports field in package.json.
@p17-350
S: nodex
D: A
T: What are the important fields in package.json?
K: package.json fields, exports field, engines field, scripts npm, dependencies vs devdependencies vs peerdependencies, main module types
X: So package.json describes a Node project or package, and a handful of fields really matter.
X: name and version identify the package, and version follows semantic versioning when you publish.
X: dependencies are packages needed at runtime. devDependencies are only for development and building, like TypeScript, test frameworks and linters, and that matters because production installs can skip them. peerDependencies declare packages the consumer has to provide, like React for a component library, so only one copy exists. optionalDependencies can fail to install without failing the whole install.
X: scripts define commands, build, test, lint, start, which you run with npm run. Pre and post hooks run automatically, so I'm careful with install scripts, because they run for dependencies too and they're a supply-chain risk.
X: type set to module makes .js files ES modules.
X: exports is the modern way to define a package's public entry points, with conditions for import versus require, types, and subpaths. It also hides internal files, anything not listed can't be imported, which is great for library authors. main and module are the older entry fields.
X: types points to the TypeScript declarations. engines declares supported Node versions, and with engine-strict, npm can enforce it. files lists what gets published, and private true stops you accidentally publishing an application.
X: And along with package.json, the lockfile has to be committed, so installs are reproducible. That one's non-negotiable for me.
@p17-351
S: nodex
D: A
T: npm install vs npm ci, and how do semantic version ranges work?
K: npm ci vs npm install, caret vs tilde version, semver ranges, package-lock.json, reproducible builds node
X: See, npm install installs dependencies from package.json, and it may update package-lock.json if versions within the allowed ranges changed, or if package.json changed. It's what developers use when adding or updating packages.
X: npm ci is for CI and production builds. It deletes node_modules, installs exactly the versions in package-lock.json, and fails if package.json and the lockfile don't match. It never touches the lockfile. So builds are reproducible, and usually faster too. In pipelines I always use npm ci, often with the npm cache directory cached.
X: Version ranges follow semantic versioning, major dot minor dot patch. A caret, like caret 4.2.1, allows anything below the next major. So 4.3.0 is fine, 5.0.0 isn't. It assumes minor and patch releases are backward compatible. For 0.x versions, caret is stricter, because 0.x minors can break things. A tilde, like tilde 4.2.1, allows only patch updates, 4.2.9 but not 4.3.0. And an exact version pins it precisely.
X: The thing people miss is the lockfile is what really decides what gets installed. The ranges only decide what updates are allowed when someone runs npm update or regenerates the lockfile.
X: In practice, I commit the lockfile, let Dependabot or Renovate propose updates as pull requests with the test suite running, and use exact versions for packages known to break in minor releases. pnpm and Yarn have equivalents, like pnpm install with frozen-lockfile.
@p17-352
S: nodex
D: A
T: Express vs Fastify vs NestJS: how do you choose?
K: express vs fastify vs nestjs, node framework comparison, nestjs, fastify performance, which node framework
X: Okay, Express is the classic, minimal web framework for Node. Simple, extremely well known, huge middleware ecosystem. But it's unopinionated, so big projects need their own structure, and historically it had weak async error handling and limited TypeScript support. Express 5, which came out in late 2024, finally handles rejected promises in route handlers properly.
X: Fastify is a performance-focused framework with a similar feel. It's noticeably faster than Express, thanks to optimised routing and schema-based JSON serialisation. It has built-in JSON Schema validation for requests and responses, a structured plugin system with encapsulation, first-class async support, built-in logging with Pino, and good TypeScript support.
X: NestJS is a full application framework built on top of Express or Fastify. It brings structure inspired by Angular and ASP.NET Core. Modules, controllers, providers, dependency injection with decorators, guards, interceptors, pipes for validation, plus integrations for GraphQL, microservices, queues and OpenAPI. For someone coming from .NET or Angular, like me, it feels very familiar.
X: How I'd choose, a small focused service or a simple BFF, Fastify, or Express if the team already knows it well. A bigger application with many developers and a complex domain, NestJS, because the enforced structure and DI keep it maintainable. And for performance-critical endpoints, Fastify, maybe as NestJS's underlying adapter. So it really depends on the size and the team.
@p17-353
S: nodex
D: A
T: How does dependency injection work in NestJS?
K: nestjs dependency injection, nestjs modules providers, injectable nestjs, nestjs vs asp.net core di, provider scopes nestjs
X: NestJS has a dependency injection container that's very similar to ASP.NET Core's and Angular's, so honestly it felt natural to me.
X: A class marked with the Injectable decorator is a provider. You register providers in a module's providers array and inject them through constructor parameters, and Nest resolves them using TypeScript metadata about the parameter types. Controllers, guards, interceptors and pipes all get their dependencies this way.
X: Modules organise the app into features. Each module declares its providers and controllers, exports the providers other modules may use, and imports the modules it depends on. A provider is private to its module unless exported, which keeps features encapsulated. Global modules, or dynamic modules with forRoot and forFeature, are for shared infrastructure, like configuration or database connections.
X: Custom providers cover more cases. useValue for constants or mocks, useClass to swap implementations, useFactory for values that need logic or async setup, like creating a database client. And injection tokens, strings or symbols, for things that aren't classes, since TypeScript interfaces don't exist at runtime.
X: Scopes are like .NET lifetimes. Default is singleton, shared across the app. REQUEST scope creates a new instance per request. TRANSIENT gives each consumer its own instance. Request scope bubbles up the dependency chain and costs performance, so I only use it when I really need it.
X: Testing is easy too. The testing module lets you override providers with mocks.
@p17-354
S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you handle unhandled promise rejections and graceful shutdown in Node.js?
K: unhandled rejection node, uncaughtexception, graceful shutdown node, sigterm node, process exit node
X: Actually since Node 15, an unhandled promise rejection crashes the process by default, just like an uncaught exception. And that's on purpose. Carrying on after an unexpected error can leave the app in an inconsistent state.
X: I handle errors where they happen, try-catch around awaits, and catch on promises that aren't awaited. As a safety net, I register process.on for unhandledRejection and uncaughtException to log the error with full details. But after an uncaught exception, the process state is unknown. So I log, exit with a non-zero code, and let the orchestrator, ECS, Kubernetes or PM2, restart a fresh instance. I don't try to keep running.
X: Graceful shutdown is about planned stops, like deployments or scale-in. The orchestrator sends SIGTERM, and after a grace period, SIGKILL. On SIGTERM, the app should stop accepting new connections with server.close, fail its readiness check so the load balancer stops sending traffic, let in-flight requests finish, stop consuming new messages from queues and finish or release the current ones, close database pools and other connections, and then exit. A timeout forces the exit if something hangs.
X: One thing people miss in Docker, the Node process has to actually receive the signals. If it's started through npm start or a shell script, signals might not reach it. So I run node directly as the main process, or use an init like tini, or the init flag.
@p17-355
S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you find a memory leak in a Node.js application?
K: node memory leak, heap snapshot node, inspect node memory, heap out of memory, chrome devtools node memory
X: So the symptom is memory growing steadily over time, until the process crashes with "JavaScript heap out of memory", or the container gets killed for going over its memory limit.
X: The first thing I do is confirm it's actually a leak, and not just a high but stable working set. Watching process.memoryUsage, especially heapUsed, over hours shows whether memory comes back to a baseline after garbage collection or keeps climbing.
X: To find the cause, I take heap snapshots. Run Node with inspect and connect Chrome DevTools, or use the inspector API, or start with the heapsnapshot-signal flag, so sending a signal writes a snapshot, which is handy in a container. I take one snapshot after warm-up, run some load, take another, and compare. The comparison view shows which object types grew, and the retainers path shows what's keeping them alive.
X: Common causes in Node, honestly I've seen most of these. Global or module-level caches, like a plain object or Map used as a cache with no size limit or expiry. Event listeners added repeatedly and never removed, often with the MaxListenersExceededWarning as a hint. Closures capturing big objects, held by long-lived timers or callbacks. Unbounded arrays, like collecting metrics or logs in memory. And unresolved promises piling up.
X: Fixes are usually bounded caches, like lru-cache, removing listeners, and clearing timers. The max-old-space-size flag only delays the crash, though you should set it to suit the container's memory.
@p17-356
S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you profile CPU usage in a Node.js service?
K: node cpu profiling, node --prof, clinic.js, flame graph node, event loop lag, blocked event loop
X: See, high CPU in Node often shows up as slow responses for everyone, because one busy main thread delays every request. So the first thing I measure is event loop lag, how long callbacks wait to run, using perf_hooks' monitorEventLoopDelay or metrics from APM tools. High lag means something's blocking the loop.
X: To find what, I take a CPU profile. You can run with inspect and record a profile in Chrome DevTools. Or use the cpu-prof flag, which writes a profile file when the process exits. Or Clinic.js, which runs the app under load and gives you a flame graph plus a diagnosis of whether the issue is CPU, I/O or the event loop. Linux perf with perf-basic-prof works for system-level profiling, and APM tools like Datadog or New Relic offer continuous profiling in production.
X: In a flame graph, wide bars are functions eating lots of CPU time. What I usually find is synchronous functions like readFileSync or crypto's sync methods in request paths. JSON.parse and JSON.stringify on huge payloads. Expensive regular expressions, sometimes even vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. Heavy loops over big arrays. And too much synchronous logging.
X: Fixes include switching to async APIs, streaming large payloads, caching results, moving CPU-heavy work to worker threads or another service, and simplifying regexes. Then I profile again to confirm it actually helped.

T: How do you manage and validate configuration in a Node.js service?
K: node configuration, dotenv, validate env variables, zod env, process.env, config management node
X: Okay, so configuration comes from environment variables, the twelve-factor way. The same build runs everywhere, with different environment variables set by the platform, like ECS task definitions or Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets.
X: For local development, a .env file loaded with dotenv, or Node's built-in env-file flag since Node 20, provides values. The .env file is in .gitignore, and a .env.example with dummy values documents what's needed.
X: The important part, honestly, is validating configuration at startup. process.env values are all strings or undefined, so a typo or a missing variable otherwise causes some confusing failure much later. What you get is a typed config object that the rest of the app imports, instead of reading process.env all over the code.
X: Secrets, like database passwords and API keys, come from a secret store. Either injected as environment variables by the platform, or fetched at startup from AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store. And they're never logged.
X: In NestJS, the ConfigModule supports the same validation approach.

T: How do you do structured logging in Node.js?
K: node logging, pino, winston, structured logging node, json logs node, log correlation id node
X: Honestly, I always use structured logging. Each log entry is a JSON object with fields, not just a text line, so logs can be searched and filtered in a central system, by request id, user id, error type, whatever.
X: Pino is my preferred library, because it's very fast and does JSON by default. Logging is a hot path, and slow logging blocks the event loop. Winston is another popular option, more flexible but slower. Redact sensitive fields, which Pino supports with paths like headers.authorization. Don't log whole request bodies. And write to standard output and let the platform collect logs, instead of writing files inside containers.
X: In development, pino-pretty makes the JSON readable for humans.

T: How do you validate request input in a Node.js API?
K: node request validation, zod express, joi validation, class-validator nestjs, json schema validation fastify, validate body node
X: So every request body, query string and path parameter is untrusted input, so I validate it at the edge, before it ever reaches business logic.
X: How depends on the framework. With Express, I use a schema library like Zod or Joi, and a small middleware that validates req.body, req.query and req.params against the route's schema. If validation fails, it responds with 400 and a structured list of errors. If it passes, it replaces the raw input with the parsed, typed values, so defaults and type coercion get applied. X: Whatever the tool, I validate types, required fields, lengths, ranges, formats and allowed values, limit body size, and reject unknown fields for sensitive endpoints. Business-rule validation, like whether a site is active, happens later in the service layer. That's how I keep the two separate.

T: Prisma vs TypeORM vs Knex vs Drizzle: how do you choose a data access library in Node?
K: prisma vs typeorm, knex query builder, drizzle orm, node orm comparison, database access node typescript
X: Okay, so these are the main options for database access in Node with TypeScript, just at different levels of abstraction.
X: Prisma defines the data model in its own schema file, generates a fully typed client, and handles migrations. Queries are very type-safe and the autocomplete is excellent. It's productive and popular. The downsides are its own schema language, less control over the generated SQL, and some complex queries needing raw SQL anyway.
X: TypeORM is a classic ORM with decorators on entity classes, kind of like Entity Framework or Hibernate. It supports Active Record and Data Mapper patterns, relations and migrations. X: Drizzle is a newer, lightweight, TypeScript-first ORM. Schema defined in TypeScript, queries that look like SQL but are fully typed, fast, and it works nicely in serverless environments.
X: How I'd pick, Prisma or Drizzle for new TypeScript services. Drizzle when I want SQL-like control and a small footprint. Plain SQL with a driver like pg for really simple services or heavy reporting.
X: Whatever I pick, it's parameterised queries, connection pooling, and migrations run in the pipeline.

T: How should you run a Node.js app in Docker?
K: node docker best practices, node dockerfile, node user docker, npm ci docker, multi stage node docker, node pid 1
X: Honestly, for Node containers I always follow a few things, almost like a checklist.
X: Use an official slim base image with a specific Node LTS version, like node 22 slim or Alpine, pinned. Never latest.
X: Use a multi-stage build. The build stage installs all dependencies with npm ci and compiles TypeScript. The final stage copies only the compiled output and production dependencies, installed with npm ci omitting dev, so dev tools and source files don't end up in the image.
X: Order the Dockerfile for caching. Copy package.json and the lockfile first, install dependencies, then copy the source. That way code changes don't reinstall everything.

X: Set memory limits consistently. Node's heap limit should fit inside the container's memory limit, using max-old-space-size if needed.
X: Add a health check endpoint for the orchestrator, and log to standard output.
X: And on top of all that, scan the image for vulnerabilities in the pipeline. So that's my usual setup.

S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you run TypeScript in Node.js: tsc, tsx, or native type stripping?
K: run typescript node, ts-node vs tsx, node type stripping, tsc build node, typescript node 22 23
X: So basically you've got a few ways now, and they fit different stages.
X: Compiling with tsc is the traditional one. TypeScript compiles .ts files to JavaScript in a dist folder, and Node runs the JavaScript. It's the reliable production approach, and tsc also does full type checking, which the runtime tools skip.
X: Running directly in development with a loader is the next one. ts-node was the original tool, but it's slower and had ES module issues. tsx, which uses esbuild, is popular now. tsx watch on your server file runs TypeScript directly, very fast, with reload on changes. It strips types without checking them, so I run tsc with noEmit separately, in the editor or the pipeline.
X: Then native type stripping. Since Node 22.6 behind a flag, and on by default from Node 23.6 and later 22.x versions, Node can run .ts files directly by removing type annotations. It only supports erasable syntax, meaning types you can simply delete. Features that generate code, like enums, namespaces, and parameter properties in constructors, aren't supported unless you use the transform option, and TypeScript added the erasableSyntaxOnly setting to flag them. It doesn't read tsconfig paths and it doesn't type-check.
X: Bundlers like esbuild or tsup can also produce a single optimised JavaScript file, which is great for Lambda functions.
X: My setup is tsx or native stripping for development, tsc type checking in CI, and compiled JavaScript or a bundle in production images.

T: What is AsyncLocalStorage in Node.js?
K: asynclocalstorage, async context node, request context node, correlation id node, cls hooked
X: Okay, so AsyncLocalStorage, from the async_hooks module, lets you store data that's available throughout an async call chain, without passing it explicitly through every function. It's similar to AsyncLocal in .NET, or thread-local storage, but it follows async operations instead of threads.
X: You create one AsyncLocalStorage instance. At the start of each request, a middleware calls run with a context object, like the request id, the user id and a request-scoped logger, and the rest of the request handling runs inside that callback. Then anywhere deeper in the code, services, repositories, the logger, getStore returns the context for the current request. Even after lots of awaits, timers and promise chains. And concurrent requests each see their own context.
X: Where I use it, adding the correlation or trace id to every log line automatically. Tracking the current user or tenant for auditing or multi-tenant data access. And request-scoped caching. OpenTelemetry's Node SDK actually uses it to track the active span, which is how traces propagate automatically.
X: A few cautions. Context can get lost with some older callback-based libraries or custom thenables, though that's rare now. It adds a small performance cost. And it's easy to overuse. For core business data, explicit parameters are clearer, so I keep it for cross-cutting things like logging and tracing.
X: Node 24 improved its implementation and performance too.
@p17-364
S: nodex
D: A
T: Why does Node warn about MaxListenersExceeded, and how do EventEmitters leak?
K: eventemitter memory leak, maxlistenersexceededwarning, remove event listener node, eventemitter node, once listener
X: See, EventEmitter is Node's built-in publish-subscribe mechanism. Lots of core objects, streams, servers, sockets, are emitters, and code subscribes with on and unsubscribes with off or removeListener.
X: By default, an emitter warns when more than 10 listeners get added for the same event. "MaxListenersExceededWarning, possible EventEmitter memory leak detected." It's a heuristic, not an error, but honestly it usually points to a real bug. Code that adds a listener repeatedly, like on every request or every retry, without removing it. Each listener stays referenced by the emitter, along with everything its closure captured, so memory grows. And the handler runs many times per event, so you get duplicate work.
X: Typical examples I've seen. Adding an error or close listener to a long-lived shared connection inside a request handler. Subscribing to process events in a function that gets called again and again. Or a reconnection loop that re-registers handlers every time.
X: The fixes, register listeners once at setup time, not per operation. Use once for listeners that should only fire one time. Always remove listeners when the work's done, in a finally block or a cleanup function. And use AbortSignal with events.on or the signal option, which removes listeners automatically when aborted. events.once also returns a promise if you're waiting on a single event.
X: Raising the limit with setMaxListeners is only right when many listeners are genuinely expected, not just to silence the warning.
@p17-365
S: nodex
D: A
T: How does error handling work for async route handlers in Express?
K: express async error handling, express 5 promises, express error middleware, async handler express, unhandled rejection express
X: Actually in Express 4, if an async route handler threw an error or a promise rejected, Express didn't catch it. The rejection went unhandled, the request hung until it timed out, and in modern Node, the unhandled rejection could crash the whole process. So everyone wrapped handlers with try-catch and called next with the error, or used a helper like express-async-handler, or the express-async-errors package, which patches Express.
X: Express 5, which became the stable release in late 2024, fixed this. When a handler or middleware returns a rejected promise, Express automatically passes the error to the error-handling middleware. So async handlers can just throw.
X: Either way, I have one central error-handling middleware, the special four-argument function, registered after all the routes. It maps known error types to responses. A ValidationError to 400 with details, NotFoundError to 404, and a custom AppError with its own status code and error code. For anything unexpected, it logs the full error with the request id and returns a generic 500 without internal details. Responses use a consistent format, like Problem Details.
X: I also add a 404 handler for unknown routes. And I make sure errors in streams or background callbacks are handled right where they happen, because they're not part of the request's promise, so the central handler never sees them. That one's caught people out in my team.
@p17-366
S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you avoid blocking the event loop in Node.js?
K: blocking event loop, sync functions node, json parse large, redos, cpu work node, event loop blocked
X: So Node runs all JavaScript for all requests on one thread. If one operation takes 200 milliseconds of CPU, every other request waits 200 milliseconds. So keeping each piece of work short is really critical.
X: The common ways the loop gets blocked, and what I do about each.
X: Synchronous APIs in request paths. readFileSync, existsSync, execSync, and crypto's sync functions, like pbkdf2Sync. I use the async versions. Sync APIs are fine only during startup.
X: Large JSON. JSON.parse and JSON.stringify are synchronous and can take a long time on very big payloads. I limit payload sizes, paginate, or stream JSON.
X: Heavy computation. Big loops, sorting huge arrays, image processing, compression, PDF generation. These go to worker threads, a separate service, or a job queue.
X: Catastrophic regular expressions. Certain regex patterns with nested quantifiers take exponential time on crafted input, that's the ReDoS attack. I keep regexes simple, limit input length, and use linting tools that detect unsafe patterns.
X: Processing a large collection in one go. I split the work into chunks and yield between them with setImmediate, so other requests get a turn.
X: To catch blocking, I monitor event loop delay with perf_hooks and alert when it's high, and use CPU profiles to find the culprit. Honestly, that monitoring has saved us more than once.
@p17-367
S: nodex
D: A
T: What is prototype pollution, and how do you protect a Node.js app?
K: prototype pollution, __proto__ attack, object merge vulnerability, javascript security, json parse proto
X: Okay, prototype pollution is a JavaScript-specific vulnerability. Every object inherits from Object.prototype. If an attacker can make the app set a property on Object.prototype itself, that property suddenly shows up on every object in the process. That can change application logic, like an isAdmin property becoming true everywhere, bypass security checks, crash the app, or in some cases lead to remote code execution through template engines or child process options. Scary stuff.
X: It usually happens through unsafe recursive merge, deep clone, or set-by-path functions that copy user-controlled JSON into objects. If the input has a key like underscore-underscore proto, or constructor.prototype, a naive merge walks into the prototype and writes there. Plenty of popular libraries had bugs like this over the years.
X: What I do to protect against it. Validate input with a schema that only allows expected properties, like Zod or JSON Schema, which also strips unknown keys. Don't write your own deep merge of untrusted data, and keep libraries like lodash updated. Block the dangerous keys, proto, constructor and prototype, in any code that sets properties by a dynamic key. Use Map instead of plain objects for user-keyed data, or objects created with Object.create of null, which have no prototype. Freezing Object.prototype at startup is strong but blunt, and it can break some libraries. Node also has a flag to disable proto.
X: And dependency scanning catches the known vulnerable package versions.

S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you protect a Node.js project from npm supply chain attacks?
K: npm supply chain attack, malicious npm package, typosquatting, npm audit, lockfile security, install scripts risk
X: Honestly, the npm ecosystem has had a lot of supply chain attacks. Typosquatted package names, maintainer accounts compromised and malicious versions published, and in 2025, self-spreading worms that stole tokens through install scripts. A typical project has hundreds of transitive dependencies, so the risk is very real.
X: What I do about it. Commit the lockfile and install with npm ci, so builds use exactly the reviewed versions, and a newly published malicious version doesn't sneak in automatically. Review new dependencies before adding them. Is it needed, is it maintained, how popular is it, and is the name spelled right? Fewer dependencies is better. Disable or restrict install scripts, which run arbitrary code at install time, with ignore-scripts, or pnpm's approach of only allowing scripts for approved packages. Run dependency scanning, npm audit, Dependabot, Snyk or Socket, in the pipeline, failing on high-severity issues. Hold off on brand-new versions for a few days, since malicious releases are usually caught quickly, and tools like Renovate support a minimum release age. Use a private registry or proxy, like Azure Artifacts or AWS CodeArtifact, so packages come through a controlled source. And protect our own publishing with 2FA and short-lived tokens, and publish with provenance from CI.
X: One more, CI build agents shouldn't have more secrets than they need, because a malicious package runs with the agent's permissions. People forget that part.

S: nodex
D: A
T: What is the native fetch API in Node.js, and how do you use it well?
K: fetch in node, undici, node 18 fetch, http client node, axios vs fetch, fetch timeout abortsignal
X: See, since Node 18, fetch is available globally, stable since Node 21, implemented by the undici library. So for HTTP calls you don't need axios or node-fetch anymore, and the same API works in browsers and Node.
X: But using it well on a server needs a few things fetch doesn't do by default.
X: Timeouts. fetch has no default timeout, so a hanging server can hold the request forever. I pass a signal from AbortSignal.timeout of, say, 5,000 milliseconds, or combine signals with AbortSignal.any to support cancellation too.
X: Error handling. fetch only rejects on network errors. A 404 or 500 response resolves successfully, so I always check response.ok or the status, and throw or handle errors explicitly. That catches people a lot.
X: Consuming the body. If you don't read or cancel the response body, the connection might not go back to the pool, so I always read it, even on errors.
X: Connection pooling and keep-alive are handled by undici's global agent, and for heavy use, you can configure an undici Agent or Pool with connection limits.
X: Retries, backoff and circuit breaking aren't built in, so I add them with a small wrapper or a library, and only retry safe requests.
X: Axios is still a fine choice in existing code, especially for its interceptors, which our React apps use for adding tokens. In Node services though, I go with native fetch plus a thin wrapper.
@p17-370
S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you choose between Promise.all, allSettled, race and any?
K: promise.all vs allsettled, promise race, promise any, parallel promises javascript, promise combinators
X: So these all take several promises and combine them, but they resolve or reject differently.
X: Promise.all resolves with an array of all results once every promise resolves, and rejects immediately if any one rejects, with that first error. The other operations keep running, but their results get ignored. I use it when every result is required, like loading a page's essential data in parallel.
X: Promise.allSettled waits for all of them, success or not, and resolves with an array of objects, each with a status, fulfilled or rejected, and a value or reason. It never rejects. I use it when operations are independent and I want each outcome. Like sending notifications to several recipients, or loading optional dashboard widgets, where one failure shouldn't hide the rest.
X: Promise.race settles as soon as the first promise settles, whether it resolves or rejects. The classic use was a timeout, racing the operation against a timer, though AbortSignal.timeout is cleaner now because it also cancels the operation.
X: Promise.any resolves with the first promise that fulfils, ignoring rejections, and only rejects, with an AggregateError, if all of them reject. Handy for redundancy, like trying several mirrors or replicas and taking the fastest successful response.
X: And one thing people forget, none of them limit concurrency. For hundreds of operations, I use a concurrency limiter, like p-limit, instead of firing them all at once.
@p17-371
S: pyx
D: A
T: What is the GIL in Python, and how does it affect performance?
K: gil, global interpreter lock, python threading cpu, free threaded python, python 3.13 no gil, python multicore
X: Okay, the Global Interpreter Lock is a lock in CPython, the standard Python interpreter, that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. It simplifies memory management, since reference counting doesn't need fine-grained locks, and makes C extensions easier to write.
X: The effect is Python threads can't run CPU-bound Python code in parallel on multiple cores. Ten threads doing heavy calculations take about as long as one thread, or even longer.
X: But for I/O-bound work, HTTP calls, database queries, file reads, the GIL is released while waiting on I/O, so threads, or asyncio, work well for concurrency. And many C-based libraries, like NumPy, release the GIL during heavy computations, so they can use multiple cores.
X: For CPU-bound Python code, the usual options are multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor from concurrent.futures, which use separate processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL. Or moving the hot code into a compiled library. Or running multiple worker processes, which web servers like Gunicorn do anyway.
X: Things are changing though. Python 3.13 introduced an experimental free-threaded build without the GIL, and in 3.14 the free-threaded build became officially supported, though not the default. Many libraries are still catching up, and single-threaded code can be slightly slower in that build.
X: For our RAG service, the work is mostly I/O, calling embedding APIs and the database, so async FastAPI fits well, and honestly the GIL just isn't a bottleneck there.
@p17-372
S: pyx
D: A
T: threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio in Python: when do you use each?
K: threading vs multiprocessing vs asyncio, python concurrency, concurrent futures, io bound vs cpu bound python, threadpoolexecutor
X: So basically I pick based on whether the work is I/O-bound or CPU-bound, and how many concurrent operations there are.
X: asyncio is for lots of concurrent I/O-bound work. Thousands of HTTP calls, database queries or WebSocket connections, handled on a single thread with an event loop, using async and await. It's very efficient, because waiting tasks don't hold threads. The catch is every library in the chain has to be async-aware, like httpx or aiohttp instead of requests, and asyncpg or async SQLAlchemy. One blocking call stalls everything.
X: threading is for I/O-bound work with libraries that are synchronous, or a moderate number of concurrent operations. The GIL is released during I/O, so threads overlap their waits. ThreadPoolExecutor from concurrent.futures makes it simple, you submit tasks, get futures, collect results. It's also how async code runs blocking functions, with asyncio.to_thread.
X: multiprocessing is for CPU-bound work. Data processing, parsing large files, heavy calculations. Each process has its own interpreter and GIL, so it actually uses multiple cores. ProcessPoolExecutor is the convenient interface. What you pay is higher memory, slower start-up, and data passed between processes has to be pickled, which is slow for large objects.
X: In web services, what I do is FastAPI with async endpoints for the I/O concurrency, and CPU-heavy tasks go to a process pool or a separate worker, like Celery. That's worked fine for us.
@p17-373
S: pyx
D: A
T: How does async and await in Python compare with C#?
K: python asyncio vs c# async, python async await, event loop python, coroutine python, asyncio gather
X: Okay, so the syntax looks almost the same, but the runtime model is quite different.
X: In Python, async def defines a coroutine function. Calling it doesn't run anything. It returns a coroutine object, which only runs when awaited, or scheduled on the event loop as a task with asyncio.create_task. In C#, calling an async method starts running it immediately, synchronously, until the first incomplete await, and returns a Task that's already in progress.
X: Python's asyncio runs on a single-threaded event loop. All coroutines share that thread, and concurrency comes from switching at await points. No thread pool involved unless you explicitly use one. C# continuations run on thread pool threads, so async code can also run in parallel on multiple cores.
X: And because Python's loop is single-threaded, any blocking call, like time.sleep, requests.get or a heavy computation, freezes every coroutine. In C#, blocking is wasteful too, but it blocks one thread, not everything.
X: The equivalents, asyncio.gather is like Task.WhenAll. asyncio.wait_for or asyncio.timeout is like a timeout with a CancellationToken. And asyncio.TaskGroup, since 3.11, gives structured concurrency, where if one task fails, the others get cancelled. Cancellation in Python shows up as a CancelledError raised at an await point, rather than a token you pass explicitly.
X: Coming from .NET, honestly the biggest adjustment for me was never mixing blocking libraries into async code. That one bit me early on.
@p17-374
S: pyx
D: A
T: What are generators in Python, and why use yield?
K: python generators, yield python, generator expression, lazy evaluation python, iterator protocol python, yield from
X: See, a generator is a function that uses yield to produce values one at a time, lazily. Calling it returns a generator object. Each call to next runs the function until the next yield, returns that value, and pauses, keeping its local state. When the function ends, it raises StopIteration, which for loops handle automatically. It's very similar to yield return in C#.
X: The big win is memory. Reading a 10 GB log file with a generator that yields one parsed line at a time uses almost no memory, whereas building a list of all lines would load everything. Generators also let you do infinite sequences and pipelines, where each stage is a generator consuming the previous one. Like read lines, filter errors, parse fields, and only the items actually consumed get processed.
X: Generator expressions are the lazy version of list comprehensions, written with parentheses. Sum of x squared for x in numbers doesn't create an intermediate list.
X: yield from delegates to another generator, which is handy for recursion, like walking a directory tree.
X: A few cautions. A generator can only be iterated once. After it's exhausted, it yields nothing. Errors show up when iterating, not when calling the function. And it's lazy, so code that looks like it ran may not have run at all. That last one confuses people.
X: Async generators, with async def and yield, work with async for, for streaming data from APIs or databases.
@p17-375
S: pyx
D: A
T: What are decorators in Python, and how do you write one?
K: python decorators, write decorator python, functools wraps, decorator with arguments, retry decorator python
X: Actually a decorator is just a function that takes a function and returns a new function, usually adding behaviour around the original one. The at-decorator syntax above a function definition is shorthand for replacing the function with decorator of function.
X: To write one, I define an outer function that takes the original function, and inside, a wrapper function that accepts star args and double-star kwargs, does something before, calls the original, does something after, and returns the result. The outer function returns the wrapper. I always apply functools.wraps to the wrapper, so the decorated function keeps its original name, docstring and signature. That matters for debugging, logging, and frameworks that inspect functions, like FastAPI.
X: A decorator with arguments, like retry with attempts equals 3, needs one more level. A function that takes the arguments and returns the actual decorator.
X: For async functions, the wrapper has to be async and await the original.
X: Where you see them, timing and logging, caching with functools.lru_cache or cache, retries with backoff, which the tenacity library gives you, access checks, and registering functions. Frameworks lean on them heavily. FastAPI's app.get, pytest's fixture and parametrize, and dataclass and property are all decorators.
X: They're like attributes plus middleware in .NET, a clean way to add cross-cutting behaviour without touching the function body. I just avoid stacking too many, because then control flow gets hard to follow.

T: What are context managers, and how does the with statement work?
K: context manager python, with statement, __enter__ __exit__, contextlib contextmanager, async with, resource cleanup python
X: Okay, a context manager sets something up and guarantees cleanup, even if an exception happens. The with statement uses it. With open of the file as f, then the block, and the file gets closed automatically when the block ends, normally or through an error. It's basically Python's version of using in C#.
X: A class becomes a context manager by implementing two methods. Dunder enter runs at the start and returns the resource, which gets bound by as. Dunder exit runs at the end. It receives the exception type, value and traceback if an error occurred, and does cleanup, like closing, releasing or rolling back. If it returns True, the exception is suppressed, which is rarely what I want.
X: The easier way is contextlib.contextmanager. A generator function where the code before yield is setup, the yielded value is the resource, and the code after yield, in a finally block, is cleanup.
X: Where I use them, files and network connections. Database transactions, committing on success and rolling back on exceptions. Acquiring and releasing locks. Temporarily changing settings, like a working directory. And timing a block of code.
X: Async context managers, with dunder aenter and aexit, or contextlib.asynccontextmanager, are used with async with, for things like database sessions and HTTP clients. FastAPI's lifespan function, which sets up and tears down resources at startup and shutdown, is actually an async context manager.
X: contextlib.ExitStack manages a dynamic number of context managers, if you ever need that.
@p17-377
S: pyx
D: A
T: What is the mutable default argument pitfall in Python?
K: mutable default argument, default list argument python, python function default bug, none default python
X: So in Python, default argument values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, not every time it's called. So if the default is a mutable object, like a list or dictionary, the same object gets shared across all calls that use the default.
X: Let me take an example. def add_item of item, and items equals an empty list, appends the item and returns items. First call returns a list with one item. The second call, which you'd expect to return a new list with one item, returns a list with two, because it's the same list object as before. Data leaks between calls, which causes really confusing bugs, especially in long-running services where state builds up across requests.
X: The standard fix is to use None as the default and create a new object inside the function. items equals None, then if items is None, items equals an empty list.
X: Same idea shows up in other places. Class attributes defined with mutable values are shared by all instances, so per-instance lists should be created in the init. Dataclasses protect you here, they raise an error for a mutable default, and I use field with default_factory equals list instead. Pydantic models handle mutable defaults safely by copying them.
X: Linters like Ruff flag mutable default arguments automatically, which is honestly one reason I always run a linter.
@p17-378
S: pyx
D: A
T: What is the difference between is and ==, and shallow vs deep copy in Python?
K: is vs == python, identity vs equality python, shallow copy deep copy python, copy module, list copy python
X: See, double equals checks equality of values, by calling the dunder eq method. is checks identity, whether two names point to the exact same object in memory. Two separate lists with the same contents are equal with double equals but not identical with is. My rule is use is only for singletons, mainly None, as in if value is None, and use double equals for comparing values. Using is with numbers or strings sometimes seems to work, because Python caches small integers and some strings, but that's an implementation detail and a common bug.
X: Copying ties into the same idea. Assigning b equals a doesn't copy anything. Both names point to the same object, so changing one changes the other.
X: A shallow copy, with list of a, a slice, dict.copy or copy.copy, creates a new outer container, but the items inside are the same objects. So with a list of lists, changing an inner list through the copy also changes it in the original.
X: A deep copy, with copy.deepcopy, recursively copies everything, so the copy is completely independent. It's slower, uses more memory, and can be surprising for objects holding resources, but it's what I need when duplicating nested mutable data, like a configuration template that each job modifies.
X: Immutable objects, like tuples of immutable items and frozen dataclasses, avoid a lot of these issues. That's one reason I prefer immutable data wherever I can.

T: dataclasses vs Pydantic models vs NamedTuple: when do you use each?
K: dataclass vs pydantic, namedtuple, python data classes, pydantic basemodel, typed dict, attrs
X: Honestly they all define structured data with typed fields, but they're for different purposes.
X: A NamedTuple is an immutable tuple with named fields. Lightweight, works anywhere tuples work, good for small simple return values or records. But it can't easily have per-instance computed defaults, and since it's a tuple, it can be compared and unpacked by position, which sometimes surprises people.
X: A dataclass, from the standard library, generates the init, repr and eq from type-annotated fields. It's a plain Python class, mutable by default, or immutable with frozen equals True, with slots for memory efficiency and default_factory for mutable defaults. Type hints aren't enforced at runtime, so passing a string where an int is declared just works. It's my go-to for internal domain objects and data passed between functions in trusted code.
X: A Pydantic model validates and converts data at runtime. Passing the string "5" to an int field converts it, and passing "abc" raises a clear validation error. It parses nested structures, serialises to and from JSON, and generates JSON Schema. Pydantic v2's core is written in Rust, so it's fast. It's the right choice at system boundaries. API requests and responses, which is why FastAPI uses it, configuration with pydantic-settings, and data coming from files, queues or external APIs.
X: So yeah, Pydantic at the edges where data is untrusted, dataclasses inside, and NamedTuple for tiny records.

T: How do type hints and mypy improve Python code?
K: python type hints, mypy, static typing python, typing module, pyright, type checking python
X: So type hints annotate variables, function parameters and return values with types, like def get_kit of kit_id int returning Kit or None. Python itself doesn't enforce them at runtime. They're for tools and humans.
X: Static type checkers, like mypy or Pyright, analyse the code using the hints and find errors before you run it. Passing the wrong type, forgetting that a function can return None, calling methods that don't exist, or missing cases. Editors use the same information for accurate autocomplete and safe refactoring.
X: Coming from C# and TypeScript, honestly it brings back a lot of the safety I'm used to. Useful features, Optional or the union-with-None syntax. T: venv, pip, Poetry or uv: how do you manage Python environments and dependencies?
K: python virtual environment, venv, pip requirements, poetry, uv python, pyproject.toml, dependency lock python
X: Actually the starting point is each Python project gets its own isolated environment, so different projects can use different package versions without conflicts. venv, built into Python, creates that environment, and pip installs packages into it.
X: The traditional approach is a requirements.txt file. To make builds reproducible, I pin exact versions, including transitive dependencies, often generated with pip-tools from a smaller list of direct dependencies.
X: Modern projects use pyproject.toml, the standard file for project metadata, dependencies and tool configuration, like Ruff, mypy and pytest settings.
X: Poetry manages dependencies through pyproject.toml, resolves versions, creates a lockfile, manages the virtual environment, and builds packages. It's mature and widely used.
X: uv, from the makers of Ruff, is the newer one, written in Rust and extremely fast. It can replace pip, pip-tools, venv, and even manage Python versions. uv add adds a dependency, uv lock creates a cross-platform lockfile, uv sync installs exactly what's locked, and uv run runs commands in the environment. It's got really popular because installs take seconds instead of minutes, which matters a lot in CI and Docker builds.
X: Whatever the tool, the principles are the same as npm and NuGet. Declare direct dependencies, commit a lockfile, install exactly from the lockfile in CI and Docker, and keep dependencies updated with automated pull requests and vulnerability scanning.
@p17-383
S: pyx
D: A
T: How does dependency injection work in FastAPI with Depends?
K: fastapi depends, fastapi dependency injection, yield dependency fastapi, dependency override testing, get db session fastapi
X: Okay, FastAPI's dependency injection is based on functions, not a container. An endpoint declares a parameter with Depends of some function, and FastAPI calls that function for each request and passes the result in. Dependencies can have their own dependencies, forming a tree, and FastAPI resolves it, caching each dependency's result within the same request by default. So two parameters that need the same database session get the same one.
X: The common ones I write, get_db, which yields a database session. Because it uses yield, the code after yield runs when the request finishes and closes the session, kind of like a scoped service with disposal in .NET. get_current_user, which reads the bearer token, validates it, and returns the user, or raises an HTTP 401. get_settings. Pagination parameters. And permission checks, like a require_role factory that returns a dependency.
X: Dependencies can be applied to a whole router or app, for things like authentication, so every endpoint is protected without repeating the parameter. Annotated type aliases, like CurrentUser equals Annotated of User and Depends of get_current_user, keep signatures clean.
X: For testing, app.dependency_overrides lets me swap any dependency with a fake, like an in-memory repository or a fixed test user, without changing endpoint code. Really handy.
X: The difference from .NET is there are no explicit lifetimes. Per-request caching and yield-based cleanup cover scoped behaviour, and singletons are usually module-level objects or created in the lifespan.
@p17-384
S: pyx
D: A
T: FastAPI BackgroundTasks vs Celery: when do you need a task queue?
K: fastapi background tasks, celery, task queue python, arq, background job python, redis queue python
X: See, FastAPI's BackgroundTasks lets an endpoint schedule a function to run after the response is sent, in the same process. It's simple and great for small, quick follow-up work, like sending a notification email or writing an audit entry, where the user shouldn't have to wait.
X: But it has clear limits. The work runs in the web server's process, so heavy tasks compete with request handling. Nothing is persisted, so if the process restarts or crashes, pending tasks are just gone. No retries, no scheduling, no visibility into what's running. And it doesn't spread work across machines.
X: A task queue fixes that. Celery, or lighter options like RQ, Dramatiq, or arq for async code. The API puts a task message on a broker, like Redis or RabbitMQ, and returns immediately, often with a job id. Separate worker processes, which scale independently, pick up tasks and run them. You get retries with backoff, time limits, result storage, scheduled and periodic jobs, monitoring with tools like Flower, and tasks survive web server restarts.
X: So my rule is BackgroundTasks for small, best-effort stuff, and a task queue for anything long-running, CPU-heavy, that must not be lost, or needs retries. Like re-indexing documents, generating large reports, or calling slow external APIs.
X: On AWS, SQS with a worker container or a Lambda is the managed alternative. In our developer RAG system, re-indexing runs from the pipeline, outside the API process.

T: How do you use SQLAlchemy 2.0 with async sessions in FastAPI?
K: sqlalchemy async, sqlalchemy 2.0, asyncsession, async engine, fastapi database session, sqlalchemy orm
X: So SQLAlchemy is Python's main database toolkit and ORM. Version 2.0 brought a modern, fully typed style. Models declared with Mapped and mapped_column type annotations, and queries built with select and executed through the session, instead of the old query API.
X: For async, I create an async engine with create_async_engine and an async driver, like asyncpg for PostgreSQL, set the connection pool size, and create an async_sessionmaker. In FastAPI, a get_db dependency opens an AsyncSession per request with async with, yields it to the endpoint, and closes it afterwards. Queries are await session.execute of a select statement, then scalars to get model objects. Writes add objects to the session and await session.commit, with rollback on errors.
X: A few things I've learned to watch. Lazy loading doesn't work in async code. Touching a relationship that isn't loaded triggers I/O implicitly, and that raises an error. So I load relationships explicitly with selectinload or joinedload in the query, which also avoids N+1 problems. Setting expire_on_commit to False in the sessionmaker stops attributes being expired and reloaded after commit. One session per request, never shared across concurrent tasks. And the engine is created once at startup, in the lifespan, and disposed on shutdown.
X: It's honestly quite similar to EF Core. The session is like the DbContext, with a unit of work and identity map, and Alembic is like EF migrations.

T: How do you manage database migrations in Python with Alembic?
K: alembic, alembic migrations, sqlalchemy migrations, autogenerate alembic, database migration python, alembic upgrade head
X: Okay, so Alembic is the migration tool for SQLAlchemy, similar to EF Core migrations.
X: After initialising it, I configure env.py to use the app's database URL and SQLAlchemy metadata, so it knows the models. When I change a model, alembic revision with autogenerate compares the models against the current schema and generates a migration script with upgrade and downgrade functions, using operations like add_column, create_table and create_index. Each migration has a revision id and points to its parent, so they form a chain. alembic upgrade head applies all pending ones, and the current version sits in an alembic_version table.
X: But autogenerate is a starting point, not the final answer, so I always review the generated script. It doesn't catch everything. Some renames it sees as drop and add, which loses data. Some constraint or server default changes. Custom types. And data migrations, like backfilling a new column, I write by hand with op.execute or batch updates.
X: In production it's the same practices as with any database. Migrations stay backward compatible with the code that's currently running, expand and contract style. They run as a separate step in the deployment pipeline, not automatically on every app start, especially with several instances. Big table changes are done carefully, like creating indexes concurrently in PostgreSQL. And I test migrations against a copy of production-sized data, because that's where the surprises come from.

T: How do you do structured logging in Python?
K: python logging, structlog, json logging python, logging configuration python, python logger best practices
X: Actually Python's built-in logging module is the foundation. Each module gets a logger with logging.getLogger of dunder name, and configuration, done once at startup, decides levels, formats and handlers. Libraries should only create loggers, never configure logging themselves.
X: For services I want structured JSON logs, so the central log system can search by fields. You can go two ways here. A JSON formatter, like python-json-logger, on top of standard logging, where extra fields go in the extra parameter. Or structlog, which I prefer. It also hooks into standard logging, so library logs come out in the same format.
X: For request context, I use contextvars, Python's version of AsyncLocal, which works with asyncio. A middleware binds the request id and user id at the start of each request, and structlog's contextvars processor adds them to every log line in that request automatically. OpenTelemetry's logging instrumentation can add trace and span ids too, linking logs with traces.
X: My habits, log events with key-value context instead of formatted sentences. Use the right levels. Log exceptions with logger.exception, which includes the traceback. Never log secrets, tokens or personal data. And write to standard output in containers.

@p17-390
S: pyx
D: A
T: ASGI vs WSGI, and how do Gunicorn and Uvicorn fit together?
K: asgi vs wsgi, uvicorn, gunicorn, python web server, uvicorn workers, production fastapi server
X: Okay, WSGI is the original standard interface between Python web servers and frameworks, used by Flask and Django traditionally. It's synchronous. Each request occupies a worker, a process or thread, until it's done. So concurrency is limited by the number of workers, and long-lived connections like WebSockets don't really fit.
X: ASGI is the async successor. It supports async request handling, so one worker can handle lots of concurrent requests while they wait on I/O, and it supports WebSockets, HTTP/2, and lifespan events for startup and shutdown. FastAPI and Starlette are ASGI frameworks, and Django supports ASGI too.
X: Uvicorn is a fast ASGI server, built on uvloop and httptools. It runs the FastAPI app. On its own it can run several worker processes with the workers option.
X: Gunicorn is a mature process manager and WSGI server. For ASGI apps, it's used as a process manager with Uvicorn's worker class. Gunicorn starts several Uvicorn worker processes, monitors them, restarts any that crash, and handles graceful restarts and timeouts. That combo was the classic production setup, because one Python process only uses one core for Python code.
X: In containers, what I've seen more and more is a different approach. Run a single Uvicorn process per container, and let ECS or Kubernetes run multiple containers and restart them. That's simpler and gives the orchestrator better visibility, so it's what I lean towards.
X: Either way, the number of workers is roughly tuned to CPU cores and memory.

D: A
T: How do you profile a slow Python service?
K: python profiling, cprofile, py-spy, line profiler, python performance, slow python code
X: See, I always start by working out where the time actually goes, rather than guessing.
X: At the service level, tracing with OpenTelemetry shows whether a slow request is spending time in our code, the database, or external calls like an embedding API. Often it's I/O. An N+1 query, a missing index, or calls made one after another that could run concurrently with asyncio.gather.
X: If the time is in Python code itself, then a profiler. cProfile, built in, records every function call with call counts and cumulative time. I view the output with snakeviz as a graph, or sort by cumulative time. It has overhead though, and the code has to run under it.
X: py-spy is a sampling profiler that attaches to a running process without restarting it or changing code, so it's safe in production. py-spy top shows live hot functions, and py-spy record produces a flame graph. py-spy dump shows what every thread is doing right now, which is great for hangs. Newer ones include Scalene, which also profiles memory and separates Python time from native time, and Pyinstrument.
X: For one specific hot function, line_profiler shows time per line.
X: The usual fixes, better algorithms or data structures, like a set for membership checks instead of a list. Vectorising with NumPy or pandas instead of Python loops. Caching with functools.cache. Batching database or API calls. And moving CPU-heavy work to a process pool.
@p17-392
S: pyx
D: A
T: EAFP vs LBYL: how do you handle errors in Python?
K: eafp vs lbyl, python exceptions best practices, custom exceptions python, try except python, raise from python
X: So LBYL, look before you leap, means checking conditions before acting. If key in dictionary, then read it. EAFP, easier to ask forgiveness than permission, means just trying the operation and handling the exception. Try reading the key, except KeyError.
X: Python culture generally prefers EAFP. It avoids race conditions where the condition changes between the check and the action, like a file getting deleted right after you checked it exists. It's often cleaner, and exceptions in Python are fairly cheap. LBYL is still fine for simple expected cases, and things like dict.get with a default sidestep both.
X: What I do in practice with exceptions. Catch specific exceptions, never a bare except, which also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, and avoid catching Exception broadly except at the top level of a request or job, where I log it and return an error. Keep the try block small, so I only catch errors from the line I expect. Use raise from to chain exceptions when translating them, like raising a custom EmbeddingServiceError from the original httpx error, which keeps the original traceback. Have a small hierarchy of custom exceptions, like a base AppError with NotFoundError and ValidationError, which FastAPI exception handlers map to HTTP responses. And finally blocks or context managers for cleanup.
X: Python 3.11 added exception groups and except star for handling multiple errors from concurrent tasks, like the ones in a TaskGroup.

S: pyx

T: How do you call external REST APIs robustly from Python?
K: httpx, requests python, retry python tenacity, python http client timeout, connection pooling python, call api python
X: Okay, for HTTP calls in Python I use httpx, which does both sync and async with the same API, or requests for simple synchronous scripts.
X: What makes it reliable is a handful of things.
X: Reuse the client. Creating a new client per request loses connection pooling and keep-alive, so I create one httpx.AsyncClient at startup, in the FastAPI lifespan, with a base URL, default headers and limits, and close it on shutdown. Same lesson as HttpClient in .NET, honestly.
X: Timeouts. requests has no default timeout at all, so a hung server blocks forever. httpx defaults to five seconds. I set explicit connect and read timeouts suited to the API.
X: Check status codes. Call raise_for_status, or check the status explicitly and handle errors.
X: Retries with backoff. The tenacity library gives you a retry decorator with stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential with jitter, and retry_if_exception_type, so I retry only transient failures, connection errors, timeouts, 429 and 503, and respect Retry-After. For non-idempotent POST requests, I retry only with an idempotency key.
X: Concurrency limits. When making lots of calls with asyncio.gather, I use an asyncio.Semaphore to cap concurrent requests and respect the API's rate limits.
X: And logging with the request id, plus OpenTelemetry instrumentation for httpx, so external calls show up in traces.
X: For the embedding API calls in our RAG service, batching and rate-limit-aware retries were essential.
@p17-394
S: pyx
D: A
T: What Python security issues should you watch for?
K: python security, pickle security, eval exec security, bandit, yaml safe load, subprocess shell injection
X: Honestly Python has a few specific risks on top of the usual web security stuff.
X: pickle. Unpickling data can execute arbitrary code, so I never unpickle data from untrusted sources, like uploads, network messages or shared caches. JSON is the safe choice for data exchange. Same applies to tools built on pickle, like some model file formats. For ML models, safer formats like safetensors exist.
X: eval and exec. Running strings as code is dangerous with any user input. For parsing simple literals, ast.literal_eval is safe.
X: YAML. yaml.load with the default or full loader can create arbitrary Python objects, so I always use yaml.safe_load.
X: subprocess. Passing a command string with shell equals True and user input allows shell injection. I pass arguments as a list without the shell.
X: SQL. Always parameterised queries, through SQLAlchemy or the driver's parameters. Never f-strings in SQL.
X: Path traversal. Building file paths from user input means resolving the path and checking it stays inside the allowed directory.
X: Insecure randomness. random is predictable, so for tokens and passwords I use the secrets module.
X: Dependencies. Typosquatted packages on PyPI are real, so I pin dependencies with a lockfile, scan them with pip-audit, and review new packages.
X: And tools help a lot. Bandit, or Ruff's security rules, flag many of these patterns automatically in the pipeline.
@p17-395
S: pyx
D: A
T: How do you process a large CSV file efficiently in Python?
K: large csv python, pandas chunksize, csv module python, polars, process big file python, memory efficient python
X: Actually the key is not loading the whole file into memory at once, unless it comfortably fits.
X: For row-by-row processing, the built-in csv module with DictReader reads one row at a time from a file object, kind of a generator-like stream. Memory stays flat no matter how big the file is. I combine it with batching. Collect rows into batches of, say, 5,000, validate them, and write each batch to the database with a bulk insert, like executemany or PostgreSQL's COPY, which is way faster than inserting rows one by one.
X: For analysis and transformation, pandas is convenient, but it loads data into memory, which can be several times the file size. read_csv with chunksize returns an iterator of DataFrames, so you can process a large file in chunks. Specifying dtypes and usecols, so you only read the needed columns with the right types, cuts memory and speeds up parsing a lot. The pyarrow engine is faster too.
X: Polars is a newer DataFrame library written in Rust. Much faster than pandas, uses all CPU cores, and its lazy API with scan_csv builds a query plan and processes data in a streaming way, even for files bigger than memory. For heavy data work it's my preferred choice now. DuckDB is another great option, it can query CSV files with SQL directly.
X: Whatever the tool, I collect invalid rows with their line numbers into an error report instead of failing the whole file.
