T: How do API Gateway authorizers work?
K: api gateway authorizer, lambda authorizer, jwt authorizer, cognito authorizer, iam authorization api gateway, authorizer caching
X: So authorizers let API Gateway authenticate and authorise requests before they reach the backend, so bad requests get rejected early.
X: JWT authorizers, in HTTP APIs, validate JSON Web Tokens from any OIDC-compliant provider, like Cognito, Keycloak, Entra ID or Auth0. You configure the issuer and audience, and API Gateway checks the signature using the provider's published keys, plus expiry, issuer and audience, and can require specific scopes per route. Claims are passed to the backend. No code needed.
X: Cognito user pool authorizers are the REST API equivalent for Cognito tokens.
X: Lambda authorizers run your own function to make the decision. A token-based one gets the bearer token, and a request-based one gets headers, query strings and context. The function validates the request, maybe checking a custom token, an API key in a database, or calling an external authorisation service, and returns an IAM policy allowing or denying, or a simple boolean for HTTP APIs, plus context values passed to the backend, like user id and tenant. Results can be cached for a TTL, keyed by the token, to cut latency and cost. But caching means revoked access may still work until the cache expires, and a cached policy has to cover all the routes the token will be used for. That second bit can catch people out.
X: IAM authorisation needs requests signed with AWS Signature Version 4, which suits service-to-service calls inside AWS.
X: And fine-grained authorisation, like whether this user can see this shipment, still belongs in the service.
@p17-444
S: awsx
D: A
T: How does SnapStart improve Lambda cold starts for .NET?
K: lambda snapstart, snapstart dotnet, lambda cold start dotnet, native aot lambda, reduce cold start lambda
X: Okay, so cold starts happen when Lambda creates a new execution environment. Downloading code, starting the runtime, running initialisation code. For .NET, JIT compilation and loading dependencies, like dependency injection setup and SDK clients, can push cold starts to a second or more.
X: SnapStart, available for .NET 8 and later managed runtimes since late 2024, as well as Java and Python, tackles this. When you publish a function version, Lambda runs the initialisation phase once, takes a snapshot of the memory and disk state of the initialised environment, encrypts it and caches it. New execution environments are resumed from the snapshot instead of initialising from scratch, which can cut cold start times dramatically.
X: Things to be careful about. Uniqueness, anything generated during init, like random seeds, unique ids or cached credentials, is the same in every environment restored from that snapshot. There are runtime hooks, before snapshot and after restore, to refresh that kind of state, and network connections opened during init may need re-establishing after restore. It works with published versions and aliases, not dollar LATEST. There's a cost for caching and restoring snapshots for .NET. And you can't combine it with provisioned concurrency.
X: The alternatives I'd look at, Native AOT compilation, which removes JIT and gives very fast starts, but needs trimming-compatible code and libraries. Provisioned concurrency, which keeps environments warm, at a cost. And honestly just reducing init work, lazy loading what isn't always needed, and choosing more memory, which also gives you more CPU.

T: ElastiCache Redis vs Memcached vs Valkey: what are the differences?
K: elasticache redis vs memcached, valkey, elasticache serverless, redis cluster mode, elasticache options
X: So ElastiCache is AWS's managed in-memory cache, and it supports a few engines.
X: Memcached is a simple, multi-threaded key-value cache. Good for straightforward caching of strings and objects, scales by adding nodes with client-side sharding, and uses multiple cores well. But no persistence, no replication, no rich data types, and no failover. If a node dies, its cached data is just gone.
X: Redis, and now Valkey, the open-source fork of Redis that AWS backs after the Redis license change, give you much more. Data structures like hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and streams. Atomic operations and Lua scripting. Pub-sub. Replication with automatic failover across availability zones. Optional persistence and backups. And cluster mode, which shards data across multiple node groups for horizontal scaling. So they work not just for caching but for sessions, leaderboards, rate limiters, distributed locks and queues. Valkey on ElastiCache is cheaper than Redis OSS and fully compatible, so it's the default for new clusters.
X: ElastiCache Serverless removes capacity planning, scaling automatically with usage, priced per GB and per request, which suits variable workloads.
X: MemoryDB is related. Redis or Valkey compatible, but durable, with a multi-AZ transaction log, so it can actually be a primary database, not just a cache.
X: I'd pick Valkey for nearly everything new. IQVIA's newer AWS services use ElastiCache for caching. On-premise, our CIRT platform uses Redis in a similar way.

T: How do .NET apps get AWS credentials, and why should you never use access keys in code?
K: aws credentials dotnet, default credential chain, aws sdk credentials, access keys in code, iam roles anywhere, aws sso credentials
X: Actually the AWS SDK for .NET resolves credentials through a default credential provider chain. It checks several sources in order, so the same code works everywhere without changes.
X: Roughly the order is credentials passed explicitly in code. Then environment variables, like AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID. Then the shared credentials and config files with profiles, including IAM Identity Center SSO profiles for developers. Then web identity tokens, used by EKS IRSA and OIDC in CI. Then the ECS container credentials endpoint, which gives tasks their task role credentials. And the EC2 instance metadata service, for the instance role.
X: So in practice, developers run aws sso login and use a profile with short-lived credentials. CI pipelines assume a role through OIDC federation, with no stored secrets. ECS tasks use their task role. Lambda functions use their execution role. EKS pods use Pod Identity or IRSA. All temporary credentials that rotate automatically.
X: Long-lived access keys in code, config files, or environment variables are a serious risk. They get committed to Git, leaked in logs or container images, they never expire unless someone rotates them by hand, and they're usually over-privileged. Attackers scan public repos for AWS keys within minutes. Honestly, minutes.
X: For workloads outside AWS, like on-premise servers that need AWS access, IAM Roles Anywhere issues temporary credentials based on X.509 certificates from a trusted certificate authority, instead of access keys.
X: And if keys really can't be avoided, they get least privilege, rotation, and storage in a secrets manager.

X: Okay, Terraform's state file maps configuration to real resources, so for a team it has to be stored remotely, shared and locked.
X: On AWS the standard backend is S3. T: How do you safely refactor Terraform: import, moved and removed blocks?
K: terraform import block, terraform moved block, terraform removed block, terraform refactor without destroy, terraform state mv
X: So as Terraform code evolves, you often need to change how resources are tracked without destroying and recreating them. Get this wrong and you can delete a production database, so modern Terraform gives you declarative blocks that get reviewed in pull requests like any other code.
X: Import blocks bring existing resources, created manually or by another tool, under Terraform management. You write an import block with the resource address and the real resource id, and run terraform plan with the generate-config-out flag to generate a starting configuration, then clean it up. The plan shows the import, and apply records it in state without changing the resource. Import blocks can use for_each for many resources.
X: Moved blocks handle renames and restructuring. Renaming a resource, moving it into a module, or converting from count to for_each. Without a moved block, Terraform would plan to destroy the old address and create a new one. With moved from and to, it just updates the state. These replace manual terraform state mv commands, which weren't reviewed or repeatable across environments.
X: Removed blocks, since Terraform 1.7, stop managing a resource without destroying it, using a lifecycle setting with destroy set to false. Like when you're handing a resource over to another team's configuration.
X: Through all of it, the plan is my safety net. Before applying, I check it shows no unexpected destroys or replacements. I also add prevent_destroy to critical resources, like databases and state buckets. Trust me, that one's worth it.

T: How do App Service deployment slots and slot swaps work?
K: deployment slots, slot swap, staging slot app service, zero downtime app service, sticky settings, swap with preview
X: See, deployment slots are live copies of an App Service app, like a staging slot next to production, each with its own hostname, running on the same App Service plan. You get them on Standard tier and above.
X: The flow is, I deploy the new version to the staging slot, warm it up and test it at its own URL, then swap staging with production. During a swap, App Service first applies the production slot's settings to the staging instances, restarts them, and warms them up by calling the site, optionally a specific warm-up path set with applicationInitialization. Only when they're ready does it switch the routing, so production traffic lands on already-warm instances with no downtime. The old version is now sitting in the staging slot, so rollback is just swapping back.
X: Settings matter here. App settings and connection strings can be marked as deployment slot settings, or sticky, so they stay with the slot instead of moving with the code. Like the staging slot keeps pointing to a staging database, or has a flag disabling background jobs. Non-sticky settings move with the app during the swap.
X: Swap with preview does it in two phases, applying production settings to staging first, so you can validate before completing. Auto swap swaps automatically after a deployment to a slot, which suits continuous deployment.
X: Traffic routing can also send a percentage of production traffic to a slot, for simple testing in production.
X: One caution I always mention, database schema changes have to work with both versions, because the swap is instant but the database is shared.

T: How do App Service plans and scaling work?
K: app service plan, scale up vs scale out app service, app service autoscale, app service tiers, automatic scaling azure
X: Okay, an App Service plan defines the compute your apps run on. The region, the OS, the pricing tier, the instance size, and the number of instances. Several apps can share one plan, so they share and compete for the same VMs. Putting a heavy app with others can cause noisy neighbour issues, so I keep critical apps in their own plans.
X: Tiers, Free and Shared for experiments. Basic for low-traffic apps without slots or autoscale. Standard and Premium, with Premium v3 or v4 recommended, for production with deployment slots, autoscale, VNet integration and zone redundancy. And Isolated, in an App Service Environment, for single-tenant network isolation.
X: Scaling up means a bigger instance size, more CPU and memory. Scaling out means more instances, with the load balancer spreading traffic across them, so apps have to be stateless, with sessions and caches in external stores.
X: For scaling out, you can go two ways. Autoscale rules, through Azure Monitor, scale based on metrics like CPU percentage, memory, or HTTP queue length, or on schedules, with min, max and default instance counts and cool-down periods. Or automatic scaling, on Premium plans, which the platform manages based on HTTP traffic, with prewarmed instances and a maximum burst, without you writing rules.
X: I also turn on Always On to avoid idle unloading, and turn ARR affinity off for stateless apps, so traffic spreads evenly. People forget that affinity setting a lot.

T: What are managed identities, and system-assigned vs user-assigned?
K: managed identity, system assigned vs user assigned, azure managed identity key vault, defaultazurecredential, no secrets azure
X: So managed identities give Azure resources, like App Service, Functions, Container Apps, AKS workloads and VMs, an identity in Entra ID, so they can authenticate to other Azure services without storing any credentials. Azure manages the identity's credentials and rotates them automatically.
X: They come in two flavours. A system-assigned identity is created for one specific resource and tied to its lifecycle, so when the resource is deleted, the identity goes too. Simple, and good when one resource needs its own permissions. A user-assigned identity is a standalone Azure resource, created separately and attached to one or more resources. It survives resource deletion, can be created and granted permissions before the app is deployed, which helps infrastructure as code, and can be shared, like by all instances of a scaled set of resources. You also need it for things like AKS workload identity and some deployment cases.
X: What I do is grant the identity an Azure RBAC role on the target. Key Vault Secrets User on a Key Vault, Storage Blob Data Contributor on a storage account, or a database user in Azure SQL created from the identity. In .NET, the Azure.Identity library's DefaultAzureCredential, or ManagedIdentityCredential in production, gets tokens automatically. Locally, the same code uses my developer login through Visual Studio or the Azure CLI.
X: End result, no connection string passwords or client secrets in config, nothing to rotate or leak, and access is auditable and revocable through RBAC.
@p17-454
S: azx
D: A
T: Azure RBAC vs Entra ID roles: what is the difference?
K: azure rbac vs entra roles, azure role assignment, owner contributor reader, azure ad roles, scope management group subscription
X: Actually these are two separate role systems that people mix up all the time.
X: Entra ID roles, formerly Azure AD roles, control administration of the directory itself. Managing users, groups, app registrations, licences and identity settings. Examples are Global Administrator, User Administrator, Application Administrator and Security Reader. They apply to the tenant, or to administrative units.
X: Azure RBAC roles control access to Azure resources. Subscriptions, resource groups, and resources like VMs, storage accounts and databases. Built-in roles include Owner, full access including granting access to others. Contributor, which can manage resources but not grant access. Reader. And lots of service-specific roles, like Storage Blob Data Reader or Key Vault Secrets User, which control data-plane access, meaning reading the actual data rather than managing the resource.
X: A role assignment has three parts. A security principal, like a user, group, service principal or managed identity. A role definition, which is a set of allowed actions. And a scope, management group, subscription, resource group or resource. Permissions inherit downward, so a role at the subscription applies to everything in it. Deny assignments and Azure Policy can restrict further.
X: What I do, assign roles to groups, not individuals. Use the narrowest scope and the least powerful role. Use data-plane roles instead of keys. Use Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time, time-limited elevation to powerful roles, with approval. And review assignments regularly.
X: A Global Administrator can elevate themselves to manage all subscriptions, so that role is tightly controlled.

T: App registrations vs enterprise applications in Entra ID: what is the difference?
K: app registration vs enterprise application, service principal entra, register app entra id, client id tenant id, multi tenant app
X: Okay, so when you integrate an app with Entra ID, two objects are involved, and the portal shows them in two places. That's where the confusion comes from.
X: An app registration is the application object, the global definition of the app, living in its home tenant. It has the client id, redirect URIs, supported account types like single-tenant or multi-tenant, certificates and secrets or federated credentials, the API permissions the app requests, scopes and app roles it exposes if it's an API, and token configuration, like optional claims.
X: An enterprise application is the service principal, the local instance of the app in a specific tenant. It's what actually gets access in that tenant. Which users and groups are assigned, whether user assignment is required, admin consent for permissions, single sign-on settings, conditional access, and sign-in logs. For a single-tenant app, there's one app registration and one service principal in the same tenant. For a multi-tenant app, each customer tenant that consents gets its own service principal, all pointing to the one app registration. Gallery apps from vendors, like a SaaS tool, only show up as enterprise applications in your tenant.
X: Practical bits, to restrict an app to certain users, set assignment required on the enterprise application. App roles are defined on the registration and assigned on the enterprise application. And for app credentials, prefer managed identities or federated credentials over client secrets, which expire and leak.
X: In our on-premise platform, Keycloak plays this role, with clients and roles, but the concepts map pretty closely.

T: Azure SQL Database vs Managed Instance vs SQL Server on a VM: how do you choose?
K: azure sql database vs managed instance, sql server on azure vm, azure sql options, migrate sql server to azure, elastic pool
X: So Azure gives you three main ways to run SQL Server workloads.
X: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed, platform-as-a-service database. Each database is independent, with built-in high availability, automatic backups with point-in-time restore, automatic patching, and features like serverless compute, Hyperscale for very large databases, and elastic pools that share resources between lots of databases with varying usage, which suits a database-per-tenant model. But it's missing some instance-level features. Cross-database queries are limited, there's no SQL Agent, CLR is restricted, and you can't touch the file system.
X: Azure SQL Managed Instance is also fully managed, but gives near-complete compatibility with an on-premise SQL Server instance. SQL Agent jobs, cross-database queries, Database Mail, CLR, linked servers, Service Broker, and native backup and restore from on-premise. It's the easiest path for lifting and shifting existing apps that rely on instance features, and it's VNet-integrated by default.
X: SQL Server on Azure VMs gives full control of the OS and SQL Server, any version and feature, including SSIS and SSRS on the same machine. But you manage patching, backups and high availability yourself, with some help from the SQL IaaS extension.
X: My choice, SQL Database for new cloud-native apps. Managed Instance for migrating existing on-premise apps that use instance features, which is honestly how I'd look at our CIRT setup, with a database per study plus a master database [and some cross-database queries]. VMs only when OS access or unsupported features are really needed.

T: DTU vs vCore and serverless in Azure SQL: how do you choose?
K: dtu vs vcore, azure sql serverless, azure sql pricing, auto pause azure sql, hyperscale
X: Okay, Azure SQL Database has two purchasing models.
X: The DTU model bundles CPU, memory and I/O into a single measure, Database Transaction Units, in Basic, Standard and Premium tiers. It's simple and fine for small, predictable databases, but you can't scale compute and storage independently, and it's hard to compare with on-premise hardware.
X: The vCore model lets you pick virtual cores, with memory proportional, and storage separately. It's more transparent, maps to on-premise sizing, and lets you use Azure Hybrid Benefit, bringing existing SQL Server licences for big savings, plus reserved capacity. It has service tiers. General Purpose, for most workloads, with remote storage. Business Critical, with local SSD storage, higher I/O, built-in readable replicas and faster failover. And Hyperscale, which scales storage up to 128 TB, with fast backups and restores, and quickly added read replicas. Hyperscale has become the recommended choice for a lot of new workloads, because its pricing got competitive.
X: Serverless is a compute option in the vCore General Purpose and Hyperscale tiers. It scales automatically between a min and max number of vCores based on load, billed per second for compute used, and in General Purpose it can auto-pause after a period of inactivity, so you only pay for storage. The catch is a delay of up to a minute or so on the first connection after a pause, which can catch people out the first time.
X: So serverless suits dev, test and intermittent workloads, and provisioned vCore suits steady production.
@p17-458
S: azx
D: A
T: What are the Cosmos DB consistency levels?
K: cosmos db consistency levels, session consistency, bounded staleness, eventual consistency cosmos, strong consistency cosmos
X: See, Cosmos DB gives you five consistency levels, trading consistency against latency, availability and throughput, especially with multiple regions.
X: Strong means reads always return the latest committed write, linearisability. Writes have to be acknowledged across regions, so latency is higher, and it's not available with multiple write regions.
X: Bounded staleness means reads can lag behind writes, but by no more than a configured number of versions or a time interval. Within that bound, order is guaranteed. It suits globally distributed apps that need near-strong guarantees.
X: Session is the default and the most popular. Within a client session, identified by a session token, you read your own writes, and reads are monotonic, they never go backwards. Other clients might see slightly older data. That fits most apps, since a user always sees their own changes immediately.
X: Consistent prefix means reads never see out-of-order writes. You might see older data, but never a gap, like seeing update three without update two.
X: Eventual has no ordering guarantee, replicas just converge eventually. Lowest latency, highest throughput, fine for things like like-counts or non-critical data.
X: The level is set on the account, and requests can relax it, but not make it stronger than the account default. Weaker levels also cost fewer request units for reads.
X: For a web app, session is usually right, as long as the session token is passed consistently, which the SDK does inside one client instance. Across instances behind a load balancer, I'd pass the token explicitly when read-your-writes matters. That's an easy one to miss.
@p17-459
S: azx
D: A
T: How do you choose a Cosmos DB partition key, and what are request units?
K: cosmos db partition key, request units, ru cosmos, hot partition cosmos, cross partition query, hierarchical partition key
X: Actually Cosmos DB measures cost and throughput in request units. Every operation costs RUs, based on CPU, memory and I/O. A point read of a 1 KB item by id and partition key costs one RU, writes cost more, and queries cost more depending on how much data they scan. Throughput is provisioned in RU per second, manual or autoscale, or you go serverless and pay per RU consumed. Going over throughput returns 429 errors, which the SDK retries.
X: The partition key is the most important design decision, because it decides how data and throughput get distributed. Items with the same partition key value live in the same logical partition, limited to 20 GB, and logical partitions are spread across physical partitions, each limited to 10,000 RU per second.
X: A good partition key has high cardinality, lots of distinct values. It spreads reads and writes evenly, so no hot keys. And it matches the most frequent queries, so they hit a single partition. A query filtering on the partition key is efficient. One that doesn't becomes a cross-partition query, fanning out to every partition, which costs more RUs and more latency.
X: Let me take an example. In a multi-tenant app, tenantId feels natural, but a huge tenant can go past 20 GB or become hot. Hierarchical partition keys fix that, using tenantId then userId or shipmentId as sub-keys, so a big tenant spreads across partitions while queries by tenant stay targeted.
X: And the partition key can't be changed easily later, so I design it from access patterns first.
@p17-460
S: azx
D: A
T: What is the Cosmos DB change feed, and what is it used for?
K: cosmos change feed, change feed processor, cosmos db trigger azure function, react to cosmos changes, all versions and deletes mode
X: Okay, so the change feed is a persistent, ordered record of changes to items in a Cosmos DB container. By default, in latest version mode, it shows inserts and updates. Each changed item shows up with its latest version, ordered within each partition key. The newer all versions and deletes mode shows every change, including intermediate versions and deletes, within the retention window.
X: How you consume it. The change feed processor in the .NET SDK, which distributes partitions across multiple instances, with a lease container tracking progress for each, so it scales out and resumes after failures. An Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger, which uses the processor internally. Or the pull model, if you want more control.
X: Where it's useful. Event-driven processing, when an order is inserted, trigger downstream actions, like notifications or workflows, so Cosmos becomes a reliable source of events without a separate outbox. Materialised views, keeping a second container partitioned differently for another query pattern, like orders by customer and orders by status. Syncing to other stores, pushing changes to Azure AI Search, a cache, or a data warehouse for analytics. Auditing and data movement, like migrating data with zero downtime.
X: A few things that bite people. Processing is at-least-once, so handlers have to be idempotent. In latest version mode, deletes aren't captured, so soft deletes with a TTL are the usual workaround. And order is only guaranteed within a partition key.

T: How do you secure Azure Blob Storage access: keys, SAS tokens or Entra ID?
K: azure blob sas token, user delegation sas, storage account keys, blob storage security, private endpoint storage, shared key access disabled
X: Honestly the options differ a lot in how safe they are.
X: Storage account keys give full access to the whole account. Anyone with a key can do anything, and rotating them breaks every client using them. I avoid them, and ideally disable shared key authorisation on the account entirely.
X: Shared access signatures, SAS, are URLs with a signed token granting limited access. Specific permissions, like read or write. Specific containers or blobs. A time window. And optionally IP ranges and HTTPS only. They're useful for giving clients direct, temporary access, like a browser uploading a file directly or downloading a report. You get account SAS and service SAS, signed with the account key, and user delegation SAS, signed with credentials from Entra ID. User delegation SAS is the one to use, because it's tied to an identity, can be revoked by revoking the delegation key, and doesn't depend on account keys. And keep SAS tokens short-lived, like 15 minutes.
X: Entra ID with Azure RBAC is the best option for applications. Managed identities with roles like Storage Blob Data Reader or Contributor, scoped to a container. No secrets at all.
X: On top of that, network and data protection. Disable public blob access, use private endpoints or firewall rules, turn on soft delete and versioning for recovery, use immutability policies for compliance data, and enable Defender for Storage to catch malware uploads and unusual access.
@p17-462
S: azx
D: A
T: What are the Azure Storage redundancy options?
K: lrs zrs grs gzrs, storage redundancy azure, geo redundant storage, read access geo redundant, storage failover
X: So Azure Storage always keeps multiple copies of data, and the redundancy option decides where those copies live.
X: Locally redundant storage, LRS, keeps three copies within a single data centre in one region. Cheapest, protects against disk and server failures, but not a data centre or zone outage.
X: Zone-redundant storage, ZRS, keeps three copies across three availability zones in the region. It survives a whole zone going down, with data still readable and writable, so it's the recommended option for high availability within a region.
X: Geo-redundant storage, GRS, keeps three copies with LRS in the primary region and replicates asynchronously to a paired secondary region, which also keeps three copies with LRS. It protects against a regional disaster, but since replication is async, recent writes might be lost, and you measure that by the last sync time.
X: Geo-zone-redundant storage, GZRS, combines ZRS in the primary region with geo-replication to the secondary, giving the best durability and availability.
X: Read-access variants, RA-GRS and RA-GZRS, let apps read from the secondary region any time, even when the primary is healthy, which helps read availability during an outage.
X: If the primary region fails, Microsoft may start a failover, or customers can trigger a customer-managed failover, which promotes the secondary.
X: I'd go with ZRS for most production data, and GZRS or RA-GZRS for critical data that needs regional disaster recovery. That's usually the conversation I'd have with the team, cost versus how bad losing a region would be.

S: azx
D: A
T: Event Grid vs Event Hubs vs Service Bus: how do you choose?
K: event grid vs event hubs vs service bus, azure messaging services, event grid topics, event hubs kafka, choose azure messaging
X: See, Azure has three main messaging services, each for a different job.
X: Service Bus is an enterprise message broker for commands and business transactions, where every message matters. Queues and topics with subscriptions, at-least-once delivery with peek-lock, dead-letter queues, sessions for ordered processing per key, duplicate detection, scheduled messages, and transactions. It's for order processing, workflows between services, and anything that needs reliable, ordered, transactional messaging.
X: Event Grid is an event routing service for reactive, discrete events, like "a blob was created" or "a resource was deleted", plus custom events from apps. It pushes events to subscribers, like Functions, webhooks, Service Bus or Event Hubs, with filtering, retries with backoff and dead-lettering to storage. It's lightweight, serverless, and lots of Azure services are built-in event sources. It also supports MQTT and pull delivery in namespaces.
X: Event Hubs is a big-data streaming platform for high-volume event ingestion. Telemetry, logs, clickstreams and IoT data, millions of events per second. Events are kept in partitions for a period, and multiple consumer groups read independently and can replay. It speaks the Kafka protocol, so Kafka clients work unchanged, and Capture writes events to storage automatically.
X: How I'd sum it up, Service Bus for high-value messages between services, Event Grid to react to things that happened, Event Hubs for streams of data to analyse. And they're often combined, like Event Grid forwarding blob events into Service Bus for reliable processing.
@p17-464
S: azx
D: A
T: How do Service Bus sessions and duplicate detection work?
K: service bus sessions, ordered messages service bus, session id, duplicate detection service bus, message id dedup, fifo azure
X: Okay, Service Bus sessions give you ordered, first-in first-out processing of related messages. Each message has a SessionId, like a shipment id or order id. Messages with the same SessionId are delivered in order, and a session can be locked by only one receiver at a time. So all messages for that shipment get processed sequentially by one consumer, while different sessions are processed in parallel by different consumers. Ordering per entity with horizontal scale, similar to Kafka partition keys or SQS FIFO message groups.
X: Sessions also have session state, a small storage area per session that the receiver can read and update, handy for tracking workflow progress across messages. The queue or subscription has to be created with sessions on, and then every message must have a SessionId. Receivers use a session processor in the SDK, with a setting for max concurrent sessions.
X: Duplicate detection protects against producers sending the same message twice. Like when a send times out and gets retried, but the first send actually succeeded. When it's on for a queue or topic, Service Bus remembers the MessageId of messages received within a time window, up to seven days, and silently drops any new message with the same MessageId. The producer has to set a meaningful, deterministic MessageId, like an event id, not a random one per send. I've seen people miss that and wonder why dedup isn't working.
X: And duplicate detection doesn't help with duplicates on the consumer side, from lock expiry and redelivery, so consumers still need to be idempotent.
@p17-465
S: azx
D: A
T: How do Service Bus topics, subscriptions, filters and dead-lettering work?
K: service bus topic subscription, subscription filters, sql filter service bus, dead letter queue service bus, max delivery count, auto forwarding
X: So a Service Bus topic is for publish-subscribe. Publishers send messages to the topic, and each subscription gets its own copy of every message that matches its filter. Each subscription behaves like a separate queue with its own consumers, so services process events independently.
X: Filters decide which messages a subscription gets. A SQL filter uses a SQL-like expression on message properties, like eventType equals Delivered and region equals EU. A correlation filter matches on properties exactly, and it's more efficient. A subscription can also have actions that modify properties. With no filter, a subscription gets everything. Filtering at the broker means consumers don't receive and throw away irrelevant messages.
X: Dead-lettering. Each queue and subscription has a dead-letter sub-queue. Messages land there when they go over the max delivery count, say after ten failed attempts. When they expire, if dead-lettering on expiration is on. When filter evaluation fails. Or when the consumer explicitly dead-letters a message it knows can't be processed, like invalid data, with a reason and description. Messages in the dead-letter queue stay until someone reads them, so what I do is monitor the dead-letter count with alerts, investigate, fix the cause, and resubmit or discard messages, through Service Bus Explorer in the portal or a tool.
X: Auto-forwarding chains a subscription or queue to another queue or topic, which helps build routing topologies.
X: Our on-premise RabbitMQ setup uses the same ideas, exchanges, bound queues, retry and dead-letter exchanges.

T: Azure Container Apps vs AKS vs App Service: how do you choose?
K: azure container apps vs aks, container apps, aks vs app service, run containers azure, dapr container apps, keda
X: Actually all three can run containers, just at different levels of control and complexity.
X: App Service is a platform for web apps and APIs. It can run code directly, or a single container, or a few with sidecars. It has deployment slots, easy authentication, autoscale and VNet integration. It's the simplest choice for typical web apps and APIs, especially for teams that don't want to deal with container orchestration.
X: Azure Container Apps is a serverless container platform built on Kubernetes, but it doesn't expose Kubernetes to you. You deploy containers, and it gives you ingress with HTTPS, revisions with traffic splitting for blue-green and canary releases, autoscaling with KEDA, including scale to zero, based on HTTP traffic, queue length, Kafka lag or other events. But the team has to operate the cluster. Upgrades, node pools, networking, security and policies. AKS Automatic cuts that down with opinionated defaults.

@p17-467
S: azx
D: A
T: Azure Front Door vs Application Gateway vs Load Balancer vs Traffic Manager?
K: front door vs application gateway, azure load balancer, traffic manager, azure waf, global load balancing azure
X: Okay, Azure has four load balancing services, and they differ by scope and layer.
X: Azure Front Door is global and works at layer 7, HTTP and HTTPS. It's a CDN and global entry point. Requests enter Microsoft's edge network near the user, with TLS termination, caching, path-based routing to backends in multiple regions, health probes with fast failover between regions, and an integrated Web Application Firewall and DDoS protection. It's the front door for global web apps and APIs, and it can reach private backends through Private Link.
X: Application Gateway is regional and works at layer 7. It's a reverse proxy inside a virtual network, with URL path and host-based routing, TLS termination and end-to-end TLS, WAF, cookie-based session affinity, and autoscaling. It fronts web apps in one region, often for VMs, App Service or AKS, where the Application Gateway for Containers option integrates with Kubernetes.
X: Azure Load Balancer is regional or cross-regional and works at layer 4, TCP and UDP. Very fast, high-throughput, protocol-agnostic, for non-HTTP traffic or internal load balancing between VMs. No TLS termination, no URL awareness.
X: Traffic Manager is global and DNS-based. It returns the address of the best endpoint by priority, weight, performance or geography, with health checks. Since it's DNS, failover depends on DNS TTLs and client caching, so it's slower to react.
X: The setup I've seen most is Front Door globally, with WAF, routing to Application Gateway or straight to regional services.

T: What can Azure API Management policies do?
K: api management policies, apim policies, apim rate limit, validate jwt apim, apim transformation, apim backend
X: So Azure API Management is a gateway that sits in front of your APIs, with a developer portal and analytics. Policies are where its real power is. They're XML statements executed on requests and responses, in four sections, inbound, backend, outbound and on-error. You can apply them globally, per product, per API or per operation, and they inherit using the base element.
X: The ones I've used most. Security, validate-jwt to check tokens from Entra ID or any OIDC provider, including audience, issuer and required claims. Header checks or IP filtering. Authentication to backends using managed identity, so backends trust APIM without secrets. And validate-content to check request bodies against schemas. Traffic control, rate-limit and quota per subscription key or any key, like a user id or IP, returning 429 when exceeded, which protects backends. Transformation, rewrite URLs, set or remove headers, convert between JSON and XML, and modify bodies, handy for legacy backends or hiding internal details. Caching, in the built-in cache or external Redis. Routing, set-backend-service to route to different backends based on conditions, with load balancing and circuit breakers across backend pools. Retry policies for resilience. And logging to Application Insights and Event Hubs, with correlation ids.
X: There are also AI gateway policies for Azure OpenAI, like token limits and semantic caching.
X: Products and subscriptions group APIs for different consumers, like internal teams or partners, with different quotas.
X: One rule I stick to, business logic stays out of policies. They're for cross-cutting gateway concerns only.

T: How do VNet integration and private endpoints work for Azure PaaS services?
K: vnet integration, private endpoint azure, private link azure, app service private database, disable public access azure
X: Okay, by default PaaS services like App Service, Azure SQL, Storage, Key Vault and Cosmos DB have public endpoints on the internet. For secure architectures, I keep traffic on private networks, and that uses two features that work together.
X: Private endpoints handle inbound access to a service. A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP from your virtual network, connected to one specific resource, like a storage account or SQL server, through Private Link. Clients in the VNet, or on-premise networks connected through VPN or ExpressRoute, reach the service at that private IP. Then you disable public network access on the service completely. DNS is the key detail. A private DNS zone, like privatelink dot database dot windows dot net, linked to the VNet, makes the normal hostname resolve to the private IP, so connection strings don't change. Honestly, misconfigured DNS is the most common reason connections still go to the public endpoint, or just fail.
X: VNet integration handles outbound traffic from App Service or Functions into a VNet. It lets the app call resources in the VNet, like a database behind a private endpoint, internal APIs or VMs, and route all outbound traffic through the VNet, for example through a firewall with a fixed outbound IP.
X: Put together, the web app uses VNet integration to reach the database's private endpoint, the database has public access turned off, and the web app itself can have a private endpoint too, with Front Door or Application Gateway as the only public entry point.

S: azx
D: A
T: NSG vs Azure Firewall: what is the difference?
K: nsg vs azure firewall, network security group, azure firewall rules, application security groups, hub spoke azure
X: See, both filter network traffic, but at really different levels.
X: Network security groups, NSGs, are basic stateful filters at layers 3 and 4, applied to subnets or network interfaces. Rules allow or deny traffic by source and destination IP or CIDR, port and protocol, with priorities. They can use service tags, like Storage or AzureLoadBalancer, instead of IP ranges, and application security groups, which group VMs by role, like web or database servers, so a rule can say "web servers can talk to database servers on 1433" without listing IPs. NSGs are free, distributed, and good for micro-segmentation inside a VNet. But they don't understand domain names or applications, and they don't inspect traffic.
X: Azure Firewall is a managed, centralised network firewall, usually deployed in a hub VNet, with spoke VNets routing traffic through it using route tables. It supports network rules, application rules with fully qualified domain names, like allowing outbound traffic only to api.github.com, threat intelligence filtering, and NAT rules for inbound traffic. The Premium tier adds TLS inspection, intrusion detection and prevention, and URL filtering. It logs all traffic centrally and is managed with firewall policies across regions. It does cost a lot more though.
X: In practice you use them together. Azure Firewall for central control of traffic between spokes, to the internet, and to on-premise networks, and NSGs for fine-grained filtering within each subnet.

T: What are Azure Policy and management groups used for?
K: azure policy, management groups, governance azure, policy initiative, deny effect, deployifnotexists, compliance azure
X: Actually management groups organise subscriptions into a hierarchy, under the tenant root group. Let me take an example. A root, then Platform, with identity, management and connectivity subscriptions, and Landing Zones, split into Corp and Online, then Sandbox and Decommissioned. Policies and role assignments applied to a management group are inherited by all subscriptions and resources under it, so governance gets applied once, consistently.
X: Azure Policy evaluates resources against rules and enforces standards. Each policy definition has a condition and an effect. Deny blocks non-compliant resources from being created or updated, like storage accounts that allow public access. Audit flags non-compliance without blocking. Modify and Append change requests, like adding required tags. DeployIfNotExists automatically deploys a related resource, like diagnostic settings sending logs to Log Analytics, or Defender for a resource type. And DenyAction blocks specific actions, like deleting critical resources.
X: Initiatives group lots of policies, like the Microsoft cloud security benchmark or regulatory standards. The compliance dashboard shows non-compliant resources across the estate, and remediation tasks fix existing resources for Modify and DeployIfNotExists policies. Exemptions handle justified exceptions, with expiry dates.
X: Common policies I've seen, allowed regions, required tags, allowed SKUs, enforcing HTTPS and TLS versions, requiring private endpoints, and disabling local authentication on services.
X: Together with landing zones, this is how organisations let teams move fast but still stay inside the guardrails.

T: How do Bicep modules and what-if deployments work?
K: bicep modules, bicep what if, deployment stacks, bicep parameters file, azure deployment validation
X: Okay, so Bicep is Azure's domain-specific language for infrastructure as code. It compiles to ARM templates, but it's much more readable, with type safety and good tooling.
X: Modules let you break infrastructure into reusable pieces. A module is just another Bicep file with parameters and outputs, like a storage account module that enforces our standards, TLS 1.2 minimum, no public access, a private endpoint and diagnostics. The main file calls modules with parameters and wires up outputs, like passing a Key Vault id into an app module. Modules can be shared through a private Bicep registry in Azure Container Registry, versioned, and Azure Verified Modules give you well-maintained, Microsoft-supported modules for most resources.
X: Parameter files, in the .bicepparam format, hold environment-specific values, like dev, test and prod, with the same template for all environments. Secrets are referenced from Key Vault, never stored in files.
X: What-if is a preview of a deployment. az deployment group what-if shows what will be created, modified and deleted, plus property-level differences, without changing anything. I run it in pull request pipelines and before production deployments, kind of like Terraform plan. It can be noisy for some resource properties, so reviewers kind of learn to read through it.
X: Deployment stacks manage a group of resources as a unit, so resources removed from the template can be deleted or detached automatically, and deny settings protect managed resources from changes outside the stack.
X: The Bicep linter and policy checks round off the pipeline.

T: How do you use Key Vault references and App Configuration in .NET apps?
K: key vault references app service, azure app configuration, feature flags azure, configuration refresh dotnet, sentinel key
X: So two services work together for configuration in Azure.
X: Key Vault references let App Service and Functions app settings point to secrets instead of holding them. An app setting value that starts with at-Microsoft-dot-KeyVault and gives the secret URI is resolved by the platform using the app's managed identity, and the app just reads a normal setting. Without a version in the URI, it picks up the latest version of the secret, refreshed periodically. So the code doesn't change, and secrets never show up in configuration or pipelines.
X: Azure App Configuration is a central store for app settings and feature flags, shared across services and environments. Keys can have labels, like dev or prod, and the .NET configuration provider loads them into IConfiguration, alongside appsettings.json, so options classes just work. App Configuration can also hold Key Vault references, which the provider resolves with the app's identity.
X: Dynamic refresh, the provider can watch settings and reload them without restarting the app. The usual pattern is a sentinel key. The app checks just one key periodically, and when it changes, all settings reload, so a set of related changes lands together. IOptionsSnapshot or IOptionsMonitor then gives the code the new values.
X: Feature flags, the Microsoft.FeatureManagement library reads flags from App Configuration, with filters for percentage rollouts, targeting specific users or groups, and time windows. So features get turned on without deployments and can be switched off quickly if something goes wrong.
X: And access uses managed identities with data reader roles, not connection strings. In our team that's pretty much non-negotiable.

D: A
T: How do you query logs with KQL in Log Analytics?
K: kql query, kusto query language, log analytics workspace, application insights query, kql summarize, find exceptions kql
X: Honestly KQL is one of my favourite tools. Log Analytics workspaces collect logs from Azure Monitor, Application Insights, VMs, containers and more, and KQL, the Kusto Query Language, is how you query them. It reads like a pipeline, you start with a table and pipe it through operators.
X: Let me take a spike in failures in a web API, using Application Insights tables.
X: I start with AppRequests, filter where TimeGenerated is within the last hour and Success is false, then summarize the count by five-minute bins and ResultCode, and render a timechart. That shows when failures started and which status codes.
X: Then the top failing operations. AppRequests where Success is false, summarize the failure count by OperationName, and take the top 10.
X: Then exceptions. AppExceptions, summarize the count by ProblemId and OuterMessage, which groups identical exceptions together.
X: To trace one request across components, I union AppRequests, AppDependencies, AppExceptions and AppTraces, filter where OperationId equals the id, and order by TimeGenerated. Everything sharing that operation id is one end-to-end transaction.
X: For latency, summarize the 50th, 95th and 99th percentiles of DurationMs by OperationName.
X: Other operators I use a lot, extend to compute columns, project to pick columns, join to combine tables, parse and extract for text, and mv-expand for arrays. Custom dimensions from structured logging sit in a dynamic Properties column, which you read by converting, say, Properties dot TenantId to a string.
X: Queries can become alert rules, or get pinned to workbooks and dashboards. And the same KQL works in Azure Data Explorer, Microsoft Sentinel and Fabric.

T: How do Azure Monitor alerts and action groups work?
K: azure monitor alerts, action groups, log search alert, metric alert azure, alert processing rules, smart detection
X: See, Azure Monitor alerts notify people or trigger automation when something in the monitoring data needs attention.
X: You've got a few kinds. Metric alerts evaluate platform or custom metrics at short intervals, like CPU above 80 percent for 10 minutes, HTTP 5xx count, or Service Bus dead-letter messages above zero. They support dynamic thresholds, which learn normal patterns and alert on deviations, and multiple dimensions, like one alert per instance. Log search alerts run a KQL query on a schedule, like failed requests for a specific operation above a threshold, so you can do complex conditions across tables. Activity log alerts fire on control-plane events, like a resource getting deleted or a service health incident in your region. Application Insights also has smart detection for anomalies like failure rate spikes.
X: Action groups define what happens. Email, SMS, push or voice notifications. Webhooks. Azure Functions, Logic Apps or Automation runbooks for automatic remediation. And integrations with ITSM tools, or Teams and incident management tools through webhooks. One action group can be reused by lots of alerts, like a production on-call group.
X: Alert processing rules suppress notifications during planned maintenance windows, or add action groups to alerts at scale.
X: What I've learned, alert on symptoms users actually feel, like errors and latency, not every resource metric. Set severity levels properly, so only severity zero and one wake people up at night. Put links to runbooks and dashboards in alert descriptions. And review noisy alerts regularly, otherwise people just start ignoring them.

A single, long-lived ConnectionMultiplexer per app, because creating connections per request is a classic cause of timeouts. Sensible timeouts and retries. Monitoring server load, memory, evictions and connected clients. And designing for the cache being briefly unavailable, falling back to the database instead of failing.

T: How do you design for high availability and disaster recovery in Azure?
K: availability zones azure, paired regions, azure disaster recovery, zone redundant, rto rpo azure, sql failover group
X: Actually HA and DR in Azure work at two levels, zones within a region, and regions.
X: Availability zones are physically separate data centres within a region, with independent power, cooling and networking. Zone-redundant services spread instances across zones automatically. Zone-redundant App Service plans, Azure SQL zone redundancy, ZRS storage, zone-redundant Service Bus Premium, AKS node pools across zones, and so on. That protects against a data centre failure with very little effort, and it's my default for production.
X: Regions protect against a whole-region outage. Lots of regions have a paired region, used for geo-redundant storage replication and staggered platform updates, though newer regions may not have pairs, so you pick the secondary region yourself.
X: DR patterns, roughly by cost and recovery time. Backup and restore to another region, with hours of recovery time. Pilot light or warm standby, with data replicated and minimal compute ready to scale up. And active-active, with traffic in both regions through Front Door, for near-zero downtime.
X: Data replication is honestly the hard part. Azure SQL failover groups with a listener endpoint that stays the same after failover. Cosmos DB multi-region with automatic failover. GZRS storage. And Service Bus geo-replication.
X: It all starts from the business's RTO and RPO, how long can the system be down, and how much data can we lose. Infrastructure as code makes rebuilding possible, and DR has to be tested regularly with real failovers, not just on paper.

T: How do you secure CI/CD connections from Azure DevOps to Azure without secrets?
K: workload identity federation, azure devops service connection oidc, federated credentials, service principal secret expiry, github actions azure oidc
X: Okay, traditionally Azure DevOps service connections to Azure used a service principal with a client secret. Secrets expire, usually every year or two, which breaks pipelines out of nowhere, and they can leak, giving attackers access to deploy or change resources.
X: Workload identity federation removes the secret completely. It uses OpenID Connect. Azure DevOps issues a short-lived token for each pipeline run, identifying the organisation, project and service connection. In Entra ID, the app registration or user-assigned managed identity has a federated credential that trusts tokens from Azure DevOps with that specific issuer and subject. The pipeline exchanges the token for an Azure access token that's only valid for that run. Nothing long-lived is stored anywhere.
X: Setting it up, you create a service connection using the workload identity federation option, either automatic, where Azure DevOps creates the identity and federated credential, or manual, using an existing identity. Then assign Azure RBAC roles to the identity, scoped narrowly, like Contributor on one resource group, not the whole subscription. Existing secret-based connections can be converted.
X: GitHub Actions works the same way, with federated credentials trusting tokens for a specific repository, branch or environment.
X: Extra controls I'd add, separate service connections per environment, with production ones needing approvals and checks, and restricted to specific pipelines and branches.
X: For on-premise Azure DevOps Server, like our setup, federation depends on the version and network reachability, so we follow the same least-privilege idea with whatever the server supports.

T: Azure Files vs Blob Storage: when do you use each?

X: Blob Storage is object storage, accessed over HTTPS APIs and SDKs. It's for unstructured data at scale. T: What is AKS workload identity, and how do pods access Azure resources?

X: Actually the right way now is Microsoft Entra Workload ID, which replaced the deprecated pod-managed identity. Pods in AKS often need Key Vault, Storage or Azure SQL, and this is how they get in without secrets.
X: How it works. The AKS cluster has an OIDC issuer turned on. X: The cluster has its own identities too. The control plane identity, and the kubelet identity, which pulls images from Azure Container Registry and should only get the AcrPull role. In my experience people over-grant that one.

T: What is Azure SignalR Service, and when do you need it?
K: azure signalr service, real time azure, scale signalr, signalr backplane, websockets azure, web pubsub
X: So SignalR is ASP.NET Core's library for real-time communication, pushing messages from server to clients over WebSockets, with fallbacks. Self-hosted SignalR has a scaling problem though. Each client is connected to one server instance, so to send a message to all users, or to a user connected to a different instance, the servers need a backplane, like Redis, and load balancers need sticky sessions. Each server also holds lots of open connections, which eats resources.
X: Azure SignalR Service fixes that. It's a managed service that holds all the client connections. The app servers connect to the service and send messages through it, so the service handles fan-out to the right clients, no matter which app instance sends the message. No backplane, no sticky sessions, and app servers don't hold thousands of connections anymore. It scales to very large numbers of concurrent connections through units. Integration is mostly configuration, you call AddSignalR and then chain AddAzureSignalR onto it.
X: It also has a serverless mode, used with Azure Functions bindings, where functions send messages through the service without any hub server. That suits event-driven notifications, like pushing a status update to a user when a background process finishes.
X: Azure Web PubSub is a related service for plain WebSocket clients, without the SignalR protocol, useful for non-.NET clients and other frameworks.
X: For me the use cases are live dashboards, notifications, collaborative editing, chat and progress updates. Authentication uses access tokens, and user ids let you target specific users and groups.

T: What is Conditional Access and Privileged Identity Management in Entra ID?
K: conditional access, pim, privileged identity management, mfa policy entra, just in time admin access, zero trust azure
X: Okay, both are key Entra ID security features, part of a zero trust approach.
X: Conditional Access is Entra's policy engine for sign-ins. Policies are if-then rules, if a sign-in matches certain conditions, then enforce controls. Conditions include which users or groups, which apps, the sign-in risk and user risk detected by Identity Protection, the device platform, whether the device is compliant or joined, the location, like trusted office networks or countries, and the client app. Controls include requiring MFA, requiring phishing-resistant MFA like passkeys for admins, requiring a compliant device, forcing a password change for risky users, limiting session lifetime, or just blocking access. Common policies, MFA for everyone, block legacy authentication, stronger requirements for administrators, and block access from unexpected countries. Report-only mode lets you test policies before enforcing them.
X: Privileged Identity Management handles privileged roles, both Entra roles and Azure resource roles. Instead of permanent admin assignments, users are eligible for a role and activate it just in time, for a limited duration, like two hours, with MFA, a justification, a ticket number, and optionally approval from someone else. Activations are audited and alerts can be raised. Access reviews regularly ask owners to confirm whether people still need their roles, which clears out stale access.
X: Put together, they cut the risk of stolen credentials a lot. Even a compromised account has no standing admin rights, and risky sign-ins get challenged or blocked. I'd say that's the bit to stress in an interview.

@p17-490
S: dkx
D: A
T: Resource requests vs limits in Kubernetes: what is the difference?
K: requests vs limits, kubernetes resources, qos class, guaranteed burstable besteffort, cpu request memory limit
X: Actually every container in a pod can declare requests and limits for CPU and memory, and they do quite different jobs.
X: Requests are what the container is guaranteed. The scheduler uses them to place pods. A node only accepts a pod if the sum of requests on it fits the node's allocatable capacity. So requests decide where pods go and how many fit on a node. Too low, and nodes get overpacked and pods fight for resources. Too high, and you're paying for idle capacity.
X: Limits are the ceiling. For memory, if a container goes over its limit, the kernel kills it, and you see OOMKilled. For CPU, a container over its limit isn't killed, it's throttled, which shows up as latency. That difference trips people up a lot.
X: Together they decide the pod's quality of service class. Guaranteed, when requests equal limits for every container, and those pods are the last to be evicted under node pressure. Burstable, when requests are lower than limits. BestEffort, when nothing is set, and those go first.
X: My defaults for a .NET API, memory request and limit set to the same value, based on observed usage plus headroom, because memory isn't compressible. A CPU request based on typical usage, and often no CPU limit, or a generous one, to avoid throttling. Then I check actual usage in metrics and adjust, because the first guesses are usually wrong.
@p17-491
S: dkx
D: A
T: A pod keeps getting OOMKilled. How do you troubleshoot it?
K: oomkilled, exit code 137, pod out of memory, container memory limit exceeded, dotnet memory kubernetes
X: Okay, OOMKilled means the container used more memory than its limit and the kernel killed it. kubectl describe pod shows the last state as OOMKilled with exit code 137, and the restart count keeps climbing.
X: One thing I always check first is whether it's a real leak or just a limit that's too low. I look at the container's memory graph over time, in Prometheus or Container Insights. A sawtooth that climbs steadily until the kill, after every restart, points to a leak. A sudden spike points to one big operation, like loading a large file or a huge query result into memory. A flat line just under the limit means the limit is simply too tight for normal work.
X: For .NET specifically, the runtime reads the container's memory limit and sizes the GC heap from it, but if the limit is really small, server GC with many heaps can still push close to it. Options are setting GCHeapHardLimitPercent, using workstation GC for small containers, or just giving a realistic limit.
X: If it's a leak, I reproduce it, take a memory dump with dotnet-dump or dotnet-gcdump before the kill, and look for what's growing. Caches without expiry, static collections, event handlers not removed, or undisposed objects.
X: For spikes, I stream instead of buffering, page large queries, and limit concurrency of heavy jobs.
X: Only after I understand the cause do I raise the limit. And I set an alert on memory near the limit, so we hear about it before the kills start, not after.
@p17-492
S: dkx
D: A
T: Why is my container being CPU throttled, and what do you do about it?
K: cpu throttling kubernetes, cfs quota, cpu limit latency, throttled container, remove cpu limits
X: So CPU limits in Kubernetes are enforced by the Linux CFS quota. The CPU limit gets converted into a time budget per 100-millisecond period. A limit of 500m means the container can use 50 milliseconds of CPU time in each 100-millisecond window. If it burns that early, say because several threads run in parallel, it's paused until the next window. That's throttling.
X: The symptom is really confusing. Average CPU looks fine, maybe 40 percent of the limit, but latency spikes, especially p99. Multi-threaded runtimes like .NET make it worse, because GC and the thread pool can burn the budget in one short burst. The metric to check is container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total compared with total periods. A high throttled ratio confirms it.
X: Fixes, depending on the situation. Raise the CPU limit, or remove CPU limits for latency-sensitive services and rely on requests, which still guarantee a fair share, because CPU is compressible and unused CPU on the node is otherwise just wasted. A lot of teams now keep memory limits but drop CPU limits. Also make sure the runtime sees a sensible CPU count. .NET uses the limit to size the thread pool and GC heaps, and DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT can be set if needed.
X: And if CPU is genuinely saturated, then honestly the real fix is scaling out with the HPA or optimising the hot code path. No setting will save you there.
