T: How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler work, and which metrics should it use?
K: hpa, horizontal pod autoscaler, scale on custom metrics, hpa behavior, metrics server, autoscaling v2
X: Okay, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of replicas of a Deployment based on metrics. Every 15 seconds or so, it compares the current metric with the target and works out the desired replicas. Current replicas times current value divided by target, within the min and max you set.
X: CPU utilisation is the classic metric, measured as a percentage of the pod's CPU request, from the metrics server. So the HPA only works properly if requests are realistic. Memory is usually a poor scaling signal for .NET, because the GC doesn't hand memory back quickly, so pods never scale back in.
X: Better signals are often application metrics. Requests per second per pod, in-flight requests, or queue length for workers. With the autoscaling v2 API, the HPA can use custom metrics through an adapter, like the Prometheus adapter, or external metrics, like the length of a RabbitMQ queue.
X: The behaviour section controls how fast it scales. What I usually do is scale up quickly, say double the pods within a minute, and scale down slowly, with a stabilisation window of five minutes or more, so it doesn't flap when traffic dips for a moment.
X: Things that break it, missing requests, a minReplicas of one in production, which gives you no redundancy, and pods with long startup times, where readiness probes and enough headroom matter, because new pods take time before they actually help.
@p17-494
S: dkx
D: A
T: What is KEDA, and when would you use it instead of a plain HPA?
K: keda, event driven autoscaling, scale to zero, scale on queue length, scaledobject, kafka lag scaling
X: See, KEDA, Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling, is a CNCF project that scales workloads based on event sources. It installs as an operator, and you describe scaling with a ScaledObject that points at a Deployment and lists triggers.
X: Under the hood, KEDA feeds external metrics into a normal HPA, so it doesn't replace the HPA, it makes it smarter. It has scalers for dozens of sources. RabbitMQ queue length, Kafka consumer lag, Azure Service Bus, AWS SQS, Redis lists, Prometheus queries, cron schedules, databases and more.
X: It adds two things the plain HPA can't easily do. One is scaling to zero. When there are no messages, KEDA scales the worker to zero replicas, and when a message arrives, it activates the deployment again. Great for background workers that sit idle most of the day. The other is scaling on the real backlog instead of CPU. A queue worker might be mostly waiting on I/O, so CPU stays low even with thousands of messages waiting. Scaling on queue length per replica, like one pod per 100 messages, matches the actual work.
X: KEDA also has ScaledJobs, which start a Kubernetes Job per batch of events, good for long-running tasks.
X: Things to watch. Scale-to-zero adds a cold start delay, the target value needs tuning, and consumers have to handle being stopped mid-work, so graceful shutdown and idempotent processing still matter.
@p17-495
S: dkx
D: A
T: Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter vs VPA: what does each scale?
K: cluster autoscaler, karpenter, vertical pod autoscaler, node autoscaling, vpa, pending pods scale nodes
X: Actually you can scale three different things in Kubernetes, and each tool handles one of them.
X: The HPA scales the number of pods. But if new pods don't fit on any node, they just sit Pending, so you also need node scaling.
X: Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes. It watches for pods that can't be scheduled because of insufficient resources, and adds nodes to a node group, like an AWS Auto Scaling group or an AKS node pool. It also removes underused nodes when their pods can be moved elsewhere. It works with predefined node groups, so you decide the instance types up front.
X: Karpenter, which started at AWS and is used more widely now, is a more flexible node provisioner. Instead of fixed node groups, it looks at the pending pods' requirements, like CPU, memory, architecture, zone, and spot or on-demand, and launches the best-fitting instance directly, often within a minute. It also consolidates, replacing several half-empty nodes with fewer, cheaper ones. On EKS it's become the common choice, and EKS Auto Mode uses it under the hood.
X: The Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts a pod's requests and limits based on observed usage. I find it most useful for recommendations, running in recommendation-only mode to right-size requests. Applying changes used to need pod restarts, though in-place resizing is arriving. And VPA and HPA shouldn't both act on CPU for the same workload, they'll fight each other.
@p17-496
S: dkx
D: A
T: What is a PodDisruptionBudget, and why does it matter?
K: pod disruption budget, pdb, voluntary disruption, node drain, minavailable maxunavailable, cluster upgrade downtime
X: Okay, so a PodDisruptionBudget protects an app's availability during voluntary disruptions. Voluntary means planned actions, like draining a node for an upgrade, the cluster autoscaler or Karpenter removing a node, or someone running kubectl drain. Involuntary ones, like a node crashing, aren't covered.
X: A PDB selects pods by label and says either minAvailable, like at least two pods must stay running, or maxUnavailable, like at most one pod can be down at a time. When a drain tries to evict pods, the eviction API checks the budget and refuses evictions that would break it. The drain then waits and retries, so pods move one at a time and the service stays up.
X: Without a PDB, a node drain can evict all replicas of a service at once if they happen to sit on the same node, or a rolling node upgrade can take down too many replicas together. Then you get an outage during routine maintenance, which is embarrassing.
X: Some practical rules. A PDB only helps if you have more than one replica, so production services run at least two or three, spread across nodes and zones. Don't set minAvailable equal to the replica count, or maxUnavailable to zero, because then the node can never be drained and upgrades get stuck. And pods failing readiness count as unavailable, so an unhealthy deployment can block drains too.
X: My approach is to add a PDB to every production Deployment as part of the Helm chart.
@p17-497
S: dkx
D: A
T: Ingress vs Gateway API in Kubernetes: what is the difference?
K: ingress vs gateway api, ingress controller, httproute, gatewayclass, ingress nginx retirement, kubernetes routing
X: So both expose HTTP services from inside the cluster to the outside, but they're different generations.
X: Ingress is the original API. An Ingress resource lists host and path rules, like api.example.com slash shipments going to the shipments service, plus TLS settings. It needs an ingress controller to actually do the work, like ingress-nginx, Traefik, or a cloud load balancer controller. Its weakness is the API is small, so anything advanced, like rewrites, timeouts, canary weights or header-based routing, goes into controller-specific annotations, which aren't portable and are easy to get wrong. The community ingress-nginx controller has also been announced for retirement in 2026, so lots of teams are planning migrations.
X: Gateway API is the newer, official successor, and it's generally available now. It splits responsibilities into roles. A GatewayClass is defined by the infrastructure provider. A Gateway, owned by the platform team, describes the listeners, ports and certificates. HTTPRoutes, owned by app teams, attach to a Gateway and describe routing. Path and header matching, traffic splitting by weight for canaries, redirects, rewrites and timeouts, all as first-class fields instead of annotations. There are also GRPCRoute and TLSRoute types, and cross-namespace references with explicit permission.
X: For a new cluster, I'd go with Gateway API, because it's more expressive, portable across implementations, and that's where the ecosystem is heading. For existing Ingress setups, I'd migrate gradually, since both can run side by side.
@p17-498
S: dkx
D: A
T: StatefulSet vs Deployment: when do you need a StatefulSet?
K: statefulset vs deployment, stateful workloads kubernetes, stable network identity, persistent volume claim template, headless service
X: Honestly the simple way to put it is a Deployment is for stateless pods. All replicas are interchangeable, they get random names, they can be created and killed in any order, and if they use storage, they usually share it or don't need it. Web APIs and workers are Deployments.
X: A StatefulSet is for workloads where each replica has its own identity and data. It gives you three guarantees. Stable names, pods are named app-0, app-1, app-2, and keep those names when rescheduled. Stable network identity, with a headless service each pod gets its own DNS name, like app-0.app.namespace.svc, so peers can find each other. Stable storage, volumeClaimTemplates create a separate persistent volume for each pod, and that volume follows the pod when it moves to another node. It also starts, scales and updates pods in order, one at a time, by default.
X: That's what clustered systems need. Databases like PostgreSQL with replicas, Kafka brokers, RabbitMQ clusters, Elasticsearch, Redis with persistence, or ZooKeeper, where each member has to know who it is and keep its own data.
X: In practice, I'd think twice before running databases on Kubernetes at all. Managed services like RDS, Azure SQL or a managed message broker take away a lot of operational work. If we do run stateful systems in the cluster, I'd use a mature operator, like CloudNativePG or the RabbitMQ cluster operator, which handles failover, backups and upgrades on top of StatefulSets.
@p17-499
S: dkx
D: A
T: What are DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs used for?
K: daemonset, kubernetes job, cronjob, run task once kubernetes, scheduled job kubernetes, node agent
X: See, besides Deployments, Kubernetes has workload types for other patterns.
X: A DaemonSet runs one copy of a pod on every node, or on a selected set of nodes. When a node joins the cluster, the pod gets added automatically. It's for node-level agents. Log collectors like Fluent Bit, monitoring agents like the node exporter or the OpenTelemetry collector in agent mode, network plugins, storage drivers and security agents.
X: A Job runs pods until a task completes successfully, instead of keeping them running forever. It has settings for completions, parallelism, a backoffLimit for retries, an activeDeadlineSeconds timeout, and a ttlSecondsAfterFinished to clean up. It's for one-off work, like a database migration before a release, a data backfill, or generating a report.
X: A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule using cron syntax, with a time zone field. Useful settings, concurrencyPolicy set to Forbid, so a new run doesn't start while the previous one is still going. startingDeadlineSeconds, so missed runs after downtime don't pile up. And history limits for successful and failed jobs.
X: A few lessons I've picked up. Jobs and CronJobs have to be idempotent, because a pod can be retried or, rarely, run twice. The container must exit with a non-zero code on failure, or Kubernetes thinks it succeeded. And for business schedules, the logic is the same as our Quartz jobs on-premise. The schedule triggers the job, but the job itself has to be safe to rerun.
@p17-500
S: dkx
D: A
T: What are init containers and sidecar containers?
K: init container, sidecar container, native sidecar, restartpolicy always init, multi container pod
X: Okay, a pod can have more than one container, and two patterns come up a lot.
X: Init containers run before the main containers start, one after another, and each has to finish successfully. If one fails, the pod restarts it until it succeeds. They're for setup tasks. Waiting for a dependency to be reachable, downloading config or certificates, running a schema check, or setting file permissions on a shared volume. Since they're separate images, they can carry tools you don't want in the main app image.
X: Sidecar containers run next to the main container for the pod's whole life, adding a capability without changing the app. Like a log shipper reading log files from a shared volume, a service mesh proxy like Envoy, an OpenTelemetry collector, or a proxy that refreshes credentials.
X: Historically, sidecars were just extra regular containers, and that caused problems. No guarantee they started before the app, and in Jobs, the sidecar kept running after the main container finished, so the Job never completed. Kubernetes now has native sidecars, stable since version 1.33. You declare them as init containers with restartPolicy Always. They start before the main containers, keep running, get restarted if they crash, and shut down after the main containers stop, which fixes both problems.
X: I keep the number of containers per pod small, though, because every container adds resource requests and complexity. Pretty much my rule of thumb.
@p17-501
S: dkx
D: A
T: What are Kubernetes NetworkPolicies, and how do you use them?
K: network policy kubernetes, default deny, pod to pod traffic, namespace isolation, calico cilium, zero trust kubernetes
X: So by default, every pod in a Kubernetes cluster can talk to every other pod, in any namespace. Convenient, but it means a compromised pod can reach everything, including databases and internal admin services.
X: A NetworkPolicy restricts traffic to and from selected pods. It selects pods by label and lists allowed ingress sources and egress destinations, by pod labels, namespace labels or IP blocks, plus ports. Once any policy selects a pod for a direction, everything not explicitly allowed in that direction is denied.
X: Policies need a network plugin that enforces them, like Calico, Cilium, or the cloud provider's implementation. Without one, the objects are accepted but do nothing, which is a dangerous surprise.
X: My usual approach per namespace, start with a default deny for ingress, and often egress, for all pods. Then add explicit allows. The ingress controller can reach the API pods on port 8080. The API can reach the database or Redis on their ports. The worker can reach the message broker. Egress rules also have to allow DNS to the cluster DNS service, or nothing works at all. That's the most common mistake, people forget DNS.
X: I roll it out carefully, in audit or logging mode first where the plugin supports it, and test traffic paths in staging, because a wrong policy just shows up as mysterious timeouts.
X: For richer rules, like by DNS name or HTTP path, Cilium and service meshes offer extended policies.
@p17-502
S: dkx
D: A
T: How does RBAC work in Kubernetes?
K: kubernetes rbac, role vs clusterrole, rolebinding, service account permissions, least privilege kubernetes, kubectl auth can-i
X: Actually Kubernetes RBAC controls who can do what with the Kubernetes API, and it's built from four objects.
X: A Role lists permissions within one namespace. Which API groups, which resources, like pods, deployments or secrets, and which verbs, like get, list, watch, create, update or delete. A ClusterRole is the same but cluster-wide, or reusable across namespaces. A RoleBinding grants a Role or ClusterRole to subjects within one namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding grants a ClusterRole across the whole cluster.
X: Subjects are users, groups or service accounts. Kubernetes doesn't store users itself. Humans come from the identity provider, like Entra ID on AKS or IAM on EKS through access entries, mapped to groups. Workloads use service accounts.
X: How I apply least privilege. Developers get read access in their team's namespaces, with no access to secrets in production. Deployment pipelines get a service account that can update deployments in specific namespaces only. App pods get their own service account with no API permissions at all, unless they genuinely need them, and automountServiceAccountToken set to false otherwise. Cluster-admin is kept for a small platform group, ideally with just-in-time access.
X: One thing to watch, permission to read secrets, create pods or exec into pods is very powerful, because it can lead to reading any secret in the namespace. So I treat those verbs as sensitive.
X: kubectl auth can-i, with the as flag, is the quick way to check what a subject can do.
@p17-503
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you share a cluster between teams with namespaces, ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges?
K: namespaces multi tenancy, resourcequota, limitrange, team isolation kubernetes, namespace per team
X: Okay, namespaces are the basic unit for sharing a cluster. Each team or app gets its own namespaces, often one per environment, and namespaces give you separate names, RBAC boundaries, policies and quotas.
X: ResourceQuotas cap the total resources a namespace can use. Total CPU and memory requests and limits, number of pods, services, load balancers, persistent volume claims and storage. It stops one team's runaway deployment or a bad HPA setting from eating the whole cluster. Once a quota covers CPU or memory, every pod in that namespace has to declare requests and limits, or it gets rejected.
X: LimitRanges set per-container rules within a namespace. Default requests and limits applied when a container doesn't specify them, plus min and max values. That makes the quota work smoothly and catches containers asking for absurd amounts.
X: Together with RBAC per namespace, NetworkPolicies with default deny, and Pod Security admission labels, this gives you soft multi-tenancy, which is fine for teams within one company who reasonably trust each other.
X: It isn't strong isolation, though. All namespaces share the same nodes, kernel and control plane. For hostile or strongly regulated tenants, I'd go with separate node pools with taints, separate clusters, or virtual clusters.
X: I also label namespaces with owner and cost centre, so cost tools can show each team its share of the cluster. That makes the cost conversation way less awkward.
@p17-504
S: dkx
D: A
T: What is Helm, and how do charts, values and releases work?
K: helm chart, helm values, helm release, helm upgrade rollback, helm template, kubernetes package manager
X: So Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. Instead of maintaining loads of raw YAML files per environment, you write a chart once and install it with different values.
X: A chart is a folder with a Chart.yaml for metadata and version, a values.yaml with default settings, and a templates folder with Kubernetes manifests written as Go templates, like a Deployment whose replica count, image tag, resources and environment variables come from values. Charts can depend on other charts, and helpers in an underscore-helpers file avoid repetition, like standard labels.
X: Installing a chart creates a release, a named instance in a namespace. helm upgrade with the install flag applies a new version with new values, and Helm keeps a history of release revisions, stored as secrets in the cluster, so helm rollback can go back to a previous revision quickly. The atomic flag rolls back automatically if the upgrade fails, and the wait flag waits for resources to become ready.
X: Per environment, I keep small values files, like values-dev and values-prod, that only override what's different. Replica counts, resource sizes, hostnames and feature flags. Secrets don't go in values files, they come from a secrets manager.
X: Habits I'd recommend, run helm lint and helm template in CI to render and validate manifests before deploying. Version charts properly. Publish charts to an OCI registry. And keep templates simple, because heavy template logic gets really hard to read and debug. I've seen charts nobody wanted to touch.
@p17-505
S: dkx
D: A
T: Helm vs Kustomize: how do you choose?
K: helm vs kustomize, kustomize overlays, kubernetes configuration management, templating vs patching
X: Okay, both solve the same problem, managing Kubernetes manifests across environments, just in different ways.
X: Helm uses templating. Manifests have placeholders and logic, and values fill them in. It's a full package manager. Charts are versioned, published to registries, have dependencies, and installations are tracked as releases with history and rollback. It's the standard way to distribute software for others to install, like ingress controllers, cert-manager or monitoring stacks. The downside is templates can get hard to read, with lots of conditionals and indentation functions.
X: Kustomize uses patching, no templates. You write plain, valid Kubernetes YAML as a base, then overlays per environment that patch it. Change replicas, add a resource limit, set an image tag, add labels or generate ConfigMaps. It's built into kubectl, kubectl apply with the k flag. It's simple, transparent and easy to review, because what you see is real YAML. But no packaging, versioning or release history, and complex variations turn into lots of patch files.
X: How I'd choose. For third-party software, I use the vendor's Helm chart. For our own services, either works honestly. A team with many similar microservices benefits from one shared Helm chart with per-service values. A team that prefers plain YAML and GitOps might like Kustomize. And they combine well, Kustomize can render a Helm chart and then patch it, and Argo CD supports both.
@p17-506
S: dkx
D: A
T: What is GitOps, and how do Argo CD or Flux work?
K: gitops, argo cd, flux, pull based deployment, desired state git, drift detection kubernetes
X: See, GitOps means Git is the single source of truth for what should run in the cluster. Instead of a pipeline pushing changes into the cluster with kubectl or helm commands, an agent running inside the cluster pulls the desired state from a Git repo and keeps making the cluster match it.
X: Argo CD and Flux are the two main tools. In Argo CD, you define an Application that points to a repo path, a Helm chart or Kustomize folder, and a target cluster and namespace. Argo CD compares the rendered manifests with what's actually running, shows the difference in a UI, and syncs, automatically or after approval. Flux works similarly with Kustomization and HelmRelease objects, and it's more CLI and controller oriented.
X: Why I like it. Every change is a commit, reviewed in a pull request, so you get an audit trail and easy rollback by reverting. Drift detection, if someone changes something by hand in the cluster, the tool shows it as out of sync and can revert it. Security, CI doesn't need cluster admin credentials, because the cluster pulls changes. And disaster recovery is simpler, since the whole state can be reapplied to a new cluster.
X: A typical flow. CI builds and tests the image, pushes it, then updates the image tag in the config repo, often through a pull request. Argo CD sees the change and deploys it. Promotion between environments becomes a pull request too, which suits audited environments really well.
@p17-507
S: dkx
D: A
T: How should you tag container images, and why avoid latest?
K: image tagging strategy, latest tag problem, image digest, immutable tags, semantic version image, git sha tag
X: Actually the latest tag is just a default name. It doesn't mean newest, and it moves every time someone pushes. If deployments use latest, you can't tell which code is running, two nodes can pull different images for the same deployment, a pod restart can silently upgrade the app, and rolling back is guesswork. With the imagePullPolicy defaults, Kubernetes might not even pull the new image at all.
X: What I do instead. Tag every build with something unique and traceable, usually the Git commit SHA, and for releases also the semantic version, like 1.8.3. Both tags point to the same image. The deployment manifest references the exact tag, so every deployment is a recorded change and rollback just means deploying the previous tag.
X: Make tags immutable in the registry. ECR, ACR and Artifact Registry all support it, so a tag can't be overwritten with different content.
X: For the strongest guarantee, deploy by digest, the sha256 of the image manifest, which is content-addressed and can never change. Tools can resolve a tag to a digest at deploy time and record both.
X: Build once and promote the same image through dev, test and production, instead of rebuilding per environment. In regulated work that matters a lot, because what was tested is byte-for-byte what goes live.
X: And add OCI labels to the image, like source repo, commit and build time, so anyone can trace a running container back to its source.
@p17-508
S: dkx
D: A
T: What are distroless and chiseled images, and should you use them for .NET?
K: distroless image, chiseled ubuntu, dotnet chiseled image, minimal container image, no shell container, attack surface
X: Okay, so distroless images contain only the app and its runtime dependencies. No package manager, no shell, no extra OS tools. Google popularised them, and Microsoft provides the .NET version as Ubuntu chiseled images, like the ASP.NET 8.0 noble chiseled image from the Microsoft container registry.
X: And it's a real win. They're much smaller, a chiseled ASP.NET Core image is around a quarter of the size of the full Debian one, so pulls and startup are faster. Far fewer packages, so vulnerability scanners report far fewer CVEs, which cuts patching noise. Attackers who get code execution find no shell or tools to work with. And chiseled images run as a non-root user by default.
X: But you pay for it a bit. You can't exec into the container and poke around with bash or curl, so debugging needs other approaches, like kubectl debug with an ephemeral container that has tools, or just good logging and metrics. Some apps need native libraries, like ICU for globalisation or time zone data, and Microsoft offers extra variants that include them. Health checks can't use curl inside the container, so they have to come from the orchestrator over HTTP.
X: My approach for .NET services, build in the SDK image in a multi-stage Dockerfile, publish, and copy the output into a chiseled runtime image. Or use a self-contained or Native AOT build on the runtime-deps chiseled image for the smallest result.
@p17-509
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you make Docker builds faster with BuildKit caching?
K: buildkit cache, docker build cache, cache mount nuget, layer cache ci, docker build slow, registry cache
X: So slow image builds usually come from not using the cache well. BuildKit, the default builder in modern Docker, gives you several tools for this.
X: Layer order matters most. Docker reuses a layer only if the instruction and everything before it is unchanged. So for .NET, I copy the solution and project files first, run dotnet restore, and only then copy the rest of the source and run publish. Code changes then don't invalidate the restore layer. For Node, same thing with package.json and the lock file before npm ci.
X: A good .dockerignore keeps bin, obj, node_modules, .git and test results out of the build context, which speeds up the upload and stops cache misses from irrelevant files.
X: Cache mounts keep package caches between builds without putting them in the image. Like a RUN step with a cache-type mount on the NuGet packages folder before dotnet restore, or on the npm cache folder.
X: In CI, every build might run on a fresh agent with an empty cache. BuildKit can export and import cache, using cache-to and cache-from with a registry, local or GitHub Actions cache backend, so the next pipeline run reuses layers.
X: Multi-stage builds also let BuildKit run independent stages in parallel, like building the API and running tests at the same time.
X: And secrets needed during build, like a private feed token, go in through a secret-type mount, never as build args, which end up in the image history. I've seen that mistake leak tokens.
@p17-510
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you run containers as non-root and lock down their security context?
K: non root container, securitycontext, readonlyrootfilesystem, drop capabilities, runasnonroot, container hardening
X: Honestly by default a lot of images run as root inside the container. If an attacker breaks out of the app, root inside the container makes escaping to the host and causing damage much easier. So I harden containers at two levels.
X: In the image, create or use a non-root user and set USER in the Dockerfile. The official .NET images include an app user, and since .NET 8 they listen on port 8080, so you don't need root to bind to a low port.
X: In Kubernetes, the pod and container securityContext. runAsNonRoot true, so Kubernetes refuses to start a container that would run as root. runAsUser and runAsGroup with fixed non-zero ids. allowPrivilegeEscalation false. readOnlyRootFilesystem true, so the app can't modify its own files, with an emptyDir volume mounted only where it really needs to write, like slash tmp. Capabilities drop ALL, adding back only what's essential, which for a web API is usually nothing. And a seccompProfile of RuntimeDefault.
X: At cluster level, Pod Security admission with the restricted profile on app namespaces enforces these settings, so a manifest that forgets them gets rejected instead of silently running as root.
X: Common issues when you tighten things, apps that write logs or temp files to their own folder, which I fix by writing to stdout and mounted temp volumes. And file permissions on mounted volumes, fixed with fsGroup.
@p17-511
S: dkx
D: A
T: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD, and why does PID 1 matter for graceful shutdown?
K: entrypoint vs cmd, pid 1 container, sigterm container, exec form vs shell form, graceful shutdown docker, tini
X: See, ENTRYPOINT defines the executable the container runs, and CMD provides default arguments, or the default command if there's no ENTRYPOINT. Arguments passed to docker run, or args in Kubernetes, replace CMD, while command in Kubernetes replaces ENTRYPOINT. For a .NET app, a typical line is ENTRYPOINT in exec form, with "dotnet" and the API dll name as the array items.
X: The form matters. The exec form, a JSON array, runs the process directly as PID 1. The shell form, written as plain text, runs it through the shell with sh dash c, so the shell is PID 1 and the app is its child.
X: Why that matters. When Kubernetes or Docker stops a container, it sends SIGTERM to PID 1, waits for the grace period, 30 seconds by default, then sends SIGKILL. A shell as PID 1 usually doesn't forward SIGTERM to the app, so the app never hears it, can't finish in-flight requests or close connections, and gets killed hard after 30 seconds. Deployments get slow and requests fail. I've hit this exact issue, it's confusing until you know.
X: Also, PID 1 has special signal handling and has to reap zombie child processes. If the app starts child processes, a tiny init like tini, or docker run with the init flag, handles that.
X: For .NET, the host listens for SIGTERM and triggers graceful shutdown. Hosted services get StopAsync and Kestrel drains requests, within HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout, which has to be shorter than the Kubernetes grace period.
@p17-512
S: dkx
D: A
T: How does .NET behave inside containers with memory and CPU limits?
K: dotnet container memory limit, server gc container, gcheaphardlimit, dotnet processor count, dotnet docker performance
X: Okay, modern .NET is container-aware. It reads the cgroup limits instead of the host machine's resources, and that matters a lot.
X: Memory. The GC sets its heap hard limit to 75 percent of the container memory limit by default, leaving room for native memory, thread stacks and other overhead. You can tune it with GCHeapHardLimit or GCHeapHardLimitPercent. If you set no memory limit at all, the runtime sees the whole node's memory and can grow way more than you'd expect.
X: GC mode. ASP.NET Core uses server GC by default, which creates a heap per logical CPU and favours throughput, but uses more memory. In a small container with a tight memory limit, workstation GC, or server GC with fewer heaps through GCHeapCount, can fit better. Since .NET 8 and 9, DATAS, dynamic adaptation to application sizes, is available, and it's on by default in .NET 9 for server GC. It shrinks and grows the heap count with load and makes server GC much friendlier for containers.
X: CPU. Environment.ProcessorCount reflects the CPU limit, rounded up, and the thread pool and GC size themselves from it. DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT can override it when the limit is fractional or you want different behaviour.
X: Practically, what I do is set a memory limit, watch GC heap size and working set through dotnet-counters or OpenTelemetry runtime metrics, and test under load with the real limits before going live.
@p17-513
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you set up local development with Docker Compose or .NET Aspire?
K: local dev environment docker compose, dotnet aspire, compose healthcheck depends_on, run dependencies locally, aspire dashboard
X: So for local development, developers need the service's dependencies, like SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ and Keycloak, without installing them all by hand.
X: Docker Compose is the classic answer. One compose file defines each dependency with an image, ports, volumes and environment variables. Health checks plus depends_on with condition service_healthy make the API wait until SQL Server is actually ready, not just started. T: A pod is stuck in Pending. How do you troubleshoot it?
K: pod pending, unschedulable pod, insufficient cpu, failedscheduling, pvc pending, taint not tolerated
X: Okay, Pending means the pod's been accepted but not scheduled onto a node, or it's waiting on something before it can start. The answer is almost always in kubectl describe pod, in the Events section, under FailedScheduling.
X: The usual causes, and what the message looks like.
X: Insufficient CPU or memory. The requests don't fit on any node. Either requests are too big, the cluster is full, or the node autoscaler hasn't added capacity yet or has hit its max. Fix by right-sizing requests or adding capacity.
X: Node selectors, affinity or taints. You'll see something like "didn't match node affinity" or "had untolerated taint". The pod wants a node type that doesn't exist, or it lacks the toleration for a dedicated node pool.
X: Volumes. The PersistentVolumeClaim is itself Pending, because there's no matching StorageClass, the provisioner failed, or the volume exists in a different availability zone than the available nodes. kubectl describe pvc shows why. That zone one is honestly where I've seen people stuck the longest.
X: Quota. In a namespace with a ResourceQuota, the pod might be rejected at creation, so it shows up as a ReplicaSet event, not a Pending pod. Describe the ReplicaSet to see it.
X: Topology spread or anti-affinity rules that can't be satisfied, like requiring one pod per zone with more replicas than zones.
X: I also check kubectl get events sorted by time, and the autoscaler's logs, because they explain why no node was added.

T: A pod shows ImagePullBackOff. What do you check?
K: imagepullbackoff, errimagepull, image pull error kubernetes, registry authentication, image not found, pull secret
X: So ImagePullBackOff means the kubelet tried to pull the container image, failed, and is backing off before retrying. kubectl describe pod shows the exact error in the events, and that tells me which of a handful of causes it is.
X: Image doesn't exist. A typo in the repository name, or a tag that was never pushed, maybe because the build failed or the pipeline pushed a different tag than the manifest references. I check the registry for the exact tag.
X: Authentication. "unauthorized" or "access denied". The cluster needs permission to pull from a private registry. On EKS, the node role needs ECR read access. On AKS, the kubelet identity needs AcrPull on the registry. Elsewhere, an imagePullSecret has to exist in the same namespace as the pod and be referenced by the pod or its service account. Expired tokens, or a secret created in the wrong namespace, are really common.
X: Network. The nodes can't reach the registry, because of a firewall, missing NAT, missing private endpoints or VPC endpoints for ECR, or DNS problems. The error's usually a timeout.
X: Rate limits. Pulling from Docker Hub anonymously can hit "toomanyrequests". The fix is mirroring base images into our own registry, or authenticating.
X: Platform mismatch. An image built only for arm64 running on amd64 nodes gives "no matching manifest", so I build multi-arch images.
X: Once it's fixed, the pod retries on its own, or what I do is delete it to retry right away.

S: dkx
D: A
T: A Kubernetes Service returns 503 or has no endpoints. How do you troubleshoot it?
K: service no endpoints, 503 ingress kubernetes, selector mismatch, service not routing, endpointslice empty, targetport wrong
X: Okay, so when traffic through a Service or Ingress fails with 503 or connection refused, I follow the path from the outside in, checking each hop.
X: I start with, does the Service even have endpoints? kubectl get endpointslices for that service, or kubectl describe service. If the endpoints list is empty, the Service isn't selecting any ready pods. Usually that's one of two things. The Service selector doesn't match the pod labels, maybe a typo, or a label changed in the Deployment but not in the Service. Or the pods exist but aren't ready, because the readiness probe is failing, and Kubernetes removes unready pods from endpoints on purpose.
X: Then ports. The Service's targetPort has to match the port the container actually listens on. Classic .NET example, since .NET 8 the container images listen on 8080 by default, but the Service still points to 80, so everything gets refused. I've seen that exact one more than once.
X: Then the app itself. I port-forward straight to a pod on 8080 and call it. If that works, the problem's in the Service or Ingress. If not, it's the app.
X: After that, the Ingress or Gateway. The backend service name and port in the rule, host and path matching, TLS secrets, and the ingress controller's logs, which usually say pretty clearly there's no healthy upstream.
X: And last, NetworkPolicies that block traffic from the ingress controller's namespace to the app's namespace.

T: A node shows NotReady. What do you do?
K: node notready, kubelet not ready, node pressure, node troubleshooting kubernetes, disk pressure memory pressure
X: See, NotReady means the control plane hasn't heard a healthy status from the node's kubelet for a while, about 40 seconds by default. After a few minutes, pods on that node get marked for eviction and rescheduled elsewhere, as long as there's capacity and the workloads have more than one replica.
X: My first step is kubectl describe node, looking at Conditions and recent events. The conditions tell you a lot. MemoryPressure, DiskPressure or PIDPressure being true points to resource exhaustion. NetworkUnavailable points to the network plugin. And if the kubelet has just stopped posting status, the Ready condition shows Unknown.
X: The usual causes. The kubelet or container runtime crashed or is stuck, which you can often see in the node's system logs with journalctl. The disk filled up with images, logs or emptyDir data, which triggers disk pressure and image garbage collection. Memory exhaustion where system processes got OOM-killed because pods had no limits. Network problems between the node and the control plane, like security group or firewall changes, or expired node certificates. On cloud providers, the underlying VM might be impaired or being retired.
X: For immediate impact, I cordon the node so nothing new lands there, and drain it if it's partly working, so pods move cleanly.
X: On managed node groups, honestly the quickest fix is often to just replace the node, let the autoscaler or node group create a fresh one, and then investigate the root cause from logs instead of nursing the broken node back.

S: dkx
D: A
T: Pods are being evicted. Why, and how do you stop it?
K: pod evicted, eviction kubernetes, ephemeral storage eviction, node pressure eviction, priority class, evicted pods cleanup
X: So an evicted pod was stopped by the kubelet or the API, not because the app crashed. kubectl describe pod shows the reason, and it's usually one of these.
X: Node pressure eviction. When a node runs low on memory, disk or process ids, the kubelet evicts pods to protect the node. It picks by quality of service and usage. BestEffort pods first, then Burstable pods using more than their requests, and Guaranteed pods last. The fix is realistic requests, so heavy pods count properly at scheduling time, memory limits, and right-sized nodes.
X: Ephemeral storage. A container writing too much to its writable layer or an emptyDir volume, like big temp files or logs written to files instead of stdout, goes over its ephemeral storage limit or fills the node's disk. Fix it with ephemeral-storage requests and limits, logs to stdout, cleaning up temp files, and a persistent volume for big data.
X: Preemption. A higher-priority pod needed room, so the scheduler evicted lower-priority pods. That's by design if you use PriorityClasses, and critical services should have higher priority than batch jobs.
X: API-initiated eviction, during node drains for upgrades or autoscaler scale-down, which PodDisruptionBudgets control.
X: Evicted pods stay listed with status Failed until they're garbage collected, which is mostly noise. But a steady stream of evictions is a signal that capacity or limits need attention. That's the thing I'd actually watch for.

T: How do you debug a running container that has no shell?
K: kubectl debug, ephemeral container, debug distroless, kubectl exec no shell, node debugging kubernetes
X: Actually with distroless or chiseled images, kubectl exec with bash just fails, because there's no shell. That's good for security, but you still need ways to debug.

@p17-520
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do taints, tolerations and node affinity work?
K: taints and tolerations, node affinity, node selector, dedicated node pool, gpu nodes kubernetes, schedule on specific nodes
X: Okay, these features control which pods run on which nodes, from two directions.
X: Taints are on nodes and push pods away. A taint like dedicated equals batch with the NoSchedule effect means no pod gets scheduled there unless it tolerates that taint. NoExecute also evicts running pods that don't tolerate it, and PreferNoSchedule is a soft version. Kubernetes uses taints itself too, like on nodes that aren't ready or are under pressure.
X: Tolerations are on pods and let them onto tainted nodes. But a toleration only permits. It doesn't attract the pod to that node. People mix that up a lot.
X: Node affinity is on pods and attracts them to nodes with certain labels, like a particular instance type, zone, or a GPU label. requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is a hard rule, and preferredDuringScheduling is a weighted preference. nodeSelector is the simple, older form of a hard rule.
X: So to dedicate nodes to a workload, you combine both. Taint the node pool so other pods stay away, and give the workload a toleration plus node affinity so it goes there and only there.
X: Typical uses, GPU nodes for machine learning jobs, nodes with lots of memory for a cache, spot nodes for interruptible batch work with a toleration, separate system node pools for cluster add-ons, and Windows nodes for Windows containers, where Windows pods need a nodeSelector for the OS.
@p17-521
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you spread pods across nodes and zones for high availability?
K: topology spread constraints, pod anti affinity, spread across zones, high availability kubernetes, zone failure
X: So running three replicas doesn't help much if all three land on the same node or the same availability zone. One node failure or zone outage and the service is down. So you have to tell the scheduler to spread them.
X: Pod anti-affinity is the older way. A rule says don't schedule this pod on a node, or in a zone, that already runs a pod with the same label. The required form is strict, which can leave pods Pending if there are more replicas than nodes, and the preferred form is a soft preference. It also gets expensive to compute in large clusters.
X: Topology spread constraints are the better, more flexible tool. A constraint says spread pods matching a label across a topology key, like the standard zone label or the hostname label, with a maxSkew, the maximum allowed difference in pod count between domains. whenUnsatisfiable set to DoNotSchedule makes it strict, ScheduleAnyway makes it best-effort. What I do usually is add two constraints, one across zones and one across nodes.
X: Some details matter. Spread only applies at scheduling time, so after a zone recovers, pods don't automatically rebalance, and the descheduler can help with that. The autoscaler has to be able to create nodes in each zone. And PodDisruptionBudgets keep the spread safe during maintenance.
X: Zone spreading can add cross-zone data transfer costs, which is usually worth it for production APIs.

S: dkx
D: A
T: How do applications pick up ConfigMap and Secret changes?
K: configmap change not reflected, reload config kubernetes, configmap hot reload, reloader, rollout restart config
X: Honestly this one surprises people a lot. You update a ConfigMap, and the app keeps using the old values. It depends on how the configuration is consumed.
X: Environment variables are read only when the container starts. Changing the ConfigMap does nothing to running pods, they need a restart.
X: Mounted volumes get updated by the kubelet eventually, usually within a minute or so, because files are refreshed through a symlink swap. An app that watches the file can reload. In .NET, adding a JSON file with reloadOnChange and reading settings through IOptionsMonitor works, though file watching on these symlinked volumes can be flaky, so you might need polling. And volumes mounted with subPath never get updated.
X: Common approaches. Rollout restart, kubectl rollout restart deployment after the change, which recreates pods gradually. A checksum annotation in the Helm chart, where the pod template includes a hash of the ConfigMap contents, so any config change changes the pod template and triggers a normal rolling update automatically. That's my preferred method, because the change goes through the same safe rollout as a code change. Or a controller like Stakater Reloader, which watches ConfigMaps and Secrets and restarts deployments that reference them.
X: Immutable ConfigMaps with versioned names, like app-config-v12, are another pattern. Each change creates a new ConfigMap, and the deployment references the new name, which makes rollback clean too.
X: And real feature flags that must change instantly are better served by a feature flag service than ConfigMaps.

S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you manage secrets in Kubernetes properly?
K: kubernetes secrets base64, external secrets operator, sealed secrets, secrets store csi driver, encrypt secrets etcd
X: See, Kubernetes Secrets are only base64-encoded by default, not encrypted. Anyone who can read them through the API, or read etcd backups, can see the values. So I treat native Secrets carefully and usually source them from a real secrets manager.
X: The baseline, turn on encryption at rest for secrets in etcd, which managed clusters support with a KMS key. Restrict RBAC so very few people and service accounts can get or list secrets. And never commit secret manifests to Git in plain form.
X: Then pick how secrets get into the cluster.
X: External Secrets Operator. An ExternalSecret resource says which keys to fetch from AWS Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault or others, and the operator creates and refreshes a normal Kubernetes Secret. Apps stay unchanged, and rotation in the source flows through.
X: Secrets Store CSI Driver. Mounts secrets from the external store directly as files in the pod, optionally syncing to a Kubernetes Secret.
X: Sealed Secrets. Encrypts secrets with the cluster's public key, so the encrypted version can be safely committed to Git, which suits GitOps. Only the controller in the cluster can decrypt them.
X: Even better, avoid secrets where you can. Use workload identity, like IRSA or Pod Identity on EKS and Workload ID on AKS, so pods authenticate to cloud databases and services without any stored credentials. That's always my first choice.

S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you upgrade a Kubernetes cluster safely?
K: kubernetes upgrade, eks upgrade, aks upgrade, deprecated api removal, node pool upgrade, version skew
X: Okay, Kubernetes releases a minor version roughly every four months, and each one is supported for about a year upstream, longer on some managed services with paid extended support. So upgrades are routine, and I treat them as a process, not an event.
X: Before upgrading, read the release notes for removed or deprecated APIs. Tools like Pluto or kubent scan manifests and Helm releases for API versions that'll stop working. Check that add-ons, like the ingress controller, CNI, CSI drivers, cert-manager and monitoring agents, support the new version, and upgrade them first if needed. And go one minor version at a time, you can't skip versions on the control plane.
X: The order. Upgrade a non-production cluster first and run the test suites. Then the control plane, which managed services do for you without downtime. Then the node pools, which have to stay within the supported version skew of the control plane. For nodes, I prefer creating a new node pool on the new version and draining the old one, or using surge upgrades that add new nodes before removing old ones. PodDisruptionBudgets, multiple replicas and graceful shutdown keep services up while pods move.
X: After, watch error rates and events, then upgrade the remaining add-ons.
X: Teams that keep clusters disposable and fully defined in code sometimes do blue-green clusters instead. Build a new cluster on the new version, shift traffic, retire the old one. Pretty much the cleanest option if you can afford it.
@p17-525
S: dkx
D: A
T: What are Pod Security Standards and admission policies?
K: pod security standards, pod security admission, restricted baseline privileged, kyverno, opa gatekeeper, validating admission policy
X: So admission control is the step where the Kubernetes API checks or modifies objects before saving them. It's where you enforce security rules on every workload, instead of trusting each manifest.
X: Pod Security Standards define three profiles. Privileged has no restrictions, for system components. Baseline blocks known privilege escalations, like privileged containers, host networking and host paths. Restricted enforces hardening best practices, non-root users, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, and a seccomp profile.
X: Pod Security Admission is built into Kubernetes and applies these profiles per namespace, using labels. Each profile can be set to enforce, which rejects violating pods, audit, which logs them, or warn, which returns a warning to the user. My approach is to start with warn and audit on restricted, fix the workloads, then enforce.
X: For rules beyond pod security, policy engines help. Kyverno writes policies as Kubernetes YAML. Require labels like owner and cost centre, require resource limits, allow images only from our registry, require signed images, or add default settings automatically. OPA Gatekeeper uses the Rego language for the same things. Kubernetes also now has built-in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy using CEL expressions, which covers a lot of simple rules without installing anything.
X: I keep policies in Git, test them in CI against our manifests, and roll them out in audit mode first, so nobody's deployment breaks without warning.
@p17-526
S: dkx
D: A
T: What happens when you run kubectl apply? Walk through the control plane.
K: kubectl apply flow, kubernetes control plane components, api server etcd scheduler, controller manager, kubelet, how kubernetes works
X: Actually walking through it is the best way to show how the pieces fit together.
X: kubectl reads the manifest and sends it to the API server over HTTPS, authenticating with my credentials. kubectl apply uses server-side or client-side apply to work out what changed compared to the last applied configuration.
X: The API server authenticates me, checks RBAC authorisation, then runs admission controllers. Mutating ones first, which might add defaults or sidecars, then validating ones, like Pod Security or policy engines. If everything passes, it stores the Deployment object in etcd, the cluster's key-value database. Nothing has actually run yet, we've only recorded desired state.
X: Controllers watch the API server for changes. The Deployment controller, in the controller manager, sees the new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet. The ReplicaSet controller sees it needs three pods and creates three Pod objects, with no node assigned yet.
X: The scheduler watches for unassigned pods. For each one, it filters nodes that fit the requests, taints, affinity and spread rules, scores them, and binds the pod to the best node.
X: The kubelet on that node sees a pod assigned to it, asks the container runtime, like containerd, to pull the image and start the containers, sets up networking through the CNI plugin and volumes through CSI, runs probes, and reports status back.
X: Meanwhile, the EndpointSlice controller adds ready pods to the Service, and kube-proxy or the CNI updates routing so traffic can reach them. So yeah, that's the whole chain.
@p17-527
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims and StorageClasses work?
K: persistent volume, persistent volume claim, storage class, dynamic provisioning, access modes rwo rwx, reclaim policy
X: Okay, containers are ephemeral, so anything written inside them disappears on restart. Persistent storage in Kubernetes has three layers.
X: A PersistentVolume is a piece of storage in the cluster, like an EBS volume, an Azure Disk, or a network file share, with a size, access modes and a reclaim policy.
X: A PersistentVolumeClaim is a request for storage by a workload. I need 20 GiB, ReadWriteOnce, of this class. The pod mounts the claim, not the volume directly, so app manifests don't depend on storage details.
X: A StorageClass describes a type of storage and its provisioner, like gp3 EBS volumes, premium Azure disks, or EFS. With dynamic provisioning, creating a claim makes the provisioner create a matching volume automatically. volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer delays creation until the pod is scheduled, so the volume gets created in the same availability zone as the pod. Trust me, that setting saves a lot of pain.
X: Access modes matter. ReadWriteOnce means one node can mount it, typical for block disks. ReadWriteMany means many nodes, which needs a network file system, like EFS or Azure Files. ReadWriteOncePod restricts it to a single pod.
X: The reclaim policy decides what happens when the claim is deleted. Delete removes the underlying disk, Retain keeps it for manual recovery. For important data, I use Retain plus regular snapshots with the CSI snapshot feature.
X: For most stateless services, though, I avoid volumes completely and use object storage or managed databases.
@p17-528
S: dkx
D: A
T: containerd vs Docker: what changed when Kubernetes removed dockershim?
K: containerd vs docker, dockershim removal, container runtime interface, cri-o, oci image, docker images still work kubernetes
X: So Kubernetes talks to container runtimes through the Container Runtime Interface, CRI. Docker Engine never implemented CRI, so Kubernetes had an adapter called dockershim to talk to it. That adapter was removed in Kubernetes 1.24.
X: What that meant in practice. Clusters switched to CRI-compatible runtimes, mainly containerd, which was actually the component Docker itself used under the hood, or CRI-O. Managed services like EKS, AKS and GKE moved to containerd.
X: What didn't change, images built with Docker still work everywhere, because they follow the OCI image standard, and containerd runs OCI images. Developers keep using Docker Desktop or Docker Engine to build and run containers locally. Only the runtime on the cluster nodes changed.
X: What did break was anything relying on the Docker socket on nodes. Like CI jobs building images inside pods by mounting the Docker socket file, or monitoring agents reading Docker's API. Those moved to alternatives, like BuildKit, Kaniko or buildah for in-cluster builds, and runtime-agnostic agents. Debugging on nodes uses crictl instead of the docker command.
X: So in an interview, I'd say the key points are, Docker is a developer tool and image format ecosystem. containerd is the runtime. OCI standards make images portable between them. And Kubernetes only needs a CRI runtime on the nodes. A lot of people panicked about that change for nothing, honestly.

@p17-530
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you run database migrations when deploying to Kubernetes?
K: database migration kubernetes, ef core migrations kubernetes, migration job helm hook, init container migration, schema change deployment
X: See, running migrations from the app at startup, like calling Database.Migrate in Program.cs, is risky in Kubernetes. With several replicas starting at once, they race to apply the same migration, startup gets slow, and the app needs DDL permissions it really shouldn't have at runtime.
X: Better options.
X: A Kubernetes Job before the rollout. The pipeline runs a migration Job, using the same image or a dedicated migrator image, waits for it to finish successfully, and only then updates the Deployment. In Helm, this is often a pre-upgrade hook, so the release fails if the migration fails. The Job uses a separate database identity with schema-change rights.
X: A migration step in the pipeline itself, outside the cluster, applying an idempotent script or an EF Core migration bundle generated at build time. That makes the migration a visible, auditable release step, which I like.
X: Init containers can work for simple cases, but every pod would try to run them, so they need locking, and I don't usually go that way.
X: Whatever the mechanism, the schema changes themselves have to be backward compatible, because during a rolling update old and new versions run side by side. I use expand and contract. Add new columns or tables first, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only drop old columns in a later release. That also keeps rolling back the app safe without rolling back the database.
@p17-531
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you do progressive delivery on Kubernetes with Argo Rollouts or Flagger?
K: argo rollouts, flagger, progressive delivery, canary analysis kubernetes, automated rollback metrics, analysis template
X: Actually a plain Deployment does a rolling update. It replaces pods gradually, but it only checks readiness, not whether the new version is actually healthy for users. Progressive delivery tools add real canary and blue-green releases with automated analysis.
X: Argo Rollouts replaces the Deployment with a Rollout resource. A canary strategy lists steps, like send 10 percent of traffic, pause five minutes, run analysis, go to 30 percent, analyse again, then 100 percent. Traffic splitting can be by replica count, or precise using an ingress controller, the Gateway API, or a service mesh. Analysis templates query a metrics provider, like Prometheus, Datadog or CloudWatch, with success conditions, like error rate below one percent and p95 latency below 400 milliseconds. If analysis fails, the rollout aborts and traffic goes back to the stable version automatically. Blue-green is supported too, with preview services and promotion.
X: Flagger does the same with a different model. You keep your Deployment, and Flagger creates the canary and primary objects and drives traffic shifting with a mesh or ingress, using metric checks and webhooks for load tests or approvals.
X: What makes it work in practice, good metrics per version, labelled so you can compare canary with stable. Enough traffic for the statistics to mean something. And backward-compatible database changes, since both versions run together.
X: It's basically the automatic rollback answer for Kubernetes. Health gets judged by real user signals, not by humans staring at dashboards.
@p17-532
S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you make trunk-based development work in practice?
K: trunk based development, short lived branches, main branch always releasable, trunk based vs gitflow, continuous integration practice
X: Okay, so trunk-based development means everyone integrates into one main branch at least daily, through short-lived branches that live a day or two, instead of long-running feature or develop branches that merge weeks later with painful conflicts.
X: Making it work needs a few supporting habits.
X: Small changes. A big feature gets split into small, safe pull requests that each keep main working, like adding the database column first, then the API, then the UI.
X: Feature flags. Unfinished work merges behind a flag that's off in production, so code gets integrated before the feature is ready. Release becomes a flag switch, not a merge.
X: Fast, reliable CI. Every pull request runs build, unit tests and static checks in about ten minutes. Branch policies require a passing build and a review before merging.
X: Keep main releasable. If main breaks, fixing it is the team's top priority, and reverting is a normal, blame-free thing to do.
X: Release branches only when needed, cut from main for a release that needs stabilisation or hotfixes, and fixes go to main first, then get cherry-picked.
X: What you get is fewer merge conflicts, earlier feedback, and a codebase that's always close to shippable. In a regulated environment, the validated release is still a specific, tagged build from main, so traceability is kept. That was the main worry people had when I've seen teams move to it.
@p17-533

D: A
T: How do you use feature flags without creating a mess?
K: feature flags, feature toggles, release toggle, flag cleanup, feature management dotnet, kill switch
X: So feature flags let you change behaviour at runtime without deploying, but they turn into technical debt if nobody manages them. I think about them by type.
X: Release flags hide unfinished or new features until they're ready. They should be short-lived, removed within a few weeks of full rollout. Ops flags or kill switches let you turn off an expensive or risky path during an incident, like disabling a heavy export, and these can live longer. Experiment flags drive A/B tests. Permission flags turn on features for specific customers or plans, which is really configuration and belongs in the product's settings model.
X: In .NET, Microsoft.FeatureManagement gives you IFeatureManager and attributes for controllers, with filters for percentage rollout, user or group targeting, and time windows. Flags can come from configuration, Azure App Configuration, or a dedicated service like LaunchDarkly or Unleash, and OpenFeature gives a vendor-neutral API.
X: My rules for keeping it clean. Every flag has an owner and an expiry date, recorded when it's created. Check the flag in one place, near the edge, instead of scattering checks across the code. Test both states. Default to the safe value if the flag service is unreachable. And add a ticket to remove the flag and the dead code once rollout's done.
X: In a regulated product, a flag that changes validated behaviour is itself a configuration change, so its state per environment has to be controlled and recorded.
@p17-534
S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you version builds automatically with semantic versioning?
K: semantic versioning, semver, gitversion, conventional commits, automatic version number, build number strategy
X: See, semantic versioning is MAJOR dot MINOR dot PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. Pre-release labels, like 2.1.0-beta.3, mark builds that aren't final. For libraries and packages it's essential, because consumers rely on it to know if an upgrade is safe.
X: Editing version numbers by hand doesn't scale, so I automate it.
X: GitVersion calculates the version from Git history, tags, branch names and commit messages. A tag v1.4.0 on main marks the release, builds after it become 1.4.1-something or 1.5.0 depending on configuration, and feature branches get pre-release labels.
X: Conventional commits put intent in commit messages, like feat colon for a feature, fix colon for a fix, and feat with an exclamation mark or BREAKING CHANGE for breaking changes. Tools like semantic-release or release-please read them, bump the version, create the tag and generate a changelog. That works really well for npm packages.
X: The build then stamps the version everywhere. Assembly versions in .NET through the Version property, package versions, container image tags, and the build name in the pipeline, so the running app can show its version on a health or about endpoint. That's saved us a lot of "which version is in prod" conversations.
X: For deployable services, I also add the commit SHA in the build metadata, like 1.4.2 plus abc1234, so any running instance traces back to its exact source.
@p17-535
S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you reuse pipeline logic with Azure Pipelines YAML templates?
K: azure pipelines templates, yaml templates, extends template, template parameters, reusable pipeline, pipeline standardization
X: Honestly when lots of services have similar pipelines, copying YAML into each repo leads to drift and painful updates. Azure Pipelines templates fix that.
X: You can template at a few levels. Step templates hold a sequence of steps, like restore, build, test and publish coverage for a .NET project. Job and stage templates hold whole jobs or stages, like a standard deploy stage with approvals and smoke tests. Variable templates hold shared variables. Templates take typed parameters, like the project path, .NET version or environment name, with defaults and allowed values, and can use template expressions with each loops and conditions, evaluated at compile time.
X: Templates usually live in a central repository, referenced with a resources repositories block and pinned to a tag or branch, so a change to the shared template is versioned and teams can adopt it deliberately.
X: Extends templates go further. The pipeline in each repo just extends a central template and passes parameters, and the template controls the overall structure. Combine that with a required template check on protected resources, like production environments or service connections, and you enforce that every pipeline deploying to production runs the mandatory security scans and approvals. That's a strong governance tool.
X: What I do is keep templates simple and well documented, avoid deep nesting, and test template changes on a sample pipeline before releasing a new version. Otherwise one bad change breaks every team at once.
@p17-536
S: cdx
D: A
T: What are stages, jobs, steps and deployment jobs in Azure Pipelines?
K: azure pipelines stages jobs steps, deployment job, environments azure devops, pipeline structure, run once rolling canary strategy
X: Okay, so an Azure Pipelines YAML pipeline has a pretty clear hierarchy.
X: Stages are the big phases, like Build, Deploy to Dev, Deploy to QA and Deploy to Production. They run sequentially by default, can depend on each other with dependsOn, and can have conditions, like only deploying from main. Approvals and checks are attached at the environment level, so a stage waits until they pass.
X: Jobs run inside stages. Each job runs on one agent, from a pool, and jobs in a stage can run in parallel. A job can be a normal job or a deployment job.
X: Steps are the individual tasks or scripts inside a job, like checking out code, running dotnet build, publishing artifacts, or running a PowerShell script.
X: Deployment jobs are special jobs for releases. They target an environment, which records deployment history, which build went to which environment and when. They support strategies, runOnce, rolling across virtual machines in the environment, and canary with increments. Each strategy has lifecycle hooks, like preDeploy, deploy, routeTraffic, postRouteTraffic, and on failure or success, so you can run smoke tests after routing traffic and roll back on failure.
X: Artifacts are published in the build stage and downloaded automatically in deployment jobs, so the exact same build output moves through every stage.
X: On our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, the older classic release pipelines are still used for some apps, but YAML pipelines with environments give us code review and history for pipeline changes.
@p17-537
S: cdx
D: A
T: Why should you build once and promote the same artifact through environments?
K: build once deploy many, artifact promotion, immutable artifact, rebuild per environment problem, environment specific config
X: So build once, deploy many means the pipeline compiles and packages the app one time, and that exact artifact, the same zip, package or container image, gets deployed to dev, test, UAT and production. Only configuration differs per environment.
X: Why it matters. If you rebuild for each environment, you're not deploying what you tested. A different build agent, an updated base image, a newer dependency pulled in by a floating version, or a different commit can sneak in. Then a bug shows up in production that never existed in test, and you can't easily tell why.
X: With a single artifact, testing in each environment adds confidence to the same binary. It's faster, because the build happens once. And it's traceable, the artifact has a version and a hash, linked to a commit and a build, and each deployment records which artifact went where.
X: To make it work, configuration has to live outside the artifact. Environment variables, appsettings per environment loaded at runtime, a configuration service, or secrets managers, not build-time constants or per-environment build flags. Front ends need the same idea, loading a runtime config file instead of baking API URLs into the bundle.
X: In a validated GxP environment, this is close to mandatory, because the validated package has to be provably identical to what goes into production. In our team we keep the build artifact, its version and its approvals linked in Azure DevOps for exactly that reason.

T: GitHub Actions vs Azure Pipelines: how do they compare?
K: github actions vs azure pipelines, github actions vs azure devops, ci cd tool comparison, workflows vs pipelines
X: Actually both are mature CI/CD systems with YAML pipelines, hosted and self-hosted runners, and support for any language. The differences are mostly in ecosystem and enterprise features.
X: GitHub Actions is built into GitHub. Workflows trigger on almost any repository event, pushes, pull requests, issues, releases, schedules or manual dispatch. Its marketplace has a huge number of actions. Reusable workflows and composite actions share logic. Environments have protection rules and secrets, and OIDC federation to AWS, Azure and GCP is straightforward. It ties in naturally with GitHub's security features, like Dependabot, code scanning and secret scanning. It's the default for open source and a lot of new projects.
X: Azure Pipelines is part of Azure DevOps, alongside Boards, Repos, Test Plans and Artifacts. It works with GitHub repos too. It's strong for enterprises with complex release processes. Multi-stage pipelines, environments with approvals, checks like business hours, required templates and exclusive locks, deep traceability from work items to commits to builds to deployments, classic release pipelines for older setups, and an on-premise version, Azure DevOps Server, which matters for organisations that can't use cloud services.
X: The choice usually follows where the code and work tracking live. In our case, the on-premise platform uses Azure DevOps Server, so Azure Pipelines is natural there, while newer cloud-based work can use either. The concepts, stages, jobs, runners, environments and secrets, transfer pretty easily between them.

T: How do you deploy to AWS from a pipeline without storing access keys?
K: oidc github actions aws, assume role with web identity, pipeline aws credentials, no access keys ci, aws federation ci
X: Okay, storing an AWS access key and secret as a pipeline secret is common but risky. The keys are long-lived, often over-privileged, hard to rotate, and if leaked, they work from anywhere. The better way is OpenID Connect federation.
X: How it works with GitHub Actions. In the AWS account, I create an IAM OIDC identity provider for GitHub's token issuer, and an IAM role whose trust policy allows the STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity action from that provider, with conditions on the token's claims. The audience has to be sts.amazonaws.com, and the subject has to match a specific repository and branch or environment, like the shipments-api repo in our org with the production environment. In the workflow, I grant the id-token write permission and use the configure-aws-credentials action with the role ARN. Each run gets temporary credentials, valid for about an hour, and nothing's stored.
X: Azure Pipelines and GitLab support the same pattern, and so does Azure with federated credentials.
X: My rules here, separate roles per environment and per purpose, like a deploy role that can update ECS services and push to ECR, and a read-only plan role for Terraform pull requests. Least-privilege policies. Tight subject conditions, never a wildcard on the whole organisation. And CloudTrail monitoring of role usage.
X: For our on-premise Azure DevOps Server, federation depends on network and version support, so the same least-privilege idea applies with whatever mechanism is available, with credentials kept only in a protected library and rotated.
@p17-540
S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you secure the software supply chain in your pipeline?
K: software supply chain security, sbom, slsa, sign artifacts, pipeline security, dependency confusion
X: So supply chain attacks go after the path from source code to production rather than the app itself. A compromised dependency, a tampered build agent, or a malicious package with the same name as an internal one. So I protect each step.
X: Source. Branch protection with required reviews, signed commits where practical, and secret scanning to stop credentials getting committed.
X: Dependencies. Lock files and pinned versions, so builds are reproducible. Package source mapping in NuGet and scoped registries in npm, so internal package names can only come from the internal feed, which prevents dependency confusion. Vulnerability scanning with dotnet list package with the vulnerable flag, npm audit, Dependabot or a commercial scanner. And a review process for adding new dependencies.
X: Build. Pipelines defined as code and reviewed. Minimal permissions for the pipeline's token. Pinned versions of actions or tasks, ideally by commit SHA. Ephemeral, clean build agents. And no secrets available to builds from untrusted pull requests.
X: Artifacts. Generate a software bill of materials, an SBOM in CycloneDX or SPDX format, so we know exactly what's inside each release and can quickly answer "are we affected?" when a new vulnerability drops. Sign artifacts and images, with tools like Sigstore Cosign or Notation, and produce provenance attestations following SLSA. Verify signatures at deployment time.
X: Deployment. Only signed, scanned artifacts from the trusted pipeline can reach production. Honestly, the SBOM part is what pays off fastest when the next big CVE hits.

T: How do you keep dependencies up to date safely with Dependabot or Renovate?
K: dependabot, renovate, dependency updates, outdated packages, automated dependency pull requests, nuget updates
X: Okay, outdated dependencies pile up security vulnerabilities and make future upgrades painful, because jumping several major versions at once is way harder than small, regular steps. Automating update pull requests keeps it manageable.
X: Dependabot, built into GitHub, and Renovate, which works with GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab and others, scan manifests, like csproj files, Directory.Packages.props, package.json, Dockerfiles and pipeline files, and open pull requests to update versions. Security updates are raised as soon as a vulnerable version is known.
X: To make it workable and not just noise.
X: Group related updates, like all Microsoft.Extensions packages or all testing packages, into one pull request, and schedule non-security updates weekly.
X: Automerge low-risk updates, like patch versions of dev dependencies, when the pipeline passes. That depends on a good test suite, which is the real safety net.
X: Treat major versions separately, read the release notes and plan the changes, since they're often breaking.
X: Use central package management in .NET, so versions are defined in one place across a solution.
X: Keep base images current too, because OS packages in images are a big source of vulnerabilities.
X: The team also needs a habit, someone reviews update pull requests every week, so they don't turn into ignored noise. In a regulated product, dependency updates still go through the normal validated release process, but small regular updates make that process way lighter.

D: A
T: How do you handle a hotfix when main already contains unreleased work?
K: hotfix process, hotfix branch, cherry pick hotfix, emergency fix production, patch release, release branch hotfix
X: See, the situation is production is on version 3.4, main already has weeks of changes for 3.5 that aren't ready, and a critical bug has to be fixed in production today.
X: Here's what I'd do.
X: Branch from what's in production, not from main. That's the release branch or the tag for 3.4, like release slash 3.4. Create a hotfix branch from it.
X: Make the smallest possible fix, with a test that reproduces the bug first. Keep it focused, no refactoring or extra changes sneaking in.
X: Run it through the pipeline like any release. Build, automated tests, review and approvals. Even in an emergency, I don't skip the review or the regression tests that matter. In a regulated environment, there's often an expedited change process, but it still records the risk assessment, testing evidence and approvals.
X: Release it as 3.4.1, a new patch version, and deploy with the normal deployment pipeline, so the deployment itself is a known, tested process.
X: Bring the fix back to main. Merge or cherry-pick it into main, and into any other active release branches, so 3.5 doesn't bring the bug back. Ideally the fix is developed on main first and cherry-picked to the release branch, so it's never forgotten, but in urgent cases you can reverse the order.
X: Afterwards, a short review. Why did the bug escape, and what test or check would have caught it. That's the part people skip, and it's the part that actually prevents the next one.
