S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you speed up a slow CI pipeline?
K: slow ci pipeline, speed up build, pipeline caching, parallel tests, ci performance, incremental build
X: Actually a slow pipeline costs focus and pushes people to batch changes, which is the opposite of what we want. My target for pull request validation is around ten minutes. I start by measuring where the time goes, using the pipeline's step timings over several runs, then go after the biggest items.
X: Caching. Restore NuGet and npm packages from a pipeline cache keyed on the lock file hash, instead of downloading everything every time. For Docker, reuse layer caches through BuildKit and a registry cache.
X: Parallelism. Split independent work into parallel jobs, like backend build and tests, front-end build and tests, and static analysis. Split large test suites across agents.
X: Do less work. Path filters, so front-end changes don't trigger the backend pipeline in a monorepo. Only build affected projects with tools like Nx for front ends. And move slow, broad tests, like full end-to-end suites or long performance tests, to a nightly or post-merge pipeline, keeping a fast smoke set on pull requests.
X: Faster tests. Find the slowest ones. Replace sleeps with proper waits. Share expensive fixtures like Testcontainers databases across a test class or collection. And run tests in parallel where they're isolated.
X: Better agents. More CPU, or self-hosted agents with warm caches, if the hosted agents are the bottleneck.
X: Then track pipeline duration as a metric, so it doesn't slowly creep back up. Trust me, it always creeps.

S: cdx
D: A
T: Monorepo vs multiple repositories: how does it affect CI/CD?
K: monorepo vs polyrepo, monorepo ci, path filters pipeline, nx affected, repository strategy microservices
X: Okay, both work. The choice just changes how builds, versioning and ownership get handled.
X: In a monorepo, many services and packages live in one repository. The good side, atomic changes across services and shared libraries in a single pull request, one place to search, consistent tooling and standards, and easy refactoring. The CI/CD challenge is you don't want every commit to build and deploy everything, so pipelines need path filters or affected-project detection, like Nx affected for JavaScript, or a build graph tool. Ownership has to be explicit, with CODEOWNERS files per folder. Versioning is either one version for all, or independent versions per package with tooling. And the repo can get big, needing shallow clones and sparse checkouts.
X: With multiple repositories, each service or package has its own repo, pipeline and version. The good side, clear ownership and permissions, independent release cycles, smaller and faster pipelines. The challenges, changes across several repos need coordinated pull requests and releases, shared code becomes versioned packages, which brings dependency update work, and standards drift unless pipeline templates are shared.
X: What I've seen work is polyrepo for independently deployed services, with shared pipeline templates and packages published to an internal feed. Our React shell with npm feature packages is a good example. Each feature package is versioned and published to the Azure DevOps feed, and the shell consumes specific versions. A monorepo makes sense for tightly coupled front-end packages where changes usually span several of them.

S: cdx
D: A
T: What branch policies and pull request checks do you put on main?
K: branch policies, branch protection rules, required reviewers, pull request validation build, code owners, protect main branch
X: So protecting main is the simplest, highest-value control in the whole delivery process. Here's what I usually set up.
X: No direct pushes to main. All changes go through pull requests.
X: A required build validation. The pull request pipeline has to pass, compiling the code, running unit tests and static analysis, before merging. In Azure Repos that's a build validation policy, in GitHub it's a required status check. The build should run against the merged result, not just the branch.
X: Required reviewers. At least one or two approvals, with code owners automatically added for the areas they own, like the database schema or the security code. Approvals reset when new changes are pushed, so reviewers don't approve one version and then a different one gets merged.
X: Linked work items, so every change traces to a requirement or bug, which matters a lot in a regulated environment.
X: All comments resolved before merging.
X: A merge strategy. Squash merges for a clean history on main, or merge commits if detailed history matters.
X: Quality gates. A SonarQube or similar gate on new code, like no new critical issues and coverage on new code above a threshold, plus secret scanning and dependency checks.
X: Exceptions. Admins can bypass in emergencies, but bypasses are logged and reviewed.
X: These rules are only as good as the checks behind them, so I keep the pull request pipeline fast and reliable. Otherwise people honestly start looking for ways around it.
@p17-546
S: cdx
D: A
T: What are DORA metrics, and how do you use them?
K: dora metrics, deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, mean time to restore, delivery performance
X: See, DORA metrics come from the DevOps Research and Assessment program, and they measure software delivery performance with four key numbers.
X: Deployment frequency, how often you deploy to production. Lead time for changes, how long from a commit to that commit running in production. Change failure rate, the percentage of deployments that cause a failure needing a fix, rollback or hotfix. And time to restore service, how long it takes to recover from a failure in production. DORA has since added deployment rework rate and refined the model, but these four are the core.
X: The research shows the first two, throughput, and the last two, stability, improve together in high-performing teams. Going faster with small changes doesn't have to mean more failures. Usually it means fewer, because each change is smaller and easier to understand.
X: How I'd use them. Measure from data the tools already have, like pipeline runs, deployment records and incident tickets, not manual reporting. Look at trends for a team over time, not comparisons between teams. Use them to find bottlenecks, like a long lead time caused by waiting days for a manual test environment, or a high failure rate pointing at weak tests.
X: What to avoid is turning them into targets for individuals, which leads to gaming, like splitting deployments artificially.
X: In a regulated release process, lead time includes validation and approval steps, so measuring it shows where automating evidence collection would help most.

T: How do you handle environment-specific configuration for .NET Framework and .NET apps?
K: web.config transformation, appsettings environment, configuration per environment, parameters.xml, environment variables dotnet config
X: Okay, the goal is one build artifact and different configuration per environment, applied at deployment or runtime, never by rebuilding.
X: For .NET Framework apps, configuration lives in web.config. Traditionally, build configurations had transforms, like Web.Release.config, applied at build time, which ties configuration to the build. Better options for build once, deploy many. Apply transforms at deployment time, which Azure DevOps IIS deployment tasks support with environment-named transform files. Use token replacement, where the web.config has placeholders, like DbServer wrapped in hash and curly brace markers, replaced from pipeline variables or variable groups during deployment. Or Web Deploy parameters.xml, which declares parameters that get values per environment. Since .NET Framework 4.7.1, configuration builders can also pull values from environment variables or a secrets store at runtime.
X: For modern .NET, configuration is layered at runtime. appsettings.json, then appsettings dot environment name dot json, then environment variables, then sources like Key Vault, App Configuration or Parameter Store, with later sources overriding earlier ones. The ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT or DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT variable picks the environment. Nested keys map to environment variables with double underscores, like ConnectionStrings double underscore Default.
X: Secrets never go in config files in the repo. They come from pipeline secret variables or secrets managers.
X: I also make the app validate its configuration at startup, with options validation, so a missing or wrong setting fails the deployment right away instead of failing later on the first request. I learned that one the hard way.
@p17-551
S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you build a front-end SPA once and configure it per environment at runtime?
K: spa runtime configuration, react environment variables build time, angular environment per deployment, config.json spa, build once spa
X: So front-end frameworks push you towards build-time configuration. Vite injects import.meta.env values, Create React App had process.env, and Angular has environment files picked by build configuration. The values get baked into the JavaScript bundle. That means a separate build per environment, which breaks build once, deploy many, and in a regulated setting means the tested bundle isn't the one that goes to production.
X: The usual fix is runtime configuration. The app ships with a small config file, like a config.json at the site root or an env-config.js, that's not part of the bundle. At deployment, the pipeline writes the environment's values into that file, like the API base URL, the identity provider authority and client id, feature flags and the telemetry key. At startup, the app fetches the file before rendering, or index.html loads env-config.js, which sets a global object.
X: In Angular, an APP_INITIALIZER, or provideAppInitializer in newer versions, can load the config before the app bootstraps, and a config service exposes it. In React, the root component waits for the config before rendering the router.
X: For containers, the entrypoint can generate the file from environment variables at startup.
X: A few things matter. The config file must not be cached aggressively, or users get stale values after a change, so it gets no-cache headers. It must contain no secrets, since everything in a browser is public. And the app should fail clearly if the config is missing, not half-load. People miss that caching one a lot.
@p17-552
S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you roll out a schema change to hundreds of tenant or study databases?
K: deploy to many databases, multi tenant database migration, database per tenant deployment, schema rollout many databases, migration orchestration
X: Okay, so with a database per study, a schema change isn't one deployment, it's hundreds. Doing that reliably needs proper orchestration.
X: The change itself has to be backward compatible to begin with, because databases get updated over minutes or hours, and the app has to work with both old and new schemas during that time. Expand and contract again. Add new structures first, and remove old ones only in a later release once every database is updated.
X: Then the rollout process. Keep a registry of all target databases, from the master database, with each one's current schema version, recorded in a version table inside each database. Run the migration in waves. Internal test databases first, then a small canary group of production databases, then the rest in batches with limited parallelism, so the database server doesn't get overloaded. Each run is idempotent and records success or failure per database, with the script version and timestamps, which also gives you the audit evidence a regulated environment needs.
X: Failure handling. A failure in one database must not leave it half-migrated, so each database's change runs in a transaction where possible, or in carefully ordered idempotent steps. Failed databases get reported and retried after investigation, without blocking the others, unless the failure looks systemic, and then the whole rollout halts.
X: Long-running changes, like adding an index to a huge table, get scheduled for quiet periods per region, with online index operations where available.
X: And honestly, a dashboard showing the version of every database makes it obvious when something's behind.

T: How do you decide between rolling back and rolling forward after a bad release?
K: rollback vs roll forward, fix forward, release went wrong decision, revert deployment, incident release decision
X: See, when a release causes problems, the decision is about restoring service fastest with the least risk. It's not about pride.
X: I lean towards rolling back when the previous version is known good and rollback is cheap and safe. Stateless services, the artifact still available, no irreversible database changes, and the impact is serious. Rolling back is usually a pipeline run or a traffic switch, and it gets you back to a known state while you investigate calmly. Feature flags are even faster, just switch off the new feature without redeploying.
X: I lean towards rolling forward, deploying a quick fix, when rollback isn't safe or possible. Like the release included database changes the old version can't handle, data's already been written in the new format, external partners have already integrated with a new API, or the fix is tiny, well understood and can go through the pipeline quickly. Rolling forward under pressure is risky though, so the fix still goes through tests and review.
X: Preparation makes all this easier. Backward-compatible database changes keep rollback possible. Every release has a documented rollback plan before it goes out. Deployments are automated, so rolling back isn't a manual scramble. And monitoring with clear signals, like error rate and key business events, tells you quickly if the action actually worked.
X: In a regulated environment, either action is a controlled change, so the decision, approvals and verification get recorded in the incident and change records.

S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you work with a change advisory board without slowing delivery to a crawl?
K: change advisory board, cab approval, change management itil, standard change, regulated release approvals, change request
X: So in regulated companies, production changes often need approval from a change advisory board, a CAB. A heavyweight CAB meeting for every change slows delivery, pushes people towards big risky batches, and research shows external approval boards don't actually reduce failure rates. So the goal is to keep the control but make it lighter and smarter.
X: What's helped, in my experience.
X: Classify changes. Standard changes are pre-approved because they're low-risk and follow a proven, automated process, like a routine deployment through the validated pipeline. Normal changes get a review. Emergency changes have an expedited path with review afterwards. Getting our routine pipeline deployments classified as standard changes was a big win for us.
X: Bring evidence automatically. The pipeline produces what the CAB wants to see. Linked work items, test results, code review approvals, security scan results, the deployment plan and the rollback plan. The change record gets created and updated by the pipeline, not typed in by hand.
X: Shift approvals left. Peer review in pull requests and automated checks give most of the assurance, and the CAB focuses on genuinely risky stuff, like data migrations or infrastructure changes.
X: Make releases smaller and more frequent, so each change is easier to assess.
X: Show the data, like change failure rate, to build trust that the process works.
X: In our GxP context, validation evidence and approvals are mandatory, but automating their collection kept releases moving without cutting corners.

T: What are ephemeral preview environments, and how do you set them up?
K: preview environments, ephemeral environments, pull request environment, review apps, environment per branch
X: Actually an ephemeral preview environment is a short-lived copy of the app created automatically for a pull request, with its own URL, and destroyed when the pull request is merged or closed. Reviewers, testers and product owners can try the change for real before it merges, instead of reading code or waiting for a shared test environment.
X: How it's usually built. For front ends it's easy. Services like Azure Static Web Apps, Vercel or Netlify, or a pipeline that uploads to a bucket under a pull-request path, create a preview site per pull request automatically.
X: For back-end services on Kubernetes, the pipeline deploys the pull request's image into a new namespace named after the pull request, using the same Helm chart with a small values override, and a dynamic host name like pr-123.dev.example.com. Dependencies are either shared, like a common dev database with test data, or created per environment, like a small database container seeded with test data, depending on cost and isolation needs. A cleanup job deletes the namespace when the pull request closes, plus a nightly sweep for anything left behind.
X: On Azure Container Apps or AWS, infrastructure as code can create and destroy a small stack per pull request.
X: Watch-outs, cost, so environments are small and auto-expire. Secrets, which shouldn't be exposed to pull requests from forks. And data, which has to be synthetic, never copies of production data. That last one is non-negotiable in our domain.
@p17-556
S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you write reusable GitHub Actions workflows and composite actions?
K: reusable workflows, composite actions, github actions reuse, workflow_call, github actions templates
X: Okay, GitHub Actions gives you two main ways to reuse logic, at different levels.
X: Composite actions bundle several steps into one action, defined in an action.yml with inputs and outputs. Like a setup-dotnet-build action that installs the SDK, restores with caching, builds and runs tests with coverage. Any job can use it as a single step. They're good for sharing step sequences, and they run inside the caller's job, on the caller's runner.
X: Reusable workflows are whole workflows triggered with workflow_call, with defined inputs, secrets and outputs. A caller job references them with a uses line pointing at the workflow file in the shared repo, pinned to a tag like v2. They can contain multiple jobs, use their own runners, environments and protection rules, and they're good for standardising entire processes, like build-and-push-image or deploy-to-environment with approvals.
X: What I do, keep shared workflows in a central repository, version them with tags, and have consumers pin a tag, or for third-party actions a full commit SHA, so an upstream change can't silently alter pipelines. Pass secrets explicitly instead of using secrets inherit everywhere. Set minimal permissions for the GITHUB_TOKEN at the workflow level. And document inputs clearly.
X: Organisation-level rulesets can require certain workflows to run on all repositories, like a security scan, which gives you similar governance to required templates in Azure Pipelines.
X: And changes to shared workflows get tested on a sample repository before a new version is tagged.

T: How do you get end-to-end traceability from requirement to deployment?
K: traceability requirement to deployment, work item linking, audit trail release, gxp traceability, commit to production
X: So traceability means for any change running in production, I can answer which requirement or bug it came from, who wrote and reviewed it, which tests verified it, which build produced it, and when and by whom it was deployed and approved. In a GxP environment, auditors expect exactly this.
X: How the tooling gives it to you in Azure DevOps.

X: Test management. Test cases link to requirements, and test runs, manual or automated, link to builds, so validation evidence connects requirement to verification.
X: Going the other way, from a requirement I can find all the code and every release that included it.
X: What actually makes it work is enforcement through policies, not just discipline. And keeping retention settings long enough, because pipeline runs and artifacts get deleted by default after a while, which would break the audit trail. In our setup we set retention to match our records requirements.
@p17-558
S: tx
D: A
T: What is Testcontainers, and why use it for integration tests?
K: testcontainers, testcontainers dotnet, real database in tests, docker integration tests, sql server container tests
X: See, Testcontainers is a library that starts real dependencies in Docker containers from inside the test code, and throws them away afterwards. There's a .NET version, with ready-made modules for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, LocalStack for AWS, Azurite for Azure Storage, and lots more.
X: Why it beats the alternatives. In-memory fakes, like the EF Core in-memory provider or SQLite standing in for SQL Server, behave differently from the real database. No real transactions, different SQL translation, no stored procedures or constraints. Tests pass and production fails. A shared test database is slow to reset, and tests step on each other. Testcontainers gives each test run a real, clean instance of the same engine and version you use in production.
X: How I use it in .NET with xUnit. A fixture class implements IAsyncLifetime, creates an MsSqlBuilder and calls Build on it, starts the container in InitializeAsync, applies migrations, and exposes the connection string. WebApplicationFactory then overrides the app's connection string to point at the container, so the API runs end to end against the real database. The fixture is shared across a test collection, because starting a container takes a few seconds, and Respawn or transactions reset data between tests.
X: It runs the same on a developer laptop and in CI, as long as Docker is available on the agent, which is really the main setup requirement. Once teams try it, they honestly don't go back to in-memory fakes.
@p17-559
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you fake authentication in ASP.NET Core integration tests?
K: test authentication handler, fake jwt integration tests, webapplicationfactory auth, authorize in tests, test user claims
X: Okay, integration tests that call secured endpoints need an authenticated user, but they shouldn't depend on a real identity provider like Keycloak. I've used two approaches for this.
X: A test authentication handler. In WebApplicationFactory's ConfigureTestServices, I register a custom AuthenticationHandler under a test scheme and make it the default. Its HandleAuthenticateAsync builds a ClaimsPrincipal with the claims the test needs, user id, roles, site or study scopes, and returns success. Tests can control the claims per request, for example by reading a test header, so one test runs as a site user and another as an admin. Authorisation policies, role checks and resource-based handlers still run for real, which is exactly what I want to test.
X: Locally signed JWTs. Configure the JWT bearer options in tests to trust a signing key created in the test, then mint tokens with the claims you need. This exercises the real JWT bearer pipeline, including issuer, audience and expiry validation, which is good for testing token-related behaviour.
X: Whichever one, I always include negative tests. No token gives 401, a valid user without permission gives 403, and a user from one site can't read another site's data. Those are the tests that catch real security bugs.
X: What I avoid is disabling authorisation in tests altogether, with AllowAnonymous filters, because then the most important rules never get tested.

T: How do you stub external HTTP APIs in tests with WireMock.Net?
K: wiremock dotnet, stub http api, mock external service, fake http server tests, test third party api
X: So when a service calls an external HTTP API, like a partner's shipment API or an identity provider, tests shouldn't call the real thing. It's slow, flaky, might cost money, and you can't make it fail on demand.
X: WireMock.Net starts a real HTTP server inside the test process on a random port. I point the app's HttpClient base address at it, then set up stubs. When a GET comes in at slash shipments slash 123 with a certain header, return 200 with this JSON body. When a POST comes in, return 201. It records all requests, so tests can verify exactly what was sent, URL, headers and body.
X: Its real value is testing failure behaviour, which is hard with the real API. I can stub a 500, a 429 with a Retry-After header, a slow response that blows past the timeout, malformed JSON, or a connection reset. Then I check retries, circuit breakers and fallbacks behave as designed, like the Polly pipeline retrying twice and then the service returning a clear error.
X: Scenarios let stubs change state across calls, like failing on the first call and succeeding on the second.
X: Compared with mocking HttpMessageHandler in unit tests, WireMock exercises the real HTTP stack, serialisation and handler pipeline.
X: The stubs should match the real API's contract though. If the partner gives an OpenAPI spec or a sandbox, I check stubs against it, or use contract tests, so the fake doesn't drift from reality. That drift is where I've seen people get burned.

S: tx
D: A
T: What is consumer-driven contract testing with Pact?
K: pact contract testing, consumer driven contracts, contract test microservices, pact broker, provider verification
X: Honestly in microservices, an API change can break a consumer without anyone noticing until integration or production. End-to-end tests catch it, but they're slow and fragile. Contract testing catches it earlier and cheaper.
X: With Pact, the consumer team writes tests describing the interactions they rely on. When I call GET slash shipments slash 123, I expect 200 with a body containing id, status and site. During the consumer's test run, Pact acts as a mock provider and records these expectations into a contract file, the pact. The pact gets published to a Pact Broker.
X: The provider then runs verification in its own pipeline. Pact replays each interaction from every consumer's pact against the real provider service, using provider states to set up data, like a shipment with id 123 exists, and checks the responses match. If the provider renamed a field a consumer uses, verification fails in the provider's pipeline, before release.
X: The broker tracks which versions of consumers and providers are compatible, and the can-i-deploy check answers whether a specific version can safely go to an environment.
X: What you get, each consumer only specifies what it actually uses, so providers can change everything else freely. Teams find breaking changes early. And you need fewer slow end-to-end tests.
X: It works for messages too, like event payloads on RabbitMQ or Kafka. The investment is mainly setting up the broker and provider states, so it pays off most with several teams and lots of service interactions.

T: How do you mock APIs in front-end tests with Mock Service Worker?
K: msw, mock service worker, mock api react tests, network level mocking, msw handlers, storybook msw
X: Okay, Mock Service Worker intercepts requests at the network level. In the browser it uses a service worker, and in Node, for Jest or Vitest, it hooks into the request layer. The app code keeps using fetch or axios normally. It has no idea requests are mocked.
X: I define handlers with the http helpers, like http.get for slash api slash shipments, returning a JSON response. Tests use the real data-fetching code, like RTK Query, TanStack Query or a service, so I'm testing what users actually experience. The component renders, fetches, shows a loading state, then shows data or an error.
X: Why it's better than mocking fetch or the API module. Module-level mocks tie tests to implementation details, so refactoring how data is fetched breaks tests even when behaviour hasn't changed. MSW tests survive refactors.
X: Per-test overrides make error cases easy. server.use with a handler returning 500 or a delayed response, then assert that the error message and retry button show up. After each test, handlers reset.
X: The same handlers get reused in Storybook, so components show realistic data in isolation, and in local development, so front-end work can carry on before the back-end endpoint even exists.
X: To keep mocks honest, I generate handlers or types from the OpenAPI spec where I can, so if the API changes, TypeScript flags the mismatch.
X: One config tip, fail tests on unhandled requests, so a missing handler gets caught instead of silently hitting nothing.
@p17-563
S: tx
D: A
T: What is mutation testing, and what does it tell you that coverage doesn't?
K: mutation testing, stryker dotnet, stryker mutator, test quality, mutation score, coverage is not enough
X: So code coverage tells you which lines ran during tests, not whether the tests would notice if those lines were wrong. A test that calls a method and asserts nothing gives full coverage and catches nothing.
X: Mutation testing measures test quality directly. A tool makes small changes to the code, called mutants. Changing greater than to greater than or equal, flipping a boolean, swapping a plus for a minus, removing a method call, or returning a default value. Then it runs the tests against each mutant. If a test fails, the mutant is killed, which is good. If all tests still pass, the mutant survived, meaning nothing in the test suite would notice that bug. The mutation score is the percentage killed.
X: For .NET, Stryker.NET does this, and Stryker exists for JavaScript and TypeScript too. It produces an HTML report showing each surviving mutant in the code, which points straight to missing assertions or untested edge cases, like boundary conditions in a date or quantity check.
X: It's slow, because it runs the tests many times, so I don't run it on every build. I run it on critical modules, like calculation, validation or allocation logic, periodically or in a nightly pipeline, and use the since option to mutate only changed code in pull requests.
X: I don't chase 100 percent, some mutants are equivalent and can't be killed. The value is finding the important gaps that coverage hides. I think that's the best way to put it in an interview.
@p17-564
S: tx
D: A
T: What is property-based testing, and when is it useful?
K: property based testing, fscheck, cscheck, hypothesis python, generative testing, invariants testing
X: Okay, so normal example-based tests check specific inputs. Given 10 kits and 3 requested, 7 remain. Property-based testing instead states a rule that has to hold for all valid inputs, and the framework generates hundreds of random inputs trying to break it.
X: Examples of properties. Serialising and then deserialising any object gives you back the same object. Sorting is idempotent and keeps all the items. For any sequence of reservations and releases, available stock never goes negative, and reserved plus available always equals the total. Or a parsing function never throws for any string, it either succeeds or returns a validation error.
X: When a property fails, the framework shrinks the input down to the smallest failing example, like an empty list or a value of exactly zero, which makes the bug really easy to understand.
X: Tools, FsCheck and CsCheck for .NET, which plug into xUnit. Hypothesis for Python. fast-check for TypeScript.
X: Where it pays off, algorithms with clear invariants, like allocation, scheduling, calculations, encoders and parsers. Code with lots of edge cases. And stateful systems, where the framework generates random sequences of operations and compares the system against a simple model.
X: It doesn't replace example tests, which document specific business cases clearly. And properties take some thought to write well. A property that just reimplements the code proves nothing. I use it for the most logic-heavy parts, and honestly it often finds bugs nobody thought of.
@p17-565
S: tx
D: A
T: What is snapshot or approval testing with Verify?
K: snapshot testing, approval testing, verify dotnet, verify tests, snapshot test api response, received approved files
X: See, snapshot or approval testing checks a complex output against a previously approved version stored in a file, instead of writing loads of individual assertions.
X: With the Verify library in .NET, a test ends with await Verify on the result. The first time, Verify serialises the result, like an object graph, an API response, a generated document, or even the HTTP calls made, into a received file, and the test fails. A developer reviews it, and if it's correct, accepts it as the verified file, which gets committed to the repository. On later runs, the new output is compared with the verified file, and any difference fails the test and shows a diff.
X: It's great for API response shapes, so an accidental field rename or format change gets caught. Generated output like reports, emails, CSV or XML exports, PDFs and images. Complex mapping results. And characterising legacy code before refactoring, capturing its current behaviour.
X: Verify handles the noise. It scrubs values that change every run, like GUIDs and dates, replacing them with stable placeholders, and lets you ignore specific members.
X: The risk is if reviewers just accept every changed snapshot without reading it, the tests catch nothing. Snapshots should be small and focused enough to actually review. And for simple values, plain assertions are clearer.
X: Jest has the same idea for JavaScript, with toMatchSnapshot, usually for serialisable outputs rather than whole component trees.

D: A
T: How do you load test an API with k6 or NBomber?
K: load testing, k6, nbomber, performance testing api, load test script, thresholds k6
X: So load testing checks how a system behaves under realistic and peak traffic, before users find out the hard way.
X: k6 is a popular open-source tool where tests are JavaScript scripts. A script defines what a virtual user does. Log in, list shipments, open one, create an allocation, with realistic think times and data. Scenarios define the load shape, like ramping to 200 virtual users over five minutes, or a constant arrival rate of 50 requests per second, which is better for APIs because it doesn't ease off when the system slows down. Thresholds define pass or fail, like p95 latency below 500 milliseconds and error rate below one percent. That makes load tests usable as pipeline gates. Results can stream to Grafana or other backends.
X: NBomber is a .NET alternative, scenarios in C#, which suits teams that want to reuse existing .NET clients and models, and it's handy for non-HTTP things too, like message consumers.
X: Getting meaningful results. Test in an environment sized like production, with production-like data volumes, because a query that's fast on 1,000 rows can crawl on 10 million. Generate load from outside the system under test, with enough load-generator capacity. Watch the server side during the test, CPU, memory, database waits, thread pool queue length, GC and dependency latency, so you know where the bottleneck is, not just that there is one. And run a baseline before changes, then compare.
@p17-567
S: tx
D: A
T: What are the different types of performance tests?
K: load test vs stress test, soak test, spike test, endurance test, capacity test, performance testing types
X: Actually different performance tests answer different questions, so I pick based on the risk.
X: A load test runs the expected normal and peak traffic, like the busiest hour of a typical day, for a while. It checks response times and error rates meet the targets under the load we actually expect.
X: A stress test pushes load past expectations until the system breaks, to find the breaking point and, more importantly, how it fails. Does it slow down gracefully, shed load with 429 or 503 responses, and recover when load drops? Or does it fall over and stay down?
X: A spike test applies a sudden jump, like ten times normal traffic within seconds, which tests autoscaling speed, connection pools, caches warming up, and queues absorbing bursts. Think of a study going live at lots of sites at once, or a batch import triggering a flood of events.
X: A soak or endurance test runs a moderate load for many hours or days. It finds problems that only show up over time. Memory leaks, connection leaks, growing queues, log disks filling up, slow degradation from fragmentation, and scheduled jobs interfering with traffic.
X: A capacity test finds how much load a given configuration can handle while meeting targets, which feeds sizing and cost decisions.
X: Breakpoint and scalability tests check whether adding instances actually increases throughput, or whether a shared resource, like the database, caps it.
X: All of them need clear targets defined up front, and server-side monitoring to explain the results. Without that, honestly, you just get numbers nobody can act on.
@p17-568
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you build test data with builders, AutoFixture or Bogus?
K: test data builder, autofixture, bogus fake data, object mother, test data setup, arrange section too long
X: Okay, tests get hard to read when the arrange section is 30 lines of object construction, and fragile when a new required property means updating hundreds of tests. Good test data tools fix both.
X: The test data builder pattern. A ShipmentBuilder class with sensible defaults for every property and fluent methods to change only what matters for this test. Like a new ShipmentBuilder, then WithStatus Delivered, then ForSite with the site, then Build. The test shows only the relevant details, and when the model changes, only the builder changes. Builders can create valid object graphs that respect domain rules, which matters when constructors enforce invariants.
X: AutoFixture creates anonymous test data automatically, filling every property with generated values, and you can customise it for specific types. With xUnit's AutoData attributes, it removes boilerplate for tests where the values don't matter, and AutoMoq integration creates mocks for dependencies automatically.
X: Bogus generates realistic fake data. Names, addresses, dates, numbers in realistic ranges, with a seed for reproducibility. It's great for seeding dev databases, demo environments and load tests, and for UI work where realistic data shows layout problems.
X: My rule is, values that matter to the test's outcome should be visible in the test, not hidden in defaults. Generated data should be valid by default. Seeds make random data reproducible when a test fails. And never use real production or patient data in tests, which in a clinical domain is especially important.

T: How do you test code that depends on the current time?
K: testing datetime, timeprovider, faketimeprovider, mock datetime now, time dependent tests, clock abstraction
X: So code that calls DateTime.Now or DateTime.UtcNow directly is hard to test. A rule like "a kit expires after 30 days" or "send a reminder if a visit is overdue by two days" depends on the clock, and tests either get flaky or have to wait.
X: The fix is to inject the clock. Since .NET 8 there's a built-in abstraction, TimeProvider. Code depends on TimeProvider, registered as TimeProvider.System in production, and calls GetUtcNow, GetLocalNow, or the CreateTimer and Task.Delay overloads that accept a TimeProvider.
X: In tests, FakeTimeProvider, from Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing, lets me set the current time to an exact value and move it forward with Advance, passing TimeSpan.FromDays of 31. Timers and delays scheduled through the fake provider fire when time is advanced, so tests of timeouts, expiry, retries with delays, or periodic background work run instantly and deterministically.
X: Before .NET 8, teams wrote their own IClock or ISystemClock interface, which works the same way.
X: Things worth testing explicitly with a controllable clock. Boundaries, like exactly at the expiry moment versus one second before. Time zones, especially for sites in different countries and daylight saving transitions, where a visit window can be 23 or 25 hours. And month ends and leap years. Those daylight saving ones catch people all the time.
X: For front-end code, Jest and Vitest have fake timers and can set the system time, which does the same job.

T: How do you test background services and hosted services?
K: test backgroundservice, test hosted service, test worker service, executeasync test, test queue consumer dotnet
X: Honestly a BackgroundService is awkward to test directly. It runs a loop in ExecuteAsync, often reading from a queue or polling on a timer, so you've got the infinite loop, timing and cancellation all mixed in. So I separate concerns.
X: Keep the loop thin. The hosted service only handles the mechanics. Wait for the next item or tick, create a DI scope, call a handler, and handle errors and cancellation. The real work lives in a separate class, like ProcessShipmentEventHandler, which is a normal class with injected dependencies and gets unit-tested like anything else. That's where most tests go.
X: Test the loop's mechanics separately, with a small number of focused tests. Start the service with a cancellation token, feed it an item through a fake queue or a Channel, wait until the handler is called, using a TaskCompletionSource instead of sleeps, then cancel and check it stops cleanly. Check an exception in one item doesn't kill the loop, and that a scope gets created per item. With TimeProvider and FakeTimeProvider, periodic services can be tested without real waiting.
X: Integration tests run the whole host with WebApplicationFactory or a test host, and a real broker through Testcontainers, publishing a message and asserting the expected database change shows up, with a timeout and polling.
X: I also test graceful shutdown. Stopping the host while an item is being processed should either finish it or leave it safely to be redelivered, never half-done.
@p17-571
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you test retry and resilience logic?
K: test polly retry, test circuit breaker, test resilience pipeline, simulate transient failures, chaos testing httpclient
X: See, retry, timeout and circuit breaker logic is easy to get wrong and rarely exercised until an outage, so it deserves deliberate tests.
X: At the unit level, I test the policy configuration itself. With Polly v8, I can build the resilience pipeline and execute a delegate that fails a set number of times, like throwing HttpRequestException twice and then succeeding, and assert it was called three times. For circuit breakers, I fail enough calls to open the circuit, assert the next call fails fast with BrokenCircuitException, then advance a fake TimeProvider past the break duration and check a trial call is allowed. Injecting the TimeProvider means no real waiting on backoff delays.
X: At the integration level, I put a fake server, like WireMock.Net, behind the real typed HttpClient with its real resilience handler, configured from the real settings. Then stub sequences. 503 then 200, 429 with Retry-After, a delay longer than the attempt timeout. I assert what the caller experiences and how many requests actually reached the server.
X: The important cases, non-idempotent requests, like POSTs, shouldn't be retried unless they carry an idempotency key. The total timeout should cap the whole sequence. And no retries for 400-type errors.
X: Polly also has chaos strategies to inject faults, latency or fake results in a test environment, which validates the whole system's behaviour under failure. I've seen that surface stuff nobody expected.
@p17-572
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you test database migrations?
K: test ef core migrations, migration testing, test schema changes, migration rollback test, migration ci check
X: Okay, migrations change production data structures, often irreversibly, so they need testing beyond "it ran on my machine".
X: The checks I put in the pipeline, pretty much always.
X: Model and migrations in sync. For EF Core, a test or a pipeline step fails if there are pending model changes without a migration, which .NET 8 and later can check with dotnet ef migrations has-pending-model-changes.
X: Apply from scratch. Create an empty database in a container with Testcontainers and apply all migrations from the beginning. That catches broken or order-dependent migrations.
X: Apply to a realistic existing state. Restore a copy of the schema, or an anonymised dataset, at the current production version, then apply the new migrations. A lot of failures only happen with real data, like adding a NOT NULL column without a default, a unique index on a column that has duplicates, or a data conversion that fails on unexpected values.
X: Measure duration on production-sized data. A migration that takes two seconds on test data might lock a big table for 20 minutes. If it's slow, it needs redesigning as an online change or batched.
X: Compatibility. Run the previous app version's tests against the new schema, since during a rolling deployment the old version runs against the migrated database.
X: Rollback. If down migrations are supported, test them too, otherwise document the forward-fix plan.
X: For SSDT projects, same thing applies to the generated deployment script, reviewed and run against a production-like copy.
@p17-573
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you unit test stored procedures and SQL logic?
K: test stored procedures, tsql unit testing, tsqlt, database unit tests, sql logic testing
X: So when important business logic lives in stored procedures, which is common in older systems like ours, it deserves tests just like C# code.
X: tSQLt is a unit testing framework that runs inside SQL Server. Tests are themselves stored procedures, grouped in test classes, and each test runs in a transaction that gets rolled back, so tests don't leave data behind. The key feature is faking. FakeTable replaces a table with an empty copy without constraints, so a test inserts only the rows it needs. SpyProcedure replaces a called procedure with a spy that records calls. And assertions like AssertEqualsTable compare expected and actual result sets. That isolates the logic of one procedure from the rest of the schema.
X: The alternative is testing procedures from .NET integration tests. Spin up a real SQL Server with Testcontainers, deploy the schema from the SSDT project or migrations, insert test data, call the procedure through Dapper or ADO.NET, and assert results. That tests the procedure and the calling code's mapping together, and fits the existing .NET test tooling and CI. In our kind of setup, I'd lean towards this one.
X: What I focus on, boundary conditions, null handling, transactions and error handling with THROW, concurrency-related logic, like whether two calls can allocate the same item, and performance with realistic data volumes, checking execution plans for scans.
X: Whatever the tool, the database schema should be in source control, so tests run in CI against the exact schema being released.
@p17-574
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you keep integration tests isolated when they share a database?
K: test database isolation, respawn, reset database between tests, transaction rollback tests, parallel integration tests
X: Actually integration tests that share a database can really interfere. One test's data changes another test's results, tests pass alone but fail together, and order starts mattering. I've used a few strategies to keep them isolated.
X: Reset between tests. Respawn is a .NET library that deletes data from all tables quickly, in the right order respecting foreign keys, while keeping reference tables you list. Calling it before each test gives you a clean database in milliseconds, much faster than recreating the database.
X: Wrap each test in a transaction and roll it back at the end. Fast and clean, but it doesn't work if the code under test manages its own transactions, uses multiple connections, or if you're testing through HTTP where the request runs on a different connection.
X: Unique data per test. Each test creates its own data with unique ids or names and only asserts on that data. That allows parallel tests on one database, but queries like "count all shipments" become unreliable.
X: Database per test class or collection. With Testcontainers, each test collection can get its own database inside a shared container, created from a template or snapshot, which allows parallel collections.
X: My typical setup, one container per test run, one database per test collection, Respawn before each test, and tests that create their own data. In xUnit, collections run in parallel and tests within a collection run sequentially, which fits this model nicely.
@p17-575
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you test for race conditions and concurrency bugs?
K: test concurrency, race condition test, concurrent requests test, double booking test, optimistic concurrency test
X: Okay, concurrency bugs, like two requests reserving the same last kit, or a duplicate message being processed twice at the same time, rarely show up in normal tests, because tests run one call at a time.
X: So I test them deliberately.
X: Fire concurrent requests in integration tests. Start, say, 20 tasks that call the same endpoint at once, released together with a barrier or a SemaphoreSlim, against a real database. Then assert the invariant. Exactly one reservation succeeded, the others got a conflict, and the stock count is correct. Run it multiple times, because a race might not show up every run.
X: Test the concurrency control itself. For optimistic concurrency, load an entity in two DbContexts, save one, then assert the second save throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException, and that the app turns it into a 409 or a retry. For unique constraints, assert the database rejects duplicates and the code handles the error.
X: Test idempotency under concurrency. Deliver the same message twice in parallel to the consumer and assert the effect happened once.
X: Use deterministic tools where you can. For code using locks or channels, control the interleaving by pausing one operation at a specific point with hooks, so the test hits the dangerous window every time, not just by luck.
X: Load tests at higher concurrency also surface deadlocks and lock contention.
X: The mindset I go with is, figure out the invariant that has to hold, then try really hard to break it.

T: How do you include security testing in the delivery process?
K: security testing, sast dast, owasp zap, penetration testing, dependency scanning, security tests pipeline
X: So basically I don't treat security testing as one big activity at the end. It's layers, and most of it runs in the pipeline on its own.
X: On every pull request we've got static analysis, so things like SonarQube security rules, Roslyn analyzers, Semgrep or CodeQL. They catch injection risks, unsafe deserialisation, weak crypto, hardcoded secrets, that kind of stuff. Then dependency scanning checks our NuGet and npm packages and the container images for known vulnerabilities, and the build fails if something critical shows up. Secret scanning sits on top so credentials never get committed in the first place.

Tools won't find those for you.
X: For infra, Checkov or something similar scans Terraform and Kubernetes manifests. And before big releases, specialists do a pen test, because they find logic flaws that automation misses. Whatever comes out of all this gets tracked like a normal bug, with fix deadlines based on severity.

T: How do you test web accessibility?

@p17-578
S: tx
D: A
T: What is visual regression testing?
K: visual regression testing, screenshot comparison tests, chromatic, playwright screenshot, ui visual tests, percy
X: See, functional tests can tell you a button exists and works, but not that it's now hidden behind another element, or the layout broke on mobile, or a theme change made the text unreadable. Visual regression testing is for exactly that, catching changes in how the UI looks that nobody intended.
X: How it works is pretty simple. You take screenshots of pages or components in a known state and store them as approved baselines. On later runs it takes new screenshots and compares them, pixel by pixel or perceptually. If the difference is over a threshold, the test fails and you get a diff image with the changes highlighted. Then the developer either approves it as an intended change or fixes it.
X: For tools, Playwright has screenshot assertions built in, toHaveScreenshot. Storybook with Chromatic captures every story on each pull request, which is really nice for a design system. Percy or Applitools give smarter comparison and review flows.
X: The hard part, honestly, is making it stable. Screenshots have to be deterministic, so fixed test data and dates, animations off, fonts loaded, same browser and OS, ideally the same container image in CI. Timestamps and other dynamic bits get masked, and a small threshold absorbs anti-aliasing noise.
X: I don't screenshot everything. I focus on shared components and a few key pages at the important screen sizes, so reviewing diffs stays quick. In our component-based front end, covering the shared library visually protects every feature package that uses it.

T: How do you test Redux Toolkit slices, selectors and custom hooks?
K: test redux slice, test selectors, renderhook, test custom hooks react, test rtk query, redux testing
X: Actually, with Redux Toolkit most of the logic is just plain functions, so it's one of the easier things to test.
X: Reducers are pure. So the test just calls the reducer with a previous state and an action from the slice's action creator, say allocation added with a kit, and checks the new state. No store, no rendering. I test the meaningful transitions and edge cases, I don't bother with every trivial setter.

X: For custom hooks, renderHook from React Testing Library, with a wrapper that gives it the store, router or query client. I check the returned values, call the returned functions inside act, and check the updates.
X: But mostly I'd rather test components the way a user uses them, with a real store, and keep isolated reducer tests for the tricky logic.
@p17-580
S: tx
D: A
T: Do you practise test-driven development?
K: tdd, test driven development, red green refactor, do you write tests first, tdd benefits drawbacks
X: Honestly, yes, but selectively. I use it where it pays off, I'm not dogmatic about doing it everywhere.
X: The cycle is red, green, refactor. You write a small failing test for the next bit of behaviour, write the simplest code to make it pass, then clean up the code and tests while they stay green, and repeat in small steps.
X: Where it really works for me is business rules with clear inputs and outputs, like validation, calculations, allocation logic. Writing the test first forces me to pin down the behaviour and the edge cases before I get lost in the implementation. Bug fixes too. I always write a failing test that reproduces the bug first, so I know the fix actually works and the bug can't quietly come back. And it helps when I'm designing a class's API, because writing the test first shows you very quickly if the interface is awkward to use.
X: Where I'm more relaxed is exploratory work, where I don't know the shape of the solution yet. There I spike first, then write the tests and usually rewrite the code properly. Same for UI layout and thin glue code, where an integration test gives better value anyway.
X: What I've seen from it is cleaner, more decoupled code, because testable code tends to have clear dependencies, and a lot more confidence when refactoring.
X: Whether the test comes first or right after, my rule is the tests describe behaviour, not implementation, and no logic change goes in without one.
@p17-581
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you add tests to legacy code that has none?
K: testing legacy code, characterization tests, seams, working effectively with legacy code, refactor without tests
X: So you can't stop everything and write tests for the whole legacy codebase, that never happens. What I follow is basically the approach from Working Effectively with Legacy Code, which is you add tests where you're about to make a change.
X: I start with characterisation tests. Before touching a piece of code, I write tests that capture what it does today, not what it should do. Call it with realistic inputs and assert whatever comes back. Snapshot tools like Verify make that quick when the output is complex. Those tests protect the existing behaviour, including the weird bits other parts of the system might depend on.
X: Then you need seams. Legacy code usually creates its own dependencies directly, so new SqlConnection, static calls, DateTime dot Now, HttpContext dot Current. A seam is a place where you can swap behaviour for a test without changing the logic. So I extract an interface and inject it, or pull the hard call into a virtual method and override it in a test subclass, or wrap statics behind a small adapter, or just pass the value in as a parameter. All in small, safe refactoring steps, mostly tool-assisted.
X: For new functionality I use sprout and wrap. I write it as a new, tested class or method and call it from the old code, instead of adding more untested lines to a huge method.
X: And for really tangled code, integration tests around the edges, like the real API or stored procedure against a test database, give you protection fastest. That's how we change the risky areas in our .NET Framework core.
@p17-582
S: tx
D: A
T: How would you test a randomisation algorithm in a clinical trial system?
K: test randomization algorithm, randomisation testing, statistical testing allocation, test treatment allocation, irt randomization validation
X: Let me put it this way, randomisation decides which treatment arm a patient goes to, so if it's wrong, it hurts the scientific validity of the trial. So I test it two ways, normal tests and statistical checks.
X: For the normal tests, the algorithm has to take its random source as a dependency. Then tests can give it a seeded generator or a fixed sequence, and I can assert exact results. With block size four and a one to one ratio, each block has two of each arm. Stratification puts the patient in the right stratum based on their factors. When a site or stratum is capped, the right thing happens. And with a pre-generated randomisation list, patients get the next entry in their stratum in order, and no entry is ever used twice.
X: Then the edge cases, like the last slot in a block, the list running out, invalid strata, re-randomisation rules, and two sites randomising at the exact same moment. Those two must never get the same entry.
X: The statistical part is simulation. You run it thousands of times, [like 100,000 simulated patients], and check the allocation ratios match the design within tolerance, balance holds within strata and sites for dynamic methods like minimisation, and there's no predictable pattern. That runs as part of study configuration testing, not every build.
X: And since it's a regulated system, the tests, the simulation reports and the configuration they ran against are kept as validation evidence. The study config also goes through UAT before it goes live.
@p17-583
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you test both states of a feature flag?
K: test feature flags, feature toggle testing, flag combinations testing, feature flag test strategy
X: Yeah, so the risk with flags is they double the paths through your code, and usually one state, the one that isn't switched on in test, never gets tested. Then someone flips it and it breaks.
X: What I do is, for every flag that changes logic, unit tests for both states. The flag check is injected, through IFeatureManager or a small interface, so the test just sets it on or off. Each flagged behaviour gets one test with it on and one with it off.
X: For integration and end-to-end tests, they run against the config production will actually have at release. If prod starts with the flag off, the main run uses off, and then there's a second run, or a subset of tests, with it on. I've seen test environments with every flag switched on, and then the off path, which is literally what production runs, isn't tested at all.
X: I don't test every combination though. With a few flags that explodes fast. Flags should be independent where possible, and I only test combinations for flags that actually interact.
X: For important flags I test the flip itself. Switching at runtime shouldn't break requests in flight or leave things inconsistent, like jobs started under the old behaviour. I also test the failure default, so if the flag service is down, the code falls back to the safe value.
X: And once a flag is fully rolled out and removed, the tests for the dead path go too. Keeps the suite honest about what the code really does.

T: How do you test Azure Functions or AWS Lambda handlers?
K: test azure functions, test lambda function, unit test lambda dotnet, local testing serverless, lambda test tool
X: Honestly, the trick with serverless is keeping the handler thin, then testing is easy.
X: So the function method or Lambda handler just translates the trigger into a call. It parses the HTTP request, queue message or S3 event, calls a service class, and maps the result back. X: But emulators can't check everything. So we also deploy through the pipeline to a real cloud test environment and trigger it with a real message or HTTP call.
