D: A
T: How do you set up OpenTelemetry in a .NET service?
K: opentelemetry dotnet setup, otel dotnet, addopentelemetry, otlp exporter, instrument aspnet core opentelemetry
X: Okay, so OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs. The nice part in .NET is the runtime already produces the raw signals, Activity for traces, System.Diagnostics.Metrics for metrics, and ILogger for logs. OpenTelemetry just collects and exports them.
X: In Program dot cs, you call AddOpenTelemetry on the services, then ConfigureResource to set the service name, version and environment, which every signal carries. WithTracing adds instrumentation for ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, SQL client or EF Core, plus any custom ActivitySource the app has. WithMetrics adds ASP.NET Core, HttpClient and runtime instrumentation, so you get request durations, GC, thread pool, exception counts, plus your own Meters. For logs you add OpenTelemetry to the logging builder, so log lines carry the trace and span ids. Then UseOtlpExporter sends everything over OTLP, usually to a local Collector, which forwards to Datadog, Grafana, Azure Monitor or CloudWatch. The endpoint and headers come from the standard environment variables, like OTEL exporter OTLP endpoint, so the same code works everywhere.
X: A few habits I stick to. Clear, stable names for custom spans and metrics. Useful attributes like tenant or study id, but never personal data. Record exceptions on spans. And filter out noise, like health check requests, otherwise they flood everything.
X: In our case the newest services use OpenTelemetry with Datadog, while older parts still log to Splunk with Serilog. The good thing about standardising on OpenTelemetry is if we change the backend later, it's config, not code.
@p17-586
S: obx
D: A
T: What does the OpenTelemetry Collector do, and why use one?
K: opentelemetry collector, otel collector, collector pipeline receivers processors exporters, agent vs gateway collector
X: So the Collector is a separate process. It receives telemetry, processes it, and exports it to one or more backends. The apps just send to the collector over OTLP instead of talking to each vendor directly.
X: The config is pipelines for traces, metrics and logs, and each pipeline has receivers, processors and exporters. Receivers take data in, OTLP from apps, Prometheus scraping, host metrics, log files, Kafka and so on. Processors change it, so batching, memory limits, adding attributes like cluster and region, dropping noisy spans like health checks, redacting sensitive attributes, tail-based sampling. Exporters send it out to Datadog, Grafana, Jaeger, Prometheus, Azure Monitor, CloudWatch, or several of them at once.
X: Why bother? For me the big one is apps stay simple and vendor-neutral. Switching or adding a backend is a collector config change, not redeploying every service. Retries and buffering happen in the collector too, so if the backend has an outage, the app doesn't slow down. Redaction, sampling and enrichment rules are applied the same way for every service. And the backend credentials live in one place instead of in every app.
X: For deployment, you usually have an agent collector close to the apps, per host, as a sidecar or a DaemonSet, and optionally a gateway collector cluster for central stuff like tail sampling.
X: One catch, the collector is now part of your pipeline, so you have to monitor it and size it properly, otherwise it drops data right when load is highest.
@p17-587
S: obx
D: A
T: Counter vs gauge vs histogram: which metric type do you use when?
K: metric types, counter gauge histogram, updowncounter, percentile metrics, system diagnostics metrics
X: Picking the right type actually matters, because it decides what questions you can answer later.
X: A counter only goes up. Requests handled, orders created, errors, bytes sent. You never really look at the raw number, you look at the rate, like requests per second, or the increase over a window. And in Prometheus-style systems restarts are fine, because the rate functions handle resets.
X: Then a gauge or up-down counter is a current value that goes up and down. Up-down counter is for things you increment and decrement yourself, like active connections or items in an in-memory queue. A gauge is something you observe at a point in time, like memory used, queue depth read from the broker, or the temperature of a storage unit. For gauges you look at averages and max over time. Rates don't make sense there.
X: A histogram records the distribution, like request duration or payload size, into buckets. From that you get percentiles, p95, p99 latency, which matter way more than averages, because the average hides the slow requests users actually notice. Histograms also aggregate across instances correctly, which pre-computed percentiles can't do.
X: In .NET's System.Diagnostics.Metrics these are Counter, UpDownCounter, ObservableGauge and Histogram. So say an allocation service, I'd have a counter for allocations by outcome, a histogram for allocation duration, and an observable gauge for available kits per depot.
X: Just make sure the histogram buckets cover the expected range, or use exponential histograms so you don't have to pick them by hand.
@p17-588
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you add custom business metrics to a .NET service?
K: custom metrics dotnet, meter dotnet, business metrics, system.diagnostics.metrics, imeterfactory, instrument business events
X: So technical metrics like CPU and latency tell you the system is up. Business metrics tell you if it's actually doing its job, like orders placed, patients randomised, shipments delivered, allocations failed because there's no stock. And quite often the business metric drops before any technical alarm fires. Say an integration is quietly sending nothing, CPU looks perfectly fine.
X: In .NET I use System.Diagnostics.Metrics. I get a Meter from IMeterFactory through dependency injection, which keeps it testable, and create the instruments once. A Counter for randomisations, a Histogram for end-to-end shipment processing time, an ObservableGauge for kits available per depot, calculated from a cached query. Then I record values right where the business event happens, with tags like outcome success or failure, or region.
X: On the OpenTelemetry side you just call AddMeter with the meter name and they get exported with the built-in metrics.
X: A few rules I follow. Tags have to be low cardinality, so outcome, region, study phase, maybe study id if the number of studies is bounded. Never patient ids, kit numbers or user ids, that creates millions of time series and a huge bill. Names are consistent, with units, following the OpenTelemetry conventions. And I record after the transaction commits, otherwise a failed transaction gets counted as a success.
X: Then the dashboard shows business flow at a glance, and you can alert on something like no randomisations in the last hour during business hours at an active study. That's exactly the kind of silent failure our AlertWatchDog jobs were built to catch.
@p17-589
S: obx
D: A
T: What are SLIs, SLOs and error budgets?
K: sli slo sla, error budget, service level objective, service level indicator, reliability targets
X: Okay, these come from site reliability engineering, and they basically give you a precise way to talk about reliability instead of just saying "it should be up".
X: An SLI, service level indicator, is a measurement of what users experience, usually good events divided by total events. Like the percentage of API calls that succeed, or the percentage served within 300 milliseconds, or the percentage of shipment events processed within five minutes.
X: An SLO is the target for that SLI over a window. So 99.9 percent of requests succeed over 28 days, or 95 percent finish within 300 milliseconds.
X: An SLA is the contract with the customer, with consequences like credits if you miss it. Your SLOs should be stricter than the SLA, so you get a warning before you breach the contract.
X: The error budget is what the SLO allows to fail. With 99.9 percent that's 0.1 percent, roughly 43 minutes of full downtime in 30 days. What I like is it turns reliability into a shared thing you can measure. If there's plenty of budget left, the team can ship faster and take more risk. If it's burning fast, you slow down releases and do reliability work.
X: For alerting you use burn rates. You alert when the budget's being used much faster than it should, say 14 times the normal rate over an hour. That catches real user-facing problems and ignores small blips.
X: And pick SLOs based on what users actually need. Not 100 percent, that's impossible and makes every change scary.
@p17-590
S: obx
D: A
T: What are the RED and USE methods for monitoring?
K: red method, use method, rate errors duration, utilization saturation errors, golden signals, what to monitor
X: See, they're two simple checklists for what to monitor, just from different angles.
X: RED is for services, from the user's point of view. For every service or endpoint you track Rate, requests per second, Errors, the count or percentage of failed requests, and Duration, the response times as percentiles. If you have those for every service, you can see very quickly which one is unhappy and how. It maps nicely to dashboards too, one row per service with three panels.
X: USE is for resources, from the infrastructure side. For every resource, CPU, memory, disk, network, connection pools, thread pools, queues, you track Utilisation, how busy it is, Saturation, how much work is waiting, like the run queue or the thread pool queue, and Errors, like disk errors or dropped packets. Saturation is the one people forget, and honestly it's often the most telling. 70 percent CPU might be totally fine, but a growing thread pool queue is a real problem.
X: Google's four golden signals are pretty similar, latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
X: How I use them together is RED tells me there's a problem, like the allocation API's p95 latency has tripled. Then USE on the resources behind it tells me why, like the database connection pool is saturated and requests are sitting there waiting for a connection. So one finds the symptom and the other one finds the cause.
@p17-591
S: obx
D: A
T: What is high cardinality, and why does it blow up metrics cost?
K: high cardinality metrics, metric labels cardinality, time series explosion, metrics cost, label best practices
X: Actually it's simple once you know that every unique combination of metric name and label values is its own time series. A request counter with method, route and status code labels might give you a few hundred series, that's fine. Add a user id label and suddenly it's hundreds of thousands. That's high cardinality.
X: Why it hurts: the backend stores and indexes each series separately, so memory, storage and query time all grow with the series count. Prometheus can just run out of memory. Commercial tools like Datadog charge per custom metric series, so one careless label can create a huge bill overnight. And dashboards get slow.
X: The usual culprits are user ids, emails, request ids, raw URLs with ids in the path instead of the route template, timestamps, exception messages, kit or order numbers, and pod names in very dynamic setups.
X: What I do is keep labels to bounded values. Route templates like shipments slash id in braces, status code classes, region, outcome. The high-cardinality detail goes into traces and logs, which are built for per-request data and you can search them by id. New metrics get reviewed, and the pipeline or collector can drop or rewrite labels. I also watch the number of series per metric so growth gets caught early.
X: And if someone really needs per-entity analysis, like latency per customer, that's usually better answered from logs or traces, or an analytics store that's designed for high cardinality.
@p17-592
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you choose log levels, and what belongs at each level?
K: log levels, when to log error vs warning, log level guidelines, information vs debug logging, too many logs
X: Honestly, if levels aren't consistent, logs become noise and cost a lot. So here's roughly how I use them.
X: Critical or Fatal is when the app or a key component can't continue. Like it fails to start because config is invalid, or the database is completely gone. Someone should get woken up.
X: Error is an operation failed and needs attention. An unhandled exception in a request, a message going to the dead-letter queue, an integration call that failed after all the retries. My rule is every error log should be actionable. If nobody needs to do anything, it's not an error.
X: Warning is something unexpected but handled. A retry worked after a transient failure, a fallback kicked in, a slow query crossed a threshold, a deprecated API got called. Warnings help you spot trends before they turn into errors.
X: Information is the important business and lifecycle events. Service started, shipment created, randomisation completed, a job processed 230 records. They tell the story of what happened without every little step.
X: Debug and Trace are detailed diagnostics for developers, intermediate values, which branch it took. Off in production by default, but you can switch them on per category at runtime, so we turn it on for one component during an investigation.
X: And a few other things. Log an exception once, where it's handled, not at every layer. Use structured properties, not string concatenation. Never log secrets or personal data. And set minimum levels per namespace to quiet the noisy libraries.
@p17-593
S: obx
D: A
T: Head-based vs tail-based sampling: how do you sample traces?
K: trace sampling, head based sampling, tail based sampling, sampling rate opentelemetry, keep error traces
X: So at high traffic, recording every single trace costs a lot in network, storage and money, and most successful traces look exactly the same anyway. Sampling keeps a representative subset.
X: Head-based sampling decides at the start of the trace, in the first service, usually as a percentage, like keep 10 percent. That decision travels in the trace context, so every downstream service keeps or drops the same trace and traces stay complete. It's simple and cheap and done in the SDK, with the ParentBased and TraceIdRatioBased samplers in OpenTelemetry. The problem is it decides before you know whether the request will fail or be slow, so you also throw away 90 percent of your interesting error traces.
X: Tail-based sampling decides after the trace is complete, usually in an OpenTelemetry Collector or in the backend, which buffers all the spans for a short time. Then rules decide. Keep every trace with an error, keep everything slower than a second, keep traces for important endpoints, and a small percentage of the rest. You get all the interesting ones and only a few boring ones. What you pay for it is the collector has to receive every span and hold them in memory, and all spans of one trace must land on the same collector instance, so you need load balancing by trace id.
X: What I'd go with usually is little or no head sampling in the SDK and tail sampling in a collector gateway. One thing, compute metrics before sampling, so your rates and error percentages stay accurate.
@p17-594
S: obx
D: A
T: How does trace context propagate across HTTP calls and message queues?
K: trace context propagation, traceparent header, w3c trace context, propagate trace through rabbitmq, distributed tracing messages
X: Right, so distributed tracing only works if every hop passes the trace context along, that's how each service's spans join the same trace.
X: The standard is W3C Trace Context. The traceparent header carries the trace id, the parent span id and the sampling flag, and tracestate carries vendor-specific stuff. Then there's baggage, a separate header for app key-value pairs like tenant id that should travel with the request. You use that carefully because it goes everywhere.
X: For HTTP, .NET just does it for you. HttpClient instrumentation adds traceparent on outgoing calls and ASP.NET Core reads it on incoming ones and creates a child Activity. Most other languages' OpenTelemetry instrumentation does the same, which is why a mixed .NET and Java system can still be traced end to end.
X: Messaging is where it's more manual and, in my experience, more often broken. The producer has to inject the context into the message headers or properties, and the consumer has to extract it and start its processing span as a child or with a link. Some libraries handle it, like for Kafka, Azure Service Bus, MassTransit and NServiceBus. For the raw RabbitMQ client, I add small helpers using OpenTelemetry's propagator API to inject and extract. For batch consumers, span links connect one processing span to many producer spans.
X: And where context just gets lost, like a legacy system in the middle or a file transfer, I carry a correlation id in the payload and log it, so you can still join the pieces.
@p17-595
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you design a useful Grafana dashboard?
K: grafana dashboard design, dashboard best practices, service dashboard, too many panels, dashboard hierarchy
X: Let me start with what usually goes wrong. Most bad dashboards have way too many panels and no story. A good one answers specific questions fast, especially at 3 AM during an incident.
X: So I start from the questions. Is the service healthy for users? What changed? Which dependency is the problem? Each panel should help answer one of those.
X: Then a hierarchy. The top-level overview shows every service's health in one place with RED metrics, request rate, error percentage, latency percentiles, plus SLO status. You click through to a service dashboard with the detail, endpoints, dependencies, resource usage with USE metrics, queue depths. And deeper than that, component dashboards for things like the database or the message broker.
X: On a page, the top is the user-facing signals and SLOs, and below that the causes, dependencies, saturation, infrastructure.
X: I add deployments and incidents as annotations, so "latency went up right after release 3.4.2" is obvious just by looking. Same time ranges and units, percentiles instead of averages, same colours for the same meaning.
X: Template variables for environment, region and service, so one dashboard serves all of them instead of copies that drift apart.
X: Links out, from a latency spike to the traces for that time range through exemplars, and then to logs.
X: Dashboards live as code, JSON or Terraform or Grafana provisioning, reviewed in pull requests, so they don't rot. And I'd say delete the ones nobody uses. A few dashboards people trust beat a hundred abandoned ones.
@p17-596
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you reduce alert fatigue?
K: alert fatigue, too many alerts, noisy alerts, actionable alerts, on call burnout, alert tuning
X: Yeah, alert fatigue is when people get so many alerts, mostly unimportant or false, that they start ignoring them, and then they miss the real one. So it's a reliability risk and honestly a morale problem as well.
X: My first rule is every page has to be actionable and urgent. If the response is "let's wait and see" or "nothing to do", it shouldn't wake anyone up. That becomes a ticket, a dashboard item or a daily digest.
X: Alert on symptoms, not causes. Users care about errors, latency and business processes failing, so alerts are based on SLOs and burn rates. High CPU on one instance is a cause, and if users aren't affected, it's not a page.
X: Tune thresholds and durations. A one-minute spike shouldn't page anybody. The condition has to hold for a sensible period, you add hysteresis so it doesn't flap, and use dynamic thresholds where traffic changes a lot by time of day.
X: Deduplicate and group. One incident should be one notification, not fifty from every instance and every dependent service. A "database down" alert can suppress the downstream ones.
X: Route it to the owning team, and let severity decide paging versus just a message. Put context in the alert, a clear title, which service, the impact, a dashboard link and the runbook.
X: And review it. After every on-call week, look at what fired, what was useful, and fix or delete the noisy ones. We track alerts per week as a metric, which keeps the pressure on.
@p17-597
S: obx
D: A
T: What is synthetic monitoring, and when do you need it?
K: synthetic monitoring, synthetic checks, uptime checks, canary scripts, cloudwatch synthetics, availability tests
X: Okay so synthetic monitoring is basically scripted checks that run against the system on a schedule, from outside, like a fake user. Every few minutes it calls the health endpoint, logs in, opens the dashboard, searches for a shipment, and checks the results look right.
X: Why do you need it when you already have real-user monitoring and server metrics? Mainly because it finds problems when there's no traffic. At night, at weekends, or on a rarely used feature, real users won't show you the outage until Monday morning, the synthetic check will. It also tests from the user side, so it catches stuff server metrics can't see, DNS issues, expired certificates, CDN or load balancer misconfig, a broken login with the identity provider, a front-end bundle error. It gives a steady baseline for availability and latency from different regions, which helps for SLA reporting. And you can run it right after a deployment as an automated smoke test.
X: There are simple uptime checks on URLs with status code, content and certificate expiry, API checks with multi-step calls, and browser checks scripted with Playwright or Selenium that walk full journeys. Tools like CloudWatch Synthetics canaries, Application Insights availability tests, Datadog Synthetics, Grafana, or just a scheduled Playwright job.
X: The thing to be careful about is test data. Use dedicated test accounts so synthetic transactions never pollute production data or reports. In a clinical system that's critical, you never create real patient or shipment records. And keep the scripts maintained, or they turn into noisy false alarms.
@p17-598
S: obx
D: A
T: What is real user monitoring, and which front-end metrics matter?
K: real user monitoring, rum, core web vitals, lcp inp cls, front end monitoring, page performance real users
X: So real user monitoring collects performance and error data from actual users' browsers. A small script or SDK in the app reports page loads, route changes, API call timings, JavaScript errors and sessions. Synthetic tests run from a fast data centre, but this shows what people on real devices, networks and locations actually go through.
X: The main metrics are Google's Core Web Vitals. LCP, Largest Contentful Paint, is how fast the main content shows up, good is under 2.5 seconds. INP, Interaction to Next Paint, which replaced First Input Delay, is how quickly the page responds to clicks and key presses, good is under 200 milliseconds. CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift, is how much stuff jumps around while loading, good is under 0.1. Time to First Byte is useful too for server and network speed, and for single-page apps I look at route change duration and the key API calls.
X: Look at percentiles, the 75th is what Core Web Vitals use, and break it down by page, browser, country and device. Averages hide the people having a bad time.
X: RUM tools also capture JavaScript errors with stack traces mapped through source maps, and they can link the front-end session to the back-end trace with trace context headers, so a slow screen can be followed right into the API and the database.
X: Tools wise, Datadog RUM, Application Insights for JavaScript, CloudWatch RUM, Sentry, or the open-source web-vitals library reporting to your own backend. And privacy, you mask inputs and never capture personal or clinical data in session replays.
@p17-599
S: obx
D: A
T: What are exemplars, and how do they connect metrics to traces?
K: exemplars, metrics to traces, exemplar prometheus, link metric spike to trace, grafana exemplars
X: Honestly this is one of my favourite features. Metrics are aggregated, so they're cheap and great for spotting problems, but you lose the detail. The latency histogram says p99 jumped to three seconds, but not which requests were slow or why. Traces have that detail, but finding the right trace in millions is painful. Exemplars connect the two.
X: An exemplar is a sample data point attached to a metric value, and it carries the trace id of a real request that contributed to it. When the service records a request duration in a histogram, the OpenTelemetry SDK can attach the current trace id as an exemplar for that bucket. Backends like Prometheus or Grafana Mimir keep a few exemplars next to the metric.
X: In Grafana they show up as dots on the latency graph. So during an incident I see the spike, hover over a dot in the slow area, and click straight into the trace in Tempo or whatever tracing backend you have. The trace shows exactly where the time went, maybe a database call that took 2.8 seconds. From there I jump to logs filtered by the same trace id.
X: So the investigation becomes metric to trace to logs in a few clicks, instead of guessing time ranges and searching around.
X: To make it work, exemplars have to be enabled in the SDK, OpenTelemetry .NET supports that with an exemplar filter. The trace has to actually be sampled, otherwise the link goes nowhere. And the backend has to support storing them. Commercial APM tools give you similar navigation built in.
@p17-600
S: obx
D: A
T: What is Prometheus, and how do you write basic PromQL queries?
K: prometheus, promql, prometheus scraping, rate function promql, histogram_quantile, prometheus basics
X: Okay, so Prometheus is an open-source monitoring system and time-series database. It pulls metrics, it scrapes an HTTP endpoint, usually slash metrics, on each target every so often, like every 15 seconds. In Kubernetes it finds targets on its own through service discovery and annotations or ServiceMonitor resources. A .NET app exposes metrics with the OpenTelemetry Prometheus exporter, or pushes over OTLP to the newer Prometheus versions that accept it.
X: The data is time series identified by a metric name plus labels, like the HTTP server request duration metric with method, route and status code.
X: The queries I write most. Request rate, that's sum by route of the rate of the request duration count over five minutes. Rate gives you the per-second increase of a counter over that window. Error percentage is the rate of requests with a 5xx status divided by the rate of all requests, times 100. For latency percentiles you use histogram quantile with 0.95, over the sum by le and route of the rate of the bucket series over five minutes. The le label is basically the bucket boundary. And saturation, like memory used versus the limit per pod, is just dividing one metric by another, matched on labels.
X: Alert rules use the same expressions with a "for" duration. Prometheus evaluates them and Alertmanager groups, silences and routes the notifications.
X: For long-term storage or many clusters, people usually add Thanos or Mimir, or use a managed one, like Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus or Azure Monitor managed Prometheus, with Grafana on top.
@p17-601
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you control the cost of logging and observability?
K: logging cost, observability cost, reduce log volume, log retention, datadog bill, log sampling
X: See, observability bills can quietly get bigger than the compute they're monitoring, mostly from log volume and high-cardinality metrics. So I manage it on purpose.
X: Logs first. Log less but better, information level for events that matter, not every step, debug off in production, and no full request and response bodies by default. Noise gets dropped at the source or in the collector, health check requests, chatty library logs. High-volume, low-value stuff like successful request logs can be sampled, while warnings and errors are always kept. Retention is tiered, hot searchable storage for 7 to 30 days, then archived to cheap object storage for compliance, and only rehydrated when you need it. And if people keep running the same log query, turn it into a metric, way cheaper to store and query.
X: For metrics, watch cardinality and remove labels like user or request ids. Drop unused metrics too, a lot of exporters spit out hundreds of series nobody looks at. For traces, tail-based sampling, keep errors and slow ones, sample the rest.
X: Then visibility. Show each team the cost of its own telemetry by service tags, so whoever's generating it sees it. Put quotas or alerts on daily ingestion, that catches a bad deployment logging in a loop.
X: But I never cut audit logs or anything compliance needs, in a regulated domain those have their own retention rules. And keep enough detail to investigate incidents. Saving money and then being blind during an outage is a false economy.
@p17-602
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you monitor message queues and consumers?
K: monitor message queue, consumer lag, queue depth alert, age of oldest message, rabbitmq monitoring, kafka lag monitoring
X: Actually this one bit us early on. With async systems, a healthy API doesn't mean a healthy system. Messages can pile up silently and nothing shows as an error. So I treat queues as proper first-class components.
X: The main thing is queue depth or consumer lag, how many messages are waiting. For RabbitMQ that's ready and unacknowledged messages per queue, for Kafka it's consumer group lag per partition, for SQS the approximate number of visible messages.
X: Then the age of the oldest message, which is often more meaningful than depth. 10,000 messages that are draining fast might be fine, but 20 messages stuck for an hour means something's wrong. SQS gives you that directly. For others, the consumer can record the time between publish and processing as a histogram.
X: Throughput, publish rate versus consume rate. If consuming is always lower, the backlog just keeps growing.
X: The dead-letter queue. Anything landing there needs attention, so I alert on DLQ depth above zero, with which message types.
X: And consumer health, number of connected consumers, processing errors, redelivery counts, processing time.
X: The alerts depend on what the business expects though. Shipment events older than five minutes during business hours is a problem. A nightly batch queue with 50,000 messages at 2 AM might be totally normal.
X: In our platform the RabbitMQ queues and their retry and dead-letter exchanges are monitored like this, and the Grafana dashboards show depth and age per queue right next to the consumers' error rates.
@p17-603
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you investigate an issue with Splunk searches?
K: splunk search, spl query, splunk investigation, splunk stats timechart, search logs splunk, splunk transaction
X: So Splunk is where our older platform's logs go, through Serilog, so it's usually my first tool in an investigation. The query language, SPL, is a pipeline, kind of like KQL.
X: I start by narrowing the scope. Index, sourcetype or application, environment, and a tight time range around when the problem started. If you search everything over all time, it's slow and expensive.
X: Then find the errors and the trend. Filter on level Error and the service name, then timechart count by exception type with a five-minute span. That tells me when it started and whether it's one error type or a bunch of them.
X: Next I group to find patterns. Stats count by endpoint, study or site and error message, sorted descending. If all the failures come from one site or one integration, that's your lead.
X: Then I follow one request. I take the correlation id from an error and search it across all services, sorted by time, so I can see the whole path. Our correlation id middleware puts the same id on every log line for a request, including the calls into other services.
X: And compare with normal, same query for yesterday or last week, to see if the volume is actually unusual.
X: Commands I use a lot are rex to pull a field out of unstructured text, eval to compute values, transaction or stats by correlation id to group a request's events, and dedup to cut the noise.
X: Good searches become alerts or dashboard panels. And honestly structured logging makes a huge difference, with JSON fields your searches are precise instead of fragile text matching.
@p17-604
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you use Datadog APM to find a performance problem?
K: datadog apm, datadog traces, flame graph, datadog service map, apm performance investigation
X: In our setup the newest services send OpenTelemetry data to Datadog, so APM is where I start for anything performance related.
X: The service page gives you RED metrics per endpoint, requests, errors and latency percentiles, with deployment markers. So I check which endpoints got slower and when, and whether that lines up with a deployment, a traffic increase or a change in some dependency.
X: The service map shows the dependencies with latency and errors on each edge. That quickly tells you whether the time is going in our service or in a downstream call, the database, another API, the broker.
X: Then I open traces for the slow endpoint, filtered to the slow ones, say above p95. The flame graph shows every span, the controller, the EF Core or SQL span with the query text, HTTP calls to other services, cache calls. What I usually find is one of a few things. A single slow query. Lots of repeated queries, the N plus one pattern. Sequential calls that could have run in parallel. A gap before the first span, which points to thread pool or connection pool starvation. Or retries hiding inside an HTTP span.
X: From the trace, the logs with the same trace id are one click away, and Database Monitoring shows the execution plan and wait events for that query.
X: If the continuous profiler is on, it shows which methods burn CPU and allocate memory, which helps when it's CPU-bound and traces can't explain it.
X: Then I fix it, deploy, and compare the same views before and after to make sure it actually helped.
@p17-605
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you detect a scheduled job that silently didn't run?
K: dead man switch, heartbeat monitoring, cron job monitoring, job did not run alert, missing job execution, watchdog job
X: Yeah, this is a sneaky one. Normal alerting catches things that fail loudly, an error, an exception. A job that never starts produces no errors at all. Maybe the scheduler got stopped, a server was patched and not restarted, a trigger is misconfigured, or the job just hangs forever. Nothing alerts, and the business finds out days later that no reports or reconciliations happened.
X: So the fix is to alert on the absence of a signal. People call it a heartbeat or a dead man's switch.
X: How it works is each job, when it completes successfully, sends a heartbeat. That can be a ping to a monitoring service, a metric like last success timestamp, or a row in a job history table. Then a separate monitor knows the expected schedule, like every hour, or daily at 2 AM plus some grace period, and alerts if no heartbeat turns up in time. Healthchecks.io, Cronitor, Datadog, or CloudWatch alarms with "treat missing data as breaching" all support this.
X: I'd also watch the duration, a job that normally takes five minutes and now takes three hours is a warning. Output sanity too, like records processed being zero when it's normally thousands. And overlap, a run starting before the last one finished.
X: This is a big part of what our AlertWatchDog does on the platform side. Quartz jobs that check the expected events actually happened, and raise an alert when they didn't. And the watchdog itself is monitored, because if it stops, nothing else is going to notice.
@p17-606
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you write runbooks and organise on-call?
K: runbook, on call process, incident runbook, playbook operations, on call rotation, escalation policy
X: For me on-call works when whoever gets paged can act fast without needing the one expert who wrote the code. Good runbooks and a sensible rotation are what make that possible.
X: Every alert links to a runbook, and the runbook answers a few things. What the alert means and what the user impact is. How to confirm it's real, with direct links to the dashboard and log queries. Likely causes from past incidents. Step-by-step mitigations, like restarting a consumer, failing over, scaling out, replaying the dead-letter queue, switching off a feature flag. What not to do, like never purge a queue that has unprocessed clinical events. And when and how to escalate. Keep it short and specific, next to the code or in a wiki the team actually updates after incidents.
X: Over time the steps people repeat become automation, a button or script that does the safe mitigation and logs it. So humans decide and tools execute.
X: For the rotation, usually weekly, with a primary and a secondary, clear escalation to subject matter experts and managers, and a handover at the end of each shift covering open issues. And there's a limit on load. If someone's getting paged every night, the system needs fixing, not a tougher engineer. Severity routing makes sure only urgent, user-impacting stuff pages.
X: After incidents we do a blameless review, and the action items often improve the alerts and runbooks. And in a regulated environment, anything you do on production during on-call is a controlled change too, recorded with who did what and why.
@p17-607
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you run a blameless post-incident review?
K: postmortem, blameless postmortem, post incident review, root cause analysis, incident retrospective, five whys
X: Honestly, the whole point is to turn an outage into improvements. Blameless means we assume everyone acted reasonably with what they knew at the time, and we look at how the system, process and tools let it happen, not who messed up. If people are scared of blame, they hide details and you learn nothing.
X: How I run one. Facts first. I build a timeline from alerts, logs, chat messages and deployment records. When it started, when it was detected and by whom, what actions were taken, when it got resolved. Plus the impact, which users, how long, and whether any data was affected.
X: Then the contributing factors, not one single root cause. It's usually a few things together, a code change with an edge case, a missing test, an alert that didn't fire, an outdated runbook, a manual step done under pressure. Five whys helps, applied to each factor. And I ask what went well too, like a fast rollback.
X: I also look at detection and response, not just the trigger. Why did it take 40 minutes to notice? Why was diagnosis slow?
X: Then action items, each with an owner and a date, ordered by impact. A test, an alert, an automated safety check, maybe a design change. A few good actions that actually get done beat a long wish list.
X: The write-up gets shared widely, other teams learn from it, and we track the actions until they're closed. In our regulated context it also feeds the formal deviation or CAPA process when validated functionality was affected.
@p17-608
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you instrument a new feature before releasing it?
K: observability driven development, instrument new feature, telemetry for new feature, release monitoring plan, measure feature health
X: So I treat observability as part of the feature's definition of done. Not something you bolt on after the first incident.
X: Before I write code I ask two questions. How will we know this works in production, and how will we know when it doesn't? That gives me a short list of signals.
X: Logs, information level for the key business events in the feature, with structured fields like study, site and outcome, and clear error logs with context when it fails. No personal data, obviously.
X: Metrics, a counter for the main operations by outcome, a histogram for duration, and a business metric if there is one, like the number of returns processed in the new DARM flow.
X: Traces, custom spans around the important internal steps, like calculating an allocation or calling an external system, with useful attributes, so a slow request shows you where the time went.
X: Then a panel or small dashboard for the feature, and alerts if the failure rate crosses a threshold or the expected events just stop.
X: For the release, if it's behind a flag, I compare the signals with flag on and flag off, and check them right after rollout to each environment and each batch of users. If the numbers look wrong, the flag goes off.
X: And I test the telemetry itself. In integration tests, or with FakeLogger and metric collectors, I check the important logs and metrics actually get emitted. I learned that the hard way, missing telemetry always gets discovered at the worst possible moment.
@p17-609
S: obx
D: A
T: What is continuous profiling, and when does it help?
K: continuous profiling, production profiler, cpu profiling production, pyroscope, datadog profiler, flame graph cpu
X: Let me explain where it fits. Traces tell you which request and which span was slow, but not which line of code inside the service burned the CPU or allocated all that memory. Continuous profiling covers that.
X: A profiler runs inside the app in production, all the time, with low overhead, usually a few percent, by sampling stack traces many times a second. It records where CPU time goes, which methods allocate, where threads wait on locks, which exceptions get thrown. It's aggregated over time and shown as flame graphs you can filter by service, version, endpoint and host.
X: Tools would be Datadog Continuous Profiler, which supports .NET, Grafana Pyroscope, the Application Insights Profiler on Azure, Amazon CodeGuru Profiler for some runtimes, and the OpenTelemetry profiling signal, which is still maturing.
X: Where it helps most is when CPU is high but no endpoint looks especially slow. The profile shows the hot method, like JSON serialising a huge object, a regex getting compiled on every call, or a LINQ query re-evaluated inside a loop. Memory and GC pressure, the allocation profile tells you what's allocating, large strings or lists built per request. Comparing versions, you diff profiles before and after a deployment and see exactly what got more expensive. And cost, fixing the top hot spots can reduce instance counts.
X: Compared with a one-off dotnet-trace, the big thing is the data's already there from when the problem happened, which matters a lot for intermittent issues you can't reproduce. Profiles can have method names and types, but never actual data values.
@p17-610
S: scx
D: A
T: An IIS-hosted .NET Framework app is stuck at 100% CPU. What do you do?
K: iis high cpu, w3wp high cpu, app pool cpu 100, dotnet framework cpu spike, debugdiag, procdump cpu
X: Okay, so two things in order. Protect the users, and grab the evidence before it disappears.
X: Quick checks first. Is it one server or all of them? Did it start after a deployment, a traffic spike, a scheduled job? If it's one server behind the load balancer, I pull it out of rotation so users go to the healthy ones. But I don't recycle the app pool yet, because a recycle wipes out the evidence.
X: Then I capture. Two or three memory dumps of the w3wp process, about 10 to 20 seconds apart, using ProcDump with a CPU threshold trigger, or DebugDiag, or just Task Manager's create dump file. I also note which requests are executing, from the worker processes view in IIS Manager or the request monitoring logs, and check Performance Monitor counters like requests queued and percent time in GC.
X: Then I recycle to get the service back.
X: For analysis I open the dumps in DebugDiag's analysis or WinDbg with the SOS extension and look at what the busy threads are doing across the dumps. If the same threads are in the same code every time, that's your hot spot. What I've seen usually is an infinite or really long loop on some unexpected data, a regex with catastrophic backtracking, heavy GC from massive allocations, which shows up as high time in GC, or lock contention with threads spinning.
X: After that, fix the code, add a test with the data that triggered it, and add an alert on sustained CPU so next time we see it earlier.
@p17-611
S: scx
D: A
T: Latency spikes every few minutes in a regular pattern. How do you find the cause?
K: periodic latency spikes, latency every few minutes, regular spikes, cache expiry spike, gc pause spike, cron job latency
X: Actually a regular pattern is kind of good news. Regular means something scheduled or cyclic is causing it, so I go looking for things with the same period.
X: I measure the period exactly from the latency graph. Every 5 minutes, every 15, on the hour? Then I line it up against the usual suspects.
X: Cache expiry is a common one. Lots of entries with the same absolute expiration, say five minutes, all expire together and a burst of requests hits the database at once. The fix is jittered expiration, refresh-ahead, or stampede protection like HybridCache.
X: Scheduled jobs. A Quartz job, cron, SQL Agent job, backup or index maintenance running on that schedule and fighting for the database or CPU. So I check job schedules and database activity at those exact times.
X: Garbage collection. Big gen 2 collections when memory builds up to a threshold, you see it in the GC metrics with pause times matching the spikes. Usually it's allocation-heavy code or large object heap usage.
X: Token or connection refresh. Credentials, certificates or config refreshed periodically and blocking requests while it happens, or connection pools recycling connections at a fixed lifetime.
X: And infrastructure, health check or autoscaling cycles, log shipping bursts, or noisy neighbours on shared hosts with their own schedules.
X: Once I've got a candidate, I correlate its metric with the spikes, change one thing, and watch if the pattern goes away. Traces of slow requests during a spike usually point you straight at whatever is waiting.
@p17-612
S: scx
D: A
T: Database CPU jumps to 100% right after a release. What do you do?
K: database cpu 100 after release, sql server cpu spike, bad query after deployment, regression query plan, db cpu high
X: So the timing basically makes the release suspect number one. I work from what changed, and try to keep the system usable while I do it.
X: I find the expensive queries right away. In SQL Server that's sys dot dm exec requests and the query stats DMV ordered by CPU, or Query Store's top resource-consuming queries for the last hour compared with the previous period. Usually it's one or two queries eating everything.
X: Then the question is, is it a new query from the release, or an old query that changed plan? New queries could be an EF Core change that now loads related data with a huge join, a missing filter, an N plus one pattern firing thousands of small queries, a LINQ expression that translates badly, or a new feature without the index it needs. A changed plan would be a schema or statistics change in the release giving a worse plan, or a new parameter pattern.
X: For mitigation I go quickest first. If a feature flag controls the new code, switch it off. If it's a plan regression, Query Store can force the old good plan. If an index is clearly missing, adding it online is often quick and low risk. If none of that works and the impact is serious, roll back the app release, as long as the database changes are backward compatible.
X: Then the real fix, rewrite or index the query and test it with production-sized data. And I'd add a check to the release process, like comparing query performance in a perf environment, because slow queries usually slip through when tests run on tiny data.
@p17-613
S: scx
D: A
T: A query was fast yesterday and is slow today, with no code change. What happened?
K: query suddenly slow, parameter sniffing, statistics out of date, plan regression, same query slow today
X: Honestly, if the code didn't change, then the data changed or the plan changed. That's where I look.
X: Plan change is my first guess. SQL Server compiles a plan using the parameter values from the first execution and caches it. If it got recompiled, after a restart, a stats update, memory pressure, with some unusual value, like a site with very few rows, you might get a nested loop plan that's terrible for the typical values with lots of rows. That's parameter sniffing. Query Store shows the query's plans over time, so I can see the plan change and the duration jump. Quick fix is to force the good plan in Query Store. Longer term, OPTION RECOMPILE for queries with wildly varying parameters, OPTIMIZE FOR, or restructuring the query. SQL Server 2022 also has parameter sensitive plan optimisation.
X: Statistics. After big data loads they can be stale, so the optimiser underestimates row counts. Updating stats fixes it more often than you'd think.
X: Data growth or skew. A table crossed some size where the plan or memory grant doesn't fit anymore, or one customer's data grew massively.
X: Blocking. The query's fine but it's waiting on locks from another process, like a new batch job. Wait stats and the requests DMV tell you if it's running or waiting.
X: And resource pressure, other workloads on the same server, tempdb contention, I/O problems.
X: I compare the actual execution plans from before and after and look at the waits. That usually tells you which of these it is pretty quickly.
@p17-614
S: scx
D: A
T: The cache expired and the database got overloaded. How do you prevent a cache stampede?
K: cache stampede, thundering herd, dog piling, cache expiry overload, hybridcache stampede protection, cache warmup
X: See, a stampede is when a popular cached item expires, or a restart empties the cache, and lots of concurrent requests all miss at the same time and run the same expensive query together. The database suddenly gets hundreds of identical queries, slows down, and that makes even more requests pile up. It's a classic outage right after a cache restart or a deployment.
X: How I prevent it. Request coalescing, so only one request recomputes a given key and the others wait for that result. In .NET 9, HybridCache does this automatically for concurrent callers in the same process. Otherwise a per-key SemaphoreSlim or a Lazy task does it, and across servers a short distributed lock in Redis.
X: Jittered expiration. Add a random bit to each item's TTL so they don't all expire at the same moment.
X: Refresh ahead. Popular items get refreshed in the background before they expire, so users never see a miss. Stale-while-revalidate is similar, you serve the slightly old value while one request refreshes it.
X: Warm up the known hot keys after deployments or cache restarts, before taking full traffic.
X: And protect the database anyway. Limit concurrency on expensive queries with a bulkhead and put a circuit breaker in, so even if the cache fails badly, the database survives and recovers.
X: I'd also monitor the cache hit ratio, so a sudden drop alerts us before the database falls over. That's usually the earliest sign something's off.
@p17-615
S: scx
D: A
T: Redis goes down in production. What happens, and what do you do?
K: redis down, cache unavailable, redis outage, redis failover, cache server down, graceful degradation cache
X: It depends on how we use Redis and how the app handles it failing. That's why I'd rather design for it before it happens.
X: If Redis is purely a cache, you want graceful degradation. Cache calls fail fast with a short timeout, get caught, logged and counted, and the app goes to the database. Users see slower responses but everything works. The risks are, every request might wait for a long Redis timeout before falling back, so timeouts must be short and a circuit breaker should skip Redis completely while it's down. And the database suddenly gets the full load, so it needs headroom, or we limit concurrency on expensive queries.
X: If Redis holds state, like sessions, distributed locks, rate-limit counters or data protection keys, it's a bigger deal. Users get logged out, locks aren't available, rate limiting fails open or closed. Each one needs a deliberate choice, like fail open for rate limits but fail safe for locks.
X: During the incident, I confirm with Redis metrics and connection errors. Check if a replica failed over, in Sentinel, cluster or a managed service, because clients might need to reconnect. Check memory, evictions and maxclients, since Redis going down is very often memory exhaustion. And tell people about the impact.
X: Afterwards, replicas with automatic failover, alerts on memory and connections, and stampede protection for when the cache comes back empty.
X: In our platform, Redis caches configuration and reference data, so the fallback is just the database, with short timeouts.
@p17-616
S: scx
D: A
T: A RabbitMQ queue backlog keeps growing. What do you do?
K: rabbitmq queue growing, message backlog, queue depth increasing, consumers too slow, rabbitmq backlog, unacked messages growing
X: Okay, a growing queue means messages are coming in faster than they're processed. So I figure out which side changed.
X: What I do is check consumers first. In the management UI or metrics, how many consumers are connected and what's the consume rate? If it dropped to zero, they crashed, lost the connection, or a deployment stopped them. If they're connected but slow, I look at unacknowledged messages. High unacked with a low prefetch can mean consumers are stuck on slow work, like a slow database call or a dependency timing out. Consumer logs and traces show what each message is waiting on.
X: Then poison messages. A message that keeps failing and gets requeued goes back to the head and blocks progress. With a proper retry and dead-letter setup it moves aside after a few attempts. Without that it just loops forever.
X: Then the producer. Did the publish rate spike, like a batch import, a retry storm upstream, or a bug publishing duplicates?
X: Then act. Scale out consumers if the work can run in parallel and the downstream dependency, usually the database, can take more load. Fix the slow dependency. Move poison messages to the DLQ. Throttle the producer if you can. And with big backlogs, check the broker has enough memory and disk, because RabbitMQ blocks publishers when memory or disk alarms trigger, and then the problem spreads upstream.
X: Afterwards I'd add alerts on queue depth and age of the oldest message, and autoscale consumers on queue length so it handles itself next time.
@p17-617
S: scx
D: A
T: A production server's disk is full. What do you do?
K: disk full production, no space left on device, disk space alert, log files filling disk, clean disk server
X: Yeah, a full disk breaks things in weird ways. Logging fails, databases stop writing, uploads fail, services won't start, sometimes the OS itself gets unstable. So I move quickly, but carefully.
X: First find what's using the space. On Windows, TreeSize or a PowerShell query for the biggest folders. On Linux, df to see which volume is full, then du or ncdu to find the big directories. I never delete files I don't understand, and never touch database files or active transaction logs. Those need proper database actions, like a log backup.
X: One thing that catches people out, on Linux a deleted file that's still held open doesn't free space until the process closes it. So you might need to restart the logging process.
X: Then restore service and check everything actually recovered, because some components need a restart after write failures.
X: And prevent it. Log rotation and retention, cleanup jobs for temp files and old releases, logs shipped to central logging instead of sitting locally, and disk alerts at 80 and 90 percent with a time-to-full forecast.
@p17-618
S: scx
D: A
T: A TLS certificate expired in production. How do you recover and prevent it?
K: certificate expired, ssl certificate expired production, tls cert expiry outage, certificate monitoring, auto renew certificate
X: So an expired cert fails everything immediately. Browsers show warnings, API clients refuse to connect, service-to-service calls fail with trust errors. Recovery is all about speed.
X: First I identify exactly which certificate expired and where it's used. Sometimes it's not the website cert at all, it's an internal one, like a client certificate for a partner integration, a token signing cert, or one on an internal API. That makes it less obvious. The error logs will mention certificate validation or the remote certificate being invalid.
X: Then get it renewed from the CA or the internal PKI and install it everywhere it's used, load balancers, IIS bindings on every server, API gateways, Kubernetes secrets, and restart or rebind where needed. Monitor expiry from outside with synthetic checks alerting at 30, 14 and 7 days, including internal and client certs. And make sure the renewal reaches every location automatically, not just the first one somebody remembers. I've seen that happen, one server renewed and the other two forgotten.

@p17-620
S: scx
D: A
T: Users in another country see dates off by one day. How do you fix it?
K: date off by one day, time zone bug, utc conversion bug, date shifted timezone, datetime kind bug, visit date wrong timezone
X: Actually "off by one day" is almost always a time zone conversion happening where it shouldn't, or not happening where it should.
X: The most common one I've seen is a date-only value stored as a date-time at midnight. A visit date of 10 March gets stored as 10 March midnight local, converted to UTC, so for India it becomes 9 March 18:30 UTC, and then somewhere it's displayed as 9 March. Or the browser parses the string 2025-03-10 as UTC midnight with new Date, and users west of UTC see 9 March. The fix is to treat date-only values as dates. DateOnly in .NET, and plain date strings or a date library on the front end, with no time zone conversion at all.
X: Mixed DateTime kinds. A DateTime with Kind Unspecified gets treated as local on one server and UTC on another, especially when servers in different regions have different time zones. So store and send instants as UTC or DateTimeOffset, and convert to local only for display.
X: Wrong time zone for business rules. Something like "visit window ends at end of day" has to use the site's time zone, not the server's or the user's browser.
X: And daylight saving, where a day has 23 or 25 hours, breaks code that adds 24 hours instead of one calendar day.
X: So the fix includes tests across time zones, India, US, far-east sites, and around DST changes. I'd also run a test server in a non-UTC zone, that exposes hidden assumptions fast.
@p17-621
S: scx
D: A
T: Customers are receiving duplicate emails or notifications. How do you investigate?
K: duplicate emails, duplicate notifications, users get two emails, notification sent twice, idempotent notifications
X: Let me think about it this way, duplicates mean something ran twice. So I find what ran twice and why.
X: I start with facts. Which notifications, for which events, since when, and are the duplicates identical in content and timing? Exact duplicates seconds apart point to retries or concurrent processing. Hours apart, more like a scheduled job re-running or a replay.
X: Common causes. Message redelivery, the consumer sent the email, then failed or timed out before acking, so the broker delivered it again. With at-least-once delivery that will happen sometimes. Retries, the HTTP call to the email provider timed out but actually succeeded, and the retry sent it again. Multiple instances, a scheduled job like a daily reminder running on every server instead of one. That often shows up exactly when you scale out from one server to two. And duplicate events, the publisher emitted it twice, from two code paths or a DLQ replay.
X: The fixes. Make sending idempotent. Record each notification with a unique key, like event id plus recipient plus template, in a table with a unique constraint, and skip if it's already there, before sending or atomically with it. Use the provider's idempotency key if they support one. Make scheduled jobs run once with clustering or a distributed lock. And consumers dedupe by message id.
X: I'd also deal with the user side, explaining and apologising if needed, and add a metric for notifications per event, so duplicates actually show up somewhere.

S: scx

T: The same version works on one server but fails on another. How do you find the difference?

X: So if the code really is identical, the difference is in the environment. I compare things one by one instead of guessing.

@p17-623
S: scx
D: A
T: After a front-end release, some users see a blank page or old version. Why?
K: blank page after deployment, chunkloaderror, old version after release, spa cache issue, failed to fetch dynamically imported module
X: Honestly, it's nearly always caching plus code splitting.
X: A single-page app loads index dot html, which points to bundles with hashed names, like main dot some hash dot js, and lazy-loaded chunks. Two things go wrong after a release.
X: One is a stale index.html. If the browser, a proxy or the CDN cached it, users keep loading the old version, which might call APIs that changed. The fix is serving index.html with Cache-Control no-cache, so the browser revalidates every time, while the hashed assets get long cache times.
X: The other is missing old chunks. A user has the old app open, goes to a lazy route, and the old chunk it wants doesn't exist anymore because the deployment replaced all the files. The browser throws ChunkLoadError or "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module", and the route is just blank. So keep previous versions' assets around for a while after deploying instead of deleting them, and in the app, catch chunk load errors and reload the page once, which picks up the new index.html.
X: Service workers can also keep serving the old version until every tab closes. You need a proper update flow that detects a new version and asks the user to refresh.
X: Other blank-page causes are a JavaScript error early in startup on some browsers, missing runtime config, or a wrong base href on a sub-path. The browser console and front-end error tracking will tell you which, so I'd check those first.
@p17-624
S: scx
D: A
T: Refreshing a deep link in the SPA gives 404 on IIS. How do you fix it?
K: spa refresh 404 iis, angular deep link 404, react router 404 refresh, url rewrite spa, history api fallback iis
X: So in a single-page app with HTML5 routing, a URL like slash shipments slash 123 is handled by the router inside the browser. Moving around inside the app works fine because nothing goes to the server. But when you refresh, or open a bookmarked link, the browser actually asks IIS for slash shipments slash 123. IIS looks for that file, doesn't find it, and gives you a 404.
X: The fix is a fallback rule. Any request that isn't a real file, a real folder or an API route should return index.html, and then the router shows the right screen.
X: On IIS I install the URL Rewrite module and add a rule in web.config. Match all URLs, with conditions that it's not a file, not a directory, and doesn't start with slash api, and then rewrite, not redirect, to slash index.html or the app's base path. If the app lives under a virtual directory, say slash study-admin, the base href in index.html and the rewrite target both need that path, otherwise the assets don't load.
X: Other hosts have the same idea. try_files in nginx, custom error responses or a function in CloudFront, navigationFallback in Azure Static Web Apps, and MapFallbackToFile in ASP.NET Core when it's serving the SPA.
X: One thing people miss, API calls to a route that doesn't exist should still get a real 404, not index.html. That's why the API exclusion matters. Otherwise the client gets HTML when it expects JSON and fails with a really confusing parse error.

T: CORS errors appear right after a deployment. How do you troubleshoot?

X: I look at the actual request. Was it the OPTIONS preflight that failed or the real request? What status did it get? A CORS error often hides a different problem. T: Every API call suddenly returns 401 after an identity provider change. What do you check?

X: See, when everything returns 401 at once, it's usually token validation failing for everybody, not someone's credentials. The JWT bearer handler logs the exact reason at information or debug level, and the WWW-Authenticate header often has it too, so that's where I start.
X: Most common is signing key rotation. X: Clock skew. A server clock drifted, so tokens look expired or not valid yet. Check NTP.
X: Network. The API can't download the metadata at all, so every validation fails.
X: And the front-end side. The client id or scopes changed, so it's getting tokens for something else, or the interceptor stopped attaching tokens.
X: What I usually do is decode a failing token in a safe local tool and compare its iss, aud, kid and expiry against the API's config. That shows the mismatch in about a minute.
@p17-627
S: scx
D: A
T: A user's role was changed but they still get 403 or still have access. Why?
K: role change not applied, stale claims, permissions not updated, token claims stale, user still has access after removal
X: Actually it's usually because the role is baked into a token or session that hasn't been refreshed yet.
X: Access tokens are self-contained. When the identity provider issues a JWT, the roles in it are fixed until it expires. So if an admin adds a role, the user's current token doesn't have it, and they keep getting 403 until they get a new token. And the worse case, when a role is removed, the user keeps access until the token expires. Cookie sessions that store claims behave the same way until the session refreshes.
X: There are other places it gets stuck too. The app caches permissions in memory or Redis. The front end caches the user's profile and shows or hides menus based on old data. Or the role was changed in the identity provider, but the app maps roles from its own database, which nobody updated.
X: How I handle it. Keep access tokens short-lived, five to fifteen minutes, so changes come through on the normal refresh. For removing access, which is the security-sensitive one, don't wait. Revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens in the identity provider, and for really sensitive apps, check permissions server-side per request, or use a revocation list or a security stamp checked on each call. Clear permission caches on role changes through events. On the front end, refresh the profile after changes, and never rely on the front end to enforce anything.
X: And tell the support teams about the expected delay, so they don't raise bugs for what's normal behaviour.
@p17-628
S: scx

T: A third-party API starts returning 429 Too Many Requests. What do you do?
K: third party api 429, rate limited by partner, too many requests external api, throttled by vendor, retry-after handling
X: Honestly, the worst thing is hammering them with retries. A 429 means we're over the partner's rate limit, and retrying harder makes it worse and can get us blocked. So I handle it on our side.
X: Right away, respect Retry-After. If they say wait 30 seconds, we wait. And if our usage is legitimate, just ask the partner for a higher limit.

X: Yeah, test and production differ in a lot of ways, but nine times out of ten it's the data.

@p17-632
S: scx
D: A
T: Traffic suddenly jumps tenfold. How do you keep the system up?
K: sudden traffic spike, 10x traffic, traffic surge, handle load spike, scale under sudden load, load shedding
X: Okay, the first question is whether it's legit. A study going live at loads of sites, a batch import, a partner resending data, that's legitimate. A bot, a client stuck in a retry loop, an attack, that's not. The response is different.
X: If it's abusive or accidental, I find the source from logs, IP, API key, client id, user agent, and block or rate-limit it at the gateway or WAF. A client stuck in a retry loop can be throttled while we contact whoever owns it.
X: If it's real traffic, my approach is to go in order of what's fastest. Scale out the stateless tiers, bump instance counts or autoscaling limits. That only helps if the bottleneck isn't something shared though.
X: Then protect the shared bottleneck, which is usually the database. Serve more from cache, defer non-essential work like reports and exports, and switch off expensive optional features with flags.
X: Shed load gracefully. Rate limits per client, returning 429 with Retry-After, so most users still get served well instead of everyone failing. Queue-based workloads soak up bursts naturally, as long as the consumers don't swamp the database.
X: And communicate, tell stakeholders what's happening and what users might see.
X: Afterwards, load test for that level, add autoscaling on the right signals, and plan with the business for known events, like scaling up before a big study launch. The cheapest spike is the one you saw coming.
@p17-633

D: A
T: A nightly batch job is now running into business hours. What do you do?
K: batch job running long, nightly job overrun, job takes too long, batch window exceeded, long running job business hours
X: So once a job overruns its window, it starts fighting users for the database, locks, slowness, all that. It needs attention before it turns into an outage.
X: Short term, if it's hurting users right now, I decide whether it's safe to pause or stop it. That depends on whether it's restartable and what happens if it doesn't finish. And I tell people about the impact.
X: Then figure out why it got slower. Data growth is the usual one. The job processes everything every night and the data has grown. Jobs that scale with total data instead of changed data break eventually. The fix is incremental processing, only records changed since the last run, using a watermark like a last-modified timestamp or change tracking.
X: Inefficient processing. Row-by-row work with a query per row, which can often become set-based SQL or batched operations. Or missing indexes for the job's queries.
X: Contention. Something new runs at the same time, a backup, index maintenance, another job, and they block each other. Job schedules and wait stats show that.
X: Or an external dependency, a slow partner API or file transfer.
X: Improvements I'd make, break it into chunks with a commit per batch, so it doesn't hold long locks and can resume after a failure. Parallelise independent parts, carefully. Run heavy reads on a readable replica if there is one. Spread the jobs across the night.
X: And record duration and records processed per run, with an alert when the duration trends up. Trust me, you want to see it long before it hits business hours.
@p17-634
S: scx
D: A
T: A scheduled job ran twice and processed data twice. How do you prevent it?
K: job ran twice, duplicate job execution, scheduled job multiple servers, distributed lock job, quartz clustering
X: Right, jobs run twice for a few different reasons, and each one has its own fix.
X: The most common is multiple instances. The app got scaled from one server to two, or deployed to several nodes, and every instance has the same scheduler, so each one runs the job. Fixes are a clustered scheduler, like Quartz with a shared database job store and clustering on, so only one node fires each trigger. Or a distributed lock at the start of the job, like a Redis lock or a SQL app lock with sp_getapplock. Or move scheduling to one external trigger, a Kubernetes CronJob, EventBridge Scheduler or an Azure Functions timer, which behaves like a singleton.
X: Overlapping runs, where the previous run hadn't finished when the next started. Quartz has the DisallowConcurrentExecution attribute, or use a lock, and Kubernetes CronJobs have concurrencyPolicy Forbid.
X: Misfire handling. After downtime, the scheduler fires the missed runs on startup. Configure the misfire instructions on purpose.
X: And manual reruns or retries after a partial failure.
X: But because some duplication is always possible, my rule is the job itself has to be idempotent. Track what's been processed with a run id or a per-record processed flag, put unique constraints on outputs like invoices or notifications, and design the steps so rerunning them doesn't double the effect.
X: Then clean up the data from the double run carefully, using the job's own records to work out what got duplicated.
@p17-635
S: scx
D: A
T: A poison message keeps crashing the consumer. What do you do?
K: poison message, consumer crash loop, message causes exception, bad message queue, dead letter poison message
X: Actually let me explain what it is first. A poison message is one that can never succeed, malformed data, an unexpected null, a reference to something that doesn't exist. If the consumer crashes or rejects it with requeue, the broker delivers it again, it fails again, and the consumer's stuck in a loop blocking everything behind it.
X: The immediate fix is getting it out of the way without losing it. With a proper setup it goes to the dead-letter queue by itself after a few attempts. If not, I move it manually with the broker tooling to a parking queue so everything else starts flowing again. Never just purge the queue, especially with business events.
X: Then investigate. Look at the message, its headers and the consumer's error logs. Is it actually invalid, sent by a buggy producer, or is our consumer failing on a valid edge case?
X: Fix the cause, either the producer or the consumer, then replay the parked message, or correct it if it really is invalid.
X: For prevention, every consumer gets retry limits with backoff and a dead-letter queue, with retry counts tracked in headers. I separate error types, so transient ones like timeouts get retried, and permanent ones like validation failures go straight to the DLQ with no retries. Exceptions are caught per message, so one bad message never takes down the whole consumer process. Messages get validated at the start of processing. And we alert when anything lands in the DLQ, with tooling to inspect and replay.

@p17-638
S: scx
D: A
T: Users get intermittent 502 or 504 errors from the load balancer. How do you troubleshoot?
K: intermittent 502, 504 gateway timeout, load balancer 502, bad gateway intermittent, alb 502 troubleshooting
X: Okay so these come from the load balancer or proxy, not the app directly, which is why the app logs might show nothing at all. A 502 means the proxy got a bad response or the connection failed. A 504 means it waited too long.
X: For 504s, some requests are taking longer than the proxy's timeout. I find which endpoints from the load balancer access logs, they record the target response time. Then fix the slow operations, or make long ones asynchronous. I only raise the timeout if the long duration is genuinely legitimate.
X: 502s have a few usual causes. The one that catches people most is a keep-alive mismatch. The app server closes idle connections before the load balancer does, the load balancer reuses a connection the server just closed, and the request fails. So the rule is the app's keep-alive timeout must be longer than the load balancer's idle timeout. In Kestrel that's KeepAliveTimeout, in Node it's server keepAliveTimeout, in IIS the connection timeout settings.
X: Deployments, instances shutting down while still getting requests, with no connection draining or graceful shutdown. If the 502s cluster around deployment times, that's it.
X: App crashes or restarts, the process dies mid-request, out-of-memory kills or unhandled exceptions. Response problems, invalid or oversized headers, or the app resetting connections. And capacity, all targets briefly unhealthy, or the app hitting connection or thread limits so new connections get refused.
X: So it's mostly correlation. Load balancer logs with timestamps and target, against app logs, restarts and deployments. Whether it's random or clustered narrows it down really fast.
@p17-639
S: scx
D: A
T: New instances fail health checks after deployment because they start slowly. What do you do?
K: slow startup health check failure, startup probe, warmup dotnet, deployment fails slow start, health check grace period
X: Yeah, so if the app takes longer to get ready than the health check allows, the orchestrator kills or replaces it before it's ready. The deployment fails or loops, and old instances might get removed too early.
X: First I find out why startup is slow. I measure the phases with logs or a trace.
