D: A
T: How would you design a kit allocation service for clinical supply?
K: design allocation service, kit allocation design, drug dispensing design, clinical supply allocation, assign kit to patient design
X: So at a visit, the system has to assign the right kit to the patient. Correct treatment, available at the site, not expiring before the next visit, keeping the blind, and never assigning the same kit twice.
X: The inputs are the subject, their treatment arm from randomisation, the visit and its dosing requirements from the study config, and the site's inventory.
X: Selection logic, filter the site's kits to the kit type the arm needs, in an available status, not quarantined or damaged, with an expiry beyond the next visit plus a configured buffer. Then pick by a rule, usually first expiry first out to cut waste. Some visits need several kits.
X: I'd say concurrency is the critical bit. Two dispensing requests at the same site must never pick the same kit. Selection and status update happen atomically in one transaction, with row-level locking using UPDLOCK and READPAST, or a conditional update checking the status hasn't changed. And an idempotency key per dispensing request stops double allocation on retries.
X: Blinding, the site only sees the kit number, never the treatment, and the kit numbering itself mustn't reveal the treatment.
X: Low stock, if there's no suitable kit, return a clear error to the site and alert supply management. Separately, allocations feed the resupply calculations, which trigger shipments when inventory drops below thresholds.
X: Audit, every allocation recorded with who, when, which kit and why, including manual overrides with reasons and approvals.
X: And testing is simulation with lots of concurrent visits and edge cases around expiry, as part of validation.
@p17-718
S: msa
D: A
T: When would you use a workflow engine like Temporal or Durable Functions instead of a hand-written saga?
K: workflow engine, temporal io, durable execution, orchestration engine vs custom saga, durable functions vs saga
X: Okay, a hand-written saga stores state in a table, reacts to messages, handles timeouts with scheduled jobs, and implements compensations. For a few simple flows that's totally fine. But once workflows get longer, with timers, human approvals, retries and branches, that custom state machine code gets complex and fragile.
X: Durable execution engines, Temporal, Azure Durable Functions, AWS Step Functions, or some newer .NET options, take over the hard parts. You write the workflow as normal code, or a definition for Step Functions. Call activity A, wait up to three days for an approval signal, then call B, and on failure run the compensation. The engine persists every step's result, so if the process crashes, the workflow picks up exactly where it was. Retries with backoff, timeouts, timers lasting days or months, and visibility into each running workflow come built in.
X: When it's worth it, long-running business processes spanning hours to weeks, workflows with lots of steps, waits and human interaction, complex compensation logic, and when seeing each instance's state really helps support and audit.
X: What you pay for it is a new platform to run or pay for, a learning curve, constraints like deterministic workflow code that can't call random or the current time directly, and versioning workflows that are already running when the code changes.
X: So for a two-step flow, I'd say just use a simple outbox and consumer. For something like a multi-day approval and transfer process, an engine saves you a lot of code and a lot of bugs.
@p17-719
S: secx
D: A
T: What is the OAuth token exchange or on-behalf-of flow?
K: on behalf of flow, token exchange, obo flow, downstream api user context, delegated token microservices
X: Honestly this comes up whenever one API needs to call another as the user. Say a user calls API A, and A has to call API B as that user, so B can apply the user's own permissions. Just forwarding the user's token is a problem. Its audience is API A, so B should reject it, and passing broad tokens everywhere makes the damage worse if one service gets compromised.
X: The on-behalf-of flow in Entra ID, and the standard OAuth 2.0 token exchange, RFC 8693, which Keycloak and others support, solve it. API A sends the incoming user token to the identity provider's token endpoint, authenticating as itself, and asks for a new token for API B. The identity provider checks A is allowed to call B on behalf of users, and issues a token with audience B, carrying the user's identity and often A's identity as the actor. A calls B with that, and B validates it like any other token.
X: What you get is every token scoped to exactly one audience, so it can't be replayed against other services. Downstream services see the real user and enforce their own authorisation. And the identity provider controls which services can delegate to which.
X: The alternative, if B doesn't need the user's identity for authorisation, A calls B with its own client credentials token and passes the user id as context. Simpler, but B is trusting A to have checked permissions.
X: So I'd use token exchange when downstream authorisation depends on the user, and client credentials otherwise.
@p17-720
S: secx
D: A
T: How does mutual TLS work, and when would you use client certificates?
K: mutual tls, mtls, client certificate authentication, certificate based auth api, two way ssl
X: So in normal TLS only the server shows a certificate, so the client knows it's talking to the real server. In mutual TLS the client also presents a certificate, so the server knows exactly which client is connecting, right at the transport level, before any HTTP request is even processed.
X: How it works, the server is set up to request client certificates and trusts a specific certificate authority. During the handshake, the client proves it holds the private key for its certificate. The server validates the chain, expiry and revocation status, then maps the certificate, by thumbprint or subject, to a client identity. In ASP.NET Core that's Kestrel's ClientCertificateMode plus the certificate authentication handler. If a load balancer or gateway terminates TLS, the gateway validates the cert and forwards the details in a header, and the app must only trust that header from the gateway.
X: Where I'd use it. Service-to-service calls in a zero trust network, often automated through a service mesh that issues and rotates the certificates. Partner and B2B integrations, where a partner system connects to our API, certificates are much harder to steal and replay than API keys, and some industries require them. And device authentication, IoT devices or machines.
X: OAuth can also bind tokens to the client certificate, so a stolen token is useless without the private key.
X: The cost is certificate management. Issuing, distributing, rotating before expiry, revoking. Honestly, without automation it becomes painful very quickly.
@p17-721
S: secx
D: A
T: API keys vs OAuth client credentials for partner integrations: which do you choose?
K: api keys vs oauth, partner api authentication, client credentials flow, api key security, machine to machine auth
X: Okay, both authenticate a system, not a user, but they're really different in security terms.
X: API keys are simple static secrets sent with every request, usually in a header. Partners find them easy, which is why they're popular. But they're long-lived and sent on every call, so any leak, in logs, proxies, code, gives access until someone notices and rotates. They have no scopes or expiry on their own unless the server builds that. And rotation needs coordination with the partner.
X: OAuth 2.0 client credentials, the partner authenticates to the token endpoint with its client id and a secret, or better, a private key JWT or a certificate, and gets a short-lived access token with specific scopes, which it sends to the API. The long-lived credential only ever goes to the identity provider, not to every API. Access tokens expire in minutes, scopes limit what the partner can do, and the identity provider handles management, rotation and revocation centrally.
X: I'd say for anything sensitive, clinical or personal data, or write operations, OAuth client credentials, ideally with private key JWT or mTLS for the client authentication. API keys are fine for low-risk, read-only or public-ish APIs, or as an extra identifier for rate limiting and analytics alongside OAuth.
X: And if we do use API keys, I store only hashes, support multiple active keys so rotation is smooth, scope them, log usage per key, and make revocation fast.
@p17-722
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you prevent open redirect vulnerabilities?
K: open redirect, returnurl validation, unvalidated redirect, redirect after login security, localredirect aspnet core
X: See, an open redirect is when the app takes a URL from user input, like a return URL parameter after login, and redirects to it without checking. Attackers send phishing links that use our trusted domain, something like our site slash login with a return URL pointing at some evil site. The user sees our domain, logs in, and lands on a fake page that asks them to "log in again" and steals their credentials. In OAuth flows it can even leak authorisation codes or tokens.
X: The main fix is only allowing local redirects. In ASP.NET Core, Url dot IsLocalUrl checks the URL is relative to our site, and LocalRedirect throws if it isn't. That's what the default login templates use. Be careful with tricky inputs like double slash evil dot com, or slash backslash evil dot com, which some naive checks treat as local. The built-in helpers handle those.
X: If you genuinely need redirects to other domains, like between our own apps, compare against an explicit allowlist of hosts, not a substring match.
X: Or use indirect references. Instead of passing a URL, pass an identifier, like a page key, that the server maps to a URL.
X: For OAuth and OpenID Connect, register exact redirect URIs in the identity provider, no wildcards, so codes can only ever go to our own apps.
X: And front-end code too. SPAs that read a redirect parameter from the URL and set window location need the same validation. It's a small fix, I'd say, with a big phishing protection payoff.
@p17-723
S: secx
D: A
T: What is insecure deserialization, and how do you avoid it in .NET?
K: insecure deserialization, binaryformatter, typenamehandling, deserialization attack, json deserialization security
X: Actually it's when the app turns untrusted data into objects with a serialiser that lets the data decide which types to create. Attackers craft payloads that instantiate dangerous types, called gadgets, whose constructors or setters run code, and you end up with remote code execution.
X: In .NET the classic danger is BinaryFormatter. It's fundamentally unsafe with untrusted data, and Microsoft removed it in .NET 9. Same story for NetDataContractSerializer, SoapFormatter, LosFormatter and ObjectStateFormatter used without protection. Legacy .NET Framework apps might still use them, in caches, session state, or ViewState with MAC validation turned off.
X: Then Newtonsoft with TypeNameHandling set to Auto, Objects or All. The JSON carries a dollar type property and the serialiser creates whatever type it names. That's exploitable. Keep TypeNameHandling at None, or if you really need polymorphism, use a strict SerializationBinder that only allows specific known types.
X: How I avoid it. Use System.Text.Json, which doesn't instantiate arbitrary types, and for polymorphic JSON use its explicit JsonDerivedType attributes, which only allow declared types. Deserialise into specific DTOs, never object or dynamic. Treat anything from outside as untrusted, including cookies, message queues and caches shared with other systems. And sign or encrypt serialised data that round-trips through clients, using Data Protection.
X: Scanners and analyzers flag dangerous serialiser use, which really helps when you're hunting for it in a big legacy codebase like ours.
@p17-724
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you prevent path traversal when handling file names?
K: path traversal, directory traversal, dot dot slash attack, file download vulnerability, safe file paths
X: Honestly this one's simple but people still get it wrong. Path traversal is when user input builds a file path and the attacker sneaks in dot dot slash to escape the intended folder. A download endpoint that takes name equals report dot pdf gets called with dot dot slash dot dot slash web dot config, and the server hands back its own configuration, connection strings and all. On uploads, attackers might write files into executable locations.
X: Best is not using user input as a path at all. Store files with server-generated names, like a GUID, and keep the original name only as metadata in the database. The user asks for a file by id, the server checks authorisation and looks up the stored path.
X: If you have to use names, validate strictly. Take only the file name part with Path dot GetFileName, reject anything with path separators, dot dot, drive letters or invalid characters, and allowlist characters and extensions.
X: Then canonicalise and check containment. Combine the base folder with the name, get the full path with Path dot GetFullPath, and verify it still starts with the base folder's full path, with a trailing separator, before touching the file. That catches encoded tricks and different separator styles.
X: Least privilege, the app's identity should only access the folders it needs, read-only where possible.
X: Even better, put files in object storage like S3 or Blob Storage with server-generated keys, and the file system's out of the picture. And archives need care too. Extracting zip entries named dot dot slash something, Zip Slip, is the exact same bug.
@p17-725
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you prevent command injection?
K: command injection, os command injection, process start security, shell injection, run external process safely
X: So command injection is when user input ends up in an operating system command, and the input contains shell syntax, like a semicolon followed by rm dash rf, or double ampersand net user, which the shell happily runs. In .NET it usually shows up when code builds a command string for Process Start with cmd.exe or bash, say to run a conversion tool or a script with a file name from the user.
X: My preference order. First choice, don't shell out at all. Use a library to do the job in-process, like an image library instead of a command-line tool.
X: If you do need an external program, don't go through a shell. Start the executable directly with ProcessStartInfo, UseShellExecute false, and pass arguments through the ArgumentList collection, which passes each argument separately and handles quoting, so input can't break out into new commands. Never concatenate input into one command string for cmd slash c or bash dash c.
X: Validate input strictly with an allowlist. If a parameter should be a file id or a known option, check it matches exactly, and map user choices to fixed values instead of passing raw input.
X: Watch for argument injection. Even without a shell, input starting with a dash can be read as an option by the target program. Use double dash to end options where it's supported, or validate.
X: Run the process with least privilege, a restricted account, a timeout, and in a sandbox or container where you can.
X: And the same thinking applies to PowerShell scripts in pipelines or automation. Parameters, not string-built commands. I've seen that one in build scripts more than in app code.

D: A
T: What is an XXE attack, and is .NET vulnerable to it?
K: xxe, xml external entity, xml parsing security, dtd processing, xmlreader secure settings, xml bomb
X: Okay, XML External Entity attacks go after XML parsers that process DTDs, document type definitions. The attacker sends XML with an entity pointing to an external resource, like a file URL for win.ini on the C drive, or an internal URL. If the parser resolves it, the file's content lands in the parsed document and may get returned to the attacker, or the server makes requests into internal systems, which is SSRF. There's a related one, billion laughs or the XML bomb, where nested entities expand a tiny document into gigabytes and exhaust memory.
X: Is .NET vulnerable? Modern .NET, and .NET Framework 4.5.2 onwards, have safe defaults for most XML APIs. XmlReader prohibits DTD processing by default, and XmlDocument doesn't resolve external resources by default in newer framework versions. But older code and explicit settings can bring the risk back. Setting DtdProcessing to Parse, using an XmlUrlResolver, or old XmlTextReader usage on framework versions before 4.5.2.
X: What I do is parse untrusted XML with XmlReader Create, with DtdProcessing set to Prohibit and the XmlResolver set to null, which also stops entity expansion. Set limits like MaxCharactersFromEntities and MaxCharactersInDocument. And validate against an expected schema where it makes sense.
X: This really matters in integrations that receive XML from partners, like older clinical data exchanges or SOAP services, which you see a lot in legacy systems. Scanners and analyzers flag unsafe XML settings, so I fix any findings in the legacy code.
@p17-727
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you encrypt sensitive data in SQL Server: TDE, Always Encrypted or column encryption?
K: tde vs always encrypted, sql server encryption at rest, column level encryption, always encrypted, encrypt pii database
X: Right, SQL Server has a few encryption options and each protects against a different threat.
X: TDE, Transparent Data Encryption, encrypts the database files, logs and backups at rest. Apps don't notice it, and it protects against someone stealing disks or backup files. But anyone who can query the database, DBAs, the app, sees plain data. It's a baseline, and usually on by default in cloud databases.
X: Always Encrypted encrypts specific columns in the client driver. Data's encrypted before it leaves the application and stays encrypted in the database, in server memory and in backups. The keys sit with the client, in Key Vault or a certificate store, not in SQL Server. So DBAs and anyone with database access can't read those columns. The catch is the server can't do much with encrypted data. Deterministic encryption allows equality lookups, randomised allows nothing. Secure enclaves extend that to some range comparisons and pattern matching. It needs driver support and careful key management.
X: Cell-level encryption with ENCRYPTBYKEY uses keys inside SQL Server. You get control, but the server and its admins can decrypt.
X: Application-level encryption, the app encrypts fields itself with envelope encryption through a key management service. Flexible and database-independent.
X: I'd say the right mix is TDE everywhere plus TLS in transit, and then Always Encrypted or app-level encryption for the few really sensitive columns, like personal identifiers, where even administrators shouldn't be able to read them.

T: What do you check in a security-focused code review?
K: security code review, secure code review checklist, review for vulnerabilities, security review pull request
X: Yeah, automated tools catch the common patterns, but a lot of real vulnerabilities are logic flaws only a human spots. So in a security-focused review I run through a mental checklist.
X: Authorisation first. Does every new endpoint have the right authorisation attribute or policy? Does it check the user can access this specific record, not just that they're logged in? Are tenant or site filters applied consistently?
X: Input handling. Is external input validated for type, length and allowed values? Any SQL built by string concatenation, raw HTML rendering, file paths, redirects or commands built from input?

X: Dependencies, any new packages, are they trustworthy, which versions.
X: And concurrency and business logic. Can actions be repeated, raced or done out of order to gain something, like double-submitting or skipping a step?

T: How do you handle findings from a penetration test?
K: penetration test findings, pen test remediation, vulnerability remediation process, security findings triage, pentest report
X: So a pen test report usually has findings rated critical, high, medium, low and informational. Handling them well comes down to triage, fixing the root cause and proving the fix.
X: Triage first. For each finding, confirm it's valid in our context, understand the real risk, exploitability, data exposure, existing controls, and agree the severity with the security team. Sometimes the tester's rating gets adjusted, with justification, but I'm careful not to downplay findings just to avoid work.
X: Then plan. Each finding becomes a tracked work item with an owner and a deadline based on severity, critical within days, high within a few weeks, whatever the security policy says. Critical ones might need an immediate mitigation, like a WAF rule or switching off a feature, before the code fix lands.
X: Fix the root cause, not just the one instance. If they found an IDOR on one endpoint, review every endpoint for the same pattern. Missing output encoding in one place, find all the similar places. Often a central fix, a shared authorisation filter or a security header middleware, kills a whole class of issues.
X: Add tests, an automated test reproducing each finding so it can't come back.
X: Verify, ask the testers to retest, or verify internally with evidence, and record the closure.
X: And learn from it. Look at patterns across findings and feed them into coding guidelines, review checklists, training and automated scans. Any accepted risks get documented and approved by the right people, with review dates. That's pretty much how we close the loop.

S: secx
D: A
T: What does zero trust mean for application design?
K: zero trust, zero trust architecture, never trust always verify, zero trust network, beyondcorp
X: Honestly the core idea is no implicit trust based on network location. The old model assumed everything inside the corporate network or VPN was trusted, so once an attacker got in, they could wander freely. Zero trust says verify explicitly every time, use least privilege, and assume you're already breached.
X: For applications, what that means in practice. Every request is authenticated and authorised, including internal service-to-service calls. Services verify tokens or mutual TLS identities, instead of trusting a call because it came from the internal network.
X: Strong identity for users and workloads. MFA and conditional access for users, managed or workload identities for services, and short-lived credentials everywhere.
X: Least privilege and just-in-time access. Services get only the permissions they need, and admins get elevated access temporarily, with approval.
X: Micro-segmentation. Network policies and security groups restrict which services can talk to which, so a compromised service can't reach everything, even though the network isn't the main defence anymore.
X: Encryption in transit everywhere, internal traffic included. Device and context awareness, so access decisions consider device health, location and risk. And continuous monitoring, logging and analysing access and spotting anomalies.
X: For legacy systems that rely on network trust, like intranet apps with Windows authentication, you apply it gradually. Put them behind an identity-aware proxy, add MFA, tighten the network paths. In our on-prem world that's realistically how it would happen, step by step.

@p17-734
S: secx
D: A
T: What is ReDoS, and how do you prevent regex denial of service?
K: redos, regex denial of service, catastrophic backtracking, regex timeout dotnet, nonbacktracking regex
X: See, ReDoS is a denial of service caused by a regular expression that takes exponential time on certain inputs. Patterns with nested quantifiers or overlapping alternatives, like a group of "a plus" that's itself repeated with a plus, or word characters with an optional space, repeated with a star, can make the regex engine backtrack through a massive number of combinations when the input almost matches but fails right at the end. A short nasty string, a few dozen characters, can keep a CPU core busy for seconds or minutes. A handful of those requests can take down an API.
X: Where it shows up, validating emails, URLs or names with home-made patterns, parsing log lines, and search features that accept user patterns.
X: How I prevent it in .NET. Set timeouts. Pass a TimeSpan to the Regex constructor, or set a default with the REGEX DEFAULT MATCH TIMEOUT AppContext setting, so a pathological match throws a timeout exception instead of running forever.
X: Use the NonBacktracking option, available since .NET 7. It's an automata-based engine with linear-time guarantees, for patterns that don't need lookarounds or backreferences.
X: Write safer patterns, avoid nested quantifiers on overlapping groups, anchor the patterns, and limit input length before matching. And never run user-supplied patterns without these protections.
X: Source-generated regexes with GeneratedRegex are good for performance, combined with all the above.
X: Analyzers can flag risky patterns, and fuzz tests with long near-matching inputs catch them in testing. Honestly, most teams don't think about this until it bites them.

T: How do you build a secure password reset flow?

X: Honestly password reset is a favourite attack path, because it skips the password completely. So it needs care.

X: MFA, if the account has it, the reset shouldn't quietly bypass it. Require the second factor during or after the reset.
X: Log reset requests and completions, and alert on unusual volumes.
X: And in enterprise setups with SSO, Keycloak or Entra ID, the identity provider owns this flow and the app just links to it. For me that's better than building our own, every time.

T: How do you prevent username or account enumeration?

X: Fine-grained data permissions, like which sites or studies a user can see, usually come from the app's own database, not the token, because they change often and can be big. A claims transformation or authorisation handler loads them, with caching.
X: And I test the mapping with test tokens that have Keycloak's structure, so a config change can't silently remove someone's access.

T: How does Windows authentication work for intranet apps, and what are its limits?
K: windows authentication, kerberos vs ntlm, intranet authentication iis, negotiate authentication, integrated windows auth
X: Right, Windows authentication lets users on domain-joined machines sign in to intranet apps automatically with their Windows login, no password prompt. IIS supports it, and so does ASP.NET Core with the Negotiate handler.
X: It uses two protocols. Kerberos is the preferred one. Proxies and load balancers can also break NTLM, because it's connection-based. I've seen that cause some very confusing login loops.
X: For modern apps I'd use OpenID Connect against an identity provider like Entra ID or Keycloak. That can still use Kerberos so people sign in without a prompt on the corporate network, while supporting MFA, external access and token-based APIs.

T: What is reflection in .NET, and what does it cost?
K: reflection c#, system reflection, gettype getproperties, reflection performance, activator createinstance
X: Let me explain it with where it's used. Reflection lets code inspect and use types at runtime. List a type's properties, methods and attributes, read or set properties by name, call methods dynamically, create instances with Activator CreateInstance. A lot of framework magic runs on it. ASP.NET Core model binding and controller discovery, DI containers, serialisers, ORMs like EF Core and Dapper mapping columns to properties, test frameworks finding test methods.
X: The costs. Performance, reflective calls are much slower than direct ones, because of lookups, security checks, boxing arguments and no inlining. Calling GetProperties and GetValue in a hot loop, for every row or request, can be a real bottleneck.
X: Type safety, errors the compiler would normally catch, like a renamed property, only show up at runtime.
X: Trimming and Native AOT, the trimmer can't see what reflection will use, so it might remove code you need, and AOT doesn't support some dynamic features at all.
X: How I reduce the cost. Cache reflection results, like the PropertyInfo arrays per type, in a static dictionary. Compile expression trees or create delegates once with Delegate CreateDelegate, then call those fast delegates. And best of all, source generators that produce the code at compile time, which is what System.Text.Json, the logging generator and the regex generator do.
X: In our projects I'd use reflection for startup-time work, like scanning assemblies to register handlers or plugins, and keep it out of per-request paths, where a generated or cached approach is way faster.
@p17-741
S: csx
D: A
T: Parallel.ForEachAsync vs Task.WhenAll vs PLINQ: when do you use each?
K: parallel foreach, parallel foreachasync, plinq, asparallel, cpu bound vs io bound parallelism
X: Yeah, they all run things in parallel, but they suit different kinds of work.
X: Parallel For and Parallel ForEach are for CPU-bound work on in-memory data, like crunching thousands of records with calculations. They split the work across thread pool threads and block the calling thread until it's done. MaxDegreeOfParallelism controls how many run at once, usually around the number of cores.
X: PLINQ, with AsParallel, does the same thing for LINQ queries. Filtering, projecting and aggregating big in-memory collections across cores. Order isn't kept unless you add AsOrdered. Good for data-parallel queries, but the overhead makes it slower for small collections or cheap operations.
X: Task WhenAll is for I/O-bound async work, calling several APIs or databases at once. You start the tasks and await them together, and no threads are blocked while waiting. But starting thousands of tasks at once can flatten the downstream service or exhaust connections.
X: Parallel ForEachAsync, since .NET 6, sort of combines both. It runs an async delegate per item with a concurrency limit, like 500 files with at most 8 uploads at a time. That's my default for lots of I/O operations with throttling, instead of hand-writing SemaphoreSlim logic.
X: My rule of thumb is pretty simple. CPU-bound, Parallel or PLINQ. I/O-bound, async with WhenAll or ForEachAsync. Never use Parallel ForEach with async lambdas, because it treats them as async void and doesn't wait for them. And in ASP.NET Core request handling, avoid heavy CPU parallelism, because requests already share the thread pool.

T: What is the Mediator pattern, and what do MediatR pipeline behaviours do?
K: mediator pattern, mediatr, pipeline behavior, ipipelinebehavior, request handler pattern
X: So the Mediator pattern cuts direct dependencies between objects by having them talk through a mediator. In .NET APIs it's usually done with a library like MediatR. A controller doesn't call a service directly. It sends a request object, like CreateShipmentCommand, and the mediator finds the one handler for that request type and calls it.
X: What you get is thin controllers, and each use case is its own handler class with its own dependencies. That fits vertical slices and CQRS nicely, and handlers are easy to test.
X: Pipeline behaviours are honestly the most useful part. They wrap every request, kind of like middleware for use cases. A behaviour gets the request and a next delegate, can run code before and after, and can short-circuit. Typical ones are validation, running FluentValidation validators and returning errors before the handler even runs. Logging and timing each request. Transactions, wrapping commands in a database transaction. Caching for queries. Authorisation checks. Retry or idempotency for commands. You register them once and they apply to all handlers, or to specific request types through generic constraints.
X: The downsides, it's an extra layer of indirection, so navigating is harder, you can't just jump from controller to service. A little overhead. And for small apps it can be over-engineering. Also, recent MediatR versions moved to a commercial licence, so some teams use alternatives or a small hand-written dispatcher.
X: I like it for medium to large APIs with lots of use cases and cross-cutting concerns, and I keep it simple. One request, one handler, behaviours for the cross-cutting stuff.

S: csx
D: A
T: How do operator overloading and implicit or explicit conversions work in C#?
K: operator overloading c#, implicit operator, explicit operator, user defined conversion, value object operators
X: Okay, C# lets a type define how operators like plus, minus, double equals and less than work on it, through static operator methods. Say a Money type defines plus to add two amounts and checks they're the same currency, or a Vector type defines arithmetic. If you overload double equals, you have to overload not-equals too, and override Equals and GetHashCode consistently. Comparison operators come in pairs as well.
X: Conversion operators define how a type converts to or from another type. An implicit conversion happens automatically, like assigning a ShipmentId to a Guid variable, and should only be used when it can never fail and loses nothing. An explicit conversion needs a cast, like casting a Fahrenheit value to Celsius, and that's for conversions that might fail, lose precision or surprise the reader.
X: Where I find them useful is value objects and strongly typed ids. Like ShipmentId wrapping a Guid, where an explicit conversion from Guid stops you accidentally mixing up different ids, and an implicit conversion to Guid makes it easy to pass into data access code. Also maths or measurement types.
X: A few cautions. Don't overload operators with surprising meanings, like using plus for something that isn't addition. Avoid implicit conversions that hide expensive work or possible exceptions. And remember operators are static and resolved at compile time, so they don't behave polymorphically through base types or interfaces, except with static abstract interface members and generic math in newer C#.
X: And records give you value equality with double equals and not-equals automatically, which I think is the easiest win of the lot.

@p17-745
S: csx
D: A
T: How do memory leaks happen in .NET, and how do you find them?
K: memory leak dotnet, managed memory leak, event handler leak, find memory leak, dotnet-gcdump
X: Okay, so .NET has a garbage collector, but leaks still happen whenever objects stay reachable when they shouldn't. The GC can't collect anything that's still referenced.
X: The most common cause I've seen is event handlers. A short-lived object subscribes to a long-lived object's event, like a static event or a singleton service, and never unsubscribes. The publisher holds a reference to the subscriber forever.
X: Static collections and caches without limits. A static dictionary that only grows, or an in-memory cache with no size limit or expiry.
X: Captive dependencies, a singleton holding scoped or transient objects, which then live forever too.
X: Timers and background tasks holding on to objects they never release. Unmanaged resources not disposed, streams, connections, native handles, which leak memory outside the managed heap as well. Closures and lambdas accidentally capturing big objects and being held by long-lived delegates. And HttpClient created per request, which leaks sockets more than memory.
X: To find them, watch the trend. dotnet-counters or metrics showing the GC heap growing after each full GC instead of levelling off. Then take two memory snapshots some time apart, with dotnet-gcdump or a full dump with dotnet-dump, and compare them in Visual Studio, PerfView or another profiler. Which types grew in count, and what's the retention path, the chain of references keeping them alive. That path usually points straight at the event subscription or static collection to blame.
X: Then the fix follows the cause. Unsubscribe or use weak events, bound the caches, fix lifetimes, dispose properly.

T: Which less common .NET collections do you use: PriorityQueue, SortedDictionary, LinkedList?
K: priorityqueue c#, sorteddictionary, sortedset, linkedlist c#, queue and stack c#, specialised collections
X: See, most code only needs List, Dictionary and HashSet, but knowing the others helps you pick the right tool.
X: Queue and Stack. First in first out and last in first out, with constant-time enqueue and dequeue, or push and pop. Queues for processing work in order, stacks for undo or depth-first traversal.
X: PriorityQueue, since .NET 6, is a min-heap where Dequeue always gives you the item with the lowest priority value, in log n time. X: LinkedList is a doubly linked list with constant-time insert and remove when you already have the node. I've used it for an LRU cache together with a dictionary. In general it's slower than List because of poor memory locality, so I rarely use it otherwise.
X: For multi-threading, the concurrent collections, ConcurrentQueue, ConcurrentBag, BlockingCollection, and Channels for async producer-consumer. And immutable and frozen collections for shared read-only data.
X: Picking correctly turns order n scans into log n or constant-time operations, which really matters at scale.

T: How do you create and use custom attributes in C#?
K: custom attributes c#, create attribute, read attributes reflection, attribute usage, metadata attributes
X: Actually attributes are just metadata on code, classes, methods, properties, parameters. They don't do anything on their own. Some other code reads them and acts. Frameworks use them everywhere, Authorize, HttpGet, Required, JsonPropertyName, test attributes like Fact.
X: To create one, you write a class that inherits from Attribute, named with the Attribute suffix by convention, like AuditedAttribute, and put an AttributeUsage attribute on it saying where it can go, methods or classes, whether it can appear multiple times, and whether it's inherited. Constructor parameters and public properties become its arguments, and they have to be compile-time constants, strings, numbers, enums or types.
X: To read it, reflection, GetCustomAttribute of AuditedAttribute on a type, method or property. In ASP.NET Core, endpoint metadata makes it easy. A middleware or filter gets the current endpoint, asks its metadata for the Audited attribute, and acts on it. For example, writing an audit record only for endpoints marked Audited, or applying a specific rate-limit policy.
X: Examples I've used, marking endpoints that need audit logging, marking properties that hold sensitive data so logging and serialisation can mask them, and marking handler classes for automatic registration.
X: A couple of considerations. Reading attributes through reflection costs something, so cache the results. For performance-critical or AOT scenarios, source generators can read attributes at compile time and generate code instead. And I don't hide important business logic in attributes, because it makes behaviour less obvious to whoever's reading the code.

D: A
T: How do you design immutable types in C#?
K: immutable types c#, immutability c#, immutable class, readonly properties, record with expression
X: Honestly I like immutability a lot. An immutable object can't change after it's created, any "change" gives you a new object. That makes code easier to reason about, since nothing can modify an object behind your back, it's naturally thread-safe, and it's safe as a dictionary key or in shared caches.
X: Records are the simplest way. A positional record, like an Address record with Street and City, gives you init-only properties, value equality, and with-expressions to make modified copies, like taking an address and creating a copy with the City set to Pune.
X: For classes, properties with get only or init, set through the constructor or object initialisers, and required members to make sure they're set. Fields marked readonly. No methods that modify state. Methods return new instances instead, like Money Add returning a new Money.
X: One thing to watch is shallow immutability. A record with a List of string property isn't truly immutable, because the list itself can still change. Use IReadOnlyList with a copy, ImmutableArray or ImmutableList, or FrozenSet for collection properties, and copy incoming collections in the constructor.
X: readonly struct for small value types guarantees all fields are read-only.
X: Where I use it, value objects in the domain, like Money, DateRange or strongly typed ids. DTOs and messages, which shouldn't change after creation. Config snapshots. And front-end state, like Redux, same idea.
X: The cost is more allocations when objects change a lot. That's rarely an issue in business code, but it matters in tight loops.

T: Which timer should you use in .NET: PeriodicTimer, System.Threading.Timer or System.Timers.Timer?
K: periodictimer, system threading timer, system timers timer, timers in dotnet, run code every n seconds
X: Yeah, .NET has several timers and it does confuse people.
X: System.Threading.Timer is the lightweight one that calls a callback on a thread pool thread at intervals. Callbacks can overlap if one takes longer than the interval, exceptions in callbacks are unhandled and can crash the process, and you have to keep a reference to it so it isn't garbage collected.
X: System.Timers.Timer is a wrapper with an Elapsed event and an AutoReset property. It swallows exceptions from handlers, which hides errors, and it also allows overlapping callbacks. Mostly legacy now.
X: UI timers, the Windows Forms and WPF dispatcher timers, run on the UI thread, desktop only.
X: PeriodicTimer, since .NET 6, is built for async code. You write a loop, while awaiting the timer's WaitForNextTickAsync with the stopping token, do the work. Ticks never overlap, because the next wait only starts once the work finishes. Exceptions are handled like normal async code, and cancellation is built in. That's my default inside a BackgroundService for periodic jobs, polling an outbox table or refreshing a cache.
X: For testability, TimeProvider in .NET 8 can create timers, so tests control time.
X: And for schedules more complex than fixed intervals, like every weekday at 2 AM, or jobs that must survive restarts and run once across multiple instances, I'd go with a scheduler like Quartz.NET or Hangfire instead of a raw timer. That's how our alert watchdog runs its scheduled checks.
@p17-750
S: csx
D: A
T: What does the volatile keyword do, and what is the .NET memory model?
K: volatile keyword c#, memory model dotnet, memory barrier, instruction reordering, volatile read write
X: Let me start with the problem. Compilers, the JIT and CPUs are allowed to reorder memory reads and writes, and cache values in registers, as long as single-threaded behaviour doesn't change. In multi-threaded code, that means one thread might not see another thread's writes when you expect, or sees them in a different order.
X: The .NET memory model defines what's guaranteed. volatile on a field gives reads acquire semantics and writes release semantics. A volatile read always reads the current value from memory, and operations after it can't move before it. A volatile write makes all earlier writes visible before it. The classic use is a stop flag. A private volatile bool stop-requested field, one thread sets it, a worker loop checks it, and the JIT can't hoist the read out of the loop and spin forever.
X: What volatile doesn't do is make compound operations atomic. count plus plus on a volatile field is still a read-modify-write race, you need Interlocked Increment for that. It also doesn't give full ordering between a write followed by a read.
X: In practice I rarely use volatile directly. Higher-level tools are clearer and safer. lock, which includes full memory barriers. Interlocked for atomic updates. Volatile Read and Volatile Write methods for explicit cases. CancellationToken for stop signals instead of a volatile bool. And concurrent collections, Lazy and Channels for coordination.
X: For me, knowing the memory model mostly helps me spot subtle bugs in lock-free code, and avoid writing lock-free code unless it's really necessary.

D: A
T: What is TaskCompletionSource, and when do you use it?
K: taskcompletionsource, tcs c#, convert callback to task, manual task completion, wrap event in task
X: So TaskCompletionSource lets you create a Task that you complete yourself. You hand its Task property to callers, they await it, and later your code calls SetResult, SetException or SetCanceled, or the Try versions, to finish it.
X: Where I find it useful. Wrapping callback or event-based APIs into async ones. An older library raises a Completed event, you subscribe, and in the handler you set the result on the completion source. The method returns its Task, so callers just await it.
X: Request-response over messaging. When you send a request over a queue or WebSocket and wait for a reply with a matching correlation id, you store a TaskCompletionSource in a dictionary keyed by that id. When the response arrives, find it and complete it. Combine it with a timeout and cancellation, and remove the entry afterwards.
X: Signals between components, one part waits until another reaches some state, like "service is ready". And testing, controlling exactly when a fake async dependency completes.
X: The important detail people miss is creating it with the RunContinuationsAsynchronously option. Otherwise, when you call SetResult, the awaiting code's continuation can run synchronously on your thread, inside your lock or event handler, and that can cause deadlocks or weird re-entrancy. I learned that one the hard way.
X: Also make sure every path completes it, including errors and cancellation, by registering a cancellation callback that calls TrySetCanceled. Otherwise the awaiting code just waits forever.
@p17-752
S: csx
D: A
T: Server GC vs workstation GC: what is the difference?
K: server gc vs workstation gc, gc modes dotnet, concurrent gc, background gc, dotnet gc settings
X: Okay, the .NET garbage collector has modes tuned for different kinds of apps.
X: Workstation GC is meant for desktop and client apps. Single heap, collects on the thread that triggered the collection, lower memory usage, so it's friendly to machines running lots of processes.
X: Server GC is meant for high-throughput server apps. It creates a separate heap and a dedicated GC thread per CPU core, so allocations scale across cores and collections run in parallel and finish faster. It uses more memory, since each heap has its own budget. ASP.NET Core apps use Server GC by default.
X: Both can run with concurrent or background GC, which is the default, so full gen 2 collections mostly run in the background while app threads keep going, reducing pauses.
X: Why it matters in practice. Containers, with Server GC on a machine with lots of cores but a small memory limit, heap counts and memory usage can surprise you. .NET respects container CPU and memory limits, and you can tune with GCHeapCount, GCHeapHardLimit, or the newer DATAS mode, dynamic adaptation to application sizes. That's on by default in .NET 9 for Server GC, and it adjusts heap count to the load and cuts memory for small apps.
X: Lots of small services on one host, Workstation GC or DATAS might be better to save memory. Latency-sensitive work, GC latency modes like SustainedLowLatency can reduce blocking collections during critical periods.
X: But my rule is, I don't change GC settings on a guess. I measure with dotnet-counters, GC pause time, heap size, allocation rate, and then adjust.

T: How do you write high-performance logging with LoggerMessage in .NET?
K: loggermessage, high performance logging, logger message source generator, logging allocations, logmethod attribute
X: Right, normal logging calls, like LogInformation with a "Processed Count items for StudyId" template and the values, are convenient but have hidden costs. Value-type arguments get boxed into an object array, the template gets parsed, and all that happens even when the level is disabled, unless you check IsEnabled first. In hot paths, like per-message processing in a busy consumer, that adds allocations and CPU.
X: LoggerMessage fixes it. The modern way is the source generator. You declare a static partial method, like LogProcessed taking a logger, a count and a study id, with the LoggerMessage attribute giving an event id, a level like Information, and the message template. The generator writes an optimised implementation at compile time. It checks the level is enabled before doing any work, avoids boxing with strongly typed parameters, and pre-parses the template.
X: Beyond speed, strongly typed log methods give consistent event ids and messages across the codebase, which makes searching and alerting in Splunk or Grafana easier. Parameter names get checked at compile time. And log calls in business code read cleanly, like logger dot LogProcessed with count and study id, when you write them as extension methods.
X: What I do is use it in libraries, and high-volume paths like message handlers, middleware and data processing loops. For rare log lines, like startup messages, regular calls are fine.
X: And I avoid string interpolation in log calls, because it builds the string even when the level is off, and you lose the structured properties.

S: csx
D: A
T: How do you sort custom objects in C#: IComparable, IComparer and stable sorting?
K: icomparable, icomparer, sort custom objects c#, orderby thenby, stable sort c#
X: Actually the differences here matter more than people think.
X: IComparable defines a type's natural order. The type implements CompareTo and returns negative, zero or positive. Think of a Version or a Money type that has an obvious order. Then List Sort and SortedSet use it automatically.
X: IComparer defines an order outside the type, so you can have several, by name, by date, by priority. You pass it to Sort, OrderBy or sorted collections. Comparer Create with a lambda builds one quickly, and StringComparer OrdinalIgnoreCase is a built-in one for strings.
X: LINQ OrderBy and ThenBy are the most readable for most business code, like ordering shipments by priority, then by created date descending. It returns a new sequence, and it's a stable sort, so items with equal keys keep their original order.
X: List Sort and Array Sort sort in place, faster with less allocation, but they're unstable, equal items can get reordered. If stability matters, like sorting a table by one column while keeping a previous order, use OrderBy or add a tie-breaker key like an id.
X: Common mistakes I've seen. Inconsistent comparers that break the rules, random results or not handling nulls, which can cause exceptions or wrong results. Subtracting integers in CompareTo, which can overflow, instead of calling CompareTo on the values. And culture-sensitive string sorting when ordinal was intended.
X: For data from a database, I sort in the SQL query, with a deterministic tie-breaker, especially for pagination.

S: csx
D: A
T: What is the dynamic keyword in C#, and when is it appropriate?
K: dynamic keyword c#, dynamic vs var vs object, dlr, dynamic language runtime, expandoobject
X: So var and dynamic look similar but they're completely different. var is static typing, the compiler infers the type at compile time and you get full type checking and IntelliSense. object is also static, you need casts to use its members.
X: dynamic switches off compile-time checking for that variable. Member access, method calls and operators get resolved at runtime by the Dynamic Language Runtime. If the member doesn't exist, you get a RuntimeBinderException at runtime instead of a compile error.
X: Where it's appropriate. COM interop, like automating Office, where the APIs are loosely typed. dynamic made that a lot simpler. Interop with dynamic languages like IronPython. Truly dynamic data structures, like ExpandoObject, or dynamic JSON in some cases, though System.Text.Json's JsonNode or JsonDocument are usually the better choice. And some reflection-heavy cases where dynamic is shorter, like calling a generic method with a runtime type, where dynamic dispatch picks the right overload.
X: Why I avoid it in normal code. No compile-time safety, so typos and refactoring mistakes turn into runtime errors. Slower than static calls, though the DLR caches call sites. No IntelliSense. And it doesn't work with trimming and Native AOT.
X: For me, in business apps and APIs, strong types, DTOs and generics win. If I see dynamic in a code review outside interop, I'd usually ask whether a proper type or JsonNode would be clearer. Most of the time it is.

S: csx
D: A
T: What are the access modifiers in C#, including protected internal and private protected?
K: access modifiers c#, protected internal, private protected, internal vs public, file access modifier
X: Okay, access modifiers control which code can use a type or member.
X: public, accessible from anywhere. private, only inside the same class or struct, and it's the default for members. protected, the class and derived classes, even in other assemblies. internal, anywhere in the same assembly but not from outside, and that's the default for top-level types.
X: Then the two that confuse people. protected internal means accessible from the same assembly, or from derived classes in any assembly. So it's protected OR internal. private protected, since C# 7.2, means only derived classes that are also in the same assembly. So protected AND internal. That OR versus AND is how I remember them, and interviewers love asking it.
X: And file, since C# 11, a type visible only inside the same source file, mostly useful for source generators and helper types.
X: How I use them in practice. Default to the most restrictive access and open up only when needed. In a library or shared NuGet package, anything that isn't meant to be public API is internal, so we can change implementations without breaking consumers.
X: InternalsVisibleTo lets a test project see internal types, so I don't make things public just for tests, though honestly I prefer testing through public behaviour anyway.
X: In clean architecture solutions, keeping the infrastructure implementations internal and exposing only interfaces and a registration extension method enforces the boundaries nicely.
X: And sealed, alongside the access modifiers, stops unintended inheritance.

S: csx
D: A
T: How do you make a deep copy of an object in C#?
K: deep copy c#, shallow copy c#, clone object c#, memberwiseclone, record with shallow copy
X: So a shallow copy creates a new object, but reference-type fields just copy the reference, so the copy and the original share nested objects. Change a nested list in the copy and it changes in the original too. A deep copy duplicates the nested objects as well, so the two are fully independent.
X: The ways to copy. MemberwiseClone, a protected method on object that makes a shallow copy, you can call it from a Clone method in your class. Records with with-expressions, also shallow. Copying an order with a new status copies the top-level values, but a List property is shared. ICloneable, an old interface that doesn't say shallow or deep, so it's not recommended for public APIs.
X: For actual deep copies. Manual copy methods or copy constructors are the most explicit and the fastest. Each class copies its own nested objects, like a new Order built from another one creating new item objects. Safe, but you have to maintain it when properties get added.
X: Serialisation round-trip, serialise to JSON with System.Text.Json and deserialise into a new object. Simple and generic, but slower, and it only copies serialisable data, so you lose private state, references and cycles unless configured.
X: Mapping libraries or source-generated mappers can produce copies too.
X: But often the best answer, I think, is to not need deep copies at all. Make objects immutable so they can be shared safely, and use immutable collections. Then "changing" means creating a new version and there's no risk of accidental shared mutation.
X: And I'd never use BinaryFormatter for cloning like older articles suggest. It's insecure and it's been removed.

T: Explain the Proxy pattern and how dynamic proxies are used in .NET.
K: proxy pattern, dynamic proxy, dispatchproxy, castle dynamicproxy, interceptor pattern c#
X: See, the Proxy pattern puts a stand-in object in front of a real one, implementing the same interface, to control access to it. The caller doesn't know it's talking to a proxy. The proxy can add behaviour before or after forwarding the call.
X: The common kinds. A virtual proxy delays creating an expensive object until it's needed, like lazy loading. A protection proxy checks permissions before calling through. A remote proxy represents an object in another process, like a generated gRPC or WCF client. And caching or logging proxies add those concerns.
X: It looks a lot like the Decorator pattern. The difference is intent. Decorators add behaviour and often get stacked, proxies control access. In code they can look identical.
X: Dynamic proxies generate the proxy classes at runtime, so you don't write one per interface. In .NET there's DispatchProxy, built in, which creates a proxy for any interface and handles every call in one Invoke method. And Castle DynamicProxy, a popular library supporting interfaces and virtual class members. Moq and NSubstitute use it to create mocks, and some frameworks use it for interceptors, adding logging, timing or retries to every method of a service.
X: Where it shows up in our stack, EF Core lazy-loading proxies, which override navigation properties to load data on access. Mocking libraries in unit tests. And HTTP client libraries like Refit, which generate implementations of an interface that make the API calls.
X: Because runtime proxies use reflection, people are increasingly using source generators to produce the same thing at compile time.

T: How would you build a GraphQL API in .NET, and how do you avoid the N+1 problem?
K: graphql dotnet, hot chocolate, graphql n+1, dataloader, graphql asp.net core
X: Actually in .NET the go-to GraphQL server library is Hot Chocolate. You define the schema from C# types, a Query class with resolver methods like GetShipments, object types for Shipment and Site, and mutations for changes. Clients send one query describing exactly the fields they want, including nested data, like shipments with their site name and items, and they get back exactly that shape.
X: The N plus one problem is GraphQL's classic trap. If a query asks for 50 shipments and each one's site, a naive site resolver runs one database query per shipment. One query for shipments plus 50 for sites.
X: DataLoader solves it. Instead of loading the site right away, each resolver asks a DataLoader for a site id. The DataLoader collects all the ids requested in that execution step, makes one batched call, basically a where id is in this list query, and hands each resolver its result. It also caches within the request, so the same site isn't loaded twice. Hot Chocolate has DataLoader built in, and it integrates with EF Core projections so only the requested columns are queried.
X: Other things I'd set up. Query depth and complexity limits, so a client can't send some huge nested query that kills the server. Persisted or allow-listed queries for public APIs. Authorisation on fields and types, not just the endpoint. And cursor-based pagination.
X: When would I choose GraphQL? When lots of different front ends need different shapes of related data. For simple CRUD or service-to-service calls, I'd say REST or gRPC is simpler to run, cache and monitor.

T: AutoMapper, Mapster, Mapperly or manual mapping: how do you map DTOs?
K: automapper vs manual mapping, mapster, mapperly, object mapping dotnet, dto mapping
X: So mapping between entities and DTOs is repetitive, which is why libraries exist. Each one has its pros and cons.
X: AutoMapper uses conventions and reflection-based configuration. Properties with matching names map automatically, and profiles define the exceptions. It saves typing, and ProjectTo can turn mappings into EF Core query projections. But mistakes show up at runtime, not compile time. The mapping logic is hidden, so debugging and find-references get harder. Complex configurations turn into a puzzle. And recent versions moved to a commercial licence.
X: Mapster is similar in style, but faster, with optional code generation.
X: Mapperly is a source generator. You declare a partial mapper class with method signatures, and it generates plain mapping code at compile time. You get compile-time warnings for unmapped properties, no reflection, good performance, and generated code you can actually read and debug.
X: Manual mapping, writing the assignments yourself, often as extension methods like ToDto, or constructors. Explicit, fast, easy to debug, refactor-safe. It costs some typing, but with modern IDEs and AI assistants that's really small now.
X: My preference is manual mapping or Mapperly for most code, because mappings often contain little business decisions, formatting, combining fields, hiding data, and those are clearer in code. For EF Core queries I write Select projections directly, so only the needed columns come back. In an existing codebase that uses AutoMapper consistently I'd keep it, but always with configuration validation tests, AssertConfigurationIsValid, to catch mistakes early.
@p17-762
S: apix
D: A
T: Why do async controller actions improve scalability in ASP.NET Core?
K: async controller actions, async await scalability, why async in web api, thread pool web requests, async io scalability
X: Right, so in ASP.NET Core each request runs on a thread pool thread. If an action calls a database or another API synchronously, that thread just sits there blocked, doing nothing, until the response comes back. Under load, all the threads can end up blocked waiting on I/O. The thread pool grows slowly, requests queue up, latency spikes, while the CPU's mostly idle. That's thread pool starvation.
X: With async actions, when the code awaits an I/O operation, like awaiting ToListAsync on a DbSet, or an HttpClient GetAsync, the thread goes back to the pool while the OS waits for the I/O. When the result comes in, a pool thread continues the method. So a small number of threads can serve lots of concurrent requests that are mostly waiting.
X: A few important points. Async improves scalability and throughput under concurrency, not the speed of one request. A single request might even be a tiny bit slower because of the overhead.
X: It only helps I/O-bound work. CPU-bound work still needs a thread, and wrapping it in Task Run inside a request just moves it to another pool thread and adds overhead.
X: It has to be async all the way. Calling dot Result or dot Wait on async methods blocks a thread again and can bring the starvation right back.
X: And pass the request's CancellationToken into async calls, so work stops when the client disconnects.
X: In our legacy ASP.NET MVC applications, moving data access to async was one of the changes that helped handle peak usage better without adding servers.

T: IActionResult vs ActionResult<T> vs returning the DTO directly: which do you use?
K: iactionresult vs actionresult, actionresult t, return types web api, controller return type, typed results controllers
X: Yeah, in ASP.NET Core controllers you've basically got three return styles.
X: Returning the DTO directly, like a Get method that returns a ShipmentDto. Simple, and the framework serialises it with a 200. But you can't return other status codes like 404 without throwing exceptions or some workaround.
X: IActionResult. You can return anything, Ok with the DTO, NotFound, BadRequest with a problem, CreatedAtAction. Flexible, but the return type says nothing about the body, so OpenAPI generators can't infer the schema. You need ProducesResponseType attributes with the DTO type and status code.
X: ActionResult of T combines both. You can return a ShipmentDto directly, and it's implicitly converted to a 200 result, or return NotFound or anything else. The T tells OpenAPI and readers what the success body looks like. That's my default for controllers, an async Get returning a Task of ActionResult of ShipmentDto. I still add ProducesResponseType for the error codes so the docs are complete.
X: For minimal APIs, the equivalent is TypedResults with a Results type listing Ok of ShipmentDto or NotFound, which gives compile-time checked status codes and automatic OpenAPI metadata.
X: One caveat, ActionResult of T doesn't work with an interface as T, because implicit conversions from interfaces aren't allowed. So I return concrete DTO types, which I'd do anyway.
X: And consistency matters more than which one you pick. The team agrees on one style for new code, along with ProblemDetails for errors.

T: Should you wrap every API response in a standard envelope?
K: api response wrapper, response envelope, standard api response format, wrap response data success, apiresponse class
X: Let me be honest, I've seen both in real systems. Some teams wrap every response in an envelope with success, data, errors and message. Others return the resource directly and use HTTP status codes and ProblemDetails for errors.
X: For an envelope, you get one consistent shape for the front end to handle, a place for metadata like pagination, warnings or request ids, and it was common practice in older systems where clients couldn't easily read status codes.
X: Against it, it duplicates what HTTP already gives you. Success false with a 200 status confuses monitoring, caches, gateways and retry logic, which all rely on status codes. It adds nesting to every client call. And standard tools, OpenAPI generators, HTTP clients, API gateways, work more naturally with plain resources and standard errors.
X: My preference is return resources directly with correct status codes. Use ProblemDetails, RFC 9457, for all errors, with extensions like an error code and validation errors. Put pagination in a consistent wrapper only for list endpoints, with items, a next cursor and a total count. And use headers for cross-cutting metadata like correlation ids.
X: If an existing API already uses an envelope, I keep it consistent rather than mixing styles, but I make sure the HTTP status still reflects the outcome, so failures aren't hidden behind 200s. In our legacy APIs that the Angular sub-apps consume, consistency for the front end was the priority, so new endpoints there follow the same contract.

X: The options pattern supports validation. With data annotations, you put Required, Range and Url attributes on the options class, and register it with AddOptions, Bind to the RabbitMq section, then ValidateDataAnnotations.

T: How do you deprecate and retire an old API version?

X: Okay, versioning lets you bring in a new version, but retiring the old one needs a proper process, otherwise you end up maintaining old versions forever.

X: Then retire it. After the sunset date, return 410 Gone with a helpful message for a while, then remove the code.

T: What is YARP, and when would you use a reverse proxy built in .NET?
K: yarp, yet another reverse proxy, reverse proxy dotnet, yarp gateway, strangler proxy
X: YARP, Yet Another Reverse Proxy, is a Microsoft library for building reverse proxies on ASP.NET Core. You configure routes and clusters, usually in appsettings. Routes match incoming requests by path, host, headers or method, and clusters define the destination servers, with load balancing, health checks and session affinity. And because it's just an ASP.NET Core app, you can add any middleware you like, authentication, rate limiting, logging, request and response transforms.
X: Where I'd use it. Strangler fig migrations, honestly that's the big one. You put YARP in front of a legacy application and route specific paths, like slash api slash shipments, to a new .NET 8 service, while everything else still goes to the old system. As features move over, you change routes, and clients never notice. That fits moving from ASP.NET MVC 4.8 to ASP.NET Core gradually.
X: A lightweight API gateway or BFF, central authentication, token handling for SPAs, header transforms and routing to internal services, when a full gateway product is too heavy or just not available on-premise.
X: Internal routing in containers, or as an edge component, with custom logic off-the-shelf proxies can't easily do.
X: Compared to Nginx, Envoy or cloud gateways, those are excellent for standard proxying and might be faster or better tied into platform features. YARP shines when a .NET team needs custom C# logic in the proxy and wants familiar tools.
X: One thing to watch is it becomes critical infrastructure. So it needs high availability, monitoring, timeouts, and careful forwarding of headers like X-Forwarded-For and correlation ids.

T: What is OData, and would you use it for your APIs?
K: odata, odata asp.net core, odata query options, filter select expand, queryable api
X: Okay, OData is a standard protocol for queryable REST APIs. Clients add query options to the URL. Dollar filter to filter, like status equals Shipped, dollar select to choose fields, dollar expand to pull in related entities, dollar orderby, dollar top and dollar skip for paging, and dollar count. In ASP.NET Core, the OData package turns those into LINQ on an IQueryable, so with EF Core they become SQL queries.
X: The good side, very flexible querying with little code, standard conventions with metadata describing the model, and good support in tools like Excel and Power BI, which can read OData feeds directly. So it's attractive for reporting and data-exploration endpoints.
X: The risks. Clients can build expensive queries, filtering on non-indexed columns or deep expands, and that hurts the database. Exposing the data model that directly couples clients to it, so changes get harder. Security needs care, so users can't expand or filter into data they shouldn't see. And honestly, the URL syntax is unfamiliar to a lot of front-end developers.
X: If I use it, I lock it down. Allow only specific properties for filtering and sorting, cap page size with MaxTop and page size settings, limit expand depth, apply authorisation filters before OData's query, and expose DTO projections instead of raw entities.
X: My view is for internal reporting or admin grids with lots of filter combinations, OData can save a lot of work. For public or core business APIs, I prefer purpose-built endpoints with explicit filters, which are easier to optimise, secure and evolve.

D: A
T: FromBody, FromQuery, FromRoute, FromHeader, FromForm and FromServices: how does binding source work?
K: frombody fromquery fromroute, binding source attributes, fromservices, fromheader, model binding sources
X: Model binding decides where each action parameter comes from, and these attributes basically make that explicit.
X: FromRoute is from the URL path template, like the id in shipments slash id.
X: FromQuery is from the query string, like status equals Shipped and page equals 2. Complex types can bind from several query parameters, which is handy for filter objects.
X: FromBody is from the request body, deserialised by the input formatter, usually JSON. Only one parameter can bind from the body, because the body stream's read once.
X: FromForm is form fields and multipart data, IFormFile for uploads included.
X: FromHeader reads a request header, like X-Correlation-Id, using its Name property.
X: FromServices injects a service from DI into just that action, useful when only one action needs a dependency.
X: With ApiController, inference rules kick in. Complex types are assumed to be from the body, simple types matching route parameters come from the route, other simple types from the query, and registered services get inferred as FromServices in newer versions. Minimal APIs have similar inference, plus AsParameters to group parameters into one object.
X: Common problems I've hit. A complex filter type on a GET wrongly inferred as body, so it needs FromQuery. Content type mismatches, like sending form data to a FromBody parameter, which gives a 415 Unsupported Media Type. And JSON property names that don't match.
X: So I'm explicit with attributes whenever there's any ambiguity. It documents the API and avoids surprises.

T: How do you generate typed API clients from OpenAPI for .NET and TypeScript?

X: Tools I'd look at. For .NET, NSwag generates C# client classes with a method per operation plus DTO classes. X: Watch-outs. The OpenAPI document has to be accurate, correct nullability, enums and response types, otherwise the generated code is just wrong. Generated clients can be big. And breaking API changes show up as compile errors, which is good, but they still need coordinating.
X: Put that together with contract tests and you catch integration mistakes really early.

T: AddControllers vs AddControllersWithViews vs AddMvc: what is the difference?
K: addcontrollers vs addmvc, addcontrollerswithviews, addrazorpages, mvc service registration
X: These register different sets of MVC services, and picking the right one keeps the app lean.
X: AddControllers registers what API controllers need, controller discovery, model binding, validation, formatters, filters, authorisation and CORS integration. No views, no Razor, no tag helpers. That's the right one for Web APIs.
X: AddControllersWithViews adds view support on top. The Razor view engine, tag helpers, view components, antiforgery for forms, and temp data. You use it for traditional MVC apps that return HTML views.
X: AddRazorPages registers Razor Pages, the page-based model, and you can combine it with the others.
X: AddMvc registers everything, controllers, views and Razor Pages. It's mainly there for compatibility with older apps migrated from ASP.NET Core 2, where it was the standard call.
X: You also need the matching endpoint mapping. MapControllers for attribute-routed API controllers, MapDefaultControllerRoute or MapControllerRoute for conventional MVC routes, and MapRazorPages for pages.
X: Why does it matter? Registering services you don't need adds a bit of startup time and memory, and switches on features you don't want, like view-related behaviour in a pure API. Also AddControllers doesn't include antiforgery validation for views, so if a migrated app uses forms, you need the views version. That one can catch people out during migrations.
X: In a migration from ASP.NET MVC 4.8, a hybrid app with both views and APIs would use AddControllersWithViews and map both route styles, while new pure API services use AddControllers or minimal APIs.

T: How do you support field selection or sparse fieldsets in a REST API?
K: sparse fieldsets, field selection api, partial response, fields query parameter, select fields rest
X: Sometimes clients only need a few fields of a big resource, like a mobile app that wants the shipment id, status and date, not the whole object with items and addresses. Sending everything wastes bandwidth and database work.
X: You've got a few choices. A fields query parameter, like get shipments with fields equals id, status, shipped-at. The API returns only those. To implement it, validate the requested fields against an allowlist, then either build a dynamic projection, a Select expression built from the field list, so the database only fetches those columns, or fetch a normal DTO and shape the output by serialising just the selected properties into a dictionary or JsonObject. JSON:API standardises this with a fields parameter per resource type.
X: Predefined views. Instead of arbitrary fields, offer a few named shapes, view equals summary or view equals detail, or separate endpoints like shipments slash summary. Easier to optimise, cache and document, and usually enough.
X: Expansion the other way round, return a lean resource by default and let clients ask for related data with expand equals items and site.
X: And GraphQL, if lots of clients need lots of different shapes. It's built for exactly this.
X: What you pay for arbitrary field selection is harder caching, since every combination's a different response, messier OpenAPI docs, and careful security so clients can't select fields they shouldn't see.
X: What I do usually is predefined summary and detail shapes, because they cover most needs and performance stays predictable. I'd add field selection only with a clear, measured need, like big payloads hurting a mobile or partner client.

T: How do you write a custom output formatter, for example to return CSV?
K: custom output formatter, csv output formatter, textoutputformatter, return csv from api, custom media type
X: ASP.NET Core uses output formatters to serialise action results based on content negotiation. JSON's the default, but you can add formatters for other media types, like CSV, so a client sending an Accept header of text slash csv gets CSV from the same endpoint.
X: To write one, you create a class inheriting TextOutputFormatter. In the constructor, add the supported media types, text slash csv, and encodings, UTF-8. Override CanWriteType to say which types it handles, say an IEnumerable of some DTO. Override WriteResponseBodyAsync to write the data, a header row and then each item's values, escaping commas, quotes and newlines properly, writing to the response body asynchronously. Then register it in AddControllers by adding a new CSV output formatter to the output formatters list. Optionally add a format mapping so a format equals csv query, or a dot csv extension, works through the FormatFilter.
X: Things to watch. Use a proper CSV library like CsvHelper for escaping and culture-safe numbers and dates, not string concatenation. I learned that the hard way with decimal commas.
X: Large data, stream rows instead of building everything in memory, ideally from an IAsyncEnumerable, so big exports don't eat memory.
X: Security, CSV injection, where values starting with equals, plus, minus or at are treated as formulas when someone opens the file in Excel. Prefix or escape them for user-provided data.
X: Set Content-Disposition with a file name so browsers download it.
X: And for really large or slow exports, I'd generate the file in a background job and return a download link, instead of formatting it inside the request.
