T: What is host filtering, and why does AllowedHosts matter in ASP.NET Core?
K: allowedhosts, host filtering middleware, host header attack, host header injection, allowed hosts configuration
X: Every HTTP request has a Host header saying which host name the client wants. Apps often use it to build absolute URLs, links in password reset emails, redirect URLs, callback URLs. If the app trusts any Host header, an attacker can send a request with the host set to evil dot com, and the app might generate links pointing to the attacker's site. Think of a password reset email whose link sends the token to the attacker, or caches poisoned with wrong URLs.
X: ASP.NET Core's host filtering middleware checks the Host header against the AllowedHosts setting. The default template sets AllowedHosts to star, which allows anything. Convenient for development, not great in production. Set it to specific names, like app dot example dot com and api dot example dot com separated by a semicolon, and the app rejects other hosts with a 400 Bad Request.
X: When the app's behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, the forwarded headers middleware might replace the host with X-Forwarded-Host. So configure KnownProxies, KnownNetworks and AllowedHosts on the forwarded headers options too, so spoofed forwarded headers aren't trusted.
X: Even better, don't build security-sensitive URLs from the incoming request at all. Use a configured public base URL for emails and callbacks. That's my preferred fix, honestly.
X: Kestrel doesn't validate host headers by itself, and IIS bindings only partly protect you if a site binding accepts all hosts.
X: It's a small config change that closes a real class of attacks, so I include it in production readiness checks.

T: How do you avoid slow first requests after deployment, and warm up an ASP.NET Core app?
K: slow first request, warm up aspnet core, application initialization iis, cold start dotnet, startup warmup
X: So the first requests after a deployment or an app pool recycle are often slow. The JIT compiles code on first use, DI builds services, EF Core builds its model and compiles queries, connection pools are empty, caches are cold, and HttpClient connections and TLS handshakes are all new. Whoever hits the app first sees seconds of delay.
X: How I reduce it. Warm up before taking traffic. In rolling or slot deployments, call key endpoints or run a warm-up routine before the instance is marked ready. An IHostedService can do warm-up work at startup, touching the DbContext, loading reference data into cache, opening connections, and a readiness health check only passes once warm-up's done.
X: IIS specifics, enable the Application Initialization module with preload enabled and start mode AlwaysRunning, and configure initialisation pages, so IIS starts the app and calls warm-up URLs after a recycle, before users arrive. Also avoid unnecessary recycles, like the default idle timeout that shuts down quiet apps. That idle timeout catches people out a lot on internal apps that only get used in the morning.
X: Reduce the startup cost itself. ReadyToRun compilation to pre-compile code, EF Core compiled models for big models, which matters when you've got hundreds of tables, avoiding heavy reflection scanning at startup, and lazy initialisation only for rarely used parts.
X: Measure it. Track the latency of the first requests after deployments and the startup duration, so regressions are visible.
X: For serverless, like Lambda or Azure Functions, it's the same idea as cold starts, with provisioned concurrency or premium plans as extra options.

S: sqlx
D: A
T: Stored procedure vs function in SQL Server: what is the difference?
K: stored procedure vs function, sql function vs procedure, udf vs stored procedure, table valued function
X: Okay, both are reusable database code, but the rules and the uses are different.
X: Stored procedures run with EXEC. They can hold almost any T-SQL, inserts, updates, deletes, transactions, try-catch, temp tables, dynamic SQL, calls to other procedures. They can return multiple result sets, output parameters and a return code. But you can't use them inside a SELECT. So they're for business operations, data changes and batch processes.
X: Functions return a value and you can use them inside queries, in the SELECT, the WHERE, a JOIN. But they're not allowed to change database state. No inserts, updates or deletes on real tables, no transactions, no dynamic SQL, limited error handling.
X: Functions come in three flavours. Scalar functions return one value. Inline table-valued functions are a single SELECT and behave like a parameterised view, the optimiser expands them into the main query, so they perform well. Multi-statement table-valued functions build a table variable in several steps, and historically they had bad cardinality estimates, so they often performed badly.
X: On performance, scalar functions called per row in big queries were famously slow, though SQL Server 2019 can inline a lot of them automatically now. Inline table-valued functions are usually the best choice when you need reusable query logic.
X: My rule of thumb is procedures for operations and data changes, inline table-valued functions for reusable filters or calculations inside queries, and keep scalar and multi-statement functions out of hot queries. From .NET, procedures are easy to call with EF Core or Dapper, and functions can be mapped too.

T: How do PIVOT and UNPIVOT work in SQL Server?
K: pivot sql server, unpivot, rows to columns sql, crosstab query, conditional aggregation
X: So PIVOT turns rows into columns. Say a table has rows of site, month and shipment count, and the report wants one row per site with a column per month. PIVOT aggregates the value, like the sum of shipment count, for each listed column value, January, February, March.
X: The syntax is you select from a source subquery of site, month and count, then PIVOT with the sum of shipment count, for month, in the list of month columns, each written as a quoted identifier.
X: The limitation is the column list has to be known when you write the query. If the columns depend on data, like a variable list of studies or visit types, you need dynamic SQL to build the list, and that has to be done safely, with QUOTENAME for the column names.
X: Honestly I often prefer conditional aggregation instead. You select the site, then a sum of a CASE expression that only counts January rows as the January column, same for February and so on, grouped by site. It's more flexible, works across databases, can mix different aggregations, and most developers find it easier to read.
X: UNPIVOT does the opposite, columns into rows, like turning January, February and March columns into rows of month and value. CROSS APPLY with a VALUES list is a more flexible alternative, and you decide how NULLs are handled, while UNPIVOT just drops them.
X: In practice I'm a bit careful about pivoting in SQL for reports at all. It's often simpler to return normalised rows and let the reporting tool or the front end pivot them. The queries stay stable when new columns show up.

T: What are CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY, and when do you use them?
K: cross apply, outer apply, apply operator sql server, lateral join, top n per row
X: See, APPLY lets you run a table expression for each row of the outer table, and the inner expression can use columns from that outer row. It's like a lateral join in other databases.
X: CROSS APPLY only returns outer rows where the inner expression returns something, like an inner join. OUTER APPLY returns all outer rows, with NULLs when the inner expression returns nothing, like a left join.
X: Where I use it. The classic one is top N per group, like the latest three shipments per site. Select from sites, cross apply a top three from shipments for that site, ordered by date descending. Very readable.
X: Calling table-valued functions per row, passing columns from the outer row in as parameters.
X: Splitting or parsing values. Cross apply STRING_SPLIT on a tags column with a comma to expand a delimited column into rows, or OPENJSON to shred JSON stored in a column.
X: Computing reusable expressions. Cross apply a little select that calculates total as quantity times price, give it an alias, and then use that total in the SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY without repeating the expression. I find that one really handy.
X: And unpivoting columns into rows with cross apply over a VALUES list.
X: On performance, APPLY with a correlated subquery effectively runs per row. So it's great when the outer set is small and the inner query does an index seek. For big outer sets, a window function approach, like ROW_NUMBER partitioned by site, might be better. I check the execution plan to decide.

D: A
T: How do LAG and LEAD work, and how do you calculate running totals in SQL?
K: lag lead sql, running total sql, cumulative sum, window function over, previous row value sql
X: Actually these are window functions that read a value from a previous or next row in a defined order, without needing a self-join.
X: LAG of quantity, one row back, default zero, over a partition by site ordered by shipped date, gives you the previous shipment's quantity for the same site, or zero if there isn't one. LEAD does the same for the next row. I use them to compare each value with the previous one, like stock change since the last count, to find time between events, like days between visits, and to detect status changes.
X: Running totals use an aggregate with an OVER clause. Sum of quantity over a partition by site, ordered by shipped date, with a ROWS frame from unbounded preceding to current row, gives a cumulative quantity per site over time.
X: The important detail is always specify ROWS for running totals. Without a frame, the default with ORDER BY is RANGE unbounded preceding, which treats rows with the same order value as peers. So you get surprising totals when there are ties, and it's slower too because it might use an on-disk worktable. ROWS is precise and faster. That one catches people out.
X: Moving averages work the same way with a limited frame, like six preceding rows and the current row for a 7-day average.
X: Other useful ones, FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE, NTILE for buckets, and PERCENT_RANK.
X: For performance, an index matching the partition and order columns lets SQL Server compute these without sorting. They replaced a lot of old cursor-based or self-join report queries, and they're usually much faster.

S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you query a hierarchy with a recursive CTE?
K: recursive cte, hierarchical query sql, parent child query, org chart sql, tree query sql server
X: Honestly recursive CTEs look scary but they're quite logical. Hierarchical data, an org chart, a folder tree, a bill of materials, regions containing countries containing sites, is often stored as a parent-child table where each row has a ParentId.
X: A recursive CTE walks the tree. It has two parts joined with UNION ALL. The anchor part selects the starting rows, the root, or a specific node. The recursive part joins the table to the CTE itself, to find the children of whatever's been found so far. SQL Server keeps repeating the recursive part until no new rows come back.
X: So for example, a CTE called Tree. The anchor selects the location with the root id at level zero. The recursive part selects locations whose parent id matches an id already in Tree, with level plus one. Then you select everything from Tree.
X: You can also build a path string as you go, to sort and display the tree, and walk upwards from a node to find all its ancestors.
X: Safety, MAXRECURSION defaults to 100 levels, so if the data has a cycle by mistake, the query errors out instead of looping forever. You can change it with the MAXRECURSION query option, and detect cycles by checking whether an id's already in the path.
X: Performance, index ParentId. For large, heavily queried trees, there's the hierarchyid data type, closure tables storing every ancestor-descendant pair, or a materialised path column. Those make subtree queries fast but cost more on updates.
X: In EF Core, recursive CTEs go in raw SQL or a view, since LINQ can't express recursion directly.

T: What is the gaps and islands problem in SQL?
K: gaps and islands, consecutive rows sql, find gaps in sequence, group consecutive dates, streaks sql
X: Yeah, gaps and islands is a classic SQL pattern. Islands are runs of consecutive values, like consecutive days a temperature sensor was out of range, or continuous periods a site was active. Gaps are the missing ranges, missing ids in a sequence, days with no data.
X: To find gaps, use LEAD to compare each value with the next one. In a subquery you get each id and the next id, and then you keep rows where the next id minus the current one is more than one. The gap starts at id plus one and ends at next id minus one.
X: Finding islands is the clever bit. The trick is the difference between the value and a row number. For dates, you subtract the row number, partitioned by sensor and ordered by date, as days from the reading date. For consecutive dates that difference stays the same, and when there's a gap it changes. Then group by sensor and that group key, and take the min and max dates for each island's start and end, and the count for its length.
X: For status changes, like periods a depot was in each state, compare each row's status with the previous one using LAG, mark a change with a one, take a running sum of those flags to get a group number, and aggregate by group.
X: Real uses I've seen, temperature excursion periods for shipments, continuous enrolment periods, consecutive missed visits, finding missing sequence numbers in imported files, and outage windows from monitoring data.
X: These set-based solutions replace cursor loops and they're much faster on big data, especially with an index on the partition and order columns.

T: What regular database maintenance should be set up for SQL Server?
K: sql server maintenance, maintenance plan, dbcc checkdb, update statistics job, backup and index maintenance
X: So on-premise SQL Server doesn't look after itself. A few regular jobs keep it healthy, usually scheduled with SQL Server Agent, and often using a well-known maintenance script solution rather than the basic maintenance plans.
X: Backups first. Full backups, say weekly or daily, differentials in between, and transaction log backups every few minutes in full recovery model, which also stops the log growing forever. Backups go to separate storage, get checked with RESTORE VERIFYONLY or checksums, and the most important bit, restores get tested regularly. A backup you've never restored is just a hope.
X: Integrity checks, DBCC CHECKDB regularly, to catch corruption early while good backups still exist. For big databases, run it on a restored copy or split it across days.
X: Statistics, update them regularly, especially on tables with big data changes, because the auto-update thresholds can be too slow for large tables and you get poor plans.
X: Index maintenance, reorganise or rebuild only indexes that are actually fragmented and big enough to matter, with sensible thresholds, online where the edition allows, outside business hours. A lot of teams now care more about statistics than fragmentation, since modern storage reduces its impact.
X: Cleanup, purge old backup history, job history and maintenance logs, and keep an eye on tempdb and log file sizes.
X: Monitoring, alerts for failed jobs, low disk, long-running jobs, blocking and high-severity errors.
X: And with lots of databases, like one per study in our case, the jobs have to loop through all of them, scale well, and be staggered so they don't all hit storage at the same time.

D: A
T: How do you implement a reliable queue table in SQL Server?
K: queue table sql server, readpast updlock, database as queue, dequeue sql, outbox processing locking
X: Okay, sometimes a table is used as a work queue, like an outbox table or a list of jobs, with several workers taking items. The challenge is letting multiple workers dequeue at the same time without processing the same item twice and without blocking each other.
X: The standard pattern uses three locking hints, ROWLOCK, UPDLOCK and READPAST. UPDLOCK takes an update lock on the rows being read, so two workers can't grab the same row. READPAST skips rows another worker has already locked instead of waiting. ROWLOCK keeps the locks fine-grained.
X: You can dequeue in one statement. A CTE selects the top ten pending rows with those hints, ordered by id, and then you update that CTE, setting status to Processing, locked-by to the worker and locked-at to the current UTC time, and use OUTPUT to return the claimed rows. Or you delete them with OUTPUT if processing is idempotent and failures are handled somewhere else.
X: The other essentials. An index on status and id, or a filtered index on pending rows, so the query doesn't scan. A timeout for stuck items, so anything in Processing too long goes back to Pending, because a worker might crash. An attempt counter that moves items to a failed state after a few tries, basically a dead-letter queue. And idempotent handlers, since an item can get processed again after a timeout.
X: When not to use it, very high throughput or lots of consumers, where a real broker like RabbitMQ is better. But for outbox tables and moderate job volumes, I'd say a queue table is great because the work stays transactional with the business data.
@p17-788
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is the logical processing order of a SQL query?
K: logical query processing order, sql order of execution, why can't use alias in where, select execution order
X: Right, SQL is written in one order but processed logically in another, and knowing that order explains a lot of common errors.
X: The logical order is FROM, including joins and APPLY, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, where expressions, aliases and window functions get computed, then DISTINCT, then ORDER BY, then TOP, or OFFSET and FETCH.
X: What that explains. You can't use a column alias from the SELECT in the WHERE, because WHERE runs before SELECT. But you can use it in ORDER BY, which comes after.
X: You can't use aggregates in WHERE. Filtering on aggregates goes in HAVING, after grouping.
X: Window functions like ROW_NUMBER can't go in WHERE either, because they're computed in the SELECT phase. So you wrap the query in a CTE or subquery and filter outside. I've seen that question come up a lot.
X: With an outer join, a filter in the ON clause behaves differently from the same filter in WHERE. In ON, it decides which rows match, and unmatched outer rows are kept. In WHERE, it removes rows after the join, which can quietly turn a left join into an inner join. That one bites people in reports.
X: TOP without ORDER BY gives you arbitrary rows, because order is only guaranteed by ORDER BY.
X: And this is the logical order, not the physical execution order. The optimiser can reorder things, push filters down, choose join orders, as long as the result is the same. But for reasoning about what a query means, the logical order is the right mental model.
@p17-789
S: sqlx
D: A
T: Which SQL Server date column type should you use: datetime, datetime2 or datetimeoffset?
K: datetime vs datetime2, datetimeoffset sql, sql server date types, store dates utc sql, date column type
X: So SQL Server has several date and time types, and the choice affects precision, storage and time zone handling.
X: datetime is the old one. Range from 1753, precision about three milliseconds, it rounds to point zero zero zero, zero zero three or zero zero seven, and uses 8 bytes. That rounding can cause surprising comparisons, so I don't use it for new columns.
X: datetime2 has a range from year 1, configurable precision down to 100 nanoseconds, and 6 to 8 bytes. It's the recommended type for date and time without an offset, and EF Core maps DateTime to it by default.
X: datetimeoffset is datetime2 plus a time zone offset, like plus five thirty, in 10 bytes. It records the moment and the offset it was captured in, and maps to DateTimeOffset in .NET.
X: date is just the date, 3 bytes, for things like date of birth or a visit date with no time. Maps to DateOnly in newer .NET. And time is just the time of day.
X: How I choose. For event timestamps, created, updated, shipped, either datetime2 holding UTC with a clear naming convention like CreatedAtUtc, or datetimeoffset if the original local offset matters, like when and where a user did something.
X: Business dates without a time, use date. That avoids the off-by-one-day issues you get from time zone conversions.
X: Be consistent in comparisons, because mixing types causes implicit conversions that can stop index use.
X: And avoid GETDATE, which returns server local time. Use SYSUTCDATETIME or SYSDATETIMEOFFSET so values don't depend on the server's time zone. I've seen that cause real bugs between servers in different regions.
@p17-790
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What are computed columns, and when should they be persisted or indexed?
K: computed column sql server, persisted computed column, index computed column, derived column sql
X: Let me give examples first. A computed column is defined by an expression over other columns in the same row. Full name as first name plus a space plus last name, line total as quantity times unit price, or pulling a value out of JSON with JSON_VALUE on a payload column, reading the status property.
X: By default it's virtual, not stored, calculated whenever you read it. Storage stays small but every read costs CPU.
X: PERSISTED stores the value physically and updates it automatically when the source columns change. Reads get faster, writes a bit slower. The expression has to be deterministic, always the same result for the same inputs, so things like GETDATE aren't allowed.
X: You can index a computed column, persisted or not, if it's deterministic and precise. That's really useful for making queries SARGable. If queries filter on an expression, like the year of the shipped date equals 2025, or a JSON property, a computed column with an index lets the optimiser seek instead of scanning. SQL Server can even match the expression in the query to the indexed computed column on its own.
X: Where I find them practical, indexing JSON properties stored in a JSON column, normalised search keys like upper-cased or trimmed codes, derived values used in filters or sorting, and keeping calculated values consistent without app code.
X: Cautions, certain SET options have to be right for indexes on computed columns, which can affect older apps or connections. And complex expressions with scalar user-defined functions can hurt performance and block parallelism.
X: In EF Core, HasComputedColumnSql maps them, and the values get read back after saves.
@p17-791
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you enforce data integrity with constraints in SQL Server?
K: check constraint, default constraint, data integrity constraints, not null unique foreign key, database constraints vs application validation
X: Honestly I'm a big believer in constraints. They make the database itself reject bad data, whatever application, script or person is writing it. App validation matters, but bugs, other services or manual fixes can bypass it.
X: The main ones. NOT NULL for required columns, simple and very effective. Primary key to uniquely identify each row.
X: Unique constraints or unique indexes for business uniqueness, like one kit number per study, or one active record per patient using a filtered unique index.
X: Foreign keys, so relationships point to rows that exist. You can't have shipments for a site that doesn't exist. They document the data model too. Options like ON DELETE CASCADE need care.
X: Check constraints, rules on values, like quantity can't be negative, status must be one of pending, shipped or received, or end date has to be on or after start date. They can reference several columns in the same row.
X: Default constraints, values when none is given, like created-at UTC defaulting to the current UTC time.
X: Why I like them. They catch bugs early, protect against bad data from imports and manual scripts, help the optimiser, since trusted foreign keys and check constraints let it skip unnecessary work, and they act as documentation.
X: Things to watch. Constraints added WITH NOCHECK, or disabled during loads, become untrusted and the optimiser ignores them, so re-enable them WITH CHECK. Name constraints explicitly so deployments and error messages are predictable, SSDT handles that well. And translate constraint violations into friendly API errors instead of showing raw SQL errors.
@p17-792
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What are the high availability and disaster recovery options for on-premise SQL Server?
K: always on availability groups, failover cluster instance, log shipping, sql server high availability, sql server disaster recovery
X: So for on-premise SQL Server you've basically got a handful of options, and they're often combined.
X: Always On availability groups. A group of databases is replicated from a primary replica to secondary replicas on other servers. Synchronous commit replicas, usually in the same data centre, give zero data loss and automatic failover. Asynchronous ones, often in another data centre, give you disaster recovery with a small possible data loss. Secondaries can be readable, so you can run reports and backups there. Apps connect through a listener name, so failover is transparent apart from a short blip. One catch, only databases get replicated. Logins, jobs and linked servers have to be synced separately, and people do forget that.
X: Failover cluster instances. The whole SQL Server instance fails over to another node, using shared storage. That protects against server failure, instance-level objects included, but the shared storage is a single point of failure, so it's usually paired with something else for DR.
X: Log shipping. Transaction log backups get copied and restored on a standby server on a schedule. Simple and reliable for DR, but data loss equals the shipping interval and failover is manual.
X: And offsite backups, always, because replication also replicates mistakes, like an accidental delete.
X: Which one you pick depends on the RPO and RTO targets, budget and licensing.
X: On the app side, use the listener, set MultiSubnetFailover to true in the connection string, add retry logic for transient errors during failover, and actually practise failovers. With lots of databases, like one per study, availability groups need planning around how many databases go in each group and the sync load.
@p17-793
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How does EF Core map inheritance: TPH, TPT and TPC?
K: ef core inheritance, tph vs tpt vs tpc, table per hierarchy, table per type, discriminator column
X: Okay, say you've got a class hierarchy, a base Notification with EmailNotification and SmsNotification. EF Core can map that to tables three ways.
X: TPH, table per hierarchy, is the default. One table holds every type, with a discriminator column saying which type each row is, and columns for all properties of all types, nullable for the types that don't use them. Queries are fast, no joins, and polymorphic queries are simple. The downsides, lots of nullable columns, you can't enforce NOT NULL on subtype-specific columns at the database level, and the table gets wide if there are many subtypes.
X: TPT, table per type. A table for the base type and one for each derived type with its own columns, linked by the primary key. The schema's clean and normalised, but every query for a derived type needs joins, and polymorphic queries join all the tables, which gets slow with many types.
X: TPC, table per concrete type, since EF Core 7. Each concrete type gets its own complete table with all properties, inherited ones included, and there's no base table. Querying one specific type is fast, no joins, and polymorphic queries use UNION ALL across tables. Keys have to be unique across all the tables, so you need sequences or GUIDs instead of identity columns per table.
X: My default is TPH for small hierarchies with few differing properties, because it performs best. TPC fits when you mostly query specific types. I'd stay away from TPT on performance-sensitive paths.
X: And honestly, often the best option is to skip inheritance in the data model altogether, and use composition, or a type column with a JSON column for the type-specific details.
@p17-794
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What are ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete in EF Core?
K: executeupdate, executedelete, ef core bulk update, set based update ef core, update without loading entities
X: Before EF Core 7, updating or deleting lots of rows meant loading entities into memory, changing them and calling SaveChanges, which sends one statement per row and eats memory, or you wrote raw SQL.
X: ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, plus their async versions, run set-based statements straight in the database from a LINQ query, without loading anything. So you take the shipments, filter where status is pending and created before a cutoff, and call ExecuteUpdateAsync, setting status to expired and updated-at to now. That becomes a single UPDATE with a WHERE. ExecuteDeleteAsync becomes a single DELETE the same way. Both return the number of affected rows.
X: You get much faster bulk changes, minimal memory, and it's still type-safe LINQ instead of raw SQL strings.
X: But honestly there are some caveats I'd point out. They bypass the change tracker, so entities already loaded in the DbContext aren't updated and might be stale.
X: They don't run the SaveChanges logic. Interceptors and overrides that set audit fields, raise domain events or write audit trails just won't fire. In a regulated system where every change needs an audit record, that's a serious problem. You have to handle auditing explicitly, with triggers or temporal tables, or just not use these methods for audited data.
X: They run immediately, outside SaveChanges, so put them in an explicit transaction with other changes if consistency matters. Concurrency tokens aren't checked automatically either.
X: For huge operations, batch them, like deleting in chunks, to avoid long locks and log growth.
X: So what I do is use them for maintenance, cleanup and non-audited bulk updates, and keep normal SaveChanges for business operations that need auditing.

T: How do you query unmapped types or keyless entities in EF Core?
K: keyless entity ef core, sqlquery unmapped types, hasnokey, query view ef core, raw sql dto ef core
X: Sometimes you need query results that don't match a normal entity, like a reporting query, a view, a stored procedure, or a projection from raw SQL. EF Core has a few tools for that.
X: Keyless entity types. You configure a class with HasNoKey, and map it to a view with ToView, or to a SQL query with ToSqlQuery. Then you can query it with LINQ, filtering and sorting on top. They're read-only, EF never tracks or saves them, because there's no key to identify rows. Good for views and reporting projections you use a lot.
X: SqlQuery for unmapped types, since EF Core 8. You call Database dot SqlQuery with a DTO type and an interpolated SQL string, say counting shipments per site for a given study id, and it maps the results straight into that class without registering it in the model. The interpolated values become parameters, so it's safe from injection. You can even compose LINQ on top, add a Where or an OrderBy, when the SQL can work as a subquery. It works with scalar types too, like a SqlQuery of int.
X: FromSql on a DbSet is for raw SQL that returns a mapped entity type.
X: When I reach for these, complex reporting queries LINQ can't express well, window functions, recursive CTEs, hints, existing views or procedures in a legacy database, and read models in a CQRS-style design.
X: Dapper's the other option for heavy read queries, and some teams use it alongside EF Core.
X: Either way, my approach is to keep the SQL in one place, test it against a real database, and watch out for column name mismatches, because you only find those at runtime.
@p17-796
S: sqlx
D: A
T: Should every foreign key column have an index?
K: index foreign key, foreign key index sql server, missing index on foreign key, fk index performance, delete slow foreign key
X: Mostly yes, I'd say. SQL Server doesn't create indexes on foreign key columns automatically, unlike primary keys. Whether you need one depends on how the column's used, but most of the time you do.
X: Why it matters. Joins, because queries usually join on foreign keys, like shipments to sites on site id. Without an index, finding shipments for a site means scanning the whole shipments table.
X: Filtering, because "all shipments for this site" or "all items for this order" are some of the most common queries you'll have.
X: And deletes and updates on parent rows. This is the one people miss. When you delete a site, or change its key, SQL Server has to check the child table for referencing rows. Without an index on the child's foreign key, it scans the whole child table for every parent row, holding locks, so deletes get extremely slow and you get blocking or deadlocks. Classic hidden problem in cleanup jobs. Cascading deletes find child rows the same way.
X: When you might skip it, very small tables, or a foreign key that's never used for lookups and whose parent rows never get deleted, like a static reference table with a few rows. Even then I'd check the access patterns.
X: Often the best index has the foreign key as the leading column plus other columns used together, like site id and shipped date, which covers both the foreign key and common queries.
X: EF Core creates foreign key indexes by default in migrations, which is a good default. In databases built by hand or with SSDT, I check for missing ones with a query over the system views that lists foreign keys without a matching index.
@p17-797
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What is a heap table, and why is a table without a clustered key usually a problem?
K: heap table sql server, table without clustered index, forwarded records, rid lookup, when to use heap
X: Right, a heap is just a table with no clustered index. Rows sit in no particular order, on whatever pages have space, and nonclustered indexes point to rows with a physical row identifier, the RID, which is file, page and slot.
X: The problems. Forwarded records. When a row gets updated and grows, like a varchar getting longer, and doesn't fit on its page anymore, SQL Server moves it to another page and leaves a forwarding pointer behind. Reads then follow extra pointers, so more I/O. Over time, heavy updates make heaps slower and slower.
X: Space isn't reclaimed well after deletes either, unless the table's rebuilt or the deletes take table locks, so heaps can grow full of empty pages.
X: Lookups from nonclustered indexes are RID lookups, and range queries in any order need sorts or scans.
X: Clustered indexes are the default for good reasons. Rows are stored in key order, range scans on the key are efficient, there are no forwarded records, and space management's better. A narrow, unique, ever-increasing key, like an identity or a sequential value, makes a good clustered key.
X: When is a heap fine? Staging tables for fast bulk loads that get read once and truncated, where insert speed matters and you read all the data anyway, or temp tables.
X: To find heaps, I query sys dot indexes for index id zero, and check the index physical stats DMV for forwarded record counts. In older databases, from what I've seen, finding big, frequently updated heaps and adding a clustered index can give a really noticeable speed-up.
@p17-798
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do STRING_AGG and STRING_SPLIT work in SQL Server?
K: string_agg, string_split, concatenate rows sql, comma separated values sql, split string sql server
X: These two handle going between rows and delimited strings, which used to need pretty awkward tricks.
X: STRING_AGG, from SQL Server 2017, concatenates values from multiple rows into one string with a separator. So you select the site id and STRING_AGG of kit number with a comma and space, within group ordered by kit number, grouped by site, and you get one row per site with a comma-separated list of kits. The WITHIN GROUP part controls the order. Before this, people used FOR XML PATH with STUFF, which was hard to read and had escaping issues. Watch the result length though. Cast the input to nvarchar max if the result can go past 8000 bytes, otherwise it errors.
X: STRING_SPLIT, from 2016, splits a delimited string into rows, with a column called value. You select value from STRING_SPLIT of an ids parameter and a comma, or use it with CROSS APPLY to split a column per row. Limitations, in older versions the output order isn't guaranteed, and SQL Server 2022 adds an enable ordinal argument that gives you the position. It only supports a single-character separator.
X: Where they help, building display strings for reports or exports, accepting a list of ids as a parameter in legacy code, and parsing simple imported data. Though from .NET, for id lists I'd go with table-valued parameters or JSON with OPENJSON, which are typed and cope with bigger lists.
X: One design caution. Storing comma-separated values in a column is usually a normalisation problem. These functions make that data easier to work with, but for new designs a proper child table or a JSON column is better.
@p17-799
S: sqlx
D: A
T: What are the risks of cross-database queries and linked servers?
K: cross database query, linked server sql server, three part names, four part names, distributed query risks
X: I mean, they're convenient, that's why they're everywhere. In SQL Server you can query another database on the same instance with three-part names, database dot schema dot table, and another server with linked servers and four-part names, or OPENQUERY. It's common in older systems, like a setup with a database per study plus a master database [and some cross-database queries]. But there are real risks.
X: Coupling. Queries depend on another database's schema and name. Renaming, moving or splitting databases breaks code in places that are hard to find, and database names often differ between environments, so the code needs synonyms or dynamic names.
X: Deployment and tooling. SSDT projects need database references to validate cross-database objects, and migrations have to be coordinated across databases.
X: High availability. Databases in different availability groups can fail over separately, so a cross-database query might suddenly point at a different server or just fail. Cross-database transactions in availability groups need special support.
X: Performance with linked servers. The optimiser often knows very little about the remote data, so it might pull whole remote tables across the network and filter locally. Distributed transactions need MSDTC, which adds latency and more things to fail.
X: Security. Linked servers are often set up with a fixed, highly privileged login, which is a common gap. Permissions and ownership chaining across databases need care too.
X: What I'd do instead. Use synonyms so the names live in one place, keep cross-database access in a small number of views or procedures, put shared reference data behind an API or a cache, and replicate the data you need into the local database with ETL or change data capture, instead of querying remotely in real time.
@p17-800
S: sqlx
D: A
T: How do you add a column or change a big table without downtime?
K: add column large table, online schema change sql server, alter table without downtime, add not null column big table, schema migration downtime
X: Schema changes on big, busy tables can lock the table for ages and block users. The trick is knowing which operations are cheap, and splitting the risky ones into safe steps.
X: Adding a nullable column is metadata-only in SQL Server, instant whatever the table size.
X: Adding a NOT NULL column with a default is also metadata-only since SQL Server 2012 Enterprise, for runtime constant defaults. Older or lower editions might rewrite every row, which is slow and locks the table.
X: Changing a column's type, or making it NOT NULL, can scan or rewrite the table. The safer way is add a new column, backfill it in small batches during quiet times, switch the app over to it, and drop the old column later.
X: Indexes, use ONLINE on where the edition allows, and RESUMABLE in newer versions so you can pause and continue. Otherwise schedule it in a maintenance window.
X: Foreign keys or check constraints, add them WITH NOCHECK first to skip the long validation, then validate later at a quiet time so they become trusted.
X: Set a low lock timeout, or use wait at low priority for online operations, so a schema change waiting for a lock doesn't block everyone queued behind it. That one catches people out badly.
X: Expand and contract. Deploy the schema change in a backward-compatible way first, release code that works with both shapes, then remove the old structure in a later release.
X: And test on a production-sized copy, measuring duration and lock behaviour. Something instant on a small test database can take an hour in production, trust me.

T: How do you show a global loading indicator for HTTP calls and route changes in Angular?
K: global loading spinner angular, loading indicator interceptor, router events loading, progress bar angular, busy indicator
X: So users need some feedback when the app's waiting, but a spinner in every component gets messy fast. What I do is two global mechanisms, plus local indicators where they make more sense.
X: For HTTP, an interceptor bumps a counter in a LoadingService when a request starts, and decrements it in finalize when the request completes, errors or gets cancelled. The service exposes an isLoading signal or observable that's true when the counter's above zero, and a progress bar at the top of the shell binds to it. Using a counter instead of a boolean is the bit that matters, because it handles parallel requests properly.
X: Some requests shouldn't show the global indicator, like background polling or typeahead searches. For those I use an HttpContextToken, something like skip loading, which callers set on specific requests, and the interceptor checks it.
X: For route changes, subscribe to router events. Show loading on NavigationStart, hide it on NavigationEnd, NavigationCancel or NavigationError. That covers lazy-loaded chunks and resolvers, which can take a noticeable while.
X: To avoid flicker, only show the indicator if loading takes longer than about 200 milliseconds, and once it's shown, keep it up for a minimum time. Otherwise it just blinks and looks broken.
X: For parts of a page, like a grid reloading, a skeleton or a small spinner in that component is better than blocking the whole screen. With signals and the resource API, components get loading states pretty easily.
X: And accessibility, announce loading and completion for screen readers with aria-busy on the region or a live announcer, and don't block keyboard focus when you don't need to.

T: How do you migrate an Angular app from NgModules to standalone components?
K: migrate to standalone angular, standalone migration schematic, remove ngmodules, bootstrapapplication, standalone components migration
X: Standalone components have been stable since Angular 15 and they're the default since 19. Moving an NgModule app over cuts boilerplate and makes lazy loading and dependencies a lot clearer.
X: Angular gives you a schematic for it, ng generate at angular slash core colon standalone. It runs in three steps, and I'd run them one at a time, committing and testing after each.
X: Step one converts all components, directives and pipes to standalone, adding the imports each one actually needs based on its template.
X: Step two removes the NgModules that aren't needed anymore, the ones that only declared and exported things.
X: Step three switches bootstrapping from bootstrapModule with AppModule to bootstrapApplication with AppComponent and an app config, moving providers into an app config file with provider functions like provideRouter, provideHttpClient with interceptors, and provideAnimations.
X: Then there's manual cleanup. Routing changes lazy loading from loadChildren with modules to loadComponent for single components, or loadChildren returning a routes array.
X: Providers that came from modules, like the store's forRoot or third-party modules, move to their provide functions, or importProvidersFrom as a bridge for libraries that don't have those yet.
X: Shared modules that exported a pile of common components get replaced with direct imports, or a constant array of common imports.
X: And tests, TestBed setups need updating to import standalone components instead of declaring them.
X: I'd do it incrementally, feature by feature, since standalone and NgModules work together fine, and keep the app releasable the whole time. In a big app it's worth running the control-flow and inject migrations around the same time too.

T: How do you test HTTP calls in Angular with HttpTestingController?
K: httptestingcontroller, test http angular, provideHttpClientTesting, mock http angular, angular service test http
X: Okay, for services that call APIs with HttpClient, Angular gives you a testing backend that intercepts requests, so tests never hit a real server.
X: Setup is simple. In TestBed you provide provideHttpClient and provideHttpClientTesting, along with the service under test, and then inject HttpTestingController.
X: The flow goes like this. Call the service method and subscribe, or turn it into a promise, and capture the result. Then call expectOne with the URL or a matcher function. That asserts exactly one matching request was made and gives you a TestRequest. Check the method, headers and body on it. Then assert the subscriber got the right data or handled the error. And in afterEach, call verify on the controller so the test fails if there were any unexpected requests.
X: What I test this way is basically URL building and query parameters, request bodies and headers, mapping responses to the right model, error handling like retries or fallbacks, and interceptor behaviour, like adding tokens or refreshing them after a 401.
X: For interceptors, register them with withInterceptors inside provideHttpClient in the test and check the outgoing headers.
X: For component tests, I'd usually mock the service instead of HTTP, to keep the test focused. For bigger integration tests, Mock Service Worker mocks the network at a lower level, and it works for both Angular and React code.

T: What are component test harnesses in Angular?
K: component harness angular, test harness, angular material harness, harnessloader, cdk testing
X: Basically harnesses are classes that let a test interact with a component through a stable API, instead of poking at its internal DOM. They come from the CDK testing package, and Angular Material ships harnesses for all its components.
X: The problem they solve is tests that query DOM details, like a querySelector on some mat-mdc select trigger class, break whenever the component's internal structure changes, and that happened a lot with Material upgrades. Those tests are hard to read as well.
X: With harnesses, you get a HarnessLoader for the fixture from the TestBed harness environment, then load a harness, say a MatSelectHarness filtered to the element with the status id. Then you just call its methods. Open it, click the option with the text "Shipped", read the value text. All async, all awaited. There are similar harnesses for buttons, inputs, tables, dialogs and more.
X: What you get, tests read like user actions, they survive internal markup changes because the harness gets updated along with the component, they wait for change detection and async tasks automatically, and the same harness works in unit tests and, with a different environment, in end-to-end style tests.
X: For our own shared components, like a date picker or a site selector, we can write custom harnesses by extending ComponentHarness, with methods like select site by name. If you publish them with the component library, consuming teams write much cleaner tests.
X: So I use harnesses for anything built on Angular Material and for shared design system components. It keeps tests maintainable across upgrades, which honestly is where most test pain comes from.

X: Right, so for years Angular projects used Karma with Jasmine for unit tests. Karma runs tests in a real browser, which is accurate but slow to start and awkward in CI. It's deprecated now, and Angular's been moving to newer options.

T: How do you implement OpenID Connect login in an Angular app?
K: angular oidc, angular keycloak login, angular-auth-oidc-client, angular sso, pkce angular
X: Let me walk through it. For an Angular SPA, logging in with an identity provider like Keycloak or Entra ID uses OpenID Connect with the authorisation code flow and PKCE. The implicit flow isn't recommended anymore.
X: The flow is, when the user isn't logged in, the app redirects to the provider's login page with a code challenge. After login, the provider redirects back with an authorisation code, and the app exchanges that, along with the code verifier, for tokens. An ID token describing the user, an access token for APIs, and usually a refresh token.
X: Libraries. angular-auth-oidc-client is certified and widely used, works with any OpenID Connect provider. keycloak-angular wraps Keycloak's JavaScript adapter, and MSAL Angular is for Entra ID. They handle redirects, token storage, silent renewal, logout and session checks.
X: Where it plugs in. An app initializer checks authentication at startup, a functional route guard protects routes and triggers login, and an HTTP interceptor attaches the access token, but only for configured API URLs, so tokens never go to third-party domains.
X: Security-wise, keep tokens in memory where you can instead of localStorage, to reduce XSS impact, keep access tokens short-lived, and be careful with refresh. Even better is the BFF pattern, which keeps tokens on a server and uses secure cookies. A lot of security teams recommend that for SPAs now.
X: Roles, read them from the token to show or hide UI, but always enforce authorisation on the API.
X: And with Keycloak as the single sign-on provider across legacy and new apps, users log in once and move between the Angular sub-apps and the React shell without logging in again.

S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you use web workers in an Angular application?
K: web worker angular, angular web worker, offload cpu work browser, ng generate web-worker, comlink
X: See, JavaScript in the browser runs on one main thread, and that thread also handles rendering and user input. So heavy work, parsing a big file, processing thousands of rows, generating a report, complex calculations, blocks the UI and the page freezes.
X: Web workers run JavaScript on a separate background thread. Angular supports them directly. ng generate web-worker creates a worker file and configures the build. In your component or service you create a new Worker, pointing at a URL built from the worker file and import meta url, send data with postMessage, and get results back in onmessage. Inside the worker you listen for messages, do the work and post the result back.
X: Limitations. Workers can't touch the DOM, window, or Angular services. Data passed between threads is copied with structured cloning, which costs something for big data, though transferable objects like ArrayBuffers can be moved without copying. And debugging's a bit different.
X: To make it nicer, libraries like Comlink wrap workers so you call functions like async methods instead of juggling messages. And wrapping the worker in an Angular service that returns Observables or Promises keeps components clean.
X: When I'd use one, client-side Excel or CSV parsing before upload, big data transformations for charts, validating large config files, or searching large in-memory datasets.
X: But before reaching for workers, I'd check whether the work can just happen on the server, or be broken into smaller chunks. Moving logic to the backend is often simpler.

T: How do you warn users about unsaved changes when they leave a page in Angular?
K: candeactivate guard, unsaved changes warning, prevent navigation angular, beforeunload angular, dirty form leave page
X: Losing work to an accidental click is really frustrating, especially in long configuration forms. There are two situations to handle, navigation inside the app, and leaving the app completely, like closing the tab or refreshing.
X: Inside the app, it's a CanDeactivate guard. With functional guards you write an unsaved-changes guard that takes the component, and if the component says it has unsaved changes, it opens a confirm dialog asking "You have unsaved changes, leave anyway?", otherwise it just returns true. Then you add that to the route's canDeactivate list. Components implement a small interface with a hasUnsavedChanges method, usually checking whether the form's dirty, or comparing current state with a saved snapshot. The guard can return a boolean, a Promise or an Observable, so it can wait on a proper Material dialog instead of the browser's confirm box.
X: Leaving the app, you listen to the window beforeunload event, with a HostListener or a host binding, and call preventDefault on the event when there are unsaved changes. Browsers show their own generic message, custom text isn't allowed anymore.
X: The details that actually matter. After saving, mark the form pristine so the warning doesn't pop up wrongly. Don't warn when the user cancels on purpose, or after a successful save that navigates away. And for logout and session timeout, decide whether to warn or just auto-save drafts.
X: Auto-saving drafts every so often is honestly the nicest option for long forms, because leaving is always safe, but it needs backend support for drafts.
X: For our study configuration screens, where users enter a lot of data, this kind of protection is definitely worth adding.

S: ngx
D: A
T: How do you poll an API with RxJS and stop when the job is done?
K: polling rxjs, poll api until complete, interval switchmap, takewhile polling, rxjs timer polling
X: So a common case, the user starts a long-running job, like generating a report, and the API returns a job id. The UI has to check the status every few seconds until it's completed or failed.
X: A clean RxJS way. Start with a timer that fires at zero and then every three seconds, pipe it through switchMap to call get job status with the job id, then takeWhile the state is Running, passing true as the second argument, and finally takeUntilDestroyed with the destroy ref.
X: How it works, the timer emits straight away and then every three seconds. switchMap calls the API each time and cancels the previous call if it's still going. takeWhile keeps going while the job runs, and that true argument means the final status, Completed or Failed, also gets emitted so the UI can show it. takeUntilDestroyed stops polling if the user leaves the page.
X: Improvements I'd make. If responses can be slow, use exhaustMap instead of switchMap, so no new call starts while one's in flight, or poll with a delay after each response using repeat with a three-second delay on the request observable.
X: Backoff for long jobs, increasing the interval over time, two, four, then eight seconds.
X: For errors, retry with a count and a delay for transient failures, and a timeout so you eventually give up with a clear message.
X: Pause polling when the browser tab is hidden, using the visibilitychange event, which saves server load.
X: If there are lots of users or frequent updates, server push with SignalR or Server-Sent Events is more efficient than polling. But for the occasional long job, I'd say polling is simple, reliable and works through every proxy.
@p17-818
S: ngx
D: A
T: debounceTime vs throttleTime vs auditTime vs sampleTime in RxJS: what is the difference?
K: debouncetime vs throttletime, audittime, sampletime, rate limiting rxjs operators, rxjs throttle
X: Okay, these all limit how often values get through, but they pick different values at different times.
X: debounceTime of 300 waits until the source has been quiet for 300 milliseconds, then emits the last value. If values keep coming, it keeps waiting. Perfect for search boxes, you only search after the user stops typing. The downside is during continuous activity, nothing comes out at all.
X: throttleTime of 300 emits the first value straight away, ignores values for 300 milliseconds, then lets the next one through. Good for button clicks, to stop double submits, or scroll events where you want an immediate reaction and then regular updates. If you set both leading and trailing to true in its config, it also emits the last value at the end of the window.
X: auditTime of 300, when a value arrives, waits 300 milliseconds, then emits the most recent value. So during continuous activity it emits regularly, with the latest value, not the first. Good for window resize or drag positions, where you want the latest state at a steady rate.
X: sampleTime of 300 emits the most recent value every 300 milliseconds on a fixed clock, whenever values arrived, and only if there was a new one. Good for sampling a fast stream, like progress or sensor readings, for display.
X: The way I remember it, debounce waits for silence, throttle takes the first and ignores the rest for a bit, audit takes the last after a delay, and sample just checks on a clock.
X: Picking the right one is what makes the UI feel responsive without flooding the server or the rendering. People mix up throttle and audit a lot, in my experience.

T: How do you handle dynamic rows with FormArray in Angular reactive forms?
K: formarray angular, dynamic form rows, add remove form controls, form array validation, typed formarray
X: FormArray holds a variable number of controls or groups, which is exactly what you need for a list of shipment items, contacts, or visit schedule rows where users add and remove rows.
X: Setup, in a typed reactive form, items is built with the form builder's array of item form groups, starting empty. A helper creates one row, a create-item method that returns a group with kit type, required, and quantity, defaulting to one, required, with a minimum of one. Adding a row is pushing a new item onto items, removing is removeAt with the index, and loading existing data is clearing the array and pushing a group per item.
X: In the template you bind formArrayName to items, loop with an at-for over the item controls with a track expression, and bind each group with formGroupName set to the index. Show errors per row.
X: Validation at the array level means a validator on the FormArray itself, like at least one row, no duplicate kit types across rows, or a total quantity limit. Cross-row validation has to live on the array or the parent group, because individual rows can't see each other.
X: Performance, for big arrays use OnPush and track by a stable id, not the index, so Angular doesn't rebuild every row when one's removed. For hundreds of rows, I'd think about a virtualised grid instead.
X: Typed forms from Angular 14 make the items value strongly typed, which really helps when mapping to the API request.
X: Common pitfalls I've seen, mutating the array without updating validity, forgetting to mark controls touched before showing errors on submit, and patchValue not adding missing rows, so you have to create the groups first.

@p17-821
S: rx
D: A
T: How does cache invalidation work in RTK Query with tags?
K: rtk query tags, providestags invalidatestags, rtk query cache invalidation, refetch after mutation rtk query
X: Right, RTK Query caches responses from query endpoints, keyed by endpoint and arguments. After a mutation, say creating or updating a shipment, the cached lists and details go stale. Tags tell RTK Query which cached data to refetch automatically.
X: How it works. In createApi you declare tag types, like Shipment. Query endpoints say what data they provide. Get shipments provides a Shipment tag with the id LIST, plus one Shipment tag per returned id, and get shipment provides the Shipment tag for its id. Mutation endpoints say what they invalidate. Add shipment invalidates the Shipment LIST tag, so lists refetch. Update shipment invalidates the tag for that id, so that shipment's detail and any list containing it refetch.
X: When a mutation succeeds, RTK Query finds active queries with matching tags and refetches them. Components subscribed through hooks re-render with fresh data, no manual dispatching.
X: You can fine-tune it. Optimistic updates with onQueryStarted and updateQueryData, which change the cache straight away and undo it if the mutation fails. Pessimistic updates, where you write the mutation's response directly into the cache instead of refetching, saving a request. keepUnusedDataFor controls how long unused entries stay, and refetchOnFocus and refetchOnReconnect refresh data when users come back.
X: Common mistakes, providing only a generic tag, so every mutation refetches everything, or forgetting the LIST tag, so new items never show up in lists. That second one can catch people out.
X: In the React shell with Redux Toolkit, RTK Query keeps API state consistent without hand-written loading flags and thunks, which removes a lot of boilerplate compared to our older patterns.
@p17-822
S: rx
D: A
T: staleTime vs gcTime in TanStack Query: what is the difference?
K: stale time vs gc time, react query cachetime, tanstack query staletime, query keys react query, refetch on window focus
X: Honestly these two confuse a lot of people, because both are about caching, but they control different things.
X: staleTime is how long fetched data counts as fresh. While it's fresh, TanStack Query serves it from cache without refetching, even when a new component mounts with the same query key. The default's zero, so data's stale immediately and it refetches in the background on things like mount, window focus or reconnect. Setting staleTime to, say, five minutes for reference data, a list of countries or sites, avoids pointless requests.
X: gcTime, which was called cacheTime before version 5, is how long unused data stays in the cache once no component is using it. Default's five minutes, and then it's garbage collected. If a component mounts again before that, the cached data shows instantly, maybe with a background refetch if it's stale.
X: So staleTime decides when to refetch, and gcTime decides when to forget.
X: Query keys matter just as much. A key array of "shipments" plus an object with site id and page includes all the parameters, so different filters are cached separately. And after a mutation, invalidateQueries with just the "shipments" prefix refetches every shipment query.
X: Typical settings I use, low staleTime for data that changes a lot, like statuses, a long one for reference data, and refetchOnWindowFocus turned off for heavy queries if it causes too many requests.
X: For showing data, isPending for the first load and isFetching for background refreshes, so the UI can show a subtle indicator instead of a full spinner when it's just refreshing cached data.

T: Next.js vs a Vite single-page app: when would you choose each?
K: next js vs vite, nextjs vs react spa, when to use nextjs, ssr vs spa react, react framework choice

@p17-824
S: rx
D: A
T: What is state colocation, and when should you lift state up?
K: state colocation, lift state up react, where to put state react, local vs global state, keep state close
X: State colocation basically means keeping state as close as possible to where it's used. If only one component needs a value, like whether a dropdown's open, it lives in that component's useState, not in Redux or some parent.
X: Why it matters. When state lives high up, every change re-renders a big chunk of the tree, and the code gets harder to follow, because you have to trace where state's set and passed. Colocated state is easier to understand, delete and refactor, and it performs better.
X: Lifting state up is the opposite move, done when you need it. If two sibling components need the same state, like a filter panel and a results table, you move it to their closest common parent and pass it down as props, with callbacks to change it.
X: The order I go through in practice. Local component state for UI-only things. Lift to the nearest common parent when siblings share it. The URL for state that should survive a refresh or be shareable, filters, sorting, pagination. A server-state library like TanStack Query or RTK Query for API data, instead of copying it into global state. Context for rarely changing app-wide values, theme, current user, locale. And a global store like Redux Toolkit or Zustand for complex client state that's shared widely, like a multi-step workflow or cross-feature selections.
X: A common anti-pattern I've cleaned up is putting everything into Redux, form inputs and modal flags included. Simple components ended up depending on the global store and re-rendering for no reason.

T: How do you test custom React hooks with renderHook?
K: renderhook, test custom hooks, testing library react hooks, act testing hooks, test usefetch hook
X: Custom hooks hold real logic, data fetching, debouncing, form handling, so they should be tested too. But hooks only run inside components, so you need a harness, and that's what renderHook from React Testing Library gives you.
X: You call renderHook with a function that uses your hook, say useCounter starting at five, and you get back result, rerender and unmount. result dot current holds the hook's latest return value. You call the functions it returns inside act, like act calling increment, and then expect result dot current dot count to be six.
X: To change props, you pass initialProps, say a delay of 300 for a useDebounce hook, and then call rerender with a delay of 500.
X: For async behaviour, use waitFor to wait until the data's defined for hooks that fetch, and fake timers, like vi useFakeTimers, to control debounce or polling without actually waiting.
X: For context and providers, pass a wrapper option that renders whatever's needed, a QueryClientProvider with a fresh client per test, a Redux Provider with a test store, or a router.
X: For network calls, I'd use Mock Service Worker to return fake API responses, so the hook runs its real fetch code.
X: And call unmount to check effects clean up properly, cancelling subscriptions or timers.
X: When I don't bother with renderHook, if the hook's simple and only used by one component, testing that component's behaviour covers it. renderHook is most valuable for shared hooks in a library where the hook itself is the public API, like hooks in our npm feature packages.

X: Logging, send unexpected errors to a front-end monitoring tool with user context and the correlation id, so we can link front-end and back-end errors together.

T: How do you analyse and reduce bundle size in a React Vite app?

T: How do you write generic components in React with TypeScript?
K: generic react component, typescript generic props, generic table component, generic select react, react typescript generics
X: A generic component works with any data type but keeps full type safety. Typical examples, a Table that renders rows of any type, a Select whose options are any objects, or a List with a custom item renderer.
X: How you do it is declare a type parameter on the component function. Say table props of T has rows, which is an array of T, columns, where each column has a key that must be a key of T, a header and an optional render function that takes a T, a get-row-id function, and an optional row click callback. Then the Table function itself takes a type parameter T and props of that type.

X: A few tips. In tsx files, arrow functions with generics need a trailing comma after the T, or a constraint like T extends object, so the parser doesn't think it's JSX. That one can catch people out.
X: Use constraints, like T extends something with a string id, when the component needs certain fields.
X: Wrapping with memo or forwardRef loses the generics, so you might need a type assertion to keep the generic signature. React 19's ref-as-prop makes that easier.
X: And don't over-engineer. If a component's only used with one type, generics just add complexity.
X: Where they really pay off is shared design system packages, like our npm feature packages, where lots of teams render different data with the same grid or picker, and type safety stops integration mistakes.

T: What does the non-null assertion operator do in TypeScript, and why avoid it?
K: non null assertion, exclamation mark typescript, ! operator typescript, strictnullchecks, definite assignment
X: Okay, with strictNullChecks on, TypeScript tracks whether values can be null or undefined. The non-null assertion operator is that exclamation mark after a value, like user-bang-dot-name, or getElementById for root followed by a bang. It tells the compiler, trust me, this isn't null or undefined. And it removes those types without any runtime check.
X: The problem is if you're wrong, you get a runtime error, "cannot read properties of undefined", which is exactly the error strict null checks were meant to stop. It silences the compiler instead of handling the case. Over time, code full of exclamation marks gives a false sense of safety.
X: Better alternatives. Narrowing with checks, like if there's no user, return null, and then TypeScript knows user is defined below that.
X: Optional chaining and nullish coalescing, user question-mark-dot name, falling back to "Unknown".
X: Assertion functions that check at runtime and throw a clear error, like an assert-defined function whose return type asserts the value is non-nullable.
X: Better types. If a value's always there after loading, model the loading state with a discriminated union so the component handles loading and loaded explicitly.
X: Definite assignment on class fields set outside the constructor, like Angular ViewChild, uses a similar exclamation mark on the field, with the same risks. Signal-based queries reduce the need for that.
X: Where it's acceptable is when the guarantee's obvious and local, like the root element in main dot tsx that always exists, or in tests.
X: What I do is turn on the ESLint no-non-null-assertion rule as a warning, so each use is a conscious decision that shows up in code review.

T: CSS Modules vs styled-components vs Tailwind vs MUI sx: how do you choose a styling approach?
K: css modules vs styled components, tailwind vs mui, css in js, react styling approaches, emotion styling
X: React has loads of styling options, and honestly each one has its own pros and cons.
X: CSS Modules are regular CSS files where class names get scoped per component automatically, so no global conflicts. No runtime cost, works with any build tool including Vite, and anyone who knows CSS is comfortable. Dynamic styling is done with conditional class names.
X: CSS-in-JS, like styled-components and Emotion, means styles written in JavaScript next to the component, with props-based dynamic styles and theming. MUI uses Emotion internally. X: How I choose, consistency with the component library matters most. In a React shell built on MUI 5, I'd use the theme, sx for small tweaks and styled for reusable pieces, rather than mixing in Tailwind or another system. Two systems fighting each other is worse than either one. For a new project without a component library, CSS Modules or Tailwind are good low-runtime choices.
X: Whatever you pick, design tokens should be the single source of truth for colours, spacing and typography.

X: Thunks, with createAsyncThunk, are functions you dispatch straight from a component, like dispatching fetch shipments for a site id. X: It's kind of a lightweight alternative to Redux-Saga or Redux-Observable, no generators or RxJS, and it's already in Redux Toolkit.

@p17-838
S: rx
D: A
T: What are the Rules of Hooks, and why do they exist?
K: rules of hooks, hooks rules react, conditional hooks, eslint plugin react hooks, why hooks order matters
X: React basically has two rules for hooks.
X: One, only call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook. Not inside conditions, loops or nested functions, and not after an early return.
X: The other, only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks, never from regular JavaScript functions or class components.
X: Why? React doesn't identify hooks by name. It tracks them by the order they're called in each render. The first useState call gets the first state slot, the second gets the second, and so on. If a hook sits inside a condition, it might run in one render and not the next, so the order shifts and React hands one hook's state to another. That gives really confusing bugs, and React throws errors like "Rendered fewer hooks than expected".
X: How to handle conditional logic, put the condition inside the hook, not around it. Like an effect that returns early when enabled is false, with enabled in its dependency array, or for data fetching, TanStack Query's enabled option. If a component needs very different hooks in different cases, split it into separate components and render one or the other.
X: Custom hooks have to start with "use", so React and the lint tools know to apply the rules.
X: The eslint-plugin-react-hooks package enforces both rules, and its exhaustive-deps rule checks dependency arrays. I keep both as errors in CI, because honestly they catch real bugs.
X: React 19's use function is the exception. It can be called conditionally, because it doesn't rely on call order in the same way.
@p17-839
S: rx
D: A
T: What is the useEffect cleanup function, and when does it run?
K: useeffect cleanup, cleanup function react, unsubscribe in useeffect, clear interval react, effect cleanup timing
X: The function you return from a useEffect callback is the cleanup. React runs it to undo whatever the effect set up.
X: When does it run? Before the effect runs again because a dependency changed, with the old values, and when the component unmounts. In development with StrictMode, React also does an extra setup, cleanup, setup cycle on mount, to expose effects that don't clean up properly. People sometimes think that's a bug, but it's on purpose.
X: What needs cleanup. Subscriptions, event listeners on window or document, WebSocket or SignalR handlers, observable subscriptions, store subscriptions, remove them all in cleanup. Timers, clearInterval or clearTimeout. Network requests, abort them with an AbortController, so a slow response for old parameters doesn't update state after the parameters changed or the component unmounted. Third-party widgets, destroy chart or map instances the effect created.
X: A simple example, an effect that starts an interval calling refresh every five seconds, and returns a cleanup that clears that interval, with refresh as the dependency.
X: Without cleanup you get memory leaks, duplicate event handlers firing several times, intervals multiplying every time dependencies change, and race conditions where old responses overwrite newer data.
X: My rule is every effect that starts something should stop it. So in code review the quick mental check is "what does this effect start, and where's it stopped?"
X: And a lot of effects can be avoided altogether. Data fetching through TanStack Query or RTK Query handles cancellation and caching, and derived values can be computed during render. Fewer effects, fewer cleanup bugs.

@p17-841
S: nodex
D: A
T: What is the libuv thread pool in Node.js, and when does it become a bottleneck?
K: libuv thread pool, uv_threadpool_size, node thread pool, node fs crypto thread pool, libuv
X: So Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread, but underneath it's not really single-threaded. libuv, the C library behind Node's event loop, handles I/O two ways. Network I/O, sockets and HTTP, uses the operating system's non-blocking mechanisms, epoll, kqueue or IOCP, so it needs no extra threads. Other work that has no good non-blocking API runs on a small libuv thread pool. That's most file system operations, DNS lookups through dns lookup, some crypto functions like pbkdf2, scrypt and randomBytes, and zlib compression.
X: The default pool size is just four threads. If an app does a lot of these at once, hashing passwords for many logins, compressing responses, reading lots of files, requests queue up for the pool, and latency goes up even though CPU and the event loop look fine. A classic surprise is slow outbound HTTP calls, because dns lookup is stuck waiting behind file or crypto work.
X: What I do. Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, set as an environment variable before the process starts, up to 1024, sized to the workload and cores. Use the async versions of crypto and fs functions, never the Sync ones on request paths. Cache DNS results or use connection keep-alive so lookups are rare. And move heavy CPU work, big compression or image processing, to worker threads or separate services.
X: To diagnose it, I look at event loop delay and pool queueing in profiles or traces. If latency's climbing while CPU and event loop lag stay low, thread pool saturation is a pretty likely cause.
