@p17-973
S: scx
D: A
T: A detailed health check endpoint is causing load and outages. What went wrong?
K: health check causing outage, deep health check load, health check database calls, cascading failure health checks, liveness dependency checks
X: Health checks are supposed to protect availability, but badly designed ones can actually cause outages.
X: What usually goes wrong. Deep checks in liveness probes. The liveness endpoint checks the database, Redis and downstream APIs. When the database is slow for a moment, every instance's liveness check fails, Kubernetes or the load balancer restarts or removes all instances at once, and a small database hiccup turns into a total outage. Then instances restarting together put even more load on the database as they reconnect and warm up. I've seen exactly this happen, and it's not fun.
X: Expensive checks called too often. Each check runs real queries, and with many instances, several load balancers and monitoring tools all calling it every few seconds, the checks put real load on shared dependencies.
X: Checks calling other services' health checks, creating chains where one slow service makes everything look unhealthy.
X: No timeouts in the check, so it hangs and ties up threads.
X: Better design. Liveness is only "is this process alive and able to respond", no external dependencies.
X: Readiness is, can this instance serve traffic? It can check critical local requirements, but be careful with shared dependencies, because pulling every instance out of rotation helps nobody.
X: A separate detailed diagnostics endpoint for humans and monitoring, protected, not used by load balancers, with results cached for a few seconds so frequent calls don't hit dependencies every time.
X: Timeouts on each dependency check, and graceful degradation, report degraded rather than unhealthy when a non-critical dependency fails.
X: In ASP.NET Core, health check tags let me map different checks to liveness and readiness endpoints, which makes this separation easy.
@p17-974
S: scx
D: A
T: Retries made an outage worse. What is a retry storm, and how do you prevent it?
K: retry storm, retries amplify outage, exponential backoff jitter, retry budget, thundering herd retries
X: So a retry storm is when a service starts failing or slowing down, and its callers respond by retrying, which multiplies the traffic on the service that's already struggling. If each layer in a chain retries three times, one user request can become dozens of calls at the bottom. The service never recovers, because the load just keeps rising.
X: How it usually plays out. The database slows down, API calls time out, the API's clients retry immediately, the gateway retries too, and the front end retries as well. Load triples or worse at the worst possible time.
X: Prevention. Exponential backoff with jitter, wait longer between each retry, with some randomness, so retries spread out instead of arriving in synchronised waves.
X: Limit retries. A few attempts, only for transient errors, and only for idempotent operations.
X: Retry at one layer. Decide where retries happen, usually closest to the failing call, and don't stack them at every layer. People miss this one a lot.
X: Retry budgets, allow retries only up to a percentage of normal traffic, like 10 percent, so retries can't multiply the load.
X: Circuit breakers. After repeated failures, stop calling the failing service for a while and fail fast, giving it room to recover.
X: Respect Retry-After headers and 429 or 503 responses.
X: Timeouts that fit together, outer timeouts longer than inner ones, so callers don't give up and retry while the inner call's still running.
X: Load shedding on the server, reject excess requests quickly when overloaded, rather than queuing everything.
X: In .NET, Polly and the standard resilience handler in .NET 8 give you backoff with jitter, circuit breakers and timeouts, which I configure deliberately instead of leaving defaults on every client.
@p17-975
S: scx
D: A
T: A message consumer is slow even though CPU is idle. What do you check?
K: consumer slow cpu idle, rabbitmq prefetch 1, sequential message processing, consumer throughput low, queue backlog low cpu
X: If messages are piling up but the consumer's CPU is barely used, it's spending its time waiting, not working. So I look at what it's waiting on.
X: Processing one message at a time, that's the most common one in my experience. A prefetch count of one with sequential processing means each message waits for the full round trip, receive, process, call the database, acknowledge. If each message spends 50 milliseconds mostly waiting on I/O, one consumer handles at most 20 a second. Increasing prefetch and processing several messages concurrently, with a sensible limit, often multiplies throughput.
X: Slow downstream calls. Each message calls an API or database that's slow, and traces show where the time goes. Fixes include batching database writes, caching reference data, and fixing slow queries.
X: Synchronous I/O or locks, blocking calls in async code, or a lock around shared state that serialises processing.
X: Too few consumers or partitions. One consumer instance, or in Kafka, fewer partitions than the consumers you want, so the extra consumers just sit idle.
X: Acknowledgement overhead, acknowledging each message individually with a round trip, where batched acknowledgements would help.
X: Network latency between consumer and broker or database, like a consumer running in a different region or data centre.
X: Throttling, a rate limiter, or the broker applying flow control.
X: After changes, I measure throughput, processing time per message and queue depth, and make sure higher concurrency doesn't break ordering guarantees or overload the database. For ordered processing, I'd say parallelise across keys, like per site or study, while keeping order within each key.
@p17-976
S: scx
D: A
T: After enabling HTTPS behind a load balancer, users get "too many redirects". How do you fix it?
K: too many redirects load balancer, redirect loop https, x-forwarded-proto, https redirection behind proxy, ssl offloading redirect loop
X: Ah, this is a classic redirect loop with TLS offloading. The load balancer terminates HTTPS and forwards requests to the app over plain HTTP. The app sees HTTP, thinks the user isn't on HTTPS, and redirects to the HTTPS URL. The browser follows it, the load balancer forwards it as HTTP again, and round and round it goes until the browser gives up.
X: The fix is making the app aware of the original scheme. Load balancers add the X-Forwarded-Proto header, set to https, along with X-Forwarded-For with the client IP.
X: In ASP.NET Core, use the forwarded headers middleware early in the pipeline, set to include the forwarded proto and forwarded for headers, and configure known proxies or known networks so the app only trusts these headers from the load balancer, not from clients. Then HTTPS redirection, HSTS, generated URLs and cookie security flags all work properly. On IIS with the ASP.NET Core Module, some of this is handled automatically, but extra proxies in front still need configuring.
X: In .NET Framework apps on IIS, URL Rewrite rules that redirect to HTTPS have to check the X-Forwarded-Proto header rather than the HTTPS server variable.
X: Other places to check. Redirect rules on both the load balancer and the app doing conflicting things, like the load balancer redirecting HTTP to HTTPS and the app redirecting to a different host. Authentication redirects using the wrong scheme for callback URLs, which causes login loops. And cookies marked Secure not being sent when the app thinks the request is HTTP.
X: I'd say the other option is re-encrypting from the load balancer to the app, HTTPS end to end, which also satisfies stricter security requirements.

T: What are matrix builds, and when do you use them?
K: matrix build, matrix strategy github actions, azure pipelines matrix, test multiple versions, parallel jobs
X: Okay so, a matrix build runs the same job several times with different parameter combinations, in parallel. In GitHub Actions you define a strategy matrix, and in Azure Pipelines a strategy with a matrix of named configurations. Each combination becomes its own job with its own result.
X: Typical uses are testing a library against several runtime versions, like Node 18, 20 and 22, or Python 3.10 to 3.12, building on Windows and Linux, or testing against different database versions. It's also handy for building lots of similar services or packages from one pipeline, where each matrix entry is one service.
X: Couple of things from practice. Be careful with fail-fast. Turning it off lets you see all the failing combinations instead of stopping at the first one. Use include and exclude to skip pointless combinations, so you don't end up with an exploding number of jobs. Cache dependencies per combination, keyed by the version, or caches will clash. And keep the matrix small for pull requests, with the full matrix running nightly or on main, because every entry costs agent minutes.
X: In practice, I used a matrix for our shared front-end npm packages, building and testing against two React versions while the shell migration was going on, because some sub-apps were still on the older one. It caught a breaking peer dependency issue before it reached any app. For services though, I prefer one pipeline per service triggered by path filters, rather than one big matrix that rebuilds everything.
@p17-978
S: cdx
D: A
T: Microsoft-hosted vs self-hosted build agents: how do you choose?
K: self hosted agent, hosted agent, self hosted runner, build agent choice, private network build agent
X: Hosted agents, Microsoft-hosted agents in Azure Pipelines or GitHub-hosted runners, are fresh virtual machines created per job and thrown away afterwards. Self-hosted agents are machines you run and maintain yourself.
X: Hosted agents are clean every time, so no leftover state between builds, no patching, and they scale without effort. The downsides are limited control over installed tools, no access to private networks unless you add extra setup, caches that have to be restored every time, and cost or time limits at scale.
X: Self-hosted agents make sense when builds need to reach private resources, like an on-prem database or an internal package feed, when you need special hardware or licensed tools, when on-disk caches make builds much faster, or when the whole server's on-premises anyway. The cost is operational. You patch them, secure them, and deal with disks filling up and state leaking between builds.
X: Security really matters with self-hosted agents. Never run untrusted pull requests from forks on them, because a malicious build can attack the network. Run the agent as a low-privilege account, isolate pools per environment so a test build can't deploy to production, and ideally use ephemeral agents, container-based or autoscaled VMs that get recreated after each job.
X: In our case, the on-prem Azure DevOps Server uses self-hosted agents, since deployments go to servers inside the network. We keep separate pools for build and for production deployment, and the production pool can only be used by approved release pipelines.

D: A
T: How do you sign container images and verify them before deployment?
K: image signing, cosign, sigstore, notation, verify image signature, admission policy signed images, sbom attestation
X: Signing proves an image was built by your pipeline and hasn't been changed since. Without it, anyone with push access to a registry could swap an image, and the cluster would happily run it.
X: The common tools are Cosign from the Sigstore project and Notation from the Notary project, which Azure Container Registry supports. The pipeline builds the image, pushes it, and signs it by its digest, not its tag, because tags can move. Signing can use a key held in a key vault, or keyless signing, where a short-lived certificate is tied to the pipeline's identity through OIDC.
X: Alongside the signature you can attach attestations, an SBOM listing every package in the image, and provenance saying which commit and pipeline built it. Those help a lot when a new vulnerability shows up and you need to know which images contain the affected package.
X: Verification happens at deploy time. In Kubernetes, an admission controller like Kyverno, Gatekeeper or the Ratify project checks every pod's image and rejects anything unsigned or signed by the wrong identity. Deployments should also reference images by digest, so what was verified is exactly what runs.
X: I'd roll it out gradually. Sign everything to begin with, then turn on verification in audit mode to find unsigned images, like third-party ones, and only then enforce. Base images from trusted publishers can be allowed by their own signatures. And it gives you a solid answer when security reviewers ask how you know production runs only what CI built.

T: How do conventional commits help generate changelogs and release notes automatically?
K: conventional commits, automated changelog, release notes generation, semantic release, commit message convention
X: Conventional commits is basically a simple format for commit messages, a type, an optional scope, and a description. For example, feat for a new feature, fix for a bug fix, docs, refactor, test or chore, plus a breaking-change marker when something isn't backward compatible.
X: Because the messages are structured, tools can read them. semantic-release or release-please can work out the next version automatically. A fix bumps the patch, a feat bumps the minor, and a breaking change bumps the major. They also generate a changelog grouped by features and fixes, create a tag, and publish the package.
X: To make it reliable, you enforce the format. commitlint in a Git hook catches mistakes locally, and a pull request check validates the PR title if you squash merge, since that title becomes the commit on main. Linking each commit or PR to a work item lets the release notes include the ticket ids.
X: And honestly it pays off. Release notes stop being a manual job at the end of a sprint, versions are consistent, and consumers of shared packages can see breaking changes clearly.
X: We used this pattern for our shared front-end npm packages published to the Azure DevOps feed. The version and changelog came from the commits, so teams consuming a package knew whether an upgrade was safe. For the main application, though, release notes still need business language for the validation team, so the generated list is a starting point someone edits, not the final document.
@p17-981
S: cdx
D: A
T: Merge commit vs squash merge vs rebase: which do you use for pull requests?
K: merge vs rebase, squash merge, git rebase, linear history, git merge strategies, pull request merge type
X: All three bring a branch's changes into main, but they give you different history.
X: A merge commit keeps every commit from the branch and adds a merge commit joining the two lines. It preserves exactly what happened, but history gets noisy with lots of small commits like "fix typo", and the graph gets hard to read.
X: Squash merge combines the whole branch into one commit on main. History becomes one commit per pull request, which is clean and easy to revert, since reverting a feature is just reverting one commit. You lose the individual commits, though they still exist in the pull request.
X: Rebase replays the branch's commits on top of main, so history stays linear without a merge commit. It keeps individual commits, which is nice if they're meaningful, but because it rewrites history you should never rebase a branch others are working on, and it means force-pushing your own branch.
X: For me, the default for short-lived feature branches is squash merge, with the pull request title written as a good commit message, since that also works with conventional commits and changelogs. For long-lived release branches, I use real merges so the relationship between branches stays visible. Locally I use rebase to update my feature branch from main before opening a pull request, because it gives reviewers a cleaner diff.
X: Whatever the team picks, it should be set in branch policies so it's consistent, not left to each person.

S: cdx
D: A
T: What are deployment rings, and how do they reduce release risk?
K: deployment rings, ring based deployment, staged rollout, progressive exposure, early adopters ring
X: Deployment rings release a change to progressively bigger groups of users, with a pause and a health check between each group. It's how large products avoid exposing everyone to a bad release at once.
X: A typical setup has ring zero for the internal team, ring one for a small set of friendly customers or one region, ring two for a larger share, and then everyone. Each ring has a bake time, and the pipeline only moves forward if error rates, latency and business metrics stay normal. If something goes wrong, only that ring's affected, and you stop or roll back.
X: Rings differ from canary releases mainly in what you divide. A canary usually splits traffic randomly by percentage, while rings divide by meaningful groups like tenants, regions or customer types. In multi-tenant systems rings fit really naturally, because you can upgrade tenants or databases in batches.
X: To do it well, automate the gates, so promotion depends on metrics and not on someone remembering to check. Keep ring membership in configuration, make the code work with mixed versions, and keep database changes backward compatible.
X: In our platform, each study has its own database, so schema and data changes naturally roll out in batches. We start with internal and test studies, then low-risk studies, then the rest, with checks after each batch. A problem caught in the first batch affects a handful of non-critical databases instead of every live study.
@p17-983
S: cdx
D: A
T: What are dark launches and shadow traffic?
K: dark launch, shadow traffic, traffic mirroring, test in production safely, mirror requests
X: A dark launch, you know, deploys new code to production and runs it with real traffic, but users don't see its results. Shadow traffic, or traffic mirroring, is a common way to do it. Each real request goes to the current version as normal, and a copy goes to the new version, whose response just gets thrown away.
X: The point is testing with real production load and real data shapes, which test environments never fully reproduce. You can compare the new version's results with the old one's, watch its latency and errors, and find performance problems before switching anyone over.
X: You can do it at different levels. A service mesh or proxy like Istio or Envoy can mirror a percentage of requests. In code, you can call both implementations, return the old result, and log the differences, which is the approach libraries like Scientist take.
X: The big risk is side effects. A shadow request must not write to the real database, charge a card or send an email twice. So shadowing works best for read paths, or the new version writes to a separate store, or calls go out with a dry-run flag.
X: I'd use it when replacing a critical read path, like a new search or a new calculation engine. For example, when moving a data transfer from the old integration layer to a new .NET API, running both and comparing outputs for a while gives confidence the new one produces identical results before it becomes the real path.
@p17-984
S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you keep dev, test and production environments consistent?
K: environment parity, dev prod parity, environment drift, consistent environments, it works on my machine
X: Inconsistent environments give you the classic problem, it works in test but fails in production. What I aim for is environments that differ only in size and configuration, not in how they're built.
X: The biggest tool is infrastructure as code. If every environment comes from the same Terraform or Bicep modules with different variables, they can't quietly drift apart, and drift detection in the pipeline catches manual changes.
X: Then building once and promoting the same artifact, so test and production run identical binaries or images. Configuration comes from the environment through settings and secret stores, never baked into the build.
X: Matching dependency versions matters too. Same database engine version, same runtime, same message broker version. Containers and Docker Compose help locally, so a developer runs the same Redis and broker versions as production.
X: Data's the hard part, honestly. Test databases are often small and clean, so performance problems and odd data only show up in production. Masked copies of production data, or generated data at realistic volume, close that gap.
X: And the deployment process itself should be the same everywhere. If test is deployed by hand and production by pipeline, you're not really testing the deployment.
X: In our on-prem setup, we keep a server configuration baseline and compare IIS settings, installed runtimes and app pool settings across environments. A runtime version mismatch on one production node once caused a failure that test never showed, which is exactly why we added that check.

S: cdx
D: A
T: How do you protect CI pipelines from malicious pull requests?
K: pipeline security fork pull request, pull_request_target, untrusted code ci, poisoned pipeline execution, secrets in pr builds
X: A pull request build runs code someone else wrote, including the build scripts themselves. If that build has access to secrets or a privileged agent, a malicious pull request can steal credentials or attack your network. It's called poisoned pipeline execution.
X: The main defences are basically about separation. Pull request builds from forks must run without secrets and with a read-only token. In GitHub Actions, the pull request event does this by default, while pull request target runs with secrets in the base repo's context, so it must never check out and run the pull request's code. That one catches people out. In Azure Pipelines, settings control whether fork builds get secrets, and that should stay off.
X: Run untrusted builds on hosted, throwaway agents, not self-hosted agents inside the network. And require approval before running workflows from first-time contributors.
X: Protect the pipeline definitions too. Changes to workflow files or templates should need review from owners, using a code owners file, and deployment pipelines should come from protected templates a pull request can't modify.
X: Keep deployment credentials scoped to protected environments with approvals, so even a compromised build job on a branch can't deploy to production. Pin third-party actions to a commit hash, since a tag can be moved to malicious code.
X: For internal repos the threat's lower, but the same rules help against a compromised developer account. Secrets live in environments with approvals, not in the pipeline used for pull request validation.

S: cdx

T: How do you promote container images between registries or environments?
K: image promotion, promote container image, copy image between registries, acr import, ecr replication, registry per environment
X: Promotion means the exact image tested in one environment is the one that goes to the next, never a rebuild. With containers, that means moving or re-tagging the same digest.
X: You'll usually see two setups. With one registry, you promote by adding tags or by updating the deployment to the tested digest. It's simple, but production pulls from a registry that test pipelines can also push to.
X: With a registry per environment or per trust level, say a dev registry and a production registry, you copy the image across after it passes testing. Azure Container Registry has an import command that copies by digest between registries, ECR supports cross-account replication, and tools like crane or skopeo copy images without pulling them locally. Production clusters only get pull access to the production registry, and only the release pipeline can push to it.
X: Important details. Always copy and deploy by digest, because a tag like the version number could get overwritten. Copy signatures and SBOMs along with the image so verification still works. Run a vulnerability scan at promotion time too, since new vulnerabilities show up after build. And keep a record of which digest went to which environment, for traceability.
X: For anything regulated, I'd go with the separate production registry. It gives a clear boundary, if an image is in the production registry, it passed the gates. The extra copy step takes a few seconds and adds a lot of confidence.

T: How do you build a deployment pipeline for serverless apps with SAM or CDK?
K: sam pipeline, cdk pipelines, deploy lambda ci cd, serverless deployment pipeline, cloudformation deploy lambda
X: For serverless on AWS, the app and its infrastructure usually deploy together, because a Lambda function, its API Gateway route, its queue and its permissions all belong to the same unit. SAM and CDK both produce CloudFormation, which does the actual deployment.
X: With SAM, the pipeline runs sam build to package the functions, runs unit tests, and then sam deploy with a parameter file per environment. SAM can also set up gradual deployment for Lambda through CodeDeploy, shifting traffic to the new version over a few minutes and rolling back automatically if CloudWatch alarms fire.

Run integration tests against the deployed stack in a test stage before promotion. And watch for changes that replace resources, like renaming a table, which CloudFormation does by deleting and recreating. That one can really bite people.
X: For a small team, I think SAM is quicker to learn. For larger systems with shared constructs, CDK gives better reuse and type checking.

T: What does a good CI pipeline for a Python service look like?
K: python ci pipeline, python lint test pipeline, ruff mypy pytest ci, python build pipeline, python docker pipeline
X: A Python pipeline should check quality quickly and produce one reproducible artifact, usually a container image or a wheel.
X: The way I set it up, it starts with the exact Python version and installs dependencies from a lock file, using uv or pip with hashes, with the package cache saved between runs. Then linting and formatting checks with Ruff, which replaces flake8, isort and black and is really fast. Then type checking with mypy or pyright, which matters in a dynamic language. Then tests with pytest, with coverage reporting and integration tests that use Testcontainers or service containers for Postgres or Redis.
X: Security checks come next, pip-audit for vulnerable packages, a secret scan, and bandit for risky code patterns.
X: Then the build. For a service, I build a Docker image with a multi-stage Dockerfile, installing dependencies in a builder stage and copying only what's needed into a slim runtime image that runs as non-root. For a library, I build a wheel and publish it to an internal feed.
X: After that, tag the image with the commit and version, scan it, push it, and deploy through the same promotion flow as other services.
X: For our Python RAG service with FastAPI and pgvector, the integration tests run against a real Postgres container with the pgvector extension, because mocking vector search wouldn't prove the queries actually work. The whole pipeline runs in a few minutes, mostly thanks to caching and Ruff's speed.

T: How do you use pre-commit hooks with Husky or the pre-commit framework?
K: pre commit hooks, husky, lint-staged, pre-commit framework, git hooks, shift left checks
X: Git hooks are scripts that run at points like before a commit or before a push. Pre-commit hooks catch simple problems, formatting, lint errors, committed secrets, before code ever reaches the pull request.
X: In JavaScript projects, Husky installs the hooks automatically when someone runs npm install, and lint-staged runs tools only on the files being committed, so it stays fast. A typical setup runs Prettier and ESLint on staged files and commitlint on the commit message.
X: In Python and lots of other stacks, the pre-commit framework manages hooks from a config file, with hooks for Ruff, trailing whitespace, large files, and secret scanning with tools like gitleaks. It works for any language, so it's a good pick for repos mixing Python, YAML and Terraform.
X: In .NET, dotnet format can run in a hook, or with Husky.Net.
X: My rules are pretty simple. Keep hooks fast, a few seconds, or people will just skip them with the no-verify flag. Hooks are a convenience, not a control, because anyone can bypass them, so the pipeline must run the same checks. And don't run the full test suite in a pre-commit hook. At most, quick tests in a pre-push hook.
X: In our front-end repos, Husky with lint-staged catches most formatting and lint issues locally, so pull request reviews focus on design instead of style comments. Secret scanning in the hook has stopped a few accidental commits of local config files before they left a laptop.

D: A
T: How do you mock dependencies in Python tests with unittest.mock and patch?
K: python mock, unittest.mock, patch where it is used, MagicMock, pytest monkeypatch, mocker fixture
X: Python's unittest mock gives you Mock and MagicMock objects that record how they're called and return whatever you set up. patch temporarily replaces an object during a test, as a decorator or a context manager, and the pytest-mock plugin offers the same thing through a mocker fixture.
X: The rule that trips most people is, patch where it's used, not where it's defined. If my module does from services import send email, the name send email now lives in my module, so I have to patch it on my module. Patching it on services won't touch the copy my module already imported. Trust me, everyone hits this once.
X: Other useful points. Use autospec, or create autospec, so the mock has the real function's signature. Otherwise a typo in a method name or wrong arguments still pass silently. For async functions, AsyncMock returns awaitables. Use side effect to raise exceptions or return a sequence of values, which is how I test retry logic. Assert calls with assert called once with, but don't over-assert every internal call, or tests break on harmless refactors.
X: pytest's monkeypatch is simpler for environment variables and attributes, and it undoes changes automatically.
X: Design matters more than tooling, though. If a test needs five patches, the code probably has hidden dependencies. Passing dependencies in, like through FastAPI's Depends with dependency overrides in tests, is cleaner than patching module globals. In our FastAPI RAG service, tests override the embedding client dependency with a fake, so no test calls a real model endpoint.
@p17-991
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you test RxJS streams with marble testing?
K: marble testing, rxjs testing, TestScheduler, cold hot observables test, test debounceTime
X: Marble testing describes observable streams as little text diagrams, where each character is a frame of virtual time. A letter is an emitted value, a dash is time passing, a pipe is completion and a hash is an error. RxJS's TestScheduler runs the test in virtual time, so operators like debounceTime or delay finish instantly instead of actually waiting.
X: Inside the test scheduler's run, you create cold observables from marble strings, apply your operator chain, and use expectObservable to compare the result with an expected marble diagram and a values map. You can also write time explicitly, like 300 milliseconds, which makes debounce tests readable.
X: It's most useful for custom operators and complex chains, like a type-ahead search that debounces, ignores duplicates, cancels old requests with switchMap and handles errors. Testing that with real timers is slow and flaky, with marbles it's precise and deterministic. You can also check subscription timing with expectSubscriptions, which proves an old request really got unsubscribed.
X: For simpler cases, like a service method that just maps an HTTP response, honestly marbles are overkill. Subscribing and checking the value, or using firstValueFrom with an async test, is clearer.
X: In our Angular study builder, the search-and-filter panel used a chain of debounce, distinct and switchMap. Marble tests caught a bug where an error from one search killed the stream permanently, so later searches did nothing. Adding catchError inside the switchMap fixed it, and the marble test now guards that behaviour.
@p17-992
S: tx
D: A
T: How do xUnit fixtures and parallel test execution work?
K: xunit fixtures, IClassFixture, ICollectionFixture, xunit parallel, test collections, shared context xunit
X: xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method, so the constructor is your per-test setup and Dispose is the teardown. That isolation's good, but expensive setup, like starting a database container, shouldn't run for every single test.
X: Fixtures solve that. A class fixture creates one shared object for all tests in a class, passed into the constructor. A collection fixture shares one object across several classes that belong to the same named collection. For async setup, the fixture implements IAsyncLifetime, with an async initialise and an async dispose. A typical example is a WebApplicationFactory or a Testcontainers database shared by all integration test classes in one collection.
X: Parallelism follows collections. By default each test class is its own collection, and collections run in parallel, while tests inside one collection run one after another. So putting classes in the same collection to share a fixture also makes them run sequentially, which is usually what you want for tests sharing a database. People mix this up quite often.
X: Things to watch. Shared fixtures mustn't hold state that tests change, or test order starts to matter. Static state breaks parallel runs. And you can tune parallelism with a runner config file, or turn it off for a specific collection.
X: In our integration tests, one collection fixture starts a SQL Server container and applies the schema once. Each test then runs inside a transaction that gets rolled back, so tests stay independent and the whole suite runs in a couple of minutes.

T: How do you test async Python code with pytest-asyncio?
K: pytest asyncio, test async python, async fixtures pytest, anyio pytest, test fastapi async
X: pytest doesn't run coroutines by itself, so async tests need a plugin. pytest-asyncio is the common one. You mark a test with the asyncio marker, or set asyncio mode to auto in config, and the plugin runs it in an event loop. The anyio plugin's an alternative and also supports trio.
X: Fixtures can be async too. An async fixture with yield can open a database connection or an HTTP client before the test and close it afterwards. Fixture scope matters here. A session-scoped async fixture needs an event loop that lives for the whole session, and newer pytest-asyncio versions let you set the loop scope explicitly, because mismatched loop scopes cause really confusing errors about the loop being closed or attached to a different loop.
X: For FastAPI, I use httpx's AsyncClient with an ASGI transport pointed at the app, which calls the app in-process without a real server. Dependency overrides swap real clients for fakes.
X: To mock async functions, use AsyncMock, so awaiting the mock works. For timing behaviour, keep timeouts small in tests and avoid real sleeps. Inject a clock or patch the sleep function.
X: One thing people miss is calling an async function without awaiting it, which creates a coroutine that never runs, so the test passes without testing anything. Turning warnings into errors in pytest config catches the never-awaited warning.
X: In our RAG service, async tests cover the retrieval endpoint against a real Postgres container, with the embedding call replaced by a deterministic fake.

T: How do you test AWS code locally with LocalStack or moto?

X: Code that calls AWS services, S3, SQS or DynamoDB, is a pain to test against real AWS. It's slow, costs money and needs credentials. Two tools help here.
X: moto is a Python library that mocks AWS APIs in memory. With a decorator or context manager, boto3 calls go to moto instead of AWS, so you can create a bucket, put an object and test your code's behaviour in milliseconds. It's ideal for unit tests of Python code.

S: tx
D: A
T: What is API fuzz testing, and how do tools like Schemathesis help?
K: fuzz testing, api fuzzing, schemathesis, property based api testing, openapi fuzz, restler
X: So fuzz testing sends huge numbers of unexpected, random or malformed inputs to a system to find crashes and unhandled cases. Normal tests check the inputs you thought of, fuzzing finds the ones you didn't.
X: For APIs, schema-based fuzzers are the practical option. Schemathesis reads your OpenAPI spec and generates requests covering each endpoint with valid and edge-case values, empty strings, huge numbers, unicode, missing optional fields, boundary dates. Then it checks the responses. No 500 errors, responses match the documented schema, and status codes are ones the spec actually declares. RESTler from Microsoft does stateful fuzzing, chaining calls like create, then read, then delete.
X: What it usually finds is unhandled exceptions from unexpected nulls or formats, validation that's missing on the server even though the client validates, responses that don't match the documented contract, and now and then security issues like errors leaking stack traces.
X: I'd run it in CI against a test deployment or an in-process app, starting with a limited number of examples per endpoint so it stays fast, and run longer fuzzing nightly. Failures come with the exact request, which is easy to turn into a normal regression test.
X: For an ASP.NET Core API, it's also a good check that the generated OpenAPI document is actually accurate. When we tried it on an internal API, the first findings were 500 errors from date parameters in unexpected formats, which honestly should've been 400 validation responses.

S: tx
D: A
T: What is test impact analysis, and how do you run only the tests affected by a change?
K: test impact analysis, run affected tests, selective testing, nx affected, test selection, faster test runs
X: Test impact analysis means working out which tests a change could affect and running only those, instead of the whole suite. It matters when the full suite takes too long for every pull request.
X: You can do it at different levels. The simplest is project-level selection. In a monorepo, tools like Nx or Turborepo know the dependency graph, so changing one library runs tests only for that library and the projects that depend on it. Path filters in pipelines do a basic version of the same thing, triggering a service's pipeline only when its folder changes.
X: The finer level uses coverage data to map tests to the code they run. Azure Pipelines has a test impact analysis feature for .NET, and Jest can run tests related to changed files. When a file changes, only tests that touched it run.
X: The risk is missing something. Changes to config, shared build files or test data aren't always tracked well. So I treat it as a speed-up for pull requests, while main and nightly builds still run everything. Any change to shared infrastructure, like the build config, should trigger the full suite.
X: Before going for impact analysis though, honestly I'd check the basics, because they often give bigger wins. Run tests in parallel, cache dependencies, split slow integration tests into a separate stage, and get rid of sleep calls in tests.
X: For our front-end packages in a shared repo, running only affected projects cut pull request builds from around twenty minutes to a few minutes for most changes.

@p17-999
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you test authorization rules systematically across roles and endpoints?
K: authorization tests, role matrix tests, test permissions api, broken access control testing, endpoint security tests
X: Broken access control is the top risk on the OWASP list, and it usually comes from one endpoint missing an authorization check. Testing a few endpoints by hand won't find that, so what I do is test authorization as a matrix.
X: Start by defining the expected access. For each endpoint and each role, should the response be allowed, forbidden or not found. Keep that as data, like a table in the test project.
X: Then write a parameterised integration test that runs every combination. Using WebApplicationFactory with a test authentication handler, each test sets the user's roles and claims, calls the endpoint and checks the status code against the table. Adding a role or an endpoint is just a new row.
X: On top of that, a guard test that discovers all endpoints from the app's endpoint data sources and fails if any endpoint's missing from the matrix or has no authorization metadata, unless it's explicitly marked anonymous. That catches the new endpoint someone forgot to protect.
X: Also test resource-level rules, not just roles. User A must not read user B's record by changing an id in the URL. Those tests create two users with their own data and try cross-access.
X: In a system with site-level and study-level permissions, this approach found an export endpoint that checked the role but not whether the user belonged to that site. The matrix test covers it now, and the endpoint discovery check stops similar gaps from coming back.
@p17-1000
S: tx
D: A
T: userEvent vs fireEvent in React Testing Library: which should you use?
K: userEvent vs fireEvent, user-event library, react testing library events, simulate typing click test
X: Both trigger events in React Testing Library tests, but they work at different levels.
X: fireEvent dispatches a single DOM event. fireEvent change sets a value and fires one change event, fireEvent click fires one click. It's low level and doesn't do what a browser does around that event.
X: userEvent, from the user-event package, simulates what a real user actually does. Typing into an input fires focus, key down, key press, input and key up for every character, respects disabled and read-only fields, and moves the cursor. Clicking fires pointer events, mouse down, focus, mouse up and click. So tests catch bugs fireEvent misses, like a handler on key down, or a field that's disabled but still accepted a change.
X: In version 14, userEvent is asynchronous. The recommended pattern is calling userEvent setup at the start of the test, then awaiting each action. If you use fake timers, pass the timer advance function to setup, or tests just hang. That one catches people out.
X: My default is userEvent for anything a user does, typing, clicking, selecting, tabbing through a form. I keep fireEvent for events users can't easily trigger, like scroll or a custom event, or where userEvent doesn't support something.
X: Combined with queries by role and label, this keeps tests close to real usage. In our React shell's forms built with MUI, switching from fireEvent to userEvent exposed a validation message that only appeared on blur, which the old tests never triggered.
@p17-1001
S: tx
D: A
T: Test pyramid vs testing trophy: which shape should your test suite have?
K: testing trophy, test pyramid vs trophy, testing honeycomb, how many unit vs integration tests, kent c dodds trophy
X: The test pyramid says most tests should be fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few end-to-end. The testing trophy, which got popular in the front-end world, puts most weight on integration tests, with static analysis like TypeScript and linting as the base, fewer unit tests and a few end-to-end. In microservices, a similar idea's called the honeycomb.
X: The reasoning behind the trophy is confidence per test. A unit test of a React component with all its children mocked proves very little about whether the screen works. Rendering the real component tree with a mocked network layer gives way more confidence for similar cost. And modern tools made integration tests fast enough, Testing Library with Mock Service Worker on the front end, or WebApplicationFactory with Testcontainers on the back end.
X: The pyramid still fits code with heavy logic, calculations, rules engines, parsers, algorithms. Those deserve lots of small unit tests covering edge cases.
X: So honestly my answer depends on the code. For a business API that mostly moves data through validation into a database, I write mainly integration tests at the API level, plus unit tests for the complex rules. For a calculation-heavy module, like randomisation or dosing logic, I write extensive unit tests. Static checks come first everywhere, because the type checker catches a whole class of bugs for free.
X: The shape matters less than the outcome, tests that are fast, trusted, catch real bugs and don't break on every refactor.
@p17-1002
S: tx
D: A
T: How do you test an ETL job or data pipeline?
K: test etl, data pipeline testing, data quality tests, test data transformation, great expectations, reconciliation tests
X: Data pipelines fail more quietly than APIs, you know. They run successfully but produce wrong or incomplete data. So testing covers both the code and the data.
X: Unit tests cover transformation logic with small, hand-written inputs, including the awkward cases, nulls, duplicates, dates across time zones, unexpected codes and really long strings. If transformations are pure functions, this is straightforward.
X: Integration tests run the job end to end against real database containers with a realistic sample dataset, checking the output tables. They catch mapping mistakes, type conversion issues and performance problems with set-based SQL.
X: Data quality checks run in production too, as part of the pipeline. Tools like Great Expectations or dbt tests, or simple SQL assertions, check row counts against the source, no unexpected nulls in required columns, valid ranges, unique keys and referential integrity. A failed check stops the load or flags it, instead of quietly publishing bad data.
X: Reconciliation is the last safety net. Compare totals between source and target, like counts per day or sums of key amounts, and alert on differences.
X: Idempotency testing matters as well. Running the job twice mustn't duplicate data, and a run that fails halfway has to be safe to rerun.
X: For data transfers between systems, like moving integration flows from a middleware platform to .NET APIs, we ran old and new paths in parallel and compared the outputs record by record before switching, which was the strongest test of all.

D: A
T: How do you catch breaking API changes automatically in CI?
K: breaking api changes ci, openapi diff, oasdiff, api compatibility check, detect breaking changes openapi, public api analyzer
X: Breaking changes usually slip in by accident. A renamed field, a property made required, a removed enum value, a changed status code. Reviewers miss them because the diff looks harmless, so I check compatibility automatically.
X: For HTTP APIs, the pipeline generates the OpenAPI document from the built service, for example with build-time document generation in ASP.NET Core, and compares it with the version from main or the last release using a diff tool like oasdiff or openapi-diff. These tools classify changes, and the build fails on breaking ones, like removing an endpoint, adding a required request field, or removing a response field. Non-breaking additions just get reported.

For TypeScript packages, API Extractor does something similar with an API report file.
X: For events, a schema registry, or checked-in JSON schemas with compatibility checks, do the same job.
X: When a breaking change is genuinely needed, the check forces a conscious decision. Add a new version, mark the old one deprecated and tell consumers. Contract tests with Pact add another layer by checking what consumers actually use.
X: In my team, with many front-end sub-apps calling the same APIs, the OpenAPI diff check stopped several accidental field renames that would otherwise have broken a screen in production.

D: A
T: How do you connect logs to traces using trace ids and span ids?
K: logs and traces correlation, trace id in logs, span id logging, log trace correlation, jump from log to trace
X: Logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where the time went across services. Linking them means every log line written during a request carries that request's trace id and span id, so from one error log you can open the whole distributed trace, and from a slow span you can see its logs.
X: In .NET this mostly comes for free. Activity Current holds the current trace, and the logging infrastructure can include the trace id and span id in every log scope, either through the logger factory's activity tracking options or through the OpenTelemetry logging provider, which attaches them automatically. Serilog has an enricher that does the same. In Node, the OpenTelemetry instrumentation for pino or winston injects trace ids, and in Python, the logging instrumentation adds them to log records.
X: The backend also has to know how to link them. In Datadog, Grafana with Loki and Tempo, or Application Insights, a trace id field in structured logs becomes a clickable link to the trace.
X: Some details matter. The field name has to match what the backend expects. Background jobs and message consumers need their own spans, or their logs have no trace id. And if traces are sampled, some logs will point to traces that weren't kept, so the sampling policy should keep traces with errors. People forget that last bit a lot.
X: In older services, we already had a correlation id passed through middleware and message headers. In the newer OpenTelemetry-based services, the W3C trace id replaces that, and Datadog connects logs, traces and metrics for one request automatically.
@p17-1005
S: obx
D: A
T: What is OpenTelemetry baggage, and how is it different from span attributes?
K: otel baggage, opentelemetry baggage, context propagation baggage, baggage vs attributes, propagate tenant id
X: Span attributes are key-value pairs recorded on one span, like the HTTP route or the order id. They stay on that span and don't travel to other services.
X: Baggage is key-value data that travels with the request context across process boundaries. It goes in the baggage HTTP header, next to the traceparent header, and every downstream service can read it. A typical example is a tenant id or customer tier set at the edge, so services several hops away know it without every API passing it as a parameter.
X: Baggage isn't automatically recorded on spans or logs, though. If you want the tenant id on downstream spans, you add a span processor that copies chosen baggage entries into attributes, which also makes them searchable in the tracing backend.
X: A few cautions I'd really stress, and people miss these. Baggage goes out on every outgoing call, including calls to third parties unless you strip it, so never put sensitive data like user emails, patient details or tokens in it. Keep it small, since it adds bytes to every request. And treat incoming baggage from outside as untrusted. Anyone can send the header, so it must not drive authorization decisions.
X: In .NET, the Baggage API in OpenTelemetry, or Activity baggage, sets values, and the propagators handle the header. I'd use it for low-sensitivity routing and diagnostic context, like a tenant or region label, which makes it easy to filter traces by tenant during an incident.
@p17-1006
S: obx
D: A
T: What are OpenTelemetry semantic conventions, and how should you name spans and attributes?
K: semantic conventions, span naming, otel attribute names, http.route, low cardinality span names
X: Semantic conventions are basically OpenTelemetry's standard names for common telemetry. Attributes like http dot request dot method, http dot route, the response status code, db dot system and the messaging destination name, plus standard metric names like the HTTP server request duration. When every service and library uses the same names, dashboards and queries work across languages without any mapping.
X: The automatic instrumentation for ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, Express or FastAPI already follows them. So the question's mostly about custom spans and attributes you add yourself.
X: For span names, keep them low cardinality and describing the operation, not the data. GET plus the route template, like orders by id, is good. The full URL with an actual id is bad, because every request becomes a unique name, which breaks aggregation and pushes up cost. For a custom operation, something like process shipment or allocate kit is clear.
X: For custom attributes, follow the conventions first, then use your own namespace for business attributes, like app dot study dot phase or app dot order dot type, so they don't clash with future standard names. Put high-cardinality identifiers, like an order id, on spans as attributes, where they're useful for search, but never as metric labels.
X: Record errors with the span status set to error and the exception recorded as an event, so backends show them consistently.
X: Agreeing a short naming guide across teams was one of the most useful things we did when moving newer services to OpenTelemetry. Without it, the same field showed up under four different names, and cross-service queries were painful.
@p17-1007
S: obx
D: A
T: What are burn-rate alerts, and why are they better than simple error thresholds?
K: burn rate alert, multi window burn rate, slo alerting, error budget alert, alert on slo
X: A simple threshold alert, like error rate above two percent for five minutes, has two problems. It fires on short blips that don't matter, and it misses slow, steady problems that sit just under the threshold but burn through the error budget over days.
X: Burn rate measures how fast you're using the error budget compared with the allowed pace. If your SLO is 99.9 percent success over thirty days, a burn rate of one uses exactly the budget in thirty days. A burn rate of fourteen point four would use two percent of the monthly budget in one hour, which is serious.
X: Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting, from Google's SRE workbook, combines a fast alert and a slow one. A page fires when the burn rate is high over both a long window, like one hour, and a short window, like five minutes. The long window proves it's significant, the short window proves it's still happening, so the alert clears quickly after recovery. A ticket-level alert fires for a lower burn rate over six hours or a day, catching slow leaks.
X: What you get is alerts that map to user impact and the SLO the business agreed. People get woken up for things that threaten the budget, not for every spike, and I think that's what keeps on-call sane.
X: You need an SLI defined as good events over total events, like successful requests under a latency target. Datadog, Grafana and most monitoring tools have built-in SLO and burn-rate alerting, so the hard work is choosing good SLIs, not the maths.
@p17-1008
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you capture and debug JavaScript errors in production with source maps?
K: front end error tracking, javascript errors production, source maps, sentry, upload source maps, minified stack trace
X: Production JavaScript is minified, so a raw error stack trace points to line one, column fifty thousand of a bundle with random names, which is useless. Source maps map those positions back to the original TypeScript files and line numbers.
X: The setup has a few parts. First, capture errors: an error tracking tool like Sentry, Datadog RUM or Application Insights' JavaScript SDK listens for unhandled errors and promise rejections, and frameworks have hooks too, like a React error boundary or Angular's ErrorHandler, to report errors that the framework catches. Each report includes the browser, the route, the release version and recent user actions as breadcrumbs.
X: Second, generate source maps in the production build, but don't serve them publicly if you don't want your source readable. Instead, upload them to the error tracking tool during the pipeline, tagged with the same release version as the deployed bundle. The tool then shows readable stack traces.
X: Third, link errors to releases, so you can see that a new error started with version 2.4, and connect front-end errors to back-end traces by propagating trace headers on API calls.
X: Be careful with privacy: scrub form values, tokens and personal data from error payloads and breadcrumbs before they leave the browser.
X: In our React shell with Vite, the pipeline uploads hidden source maps per release. When a sub-app started failing for one browser version, the readable stack trace pointed straight to an unsupported API call, which saved hours of guessing.
@p17-1009
S: obx
D: A
T: What is eBPF, and why is it used for observability?
K: ebpf, ebpf observability, kernel tracing, cilium hubble, pixie, zero instrumentation monitoring
X: eBPF lets small, verified programs run safely inside the Linux kernel, attached to events like system calls, network packets or function calls, without changing kernel code or restarting anything. For observability, it means you can see what processes are doing from the outside, without adding code to the application.
X: What it can show: network flows between pods, including latency and dropped connections; HTTP and gRPC requests parsed at the kernel level; DNS lookups; file and disk activity; CPU profiles across all processes; and security events like unexpected process launches.
X: Tools built on it include Cilium with Hubble for Kubernetes network visibility, Pixie and Grafana Beyla for automatic request metrics and traces, Parca and other continuous profilers, Falco for runtime security, and the Datadog and other vendor agents, which use it for network monitoring.
X: The advantages are no code changes, very low overhead, and visibility into things applications don't report, like a connection dropped by the network or a slow DNS lookup.
X: The limits are real too. It's Linux only and needs a recent kernel and privileges. It sees bytes and calls, not business context, so it can't tell you which study or order a request belonged to. Encrypted traffic is harder to inspect, needing hooks into TLS libraries.
X: So I see eBPF as a complement to OpenTelemetry, not a replacement. It gives a baseline for every workload in a cluster, including ones nobody instrumented, while application instrumentation adds the business meaning.
@p17-1010
S: obx
D: A
T: What does 99.9 percent availability mean in downtime, and how do dependencies affect it?
K: availability nines, 99.9 uptime downtime per month, sla calculation, composite availability, dependency availability maths
X: Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by ten. Ninety-nine percent allows about seven hours of downtime a month. 99.9 percent, three nines, allows about forty-three minutes a month or under nine hours a year. 99.95 allows about twenty-two minutes a month, and 99.99, four nines, only about four minutes a month, which is less than one manual deployment going wrong.
X: Dependencies multiply. If a request needs three services in series, each 99.9 percent available, the combined availability is roughly 99.9 times 99.9 times 99.9, which is about 99.7 percent. That means you can't promise a higher SLA than your critical dependencies allow, unless you remove the dependency from the critical path.
X: Redundancy works the other way. Two independent instances, each 99 percent available, behind a load balancer give about 99.99 percent in theory, because both must fail together. In practice, shared failure causes like the same bad deployment, the same database or the same region reduce that benefit a lot.
X: So to improve availability, make fewer things critical: cache data, use queues so a downstream outage delays work instead of failing requests, degrade gracefully when an optional service is down, and run across zones.
X: Also be precise about what availability measures. Is it uptime of a health endpoint, or successful user requests? Request-based SLIs are more honest. And scheduled maintenance windows often aren't counted in contractual SLAs, but users still feel them, which is one more reason to aim for zero-downtime releases.

T: How do you change log levels at runtime without redeploying?
K: dynamic log level, change log level runtime, serilog LoggingLevelSwitch, debug logging production, reloadOnChange logging
X: During an incident, you often want detailed debug logs from one component, but production runs at Information or Warning level to control volume and cost. Redeploying to change a log level is slow and risky, so the level should be changeable at runtime.

X: Combining this with sampling helps too: debug logs for one tenant or one request header rather than all traffic. In our services, a temporary category-level override has helped diagnose integration issues without a release, which matters a lot when every release needs validation.

T: How do you monitor third-party APIs and external dependencies?

X: Many production incidents start outside your system: a partner API slows down, a payment provider has an outage, or a certificate on their side expires. You need to know quickly whether the problem is yours or theirs, and ideally before your users tell you.

@p17-1013
S: obx
D: A
T: How do you read a trace waterfall to find where the time is spent?
K: trace waterfall, read distributed trace, critical path trace, find slow span, span timeline analysis
X: A trace waterfall shows every span of a request on a timeline: the root span at the top, child spans indented, and each bar's length showing its duration. Reading it well is a quick way to find the real cause of slowness.
X: First, look at the root span's duration and compare it with what's typical, so you know you're looking at a representative slow trace. Exemplars from a latency chart or a filter for slow traces help find one.
X: Second, follow the critical path: the chain of spans that actually determined the end time. A long span that runs in parallel with others may not matter, while a short span repeated many times in sequence often does.
X: Common patterns jump out visually. A staircase of many small database or HTTP spans one after another is an N plus one problem. A big gap where no child span exists means time spent in the service itself, like CPU work, lock waits, garbage collection or thread pool starvation, or an uninstrumented call. Spans that could run in parallel but run sequentially suggest missing concurrency. A span that waits a long time before starting, like a message sitting in a queue, shows backlog.
X: Then check span attributes and events: the SQL statement, retry counts, cache hit or miss, response size.
X: Finally, compare with a fast trace for the same endpoint. The difference between the two usually points straight at the cause. In our services, the gap pattern once led us to thread pool starvation from a synchronous call inside async code.

S: obx
D: A
T: How do audit logs differ from application logs, and how long should you keep each?
K: audit log vs application log, log retention policy, how long keep logs, compliance logging, immutable audit trail
X: Application logs are for engineers: diagnosing errors, understanding behaviour and performance. They're high volume, can be sampled or dropped, and usually only need to be kept for days or weeks, because nobody investigates a debug log from last year.
X: Audit logs are for accountability: who did what, to which record, when, and sometimes why. They're a business and compliance record, so they must be complete, accurate and tamper-evident, and kept for as long as regulations or contracts require, which can be many years in regulated industries.
X: That difference drives the design. Audit records shouldn't depend on the logging pipeline, which may drop messages under load. They're usually written in the same database transaction as the change, or through an outbox, so a change can't happen without its audit record. They're append-only, with permissions that stop even administrators from editing them, and ideally protected with hashing or write-once storage. They contain old and new values and the user identity, and they're designed to be queried by business users and auditors.
X: Application logs go to tools like Splunk, Datadog or CloudWatch with retention set by cost and need, often thirty to ninety days hot, with older data archived cheaply if required.
X: Both need data protection: personal data in application logs should be minimised or masked, while audit logs, which may need personal data, require strict access control.
X: In a GxP system, the audit trail is a validated feature of the product, not a side effect of logging, and treating it that way avoids a lot of findings.

@p17-1016
S: msa
D: A
T: What is the inbox pattern for processing each message only once?
K: inbox pattern, inbox table, processed messages table, duplicate message handling, at least once delivery consumer
X: Most brokers, like RabbitMQ, SQS and Service Bus, deliver messages at least once. A consumer may receive the same message twice after a timeout, a lost acknowledgement or a redelivery. If processing has side effects, like reserving stock or sending an email, duplicates cause real damage.
X: The inbox pattern makes the consumer idempotent. Every message carries a unique message id. The consumer has an inbox table, or processed messages table, keyed by that id. When a message arrives, in one database transaction the consumer inserts the message id into the inbox and performs its business changes. If the insert fails because the id already exists, the message was already processed, so the consumer just acknowledges it and does nothing else. Because both happen in one transaction, you can't end up with the change done but not recorded, or recorded but not done.
X: It pairs naturally with the outbox pattern on the producer side: the outbox guarantees the message is published, and the inbox guarantees it's processed once.
X: Details to handle: clean old inbox rows after a retention period longer than any possible redelivery; and for side effects outside the database, like calling an external API, pass an idempotency key so the other system can also deduplicate.
X: Libraries like MassTransit and NServiceBus include inbox and outbox support. In our RabbitMQ consumers, a processed message table per database made retries from the dead-letter flow safe, because replaying a message twice simply has no effect the second time.
@p17-1017
S: msa
D: A
T: How do you implement a distributed lock, and when should you avoid one?
K: distributed lock, redis lock, redlock, sql application lock, sp_getapplock, lease lock, fencing token
X: A distributed lock makes sure only one instance across many servers does something at a time, like running a scheduled job, refreshing a shared token or processing one customer's batch.
X: Common implementations: Redis with SET using NX and an expiry, where the value is a unique token so only the owner can release it; SQL Server's sp_getapplock, which is simple if you already have a database and is released automatically with the session or transaction; blob leases in Azure Storage; DynamoDB conditional writes; or ZooKeeper and etcd for stronger guarantees. Libraries like DistributedLock for .NET wrap several of these.
X: The hard part is that locks expire. If the holder pauses, for example a long garbage collection or network delay, its lock can expire while it still thinks it owns it, and a second instance starts the same work. The fix is a fencing token: an increasing number issued with each lock, which the protected resource checks, rejecting writes with an older token. Redis-based locks can't fully guarantee safety without that.
X: So I avoid distributed locks where possible. Often a better design exists: a database unique constraint, optimistic concurrency with a row version, partitioning work so each key always goes to one consumer, a single active consumer queue, or a scheduler with built-in clustering, like Quartz.NET with a clustered job store.
X: When I do use one, I treat it as an efficiency mechanism, preventing duplicate work, and make the work itself idempotent, so a rare double run is still safe.
@p17-1018
S: msa
D: A
T: Should microservices share common libraries, and what should go in them?
K: shared libraries microservices, common nuget package, shared code between services, chassis library, coupling through shared library
X: Sharing code across services saves duplication, but a shared library is also a form of coupling. If every service must upgrade together when it changes, you've built a distributed monolith through a NuGet or npm package.
X: What's good to share is technical, cross-cutting plumbing that changes rarely: logging and OpenTelemetry setup, standard health checks, authentication configuration, a resilient HTTP client setup, error response formats, and messaging conventions. This is often called a service chassis, and it makes services consistent.
X: What shouldn't be shared is domain logic and domain models. If two services share a customer entity class, a change for one forces a change in the other, and the service boundaries become meaningless. Each service should own its models; for contracts between services, share schemas or generated clients, versioned carefully, rather than internal classes.
X: Practices that keep sharing healthy. Version libraries with semantic versioning and keep breaking changes rare. Don't force simultaneous upgrades; services should be able to lag behind for a while. Keep packages small and focused, rather than one giant common package. Avoid heavy transitive dependencies that dictate framework versions. Have a clear owner who reviews changes.
X: In our front-end work, shared npm packages on the Azure DevOps feed hold the design system, API client and auth helpers for the React shell and sub-apps. They're versioned independently, and a sub-app can stay on an older version until its team is ready, which avoids coordinated big-bang upgrades.

S: msa
D: A
T: How does request-reply over a message broker work?
K: request reply messaging, rpc over rabbitmq, reply queue, correlation id messaging, async request response
X: Sometimes you want the decoupling of a broker but still need an answer, for example asking a pricing service to calculate a quote. Request-reply over messaging does this.
X: The requester sends a message to the service's request queue with two extra properties: a reply-to address, which is a queue where it listens for answers, and a correlation id that's unique to the request. The responder processes the message and sends the result to the reply-to queue with the same correlation id. The requester matches the reply to the waiting request by correlation id.
X: The reply queue can be one temporary exclusive queue per requester instance, or RabbitMQ's direct reply-to feature, which avoids creating queues. In Azure Service Bus, sessions are often used, with the session id matching the request.
X: Important points. Always set a timeout, because a reply may never arrive. Messages can be delivered twice, so the responder should be idempotent. If the requesting instance restarts, pending replies are lost, so this suits short, interactive requests, not long processes.
X: It's worth asking whether you really need it. If the caller blocks waiting for the reply, you get the latency of the broker and most of the coupling of a direct call. For real-time answers, a direct HTTP or gRPC call is usually simpler. Request-reply over a broker makes sense when the responder must sit behind the broker, for load levelling or network reasons, or when the reply can be processed asynchronously, like an event updating status later.
@p17-1020
S: msa
D: A
T: What is the competing consumers pattern?
K: competing consumers, multiple consumers one queue, scale message processing, work queue pattern, prefetch count
X: Competing consumers means several instances of a consumer read from the same queue, and each message goes to only one of them. It's the standard way to scale background processing: if the queue is growing, add more consumers.
X: The broker handles distribution. RabbitMQ delivers messages round-robin to consumers on the same queue, limited by each consumer's prefetch count. SQS hands messages to whichever poller asks, hiding them for the visibility timeout. Service Bus uses peek-lock with similar behaviour, and in Kubernetes, KEDA can scale consumer pods based on queue length.
X: It brings a few consequences. Order isn't guaranteed, because two consumers process messages in parallel, so if order matters per entity, you need partitioning, like Service Bus sessions, SQS FIFO message groups or a consistent hash exchange, so all messages for one key go to one consumer. Messages can be redelivered if a consumer crashes, so processing must be idempotent. Poison messages that always fail need a retry limit and a dead-letter queue, or they block a consumer forever.
X: Prefetch needs tuning. A high prefetch is efficient for fast, small messages but can leave one busy consumer holding many messages while others sit idle; for slow messages, a prefetch of one or a few spreads work fairly.
X: Our notification and data processing workers use this pattern on RabbitMQ, with multiple worker instances per queue, a low prefetch for heavy messages, and retry with a dead-letter exchange, so scaling is just adding instances.
