S: msa
D: A
T: What is the claim check pattern for large messages?
K: claim check pattern, large message payload, store payload in blob, message size limit, reference message
X: Message brokers have size limits, like 256 kilobytes for SQS and Service Bus standard, and even where they allow larger messages, big payloads slow down the broker and use expensive memory. The claim check pattern avoids putting large data in the message.
X: The producer stores the large payload in external storage, such as S3, Azure Blob Storage or a database table, and sends a small message containing a reference, the claim check, like the object key, plus useful metadata such as type, size and a hash. The consumer reads the message, fetches the payload using the reference and processes it.
X: Things to get right. Write the payload before sending the message, so the consumer never gets a reference to something missing. Decide who deletes the payload: a lifecycle rule that expires objects after a few days is simpler than tracking when every consumer has finished. Secure the storage, since the payload may contain sensitive data, using encryption and access limited to the producer and consumers, or short-lived presigned URLs. Include a checksum so the consumer can verify the content.
X: The Amazon SQS extended client library does this automatically for Java and Python, and similar helpers exist for other SDKs.
X: A natural example is file processing: an uploaded file lands in storage, and a message with its location triggers the import job. In our data transfer flows, large extracts are written to storage and only the reference and metadata travel through the queue, which keeps the broker fast and messages easy to inspect.
@p17-1022
S: msa
D: A
T: How do you propagate timeouts and deadlines across a chain of service calls?
K: deadline propagation, timeout budget, cascading timeouts, grpc deadline, request timeout across services
X: When service A calls B, which calls C, each with its own timeout, the timeouts often don't add up. If A gives up after two seconds but B waits five seconds for C, B and C keep working on a request nobody is waiting for, wasting capacity exactly when the system is under stress.
X: Deadline propagation fixes this by passing the remaining time budget down the chain. The edge sets a deadline for the whole request, and each service uses whatever is left, minus a small margin, as the timeout for its own downstream calls. If little time remains, it fails fast instead of starting work that can't finish.
X: gRPC has this built in: the client sets a deadline, it travels in the request metadata, and the server's cancellation token fires when it expires. With HTTP, you can pass a custom header with the deadline or remaining milliseconds and convert it into a cancellation token.
X: In .NET, the important part is honouring cancellation: pass the request's cancellation token through to database queries and HTTP calls, so work actually stops. Combining it with a timeout using a linked cancellation token source keeps the code simple.
X: Some general rules: timeouts should get shorter as you go deeper in the chain; retries must fit inside the remaining budget, or they make things worse; and queued messages should carry an expiry, so a consumer doesn't process a request that's already stale.
X: This is one of those details that turns a small slowdown into a full outage if ignored, because abandoned work keeps piling up.
@p17-1023
S: msa
D: A
T: How do you invalidate caches across services when data changes?
K: distributed cache invalidation, cache invalidation events, redis pub sub invalidation, stale cache microservices, cache across instances
X: When several instances or services cache the same data, a change in one place must reach all the caches, or users see stale data. There are a few approaches, each with trade-offs.
X: The simplest is short expiry times. Data is allowed to be stale for a known period, like sixty seconds, and no invalidation is needed. For a lot of reference data, that's good enough.
X: Event-based invalidation is the next level. The service that owns the data publishes an event when it changes, like product updated, and every service that caches it removes or refreshes that entry. With a message broker, each instance needs its own subscription, not a shared queue, or only one instance hears the event. Redis pub/sub or keyspace notifications work well for in-memory caches across instances.
X: A shared distributed cache like Redis avoids the problem for instance-local copies, because all instances read the same entry, and the owner updates or deletes it on change. A two-level cache, with memory in front of Redis, still needs invalidation messages for the memory level. HybridCache in .NET 9 supports this layering with tag-based invalidation.
X: Version stamps are another option: include a version in the cache key, and bump the version when data changes, so old entries are simply never read again.
X: Always keep expiry as a safety net, since invalidation messages can be lost. In our IIS web farm, configuration data is cached in memory per node, with Redis pub/sub invalidation messages and a short expiry as a backup, which keeps all nodes consistent within seconds.
@p17-1024
S: msa
D: A
T: What is the tolerant reader pattern?
K: tolerant reader, robustness principle, ignore unknown fields, backward compatible consumer, postel law api
X: The tolerant reader pattern says a consumer of an API or message should be strict only about what it actually needs and ignore everything else. It's an application of the robustness principle: be conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept.
X: In practice, a tolerant reader ignores unknown fields instead of failing, so the producer can add fields without breaking anyone. It reads only the fields it uses, rather than mapping the whole payload into a strict model. It handles missing optional fields with sensible defaults. And for enums, it has a fallback for unknown values, because a new status value from the producer shouldn't crash the consumer.
X: Most serializers support this. System.Text.Json ignores unknown properties by default, though .NET 8 added an option to disallow them, which you should leave off for external contracts. In TypeScript, a runtime validator like Zod should be configured to strip unknown keys rather than reject them.
X: The pattern makes independent deployment possible. A producer can add a field, deploy, and consumers update later when they want to use it. Combined with additive-only changes from producers, versioning becomes rare.
X: There's a balance though. Being tolerant doesn't mean accepting invalid data silently: required fields and business rules must still be validated, and unknown enum values should be logged so you notice them.
X: Our front-end sub-apps consume the same APIs at different release cadences. Tolerant parsing with safe defaults means a backend can release a new field without forcing every sub-app to release at the same time.

T: What is AsyncAPI, and how do you document event-driven APIs?
K: asyncapi, document events, event catalog, message contract documentation, openapi for events
X: OpenAPI documents request-response HTTP APIs, but it doesn't describe events and message queues well. AsyncAPI is the equivalent specification for event-driven systems.
X: An AsyncAPI document describes the servers, like a RabbitMQ or Kafka broker; the channels, such as queues, topics or exchanges and routing keys; the operations, saying whether the application sends or receives on each channel; and the message payloads with JSON Schema or Avro, plus headers like correlation id and message type. It can also describe security and bindings specific to each protocol.
X: From that, tools generate human-readable documentation, code models and even boilerplate for producers and consumers. Specifications can be checked into each service's repo and validated in CI like OpenAPI files.
X: The practical value is discoverability. In an event-driven system, it's surprisingly hard to answer which events exist, who publishes them, who consumes them and what fields they contain. Without documentation, people read code or guess from messages in queues. An event catalog, like EventCatalog or a developer portal such as Backstage, can collect the AsyncAPI files from all services into one browsable place, showing producers and consumers for each event.
X: Combined with schema compatibility checks, it also supports safe evolution: a change to a message schema shows up in review, and breaking changes can fail the build.
X: For a team with many RabbitMQ queues built up over years, I'd start small: document the most widely consumed events first, with their payload schemas and owners, because that's where unclear contracts cause the most incidents.
@p17-1026
S: msa
D: A
T: Event notification vs event-carried state transfer: what is the difference?
K: event notification vs event carried state transfer, thin events vs fat events, event payload design, domain event payload
X: These are two ways to design the content of events, sometimes called thin and fat events.
X: An event notification is thin: it says that something happened and gives an id, like order 123 was updated. Consumers that care call back to the owning service's API to get the current details. Events stay small and stable, and consumers always see the latest data. The downsides are extra calls, load on the owner, and runtime coupling: if the owner is down, consumers can't process the event.
X: Event-carried state transfer is fat: the event contains the relevant data, like the order's status, items and totals. Consumers can update their own local copy without calling back, so they keep working when the owner is down, and queries become local and fast. The downsides are larger messages, more fields that become part of the contract, harder schema evolution, and data duplicated across services that is eventually consistent.
X: There's also a middle path: include the fields most consumers need, plus the id for anyone who needs more.
X: Ordering matters with fat events. If a consumer processes an older event after a newer one, it might overwrite fresh data with stale data, so include a version or timestamp and ignore older ones.
X: I choose based on the consumers. When many services need to keep their own view of reference data, like site or product details, event-carried state transfer reduces chatter and coupling. For sensitive data, a thin notification is safer, since the details stay behind the owner's API with its access controls.
@p17-1027
S: msa
D: A
T: What is a cell-based architecture?
K: cell based architecture, cells, blast radius reduction, shuffle sharding, bulkhead at infrastructure level, partitioned deployment
X: A cell-based architecture splits a system into several independent, complete copies, called cells, each serving a subset of customers or tenants. Each cell has its own application instances, databases, queues and caches. A thin routing layer sends each request to the right cell based on, say, the tenant id.
X: The main reason is to limit blast radius. A bad deployment, a noisy tenant, a poison message or a database problem affects one cell, not everyone. It's the bulkhead pattern applied to the whole infrastructure. AWS uses this extensively for its own services.
X: It also helps scaling and operations. Cells have a known maximum size, so you test that size and add new cells as you grow, instead of discovering new limits in one giant deployment. Deployments roll out cell by cell, which works naturally with deployment rings.
X: The costs are real. More infrastructure to run and pay for. The routing layer must be very simple and highly available, since it's shared. Moving a tenant between cells needs a data migration process. And cross-cell features, like global reporting or search, need separate aggregation.
X: It fits systems with natural partitioning, like multi-tenant SaaS, where each customer's data is mostly independent.
X: A per-study database model is a small step in this direction. Each study's data is isolated, so a problem with one study's data or a migration rarely affects others. A full cell design would go further by also splitting the application tier, so a group of studies runs on its own infrastructure.
@p17-1028
S: msa
D: A
T: How do you share reference data across microservices?
K: reference data microservices, shared lookup data, master data across services, country codes services, replicate reference data
X: Reference data is data that many services need but that rarely changes, like countries, currencies, product catalogues, site details or configuration lists. The question is how services get it without coupling to one central database.
X: Option one is a reference data service with an API. Every service calls it, usually with caching. It keeps one source of truth, but adds a runtime dependency; if the service is slow or down, callers suffer unless their caches are good.
X: Option two is replication through events. The owning service publishes changes, and each consumer keeps its own local copy, in its own database or cache. Reads are local and fast, and consumers keep working during outages. The cost is eventual consistency and some storage duplication, which for reference data is usually fine.
X: Option three is shipping static data with the code, as a package or configuration file. For truly static standards, like ISO country codes, this is simplest. It needs a release to change, though.
X: Avoid a shared database that every service reads directly, because then no one can change the schema safely.
X: Whatever the approach, be clear about the owner, use stable identifiers that don't change when display names do, and version changes. For data that affects business rules, like a site being closed, decide how quickly consumers must see it, because that drives the choice between caching, events and direct calls.
X: In our platform, slowly changing configuration is cached per node with invalidation messages, while truly static lists ship with the application.

T: How do you debug a running pod with kubectl debug and ephemeral containers?
K: kubectl debug, ephemeral containers, debug distroless pod, troubleshoot pod no shell, debug node kubernetes
X: Modern images are often distroless or minimal, with no shell, curl or debugging tools, which is good for security but makes troubleshooting hard. You can't just exec into the pod and run commands that don't exist.
X: Ephemeral containers solve this. kubectl debug adds a temporary container, with an image that has the tools you need, like busybox or netshoot, to a running pod without restarting it. With the target option, the debug container shares the process namespace of the application container, so you can see its processes, read its files through the proc filesystem, and use the same network namespace for testing connectivity, DNS and ports.
X: kubectl debug has two other modes. It can create a copy of a pod with changes, such as a different image or a changed command, which helps when a container crashes on startup, because you can start the copy with a shell instead. It can also debug a node, starting a privileged pod on that node with the host filesystem mounted, which replaces having to SSH into nodes.
X: For .NET, you can attach a debug container with the dotnet diagnostic tools to collect a dump or trace from the running process, since they share the process namespace.
X: Security matters here. Creating ephemeral containers needs its own RBAC permission, which should be limited to the people who need it, especially in production, and usage should be audited. Debugging this way is a last resort after logs, metrics and traces, but when you need it, it saves rebuilding images with tools inside.
@p17-1030
S: dkx
D: A
T: How do you speed up Docker builds in CI with BuildKit cache?
K: docker build cache ci, buildkit cache, cache-from cache-to, registry cache docker, docker layer caching ci, buildx
X: On a fresh CI agent, Docker has no local layer cache, so every build starts from scratch: restoring packages, compiling, everything. BuildKit, the default builder in modern Docker, can import and export cache from outside the machine.
X: With docker buildx build, the cache-to and cache-from options store and reuse layer cache. Common targets are a registry, where the cache is pushed as a separate image or tag; the GitHub Actions cache backend; or a local directory that the CI system caches. Mode max caches intermediate layers from all stages of a multi-stage build, not just the final image, which matters because the expensive work happens in the build stage.
X: The Dockerfile has to be cache-friendly too. Copy the dependency files first, like the project files for .NET or package and lock files for Node, restore dependencies, and only then copy the rest of the source. Then a code change doesn't invalidate the restore layer. A good dockerignore keeps unneeded files from breaking the cache.
X: BuildKit cache mounts help with package caches: a RUN instruction with a cache mount for the NuGet or npm cache folder keeps downloaded packages between builds without putting them in the image.
X: Other tips: pin base images by digest so cache hits are predictable, build stages in parallel where possible, and avoid steps that change every time, like writing a build timestamp early in the Dockerfile.
X: In practice, switching a .NET service pipeline to registry cache with restore-first ordering brought typical image builds down from several minutes to under one minute.
@p17-1031
S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you cancel work in Node.js with AbortController?
K: abortcontroller, abortsignal, cancel fetch node, AbortSignal.timeout, cancellation node js
X: AbortController is the standard cancellation mechanism in JavaScript, both in browsers and in Node. You create a controller, pass its signal to an operation, and call abort when you want the operation to stop. The operation listens to the signal and rejects with an AbortError.
X: Many Node APIs accept a signal now: fetch, timers in the promises module, events.once, streams, child processes, and file system functions like readFile. Libraries such as undici, axios and database drivers support it too.
X: Two helpers make it convenient. AbortSignal.timeout creates a signal that aborts after a given number of milliseconds, which is the easiest way to put a timeout on fetch. AbortSignal.any combines several signals, for example a request-level signal plus a timeout, so the operation stops when either fires.
X: In a web server, a useful pattern is creating a controller per request and aborting it when the client disconnects, by listening for the request's close event, then passing the signal down to database queries and outgoing calls. That's like passing a cancellation token through an ASP.NET Core request, and it stops wasted work for requests nobody is waiting for.
X: For your own long-running functions, check signal.aborted in loops, or call signal.throwIfAborted, and listen for the abort event to clean up resources.
X: Handle the error properly: an AbortError is usually expected, so log it at a lower level than real failures, and make sure aborted operations don't leave half-written data behind.
@p17-1032
S: nodex
D: A
T: npm vs pnpm vs Yarn: how do you choose a package manager?
K: npm vs pnpm vs yarn, pnpm workspaces, yarn berry, package manager node, corepack, node_modules disk space
X: All three install packages from the npm registry and use a lock file, but they differ in speed, disk use and strictness.
X: npm comes with Node, so it needs no setup and has the widest compatibility. It's improved a lot and supports workspaces for monorepos. Its node_modules layout is flat, which means code can accidentally import packages it never declared, because they were hoisted from another dependency.
X: pnpm stores every package version once in a global content-addressed store and links it into projects, so installs are fast and disk use is much lower, especially with many projects. Its node_modules is strict: a package can only import what it declares, which catches missing dependency mistakes early. Its workspace support is strong, which makes it popular for monorepos.
X: Yarn version one was the faster alternative years ago and is now in maintenance. Modern Yarn, called Berry, offers Plug'n'Play, which removes node_modules entirely, but some tools still struggle with it.
X: Corepack, included with Node, lets a project pin its package manager and version in package.json, so everyone and CI use the same one.
X: My choice: for a single app, npm is fine. For a monorepo with many packages, pnpm is usually the best mix of speed and strictness. Whatever you choose, commit the lock file, use the frozen or ci install mode in pipelines, and configure the private registry, like an Azure Artifacts feed, in a project-level npmrc without credentials in the file.
@p17-1033
S: nodex
D: A
T: How do you manage Node.js versions and upgrade to a new LTS release?
K: node lts upgrade, nvmrc, node version manager, node end of life, upgrade node version, volta fnm
X: Node releases a new major version every six months. Even-numbered versions become long-term support releases, with about thirty months of support in total, while odd-numbered versions are short-lived. Production should run an active or maintenance LTS version, and teams should plan an upgrade before the version reaches end of life, since security fixes stop then.
X: To keep versions consistent, pin the version per project. An nvmrc file works with nvm or fnm, Volta can pin it in package.json, and the engines field documents the supported range, with engine-strict mode making npm fail on a wrong version. The Docker base image should use the same major version, and CI should read the version from the same file.
X: For an upgrade, I start with the release notes and the list of breaking changes, check native modules, which must be rebuilt for each version and are the most common source of trouble, and check that key dependencies support the new version. Then I run the full test suite on the new version in CI, often as a matrix with both versions for a while. Deprecation warnings from the current version are a good hint of what will break.
X: Then I roll out like any risky change: one service or environment first, watching memory, CPU and error rates, since garbage collection and performance characteristics change between versions.
X: Upgrading regularly, one LTS to the next, is much easier than jumping several versions after years of neglect.
@p17-1034
S: pyx
D: A
T: requests vs httpx vs aiohttp: which HTTP client should you use in Python?
K: requests vs httpx, aiohttp, python http client, async http python, httpx async client, connection pooling python
X: requests is the classic synchronous HTTP client. It's simple and very widely used, but it has no async support, no HTTP/2, and you must remember to use a Session for connection pooling and to set a timeout, because by default it can wait forever.
X: httpx has an API very similar to requests, but offers both a synchronous Client and an AsyncClient, supports HTTP/2, and has sensible timeouts by default. It can also call an ASGI or WSGI app directly in-process, which makes it the standard choice for testing FastAPI. For new code, especially async code, httpx is my default.
X: aiohttp is async only and includes both a client and a web server. It's mature and fast, and was the main async option before httpx, so many existing async projects use it.
X: Whichever client you choose, a few rules matter more than the library. Reuse one client per application, created at startup and closed at shutdown, for example with FastAPI's lifespan, so connections are pooled; creating a client per request is a common performance problem. Always set timeouts. Never use a synchronous client inside an async endpoint, because it blocks the event loop. Add retries with backoff for idempotent calls only, using the transport retry setting or a library like tenacity.
X: In our FastAPI RAG service, one shared httpx AsyncClient calls the embedding and model endpoints with explicit timeouts, which removed connection setup overhead from every request.
@p17-1035
S: pyx
D: A
T: How do you add retries with backoff in Python using tenacity?
K: tenacity, python retry, exponential backoff python, retry decorator, retry transient errors python
X: tenacity is the most common Python library for retries. You decorate a function with retry and configure when to stop, how long to wait and which errors to retry, and it works with both normal and async functions.
X: A typical setup stops after a number of attempts or a total time, waits with exponential backoff plus random jitter, so many clients don't retry at the same moment, and retries only on specific exceptions, like connection errors, timeouts or HTTP responses with status 429 or 503. You can also retry based on the result, and add before-sleep logging so each retry is visible.
X: What to retry matters more than how. Retry transient failures, not validation errors or 404s, which will fail the same way every time. Only retry operations that are safe to repeat; for writes, use an idempotency key. Respect a Retry-After header when the server sends one.
X: Keep the total retry time inside the caller's own timeout, otherwise the caller gives up while you're still retrying. And avoid stacking retries: if the HTTP client retries, tenacity retries, and the message consumer also retries, one failure becomes dozens of calls, which turns a small problem into a retry storm.
X: For long outages, retries aren't enough; a circuit breaker stops calling a failing service for a while. Libraries like pybreaker provide that.
X: In our Python services, model and embedding calls retry a few times with jittered backoff on 429 and 503 responses, with each retry logged, which smoothed out short rate-limit spikes.
@p17-1036
S: pyx
D: A
T: How do you debug Python code with pdb, breakpoint and debugpy?
K: python debugging, pdb, breakpoint function, debugpy, remote debug python container, post mortem debugging
X: Python has a built-in debugger, pdb. Calling the built-in breakpoint function anywhere in code pauses execution and opens an interactive prompt where you can print variables, step to the next line, step into functions, continue, and move up and down the call stack. The PYTHONBREAKPOINT environment variable controls what breakpoint does, including disabling it completely, which is a safety net in production.
X: Post-mortem debugging is very useful: running a script with python -m pdb drops you into the debugger at the point where an unhandled exception happened, and pytest's pdb option does the same for a failing test, so you can inspect the state that caused the failure.
X: For IDE debugging, VS Code and PyCharm use debugpy. You can also attach remotely: the app starts with debugpy listening on a port, and the IDE connects. That works for code running in Docker containers, with the port mapped, which is how I debug a FastAPI service running inside Docker Compose. With uvicorn's reload mode, configure the debugger to follow subprocesses.
X: For async code, the debugger works, but stepping across awaits can be confusing; good logging often helps more there.
X: In production, don't attach interactive debuggers. Use logs, traces and tools that don't stop the process, such as py-spy to see what every thread is doing, which can dump stacks of a running process without restarting it. That's often how you diagnose a hung worker quickly.
@p17-1037
S: awsx
D: A
T: What are VPC endpoints, and why use them instead of a NAT gateway?
K: vpc endpoints, gateway endpoint, interface endpoint, privatelink, s3 gateway endpoint, private access aws services
X: Resources in private subnets, like ECS tasks, Lambda functions in a VPC or EC2 instances, have no direct internet access. To reach AWS services such as S3, SQS or Secrets Manager, traffic normally goes through a NAT gateway to the services' public endpoints. VPC endpoints let that traffic stay on AWS's private network instead.
X: There are two kinds. Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB. They're added as routes in the route table and are free, so there's almost no reason not to have them. Interface endpoints, powered by PrivateLink, create network interfaces with private IPs in your subnets for most other services, like ECR, CloudWatch Logs, SQS, Secrets Manager and STS. They cost a small hourly amount per availability zone plus data charges.
X: The benefits: security, because traffic never crosses the internet and subnets can be fully private with no NAT at all; and cost, because NAT gateway data processing charges can be large when containers pull big images from ECR or write heavy logs.
X: Endpoint policies add control. A policy on the S3 endpoint can allow access only to your organisation's buckets, which helps prevent data being copied out to someone else's bucket. Bucket policies can also require that access comes through a specific endpoint.
X: Private DNS on interface endpoints means the normal service hostnames resolve to the private IPs, so applications need no code change.
X: For an ECS cluster in private subnets, I'd add the S3 gateway endpoint plus interface endpoints for ECR, CloudWatch Logs and Secrets Manager.

S: awsx
D: A
T: What do GuardDuty and Security Hub do in AWS?
K: guardduty, security hub, aws threat detection, aws security posture, aws inspector, cloud security monitoring aws
X: They're two complementary AWS security services, one for detecting threats and one for collecting findings and checking posture.
X: GuardDuty is threat detection. It analyses CloudTrail events, VPC flow logs and DNS logs, plus optional sources like S3 data events, EKS audit logs and runtime monitoring for EC2, ECS and EKS. It uses threat intelligence and anomaly detection to find things like credentials used from an unusual location, an instance talking to a known malicious IP or mining cryptocurrency, unusual API calls suggesting reconnaissance, or a public bucket being accessed suspiciously. There's no agent to manage for the basic sources; you enable it per account and region, ideally across the organisation.
X: Security Hub is the central dashboard. It aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector for vulnerability scanning, Macie for sensitive data in S3, IAM Access Analyzer and third-party tools, and it runs automated checks against standards such as the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices and CIS benchmarks, giving a score and a list of failing controls like unencrypted volumes or overly open security groups.
X: Making it useful takes process. Send high-severity findings through EventBridge to the on-call channel or ticketing system, automate common fixes where safe, suppress known false positives with documented reasons, and review the posture score regularly. A delegated administrator account in AWS Organizations gives one view across all accounts.
X: Detective can then help investigate a finding by showing related activity over time. Together they turn security from occasional audits into continuous monitoring.

T: How do you run chaos experiments with AWS Fault Injection Service or Azure Chaos Studio?
K: aws fault injection service, azure chaos studio, fis experiment, managed chaos engineering, fault injection cloud
X: Both are managed services for chaos engineering on their clouds. They let you inject real failures, in a controlled and repeatable way, to prove your system handles them.
X: AWS Fault Injection Service runs experiment templates with actions such as stopping or terminating EC2 instances, stopping ECS tasks, injecting CPU or memory stress, adding network latency or packet loss, failing over an Aurora cluster, throttling API calls, or disrupting an entire availability zone's connectivity. Azure Chaos Studio has similar faults: shutting down VMs, killing processes, adding latency, failing a Cosmos DB region, rebooting a Redis cache, and Kubernetes faults for AKS through Chaos Mesh.
X: The safety features matter most. Experiments target resources by tags or explicit lists, so you control the blast radius. Stop conditions, like a CloudWatch alarm or Azure Monitor alert firing, halt the experiment automatically if things go worse than expected. Permissions go through an IAM role or managed identity limited to what the experiment needs.
X: A good experiment starts with a hypothesis: if one ECS task in each service is stopped, the error rate stays below one percent and capacity recovers within two minutes. Run it in a test environment first, watch dashboards, then compare the result with the hypothesis. Findings become fixes, like missing retries, slow health checks or alarms that never fired.
X: Once trusted, experiments can run in pipelines or game days on a schedule, so resilience is checked continuously rather than assumed.
@p17-1040
S: scx
D: A
T: A Lambda function runs out of memory while processing large files from S3. What do you do?
K: lambda out of memory, lambda large file s3, process big file lambda, lambda memory error, stream s3 object
X: First, confirm it's really memory. The function's log ends with a runtime exited error or the REPORT line shows max memory used equal to the configured memory. Then check which files fail; it's usually only the large ones.
X: The root cause is normally reading the whole object into memory: calling read on the S3 body, loading it into a string or data frame, or building a big list of parsed records. A two-gigabyte file can't fit into a function with one gigabyte of memory, and parsing often needs several times the file size.
X: The fix is streaming. Read the S3 body as a stream and process it line by line or in chunks, writing results out in batches rather than collecting everything. For CSV and JSON lines, that's straightforward with streaming readers in Python, Node or .NET. For uploads of output, use multipart upload streams. Temporary data can go to the ephemeral storage under the tmp folder, which can be configured up to ten gigabytes.
X: Increasing memory is a quick fix and also gives more CPU, but it only moves the limit.
X: Then think about fit. Lambda has a fifteen-minute limit too, so very large files may also time out. Options are splitting work: one function reads byte ranges and sends chunk references to a queue for parallel workers; Step Functions distributed map for processing large datasets in parallel; or moving heavy processing to an ECS task triggered by the upload.
X: Finally, add alerts on errors and max memory used, and test with the largest realistic file.
@p17-1041
S: scx
D: A
T: A Node.js service hits 100 percent CPU after a release, and requests time out. What do you check?
K: node cpu 100 percent, node event loop blocked, regex denial of service, node service hanging high cpu, redos production
X: Node runs JavaScript on one main thread, so one piece of CPU-heavy code blocks every request on that instance. When CPU jumps to a hundred percent right after a release and everything times out, I suspect something in the new code that blocks the event loop.
X: First, contain it: roll back if the impact is wide, since the release is the obvious trigger, and then investigate using the bad version in a test environment.
X: To find the hot code, take a CPU profile. Starting Node with the inspect flag and attaching Chrome DevTools, using the cpu-prof flag, or clinic flame gives a flame graph showing which functions use the time. Event loop delay metrics from perf_hooks confirm the loop is blocked rather than the service simply being busy.
X: Common causes after a release: a regular expression with nested quantifiers that takes exponential time on certain inputs, called ReDoS; synchronous functions like readFileSync, synchronous crypto or JSON.parse and JSON.stringify on very large payloads; a loop that became quadratic over a growing array; or a new dependency doing heavy work at import or per request.
X: Then fix it properly: rewrite the regex or use a linear-time engine like RE2, switch to async APIs, stream large payloads, move CPU-heavy work to worker threads or a separate service, and add input size limits.
X: Afterwards, add an event loop delay alert and a performance test with large and nasty inputs to the pipeline, so the next regression is caught before production.
